results.name: Schur complement elimination and inverse
results.statement: Let K be a field, p and q nonnegative integers, A in K^(p×p), B in K^(p×q), C in K^(q×p), and D in K^(q×q). Assume A is invertible. Set S=D−CA⁻¹B and M=[[A,B],[C,D]]. Then M is invertible if and only if S is invertible. In that case M⁻¹=[[A⁻¹+A⁻¹BS⁻¹CA⁻¹,−A⁻¹BS⁻¹],[−S⁻¹CA⁻¹,S⁻¹]]. The equation M(x,y)=(f,g) reduces to Sy=g−CA⁻¹f and x=A⁻¹(f−By).
hypotheses: K is a commutative field. All block products have the stated dimensions.
A has a two-sided inverse. The inverse formula requires a two-sided inverse of S.

/-- LDU decomposition of a block matrix with an invertible top-left corner, using the
Schur complement. -/
theorem fromBlocks_eq_of_invertible₁₁ (A : Matrix m m α) (B : Matrix m n α) (C : Matrix l m α)
    (D : Matrix l n α) [Invertible A] :
    fromBlocks A B C D =
      fromBlocks 1 0 (C * ⅟A) 1 * fromBlocks A 0 0 (D - C * ⅟A * B) *
        fromBlocks 1 (⅟A * B) 0 1 := by
  simp only [fromBlocks_multiply, Matrix.mul_zero, Matrix.zero_mul, add_zero, zero_add,
    Matrix.one_mul, Matrix.mul_one, invOf_mul_self, Matrix.mul_invOf_cancel_left,
    Matrix.mul_assoc, add_sub_cancel]

steps.text: Define L=[[I,0],[CA⁻¹,I]], H=[[A,0],[0,S]], and U=[[I,A⁻¹B],[0,I]]. Direct block multiplication gives LH=[[A,0],[C,S]]. Therefore LHU=[[A,B],[C,CA⁻¹B+S]]=M.
The matrices L and U have inverses L⁻¹=[[I,0],[−CA⁻¹,I]] and U⁻¹=[[I,−A⁻¹B],[0,I]]. Multiply each proposed inverse on both sides to obtain the identity. No inverse of S enters these products.
If S is invertible, then H⁻¹=[[A⁻¹,0],[0,S⁻¹]]. Both HH⁻¹ and H⁻¹H equal the identity. Thus U⁻¹H⁻¹L⁻¹ is a two-sided inverse of LHU=M.
If M is invertible, then H=L⁻¹MU⁻¹ is invertible, with inverse UM⁻¹L. Write its inverse as [[E,F],[G,J]]. The bottom-right blocks of HH⁻¹=I and H⁻¹H=I give SJ=JS=I. Thus S is invertible.
Multiply U⁻¹H⁻¹ to obtain [[A⁻¹,−A⁻¹BS⁻¹],[0,S⁻¹]]. Its product with L⁻¹ is the displayed inverse. The order of every factor matters. No interchange of matrix factors occurs.

The first block equation is Ax+By=f. Since A is invertible, x=A⁻¹(f−By). Substitute this into Cx+Dy=g to obtain Sy=g−CA⁻¹f. Conversely these two reduced equations imply both original equations. Empty blocks satisfy the same identities.

worked_application.title: A saddle-point system without a full inverse
hypotheses: The entries lie in ℝ. A=diag(2,3), B=(1,1)ᵀ, C=(1,1), and D=0.
A is invertible because 2 and 3 are nonzero.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The Schur complement reduces 3 equations to 1 scalar equation. Its nonzero value also proves that the full matrix is invertible.

steps.text: Compute A⁻¹=diag(1/2,1/3). Then S=0−(1,1)diag(1/2,1/3)(1,1)ᵀ=−5/6. Thus S has inverse −6/5.
For f=(1,2)ᵀ and g=0, the reduced right side is g−CA⁻¹f=−(1/2+2/3)=−7/6. Therefore y=(−6/5)(−7/6)=7/5.
Check the original equations. The values give 2(−1/5)+7/5=1, 3(1/5)+7/5=2, and −1/5+1/5=0. The solution is unique because A and S are invertible.

results.name: Operator Neumann series with a certified truncation error
results.statement: Let E be a Banach space over ℝ or ℂ. Let T:E→E be a bounded linear operator with q=‖T‖<1. Then I−T has bounded inverse R=∑_{n=0}^∞ Tⁿ, where the series converges in operator norm. For every integer N≥0, ‖R−∑_{n=0}^N Tⁿ‖≤q^(N+1)/(1−q), and ‖R‖≤1/(1−q).
hypotheses: E is complete for its norm. T is linear and bounded.
The operator norm satisfies q=‖T‖<1. N is an integer with N≥0.

prerequisites.reason: The scalar series ∑qⁿ converges to 1/(1−q) for 0≤q<1. This bounds every operator tail.
The worked application integrates continuous polynomial and exponential functions through their antiderivatives.

definitions.name: operator norm
definitions.text: ‖T‖ is the least bound c≥0 for which ‖Tx‖≤c‖x‖ for all x.

definitions.name: Banach space
definitions.text: A Banach space is a normed real or complex vector space in which every Cauchy sequence converges.

definitions.name: operator series
definitions.text: Convergence in operator norm means that the operator norms of the differences of partial sums and the limit tend to 0.

source.alignment: The source proves invertibility and both inverse equations in a normed ring with summable geometric series. The authored proof treats bounded operators on a Banach space and proves the quantitative tail estimate.

results.proof_status: source proof inspected; authored proof awaits inference review; no local Lean check

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: For bounded operators U and V, ‖UVx‖≤‖U‖‖V‖‖x‖. Thus ‖UV‖≤‖U‖‖V‖. Induction gives ‖Tⁿ‖≤qⁿ for n≥1. Also ‖I‖≤1, including the zero space.

Let P_N=∑_{n=0}^N Tⁿ. For m>N, the triangle inequality gives ‖P_m−P_N‖≤∑_{n=N+1}^m qⁿ≤q^(N+1)/(1−q). The linked scalar geometric series proves that this bound tends to 0. Hence the partial sums form a Cauchy sequence in operator norm.

For each x, the sequence P_Nx is Cauchy because ‖(P_m−P_N)x‖≤‖P_m−P_N‖‖x‖. Completeness of E gives a limit Rx. Limits preserve addition and scalar multiplication, so R is linear. The bound ‖P_Nx‖≤(∑_{n=0}^N qⁿ)‖x‖ gives ‖Rx‖≤‖x‖/(1−q). Thus R is bounded.

For every x, take m→∞ in the tail estimate to obtain ‖(R−P_N)x‖≤q^(N+1)‖x‖/(1−q). Continuity of the norm follows from |‖u‖−‖v‖|≤‖u−v‖. The definition of operator norm gives the stated tail bound and proves P_N→R in operator norm.

Finite cancellation gives (I−T)P_N=P_N(I−T)=I−T^(N+1). The operator norm of T^(N+1) is at most q^(N+1), which tends to 0. Products with the fixed bounded operator I−T preserve operator-norm limits by the first-step bound. Therefore (I−T)R=R(I−T)=I.
The tail and inverse bounds also hold when q=0. In that case T=0, R=I, and every tail is 0. The proof does not require different operators to commute. It uses only powers of T.

worked_application.title: A quantitative Volterra integral equation
worked_application.goal: Solve u(x)−(1/2)∫₀ˣu(t)dt=1 for x in [0,1], and bound a finite approximation.
hypotheses: E=C([0,1],ℝ) with the uniform norm is complete.
Define (Tu)(x)=(1/2)∫₀ˣu(t)dt. This operator is linear and maps continuous functions to continuous functions.

Completeness follows directly: a uniform Cauchy sequence has pointwise real limits. The same Cauchy estimate proves uniform convergence. For a point x, select one continuous approximant within ε/3 of the limit. Its continuity and the triangle inequality prove continuity of the limit at x.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The uniform estimate gives ‖T‖≤1/2<1. The Neumann theorem gives uniqueness and a uniform error bound for successive integral approximations.

steps.text: For ‖u‖∞≤1, |(Tu)(x)|≤x/2≤1/2. The function u=1 attains 1/2 at x=1. Thus ‖T‖=1/2.
Induct on n. The case n=0 gives T⁰1=1=x⁰/(2⁰0!). Integrate xⁿ/(2ⁿn!) to obtain T^(n+1)1=x^(n+1)/(2^(n+1)(n+1)!).

The inverse yields u(x)=∑_{n=0}^∞ xⁿ/(2ⁿn!). Define exp(s) by its real power series. This gives u(x)=exp(x/2). The ratio of consecutive absolute terms is at most 1/(2(n+1)) on [0,1], so the series converges uniformly. An integral of a uniform error is at most that error times the interval length. Thus the integral preserves this series limit.
Use N=6. The approximation u₆(x)=∑_{n=0}^6 xⁿ/(2ⁿn!) satisfies ‖u−u₆‖∞≤(1/2)^7/(1−1/2)=1/64. At x=1 it gives u₆(1)=75973/46080. The exact value is exp(1/2).
Check the equation directly: (1/2)∫₀ˣexp(t/2)dt=exp(x/2)−1. Thus u−Tu=1. The inverse theorem proves that no other continuous solution exists.

worked_application.result: The unique solution is u(x)=exp(x/2). The degree-6 approximation has uniform error at most 1/64.

limitations: The sufficient condition ‖T‖<1 is not necessary for invertibility.
The proof requires completeness. The bound is in operator norm, not an entrywise norm.

results.name: Finite-field Gauss sum magnitude and quadratic square
results.statement: Let F be a finite field of q elements. Let χ:F×→ℂ× be a nontrivial multiplicative character, extended by χ(0)=0. Let ψ:(F,+)→ℂ× be a nontrivial additive character. Define G(χ,ψ)=∑_{x∈F}χ(x)ψ(x). Then |G(χ,ψ)|²=q. If χ²=1 on F×, then G(χ,ψ)²=χ(−1)q.
hypotheses: F is a field with finitely many elements. q=|F|.
χ and ψ are group homomorphisms to nonzero complex numbers. Neither character is trivial.
The square formula requires χ(x)²=1 for every nonzero x.

prerequisites.reason: The worked application constructs the additive character from a primitive fifth root through de Moivre’s formula.

definitions.name: multiplicative character
definitions.text: χ(xy)=χ(x)χ(y) for nonzero field elements, and χ(1)=1. Extend χ to 0 by χ(0)=0.

definitions.name: additive character
definitions.text: ψ(x+y)=ψ(x)ψ(y), and ψ(0)=1. Nontrivial means ψ(z)≠1 for some z.

definitions.name: Gauss sum
definitions.text: G(χ,ψ)=∑_{x∈F}χ(x)ψ(x). The sum includes 0, whose term is 0.

source.excerpt:
/-- We have `gaussSum χ ψ * gaussSum χ⁻¹ ψ⁻¹ = Fintype.card R`
when `χ` is nontrivial and `ψ` is primitive (and `R` is a field). -/
theorem gaussSum_mul_gaussSum_eq_card {χ : MulChar R R'} (hχ : χ ≠ 1) {ψ : AddChar R R'}
    (hψ : IsPrimitive ψ) :
    gaussSum χ ψ * gaussSum χ⁻¹ ψ⁻¹ = Fintype.card R := by
  simp only [gaussSum, AddChar.inv_apply, Finset.sum_mul, Finset.mul_sum, MulChar.inv_apply']
  conv =>
    enter [1, 2, x, 2, y]
    rw [mul_mul_mul_comm, ← map_mul, ← map_add_eq_mul, ← sub_eq_add_neg]
--  conv in _ * _ * (_ * _) => rw [mul_mul_mul_comm, ← map_mul, ← map_add_eq_mul, ← sub_eq_add_neg]
  simp_rw [gaussSum_mul_aux hχ ψ]
  rw [Finset.sum_comm]
  classical -- to get `[DecidableEq R]` for `sum_mulShift`
  simp_rw [← Finset.mul_sum, sum_mulShift _ hψ, sub_eq_zero, apply_ite, Nat.cast_zero, mul_zero]
  rw [Finset.sum_ite_eq' Finset.univ (1 : R)]
  simp only [Finset.mem_univ, map_one, one_mul, ite_true]

/-- When `χ` is a nontrivial quadratic character, then the square of `gaussSum χ ψ`
is `χ(-1)` times the cardinality of `R`. -/
theorem gaussSum_sq {χ : MulChar R R'} (hχ₁ : χ ≠ 1) (hχ₂ : IsQuadratic χ)
    {ψ : AddChar R R'} (hψ : IsPrimitive ψ) :
    gaussSum χ ψ ^ 2 = χ (-1) * Fintype.card R := by
  rw [pow_two, ← gaussSum_mul_gaussSum_eq_card hχ₁ hψ, hχ₂.inv, mul_rotate']
  congr
  rw [mul_comm, ← gaussSum_mulShift _ _ (-1 : Rˣ), inv_mulShift]
  rfl

steps.text: Every nonzero character value has finite multiplicative order because its source group is finite. Thus |χ(x)|=1 for x≠0 and |ψ(x)|=1 for all x. Their complex conjugates equal their inverses.
Choose a∈F× with χ(a)≠1. The bijection x↦ax on F× shows ∑_{x∈F×}χ(x)=χ(a)∑_{x∈F×}χ(x). Subtract the two sides and divide by 1−χ(a). Therefore the multiplicative character sum is 0.

Choose z∈F with ψ(z)≠1. The bijection x↦x+z gives ∑_{x∈F}ψ(x)=ψ(z)∑_{x∈F}ψ(x), so this additive character sum is 0. If b≠0, multiplication by b permutes F. Hence ∑_{y∈F}ψ(by)=0. Remove the y=0 term to obtain ∑_{y∈F×}ψ(by)=−1. For b=0 the latter sum is q−1.

Expand |G|²=G conjugate(G) as a finite double sum. Terms with x=0 or y=0 vanish. For each y≠0, write x=ty. This bijection changes χ(x)conjugate(χ(y)) to χ(t), and ψ(x)conjugate(ψ(y)) to ψ((t−1)y). Thus |G|²=∑_{t∈F×}χ(t)∑_{y∈F×}ψ((t−1)y).
Separate t=1. Its inner sum is q−1 and χ(1)=1. Every other t contributes −χ(t). The zero sum in step 2 gives ∑_{t≠0,1}χ(t)=−1. Therefore |G|²=(q−1)−(−1)=q.

If χ²=1 on F×, all its values are real and equal to 1 or −1. Therefore conjugate(G)=∑χ(x)ψ(−x). Replace x by −x to obtain conjugate(G)=χ(−1)G. Since χ(−1)²=1, the magnitude equation yields χ(−1)G²=q, or G²=χ(−1)q.

worked_application.title: Exact quadratic exponential sums modulo 5
worked_application.goal: Compute ∑_{x=0}^4 exp(2πiax²/5) for a=1 and a=2.
hypotheses: F=ℤ/5ℤ is a field. Put ζ=exp(2πi/5) and ψ(t)=ζᵗ.
Define χ(1)=χ(4)=1 and χ(2)=χ(3)=−1. Extend χ(0)=0.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The Gauss theorem fixes the magnitude and square of an oscillatory sum. A sign check then gives an exact value.

steps.text: The element 2 generates F×. Its successive powers are 1,2,4,3, with χ-values 1,−1,1,−1. Thus χ is a nontrivial homomorphism. By de Moivre’s formula, ζ=cos(2π/5)+i sin(2π/5) satisfies ζ⁵=1. Its angle shows ζ≠1. Hence ψ(t)=ζᵗ is a well-defined nontrivial additive character.
The squares x² for x=0,1,2,3,4 are 0,1,4,4,1. Thus the number of roots of x²=t is 1+χ(t) for each t in F. For a≠0, the additive-character sum ∑_tψ(at) is 0. Therefore S(a)=∑_tχ(t)ψ(at).
Replace t by a⁻¹s to obtain S(a)=χ(a)⁻¹G. Here χ(a)⁻¹=χ(a), so S(1)=G and S(2)=−G.
Since χ(−1)=χ(4)=1, the theorem gives G²=5. Directly G=ζ+ζ⁴−ζ²−ζ³=2cos(2π/5)−2cos(4π/5). The first cosine is positive and the second is negative. Hence G>0 and G=√5.
Thus S(1)=√5 and S(2)=−√5. Direct enumeration also gives S(1)=1+2ζ+2ζ⁴ and S(2)=1+2ζ²+2ζ³. The identity 1+ζ+ζ²+ζ³+ζ⁴=0 makes these expressions agree with the Gauss calculation.

worked_application.result: The sums are √5 for a=1 and −√5 for a=2. The square formula alone does not select the sign.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: Neither character may be trivial. The proof requires a field, not an arbitrary finite ring.
The quadratic square formula does not determine the sign of G. A further argument must select the square root.

results.name: Exactness of module localization
results.statement: Let R be a commutative ring with identity. Let S be a multiplicative subset containing 1. For R-linear maps f:M→N and g:N→P with im(f)=ker(g), the induced maps S⁻¹f and S⁻¹g satisfy im(S⁻¹f)=ker(S⁻¹g). Localization also preserves injective and surjective maps. Thus it preserves every short exact sequence.
hypotheses: M, N and P are unital R-modules. The maps are R-linear.
S contains 1 and is closed under multiplication. S may contain 0, in which case every localized module is 0.
The sequence is exact at N. Injectivity and surjectivity assertions assume these properties for the original map.

definitions.name: localized module
definitions.text: S⁻¹M consists of fractions m/s. The fractions m/s and n/t are equal if u(tm−sn)=0 for some u∈S.

definitions.name: exactness
definitions.text: A sequence M→N→P is exact at N when the image of the first map equals the kernel of the second.

definitions.name: localized map
definitions.text: An R-linear map f induces S⁻¹f by m/s↦f(m)/s.

source.excerpt:
lemma LocalizedModule.map_exact (g : M₀ →ₗ[R] M₁) (h : M₁ →ₗ[R] M₂) (ex : Exact g h) :
    Exact (map S (mkLinearMap S M₀) (mkLinearMap S M₁) g)
    (map S (mkLinearMap S M₁) (mkLinearMap S M₂) h) :=
  fun y ↦ Iff.intro
    (induction_on
      (fun m s hy ↦ by
        rw [map_LocalizedModules, ← zero_mk 1, mk_eq, one_smul, smul_zero] at hy
        obtain ⟨a, aS, ha⟩ := Subtype.exists.1 hy
        rw [smul_zero, mk_smul, ← map_smul, ex (a • m)] at ha
        rcases ha with ⟨x, hx⟩
        use mk x (⟨a, aS⟩ * s)
        rw [map_LocalizedModules, hx, ← mk_cancel_common_left ⟨a, aS⟩ s m, mk_smul])
      y)
    fun ⟨x, hx⟩ ↦ by
      revert hx
      refine induction_on (fun m s hx ↦ ?_) x
      rw [← hx, map_LocalizedModules, map_LocalizedModules, (ex (g m)).2 ⟨m, rfl⟩, zero_mk]

source.alignment: The source proves exactness for localized modules over a commutative semiring. The authored proof specializes to modules over a ring and also derives endpoint preservation.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: The induced map is well-defined. If u(tm−sn)=0, linearity gives u(tf(m)−sf(n))=0. The same u proves equality of the image fractions. Composition commutes with localization by evaluation on every fraction.
Since gf=0, the image of S⁻¹f lies in the kernel of S⁻¹g. Conversely let n/s satisfy g(n)/s=0. The definition of equality of fractions gives u∈S with ug(n)=0. Thus g(un)=0.
Exactness gives m∈M with f(m)=un. Therefore (S⁻¹f)(m/(us))=un/(us)=n/s. The last equality follows by multiplication of numerator and denominator by u. This proves the reverse inclusion.

If f is injective and f(m)/s=0, choose u∈S with f(um)=0. Injectivity gives um=0, so m/s=0. Thus localization preserves injectivity. If g is surjective, choose a preimage n of p. Then n/s maps to p/s, so localization preserves surjectivity.

Apply these conclusions to the three maps of a short exact sequence. The kernel-image equality and both endpoint properties persist. If 0∈S, every m/s equals 0 by the fraction relation, so the same conclusions hold.

worked_application.title: Separate torsion by a local calculation
worked_application.goal: Localize 0→ℤ→ℤ→ℤ/6ℤ→0, whose first nonzero map is multiplication by 6, at powers of 2.
hypotheses: R=ℤ and S={2ⁿ:n≥0}. Multiplication by 6 is injective, and its image is the kernel of reduction modulo 6.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Exactness converts a quotient of localized modules into a localized quotient. Inverting 2 removes the 2-primary torsion and preserves the 3-primary torsion.

steps.text: The localized ring is ℤ[1/2]. Exactness gives S⁻¹(ℤ/6ℤ)≅ℤ[1/2]/6ℤ[1/2]. Since 2 is a unit, the ideals generated by 6 and 3 are equal.
Define ℤ[1/2]→ℤ/3ℤ by a/2ⁿ↦a(2⁻¹)ⁿ modulo 3. The inverse of 2 modulo 3 is 2. Equivalent fractions have the same image, because every denominator is a unit modulo 3.
The map is surjective because integer fractions supply every residue. Its kernel consists of fractions with numerator divisible by 3, which is precisely 3ℤ[1/2]. Thus S⁻¹(ℤ/6ℤ)≅ℤ/3ℤ.

The class of 3 in ℤ/6ℤ disappears because 2·3=0. The class of 2 remains nonzero and has order 3. If all nonzero integers are inverted instead, multiplication by 6 is invertible and the quotient becomes 0.

worked_application.result: Localization at powers of 2 gives ℤ/3ℤ. Localization at all nonzero integers gives 0.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: Localization can remove nonzero torsion. Exactness does not imply that the localization map is injective.
A multiplicative set that contains 0 gives the zero localization.

results.name: Vandermonde determinant and interpolation solvability
results.statement: For a field K, n≥0 and nodes a₀,…,aₙ₋₁∈K, let Vᵢⱼ=aᵢʲ for 0≤i,j<n. Then det(V)=∏_{0≤i<j<n}(aⱼ−aᵢ). Therefore V is invertible exactly when the nodes are pairwise distinct. For distinct nodes, every data vector gives one polynomial of degree less than n with those values.
hypotheses: K is a commutative field. n is a nonnegative integer.
The existence and uniqueness of interpolation require pairwise distinct nodes. The determinant formula also holds for repeated nodes.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: The proof derives the polynomial root factors and adjugate identity explicitly. It uses the determinant definition and field axioms.

definitions.name: Vandermonde matrix
definitions.text: The row for node aᵢ is (1,aᵢ,…,aᵢⁿ⁻¹).

definitions.name: interpolation
definitions.text: Interpolation asks for a polynomial whose values at specified nodes equal specified data.

source.alignment: The source gives this determinant formula over a commutative ring. The authored proof uses a field and derives interpolation solvability.

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: The determinant for n=0 is 1, which agrees with the empty product. For n=1 it is also 1. Assume the formula for n−1 and first take distinct nodes a₀,…,aₙ₋₂.

Replace the last node by an indeterminate X. Expand the determinant along its last row. This gives a polynomial D(X) of degree at most n−1. Its leading coefficient is the determinant of the first n−1 nodes, because the last cofactor has positive sign.
For X=aᵢ with i<n−1, two rows are equal and D(aᵢ)=0. This equality follows from the determinant definition: interchange those rows in each permutation term and pair terms with opposite signs.

For any polynomial P, the identity Xᵏ−aᵏ=(X−a)∑_{j=0}^{k−1}Xᵏ⁻¹⁻ʲaʲ shows P(X)−P(a) is divisible by X−a. Therefore each distinct root aᵢ gives a factor X−aᵢ. After division by earlier factors, evaluation at a later root still gives 0, since the earlier factors are nonzero there.

Thus D(X) is its leading coefficient times ∏_{i<n−1}(X−aᵢ). The induction hypothesis supplies that coefficient. Substitute X=aₙ₋₁ to obtain the full product. If the first n−1 nodes are not distinct, V has repeated rows, and both sides are 0.

If det(V)≠0, its adjugate gives the inverse V⁻¹=adj(V)/det(V). The adjugate identity follows by cofactor expansion: diagonal entries give det(V), and off-diagonal entries give determinants with a repeated row. If det(V)=0, the nodes repeat and V has two equal rows, so V cannot map onto every data vector. The interpolation equations are Vc=y. Thus distinct nodes give exactly one coefficient vector c.

worked_application.title: Reconstruct a cubic from irregular samples
worked_application.goal: Find a polynomial of degree at most 3 with values 1,0,1,33 at nodes 0,1,2,4.
hypotheses: The nodes lie in ℝ and are distinct. There are 4 values, so the coefficient vector has dimension 4.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The determinant proves unique solvability before any coefficient calculation. The interpolation basis gives the polynomial explicitly.

steps.text: The determinant is (1−0)(2−0)(4−0)(2−1)(4−1)(4−2)=48≠0. Thus the interpolation system has exactly one solution.
For each node aᵢ, define Lᵢ(x)=∏_{j≠i}(x−aⱼ)/(aᵢ−aⱼ). Every denominator is nonzero. Direct substitution gives Lᵢ(aⱼ)=1 if i=j, and 0 otherwise.

The nodes are a₀=0, a₁=1, a₂=2 and a₃=4. The data are 1, 0, 1 and 33. Only L₀, L₂ and L₃ have nonzero data. The required polynomial is L₀+L₂+33L₃. Explicitly it is −(x−1)(x−2)(x−4)/8−x(x−1)(x−4)/4+33x(x−1)(x−2)/24.
Expansion gives P(x)=x³−2x²+1. The values are P(0)=1, P(1)=0, P(2)=1, and P(4)=33. The nonzero determinant proves that this polynomial is unique.

worked_application.result: The unique interpolating polynomial is x³−2x²+1.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: Distinct nodes ensure exact solvability. They do not ensure good numerical conditioning.
Repeated nodes require derivative data and a confluent Vandermonde construction.

results.name: Singular value decomposition from the adjoint square
results.statement: Let A be a complex m×n matrix, with m,n≥1 and rank r. There are unitary matrices U and V and a rectangular diagonal matrix Σ such that A=UΣV*. Its nonzero diagonal entries σ₁≥…≥σᵣ>0 are the square roots of the positive eigenvalues of A*A. Its Euclidean operator norm is σ₁ when r>0, and 0 when r=0.
hypotheses: A acts between finite-dimensional complex Euclidean spaces. The adjoint A* is the conjugate transpose.
U and V are square unitary matrices on the codomain and domain respectively. Σ has r positive diagonal entries.

prerequisites.reason: The finite-dimensional Hermitian spectral theorem supplies an orthonormal eigenbasis of A*A.

definitions.name: unitary matrix
definitions.text: A square matrix U is unitary if U*U=UU*=I.

definitions.name: singular value
definitions.text: A singular value is the nonnegative square root of an eigenvalue of A*A.

definitions.name: rectangular diagonal matrix
definitions.text: Σ has entries only at positions (i,i). All other entries are 0.

source.alignment: The source identifies singular values with square roots of the eigenvalues of the adjoint square. The full decomposition proof is authored from the linked spectral theorem. The source excerpt alone does not prove the complete authored statement.

results.proof_status: source proof inspected; authored proof awaits inference review; no local Lean check

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: The matrix A*A is Hermitian because (A*A)*=A*A. It is positive semidefinite because v*A*Av=‖Av‖²≥0. The linked spectral theorem gives an orthonormal basis vᵢ of eigenvectors with real eigenvalues λᵢ≥0.

Let p be the number of positive eigenvalues of A*A, counted with multiplicity. Order the eigenvectors so that λ₁≥…≥λₚ>0 and λᵢ=0 for i>p. Set σᵢ=√λᵢ for i≤p. Then σ₁≥…≥σₚ>0. For i≤p define uᵢ=Avᵢ/σᵢ. Then ⟨uᵢ,uⱼ⟩=⟨vᵢ,A*Avⱼ⟩/(σᵢσⱼ)=λⱼδᵢⱼ/(σᵢσⱼ)=δᵢⱼ. Thus these uᵢ are orthonormal.

If i>p, then λᵢ=0 and ‖Avᵢ‖²=λᵢ‖vᵢ‖²=0, so Avᵢ=0. Expansion in the vᵢ basis shows that the range of A is exactly the span of u₁,…,uₚ. Its dimension is p. So p=r, and σ₁≥…≥σᵣ>0 are the square roots of the positive eigenvalues in decreasing order.

Extend the r orthonormal vectors uᵢ to an orthonormal basis of ℂᵐ. If their span is proper, choose a vector outside it. Subtract its orthogonal projections onto the existing vectors. The remainder is nonzero and orthogonal to them. Normalize it, and repeat until m vectors exist.
Let U and V have these basis vectors as columns. They are unitary. The equations Avᵢ=σᵢuᵢ for i≤r and Avᵢ=0 otherwise show U*AV=Σ. Multiply by U and V* to obtain A=UΣV*.

For x=∑cᵢvᵢ, orthonormality gives ‖Ax‖²=∑_{i≤r}σᵢ²|cᵢ|²≤σ₁²‖x‖², because σ₁ is the largest of the σᵢ by the decreasing order of step 2. Equality holds for x=v₁ if r>0. If r=0, A=0. This proves the operator norm formula.

worked_application.title: Exact singular values of a rectangular shear
worked_application.goal: Compute the singular values and Euclidean condition number of A=[[1,1],[0,1],[0,0]].
hypotheses: A is a complex 3×2 matrix with real entries. Its 2 columns are linearly independent, so r=2.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The adjoint square converts the rectangular problem into a Hermitian eigenvalue calculation. The resulting singular values measure amplification in orthogonal directions.

steps.text: Compute A*A=[[1,1],[1,2]]. Its characteristic polynomial is λ²−3λ+1. The eigenvalues are λ±=(3±√5)/2, both positive.
Put φ=(1+√5)/2. Since φ²=(3+√5)/2 and φ⁻²=(3−√5)/2, the singular values are φ and φ⁻¹.
For either eigenvalue λ, an eigenvector is (1,λ−1). Its normalized form is vλ=(1,λ−1)/√(1+(λ−1)²). The matching left singular vector is uλ=(λ,λ−1,0)/(√λ√(1+(λ−1)²)).

The two left singular vectors span the first 2 coordinate directions. Add (0,0,1) to obtain U. These vectors and the vλ give A=UΣV*. The largest amplification is φ, and the smallest amplification on the domain is φ⁻¹.

The Euclidean condition number for this full-column-rank map is their ratio φ²=(3+√5)/2. The determinant of its top 2×2 block is 1, but this does not force equal amplification in different directions.

worked_application.result: The singular values are φ and φ⁻¹. The Euclidean condition number is φ²≈2.618.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: The order of singular vectors is not unique when singular values repeat.
Finite-dimensionality is essential for this finite matrix statement. Infinite-dimensional operators need different compactness hypotheses.

results.name: Gaussian quadratic integral with a linear source
results.statement: Let d≥1, let A be a real symmetric positive definite d×d matrix, and let b∈ℝᵈ. With Lebesgue measure, ∫_{ℝᵈ} exp(−xᵀAx/2+bᵀx)dx=(2π)^(d/2)exp(bᵀA⁻¹b/2)/√det(A). The integral is finite and positive.
hypotheses: A is real, symmetric and positive definite. Thus xᵀAx>0 for x≠0.
b is any real vector. The integral uses d-dimensional Lebesgue measure.

prerequisites.reason: Tonelli permits the nonnegative product integral and its factorization before integrability is established.
The scalar Gaussian calculation uses polar coordinates with Jacobian r.
The fundamental theorem of calculus evaluates the radial integral and the scalar antiderivatives.
The spectral theorem diagonalizes the real symmetric positive definite matrix.
The affine substitution x=μ+Qy has a nonzero Jacobian and a bijective smooth inverse.
The covariance computation reduces each scalar second moment to its Gaussian normalization by integration by parts.

theorem integral_gaussian (b : ℝ) : ∫ x : ℝ, exp (-b * x ^ 2) = √(π / b) := by
  -- First we deal with the crazy case where `b ≤ 0`: then both sides vanish.
  rcases le_or_gt b 0 with (hb | hb)
  · rw [integral_undef, sqrt_eq_zero_of_nonpos]
    · exact div_nonpos_of_nonneg_of_nonpos pi_pos.le hb
    · simpa only [not_lt, integrable_exp_neg_mul_sq_iff] using hb
  -- Assume now `b > 0`. Then both sides are non-negative and their squares agree.
  refine (sq_eq_sq₀ (by positivity) (by positivity)).1 ?_
  rw [← ofReal_inj, ofReal_pow, ← coe_algebraMap, RCLike.algebraMap_eq_ofReal, ← integral_ofReal,
    sq_sqrt (div_pos pi_pos hb).le, ← RCLike.algebraMap_eq_ofReal, coe_algebraMap, ofReal_div]
  convert! integral_gaussian_sq_complex (by rwa [ofReal_re] : 0 < (b : ℂ).re) with _ x
  rw [ofReal_exp, ofReal_mul, ofReal_pow, ofReal_neg]

steps.text: First prove ∫ℝexp(−t²)dt=√π. This integral is finite: outside |t|≤1, exp(−t²)≤exp(−|t|), whose integral is finite. Let J denote the integral. Its nonnegative integrand permits the linked Tonelli theorem, so J²=∫_{ℝ²}exp(−u²−v²)dudv.

The linked polar coordinate formula gives J²=2π∫₀∞r exp(−r²)dr=π. An antiderivative is −exp(−r²)/2. Its endpoint values are −1/2 and 0. Since J>0, J=√π. Scaling t=√(λ/2)y gives ∫ℝexp(−λy²/2)dy=√(2π/λ) for λ>0.
The linked spectral theorem gives A=QΛQᵀ, with Q orthogonal and Λ diagonal with entries λᵢ>0. Positivity follows by evaluation on each unit eigenvector. Therefore A is invertible and det(A)=∏λᵢ>0.
Set μ=A⁻¹b. Expand (x−μ)ᵀA(x−μ)=xᵀAx−2bᵀx+bᵀA⁻¹b. Thus the exponent is −(x−μ)ᵀA(x−μ)/2+bᵀA⁻¹b/2.
Use x=μ+Qy. This affine map is a bijection with absolute Jacobian determinant 1, because QᵀQ=I. The linked change-of-variables formula transforms the integral into exp(bᵀA⁻¹b/2)∫exp(−∑λᵢyᵢ²/2)dy.

Tonelli factors this last nonnegative integral into d scalar integrals. Step 2 gives ∏√(2π/λᵢ)=(2π)^(d/2)/√det(A). Every scalar integral is finite, so the original integral is finite. All factors are positive.

worked_application.title: Normalize a correlated Gaussian exactly
worked_application.goal: Evaluate ∫_{ℝ²}exp(−x₁²−x₁x₂−x₂²+x₁)dx₁dx₂.
hypotheses: A=[[2,1],[1,2]] and b=(1,0)ᵀ. The exponent is −xᵀAx/2+bᵀx.
The eigenvalues of A are 1 and 3, so A is positive definite.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Completion of the square handles the linear source. The determinant gives the normalization without two nested square completions.

steps.text: Compute bᵀA⁻¹b=2/3. The source factor is exp(1/3). Since d=2, the theorem gives Z=2πexp(1/3)/√3.
Divide the original integrand by Z to obtain a probability density. In the shifted coordinates y=x−μ, its exponent is −yᵀAy/2. The change of variables proves that the density integrates to 1.

The covariance is A⁻¹. To check this directly, diagonalize A with eigenvectors (1,−1)/√2 and (1,1)/√2. The two scalar Gaussian factors have variances 1 and 1/3. Transform their diagonal covariance by the orthogonal basis to obtain (1/3)[[2,−1],[−1,2]]. For a scalar density proportional to exp(−λt²/2), symmetry gives mean 0. Integration by parts gives ∫t²exp(−λt²/2)dt=(1/λ)∫exp(−λt²/2)dt, because t exp(−λt²/2) tends to 0 at both ends.

worked_application.result: The integral is 2πexp(1/3)/√3. The normalized density has mean (2/3,−1/3) and covariance A⁻¹.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: A positive semidefinite singular A does not give a finite integral over all of ℝᵈ.
An indefinite A produces exponential growth along some direction. The stated formula does not apply.

results.name: Beta–Gamma factorization for improper integrals
results.statement: For real a,b>0, define Γ(a)=∫₀∞t^(a−1)e^(−t)dt and B(a,b)=∫₀¹s^(a−1)(1−s)^(b−1)ds. Both integrals converge, Γ(a+b)>0, and B(a,b)=Γ(a)Γ(b)/Γ(a+b). Also ∫₀∞x^(a−1)/(1+x)^(a+b)dx=B(a,b).
hypotheses: The parameters a and b are real and strictly positive.
The integrals are Lebesgue integrals of nonnegative functions on the stated open intervals.

prerequisites.reason: Tonelli factors nonnegative integrals on the positive quadrant.
The positive-quadrant substitution has a smooth inverse and Jacobian r.
The final one-dimensional substitution maps (0,∞) bijectively onto (0,1).
The worked computation derives the Gamma recurrence from the defining integral.
The scalar antiderivative gives Γ(1)=1.
Its scalar case evaluates Γ(1/2) after the substitution u=v².

theorem Gamma_mul_Gamma_eq_betaIntegral {s t : ℂ} (hs : 0 < re s) (ht : 0 < re t) :
    Gamma s * Gamma t = Gamma (s + t) * betaIntegral s t := by
  -- Note that we haven't proved (yet) that the Gamma function has no zeroes, so we can't formulate
  -- this as a formula for the Beta function.
  have conv_int := integral_posConvolution
    (GammaIntegral_convergent hs) (GammaIntegral_convergent ht) (ContinuousLinearMap.mul ℝ ℂ)
  simp_rw [ContinuousLinearMap.mul_apply'] at conv_int
  have hst : 0 < re (s + t) := by rw [add_re]; exact add_pos hs ht
  rw [Gamma_eq_integral hs, Gamma_eq_integral ht, Gamma_eq_integral hst, GammaIntegral,
    GammaIntegral, GammaIntegral, ← conv_int, ← MeasureTheory.integral_mul_const (betaIntegral _ _)]
  refine setIntegral_congr_fun measurableSet_Ioi fun x hx => ?_
  rw [mul_assoc, ← betaIntegral_scaled s t hx, ← intervalIntegral.integral_const_mul]
  congr 1 with y : 1
  push_cast
  suffices Complex.exp (-x) = Complex.exp (-y) * Complex.exp (-(x - y)) by rw [this]; ring
  rw [← Complex.exp_add]; congr 1; abel

source.alignment: The source proves the Beta–Gamma product for complex parameters with positive real parts. The authored result restricts to positive real parameters and proves the nonzero denominator and the rational-integral substitution.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: For a>0, t^(a−1) is integrable on (0,1), with integral 1/a. For t≥1, t^(a−1)e^(−t)≤Ce^(−t/2) for some finite C. If a≤1, take C=1. If a>1, differentiation shows t^(a−1)e^(−t/2) has a finite maximum. Hence Γ(a) is finite. The same proof applies to Γ(b) and Γ(a+b).

The Beta integrand is integrable near 0 because a>0 and (1−s)^(b−1) is bounded on (0,1/2). It is integrable near 1 because b>0 and s^(a−1) is bounded on (1/2,1). Thus B(a,b) is finite. Γ(a+b)>0 because its integrand is positive on (1,2).
Tonelli gives Γ(a)Γ(b)=∫_{(0,∞)²}u^(a−1)v^(b−1)e^(−u−v)dudv. The integrand is nonnegative, so the factorization is valid.

Use u=rs and v=r(1−s), with r>0 and 0<s<1. The inverse map is r=u+v and s=u/(u+v), so this is a smooth bijection. Its absolute Jacobian is r. The change-of-variables formula gives the integrand r^(a+b−1)e^(−r)s^(a−1)(1−s)^(b−1).
Tonelli factors the transformed integral into Γ(a+b)B(a,b). Divide by the positive Γ(a+b) to obtain the ratio formula.

For the second identity, set s=x/(1+x). Then x=s/(1−s) and dx=ds/(1−s)². Direct substitution gives x^(a−1)(1+x)^(−a−b)dx=s^(a−1)(1−s)^(b−1)ds. The change-of-variables formula and the convergence already proved give the result.

steps.text: The theorem gives I=Γ(3/2)Γ(5/2)/Γ(4). All convergence conditions hold because a,b>0.
Integration by parts gives Γ(t+1)=tΓ(t) for t>0. Its boundary term uᵗe^(−u) tends to 0 as u→0 and u→∞. Also Γ(1)=∫₀∞e^(−u)du=1.
Set u=v² in Γ(1/2). Its integral becomes 2∫₀∞e^(−v²)dv=√π by the Gaussian integral and symmetry. Thus Γ(3/2)=√π/2 and Γ(5/2)=3√π/4.
The recurrence gives Γ(4)=3·2·1=6. Hence I=((√π/2)(3√π/4))/6=π/16.

worked_application.result: The convergent improper integral equals π/16.

The endpoints 0 and 1 can be singular. The proof treats their integrability explicitly.

theorem deriv_gaussian_eq_hermite_mul_gaussian (n : ℕ) (x : ℝ) :
    deriv^[n] (fun y => Real.exp (-(y ^ 2 / 2))) x =
    (-1 : ℝ) ^ n * aeval x (hermite n) * Real.exp (-(x ^ 2 / 2)) := by
  rw [mul_assoc]
  induction n generalizing x with
  | zero => rw [Function.iterate_zero_apply, pow_zero, one_mul, hermite_zero, C_1, map_one, one_mul]
  | succ n ih =>
    replace ih : deriv^[n] _ = _ := _root_.funext ih
    have deriv_gaussian :
      deriv (fun y => Real.exp (-(y ^ 2 / 2))) x = -x * Real.exp (-(x ^ 2 / 2)) := by
      -- Porting note (https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/issues/10745): was `simp [mul_comm, ← neg_mul]`
      rw [deriv_exp (by simp)]
      simp [mul_comm]
    rw [Function.iterate_succ_apply', ih, deriv_const_mul_field, deriv_fun_mul, pow_succ (-1 : ℝ),
      deriv_gaussian, hermite_succ, map_sub, map_mul, aeval_X, Polynomial.deriv_aeval]

    · apply Polynomial.differentiable_aeval

steps.text: Induction on n shows Hₙ is monic of degree n. The term xHₙ has degree n+1 and leading coefficient 1. The derivative Hₙ′ has smaller degree, so subtraction cannot change that leading term.
Put φ(x)=e^(−x²/2). Since φ′=−xφ, induction and the product rule give φ^(n)=(-1)ⁿHₙφ. The induction step is D((-1)ⁿHₙφ)=(-1)ⁿ(Hₙ′−xHₙ)φ=(-1)ⁿ⁺¹Hₙ₊₁φ.

Every polynomial times φ is integrable, and tends to 0 at ±∞. For each integer k≥0, |x|ᵏe^(−x²/2) has a finite integral. For large |x|, k log|x|≤x²/4, so the expression is at most e^(−x²/4). The linked Gaussian integral proves that bound is integrable. This also proves the boundary limit.

On each finite interval, integrate Hₘφ^(n) by parts n times. Then send both endpoints to infinity. Every boundary term is a polynomial times φ, so step 3 makes it vanish. Absolute integrability permits the improper limits. The two factors (-1)ⁿ cancel, giving ∫HₘHₙφ=∫Hₘ^(n)φ.
If n>m, the nth derivative of Hₘ is 0, so the integral is 0. If n=m, monicity gives Hₙ^(n)=n!, and the linked Gaussian integral gives n!√(2π).
If n<m, interchange m and n in the integral and use the n>m case. Multiplication of the real polynomial values is commutative. This covers every pair of indices, including m=n=0.

worked_application.title: A Gaussian control variate from orthogonal polynomials
worked_application.goal: Find the best approximation of X⁴ by a+b(X²−1) in mean square, for a standard normal variable X.
hypotheses: The density of X is e^(−x²/2)/√(2π). Its normalization follows from the Gaussian integral.
Mean-square error is the Gaussian polynomial inner product of the residual with itself.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Hermite orthogonality makes the least-squares coefficients independent. It also computes the residual variance exactly.

steps.text: The recurrence gives H₂=x²−1 and H₄=x⁴−6x²+3. Therefore x⁴=H₄+6H₂+3H₀.
The residual is H₄+(6−b)H₂+(3−a)H₀. Orthogonality gives its squared norm 4!+2!(6−b)²+(3−a)²=24+2(6−b)²+(3−a)².
This expression has its unique minimum at a=3 and b=6. The best approximation is 3+6(X²−1), and its mean-square error is 24.
Orthogonality with H₀ gives E[X⁴]=3. The squared norm of X⁴ is 24+36·2+9=105. Thus Var(X⁴)=105−9=96.
The adjusted estimator X⁴−6(X²−1) still has mean 3 because E[H₂]=0. Its centered residual is H₄, so its variance is 24. The orthogonal calculation reduces the variance from 96 to 24.

worked_application.result: The best coefficients are a=3 and b=6. The residual variance is 24.

limitations: Different Hermite conventions use different Gaussian weights and normalization constants.
The polynomial projection is in Gaussian L². It does not minimize the uniform error on ℝ.

results.name: Lagrange multiplier rule for equality constraints
results.statement: Let U⊆ℝⁿ be open and x₀∈U. Let f=(f₁,…,fₘ):U→ℝᵐ and φ:U→ℝ be C¹ maps. Let S={x∈U: f(x)=f(x₀)}. Assume φ|_S has a local extremum at x₀. Then there are real numbers λ₀,λ₁,…,λₘ, not all 0, with λ₀∇φ(x₀)+∑λᵢ∇fᵢ(x₀)=0. If ∇f₁(x₀),…,∇fₘ(x₀) are linearly independent, then λ₀≠0, and one can take λ₀=1.
hypotheses: n≥1 and 0≤m≤n. For m=0 the constraint set is U and the rule reduces to ∇φ(x₀)=0.
f and φ are continuously differentiable on U. The extremum is local on S: there is a neighborhood N of x₀ with φ(x)≤φ(x₀) for all x∈S∩N, or φ(x)≥φ(x₀) for all x∈S∩N.
The normal form with λ₀=1 needs the constraint gradients to be linearly independent at x₀.

prerequisites.reason: Step 3 applies the inverse function theorem to Ĝ.

definitions.name: local extremum on S
definitions.text: x₀ is a local maximum (minimum) of φ on S if φ(x)≤φ(x₀) (respectively ≥) for all x∈S near x₀.

definitions.name: Lagrange multiplier
definitions.text: A multiplier is a coefficient λᵢ in the linear relation among ∇φ(x₀) and the constraint gradients ∇fᵢ(x₀).

definitions.name: critical point of the Lagrangian
definitions.text: For L(x,λ)=φ(x)+∑λᵢ(fᵢ(x)−fᵢ(x₀)), the conditions ∇ₓL=0 and f(x)=f(x₀) define the candidate points.

/-- Lagrange multipliers theorem: if `φ : E → ℝ` has a local extremum on the set `{x | f x = f x₀}`
at `x₀`, both `f : E → F` and `φ` are strictly differentiable at `x₀`, and the codomain of `f` is
a complete space, then there exist `Λ : dual ℝ F` and `Λ₀ : ℝ` such that `(Λ, Λ₀) ≠ 0` and
`Λ (f' x) + Λ₀ • φ' x = 0` for all `x`. -/
theorem IsLocalExtrOn.exists_linear_map_of_hasStrictFDerivAt
    (hextr : IsLocalExtrOn φ {x | f x = f x₀} x₀) (hf' : HasStrictFDerivAt f f' x₀)
    (hφ' : HasStrictFDerivAt φ φ' x₀) :
    ∃ (Λ : Module.Dual ℝ F) (Λ₀ : ℝ), (Λ, Λ₀) ≠ 0 ∧ ∀ x, Λ (f' x) + Λ₀ • φ' x = 0 := by
  rcases Submodule.exists_le_ker_of_lt_top _
      (lt_top_iff_ne_top.2 <| hextr.range_ne_top_of_hasStrictFDerivAt hf' hφ') with
    ⟨Λ', h0, hΛ'⟩
  set e : ((F →ₗ[ℝ] ℝ) × ℝ) ≃ₗ[ℝ] F × ℝ →ₗ[ℝ] ℝ :=
    ((LinearEquiv.refl ℝ (F →ₗ[ℝ] ℝ)).prodCongr (LinearMap.ringLmapEquivSelf ℝ ℝ ℝ).symm).trans
      (LinearMap.coprodEquiv ℝ)
  rcases e.surjective Λ' with ⟨⟨Λ, Λ₀⟩, rfl⟩
  refine ⟨Λ, Λ₀, e.map_ne_zero_iff.1 h0, fun x => ?_⟩
  convert! congr($(LinearMap.range_le_ker_iff.1 hΛ') x) using 1
    -- squeezed `simp [mul_comm]` to speed up elaboration

  -- squeezed `simp [mul_comm]` to speed up elaboration
  simp only [e, smul_eq_mul, LinearEquiv.trans_apply, LinearEquiv.prodCongr_apply,
    LinearEquiv.refl_apply, LinearMap.ringLmapEquivSelf_symm_apply, LinearMap.coprodEquiv_apply,
    ContinuousLinearMap.coe_prod, LinearMap.coprod_comp_prod, LinearMap.add_apply,
    LinearMap.coe_comp, ContinuousLinearMap.coe_coe, Function.comp_apply, LinearMap.coe_smulRight,
    Module.End.one_apply, mul_comm]

/-- Lagrange multipliers theorem, 1d version. Let `f : ι → E → ℝ` be a finite family of functions.
Suppose that `φ : E → ℝ` has a local extremum on the set `{x | ∀ i, f i x = f i x₀}` at `x₀`.
Suppose that all functions `f i` as well as `φ` are strictly differentiable at `x₀`.
Then the derivatives `f' i : E → L[ℝ] ℝ` and `φ' : StrongDual ℝ E` are linearly dependent:
there exist `Λ : ι → ℝ` and `Λ₀ : ℝ`, `(Λ, Λ₀) ≠ 0`, such that `∑ i, Λ i • f' i + Λ₀ • φ' = 0`.

See also `IsLocalExtrOn.linear_dependent_of_hasStrictFDerivAt` for a version that
states `¬LinearIndependent ℝ _` instead of existence of `Λ` and `Λ₀`. -/
theorem IsLocalExtrOn.exists_multipliers_of_hasStrictFDerivAt {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι]
    {f : ι → E → ℝ} {f' : ι → StrongDual ℝ E} (hextr : IsLocalExtrOn φ {x | ∀ i, f i x = f i x₀} x₀)
    (hf' : ∀ i, HasStrictFDerivAt (f i) (f' i) x₀) (hφ' : HasStrictFDerivAt φ φ' x₀) :
    ∃ (Λ : ι → ℝ) (Λ₀ : ℝ), (Λ, Λ₀) ≠ 0 ∧ (∑ i, Λ i • f' i) + Λ₀ • φ' = 0 := by
  let := Classical.decEq ι
  replace hextr : IsLocalExtrOn φ {x | (fun i => f i x) = fun i => f i x₀} x₀ := by
    simpa only [funext_iff] using hextr
  rcases hextr.exists_linear_map_of_hasStrictFDerivAt (hasStrictFDerivAt_pi.2 fun i => hf' i)
      hφ' with
    ⟨Λ, Λ₀, h0, hsum⟩
  rcases (LinearEquiv.piRing ℝ ℝ ι ℝ).symm.surjective Λ with ⟨Λ, rfl⟩
  refine ⟨Λ, Λ₀, ?_, ?_⟩
  · simpa only [Ne, Prod.ext_iff, LinearEquiv.map_eq_zero_iff, Prod.fst_zero] using! h0
  · ext x; simpa [mul_comm] using hsum x

steps.text: Let G=(f,φ):U→ℝ^(m+1). Write J for the (m+1)×n matrix of DG(x₀). Its rows are ∇f₁(x₀),…,∇fₘ(x₀),∇φ(x₀). A nontrivial vanishing combination of the rows is exactly the claimed relation. So it is enough to show that the rows are linearly dependent.

Suppose, for a contradiction, that the rows of J are linearly independent. Then J has rank m+1, so its kernel K has dimension n−m−1. Choose a linear map L:ℝⁿ→ℝ^(n−m−1) whose restriction to K is an isomorphism (for example, the orthogonal projection onto K followed by a coordinate isomorphism). If Jx=0 and Lx=0, then x∈K and L|_K x=0, so x=0. Thus x↦(Jx,Lx) is an injective linear map ℝⁿ→ℝⁿ, hence bijective.

Define Ĝ:U→ℝⁿ by Ĝ(x)=(G(x),L x). It is C¹, and DĜ(x₀)=(J,L) is invertible by step 2. The inverse function theorem gives open sets V∋x₀ and W∋Ĝ(x₀) such that Ĝ:V→W is a C¹ bijection with continuous inverse.

Put y₀=Ĝ(x₀)=(f(x₀),φ(x₀),Lx₀). For small real t, the point y_t=(f(x₀),φ(x₀)+t,Lx₀) lies in W, because W is open. Let x_t=Ĝ⁻¹(y_t)∈V. The first m coordinates of Ĝ(x_t) show f(x_t)=f(x₀), so x_t∈S. The next coordinate shows φ(x_t)=φ(x₀)+t.

The inverse is continuous, so x_t→x₀ as t→0. Thus there are points of S arbitrarily close to x₀ with φ>φ(x₀) (take t>0) and points with φ<φ(x₀) (take t<0). This contradicts the local extremum hypothesis. So the rows of J are dependent, which proves the first claim.

Now assume ∇f₁(x₀),…,∇fₘ(x₀) are independent. In a nontrivial relation λ₀∇φ+∑λᵢ∇fᵢ=0, the case λ₀=0 would give a nontrivial relation among the ∇fᵢ, which is impossible. So λ₀≠0. Divide by λ₀ to get λ₀=1 and ∇φ(x₀)=−∑μᵢ∇fᵢ(x₀) with μᵢ=λᵢ/λ₀.

worked_application.title: Extreme values of xy+yz on the unit sphere
worked_application.goal: Find the maximum and the minimum of φ(x,y,z)=xy+yz on S={x²+y²+z²=1}, and the points where they occur.
hypotheses: n=3, m=1, f(x,y,z)=x²+y²+z²−1 and φ(x,y,z)=xy+yz. Both are polynomial, so both are C¹.
∇f=(2x,2y,2z) is nonzero at every point of S, so the independence hypothesis holds at each point.
S is closed and bounded, hence compact, so φ attains a maximum and a minimum on S.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: At an extremum point of the compact set S, the rule gives ∇φ=μ∇f with a real μ. This turns an optimization over a surface into algebraic equations in x,y,z,μ.

steps.text: Set up. Take f(x,y,z)=x²+y²+z²−1 and φ(x,y,z)=xy+yz, with n=3 and m=1. Then S={f=0}=f^(-1)(f(x₀)) for every x₀ on the sphere, because f(x₀)=0. Compute ∇f=(2x,2y,2z). On S this vector has length 2, so it is nonzero and the independence hypothesis holds at every point of S. Let x₀ be a point where φ|_S has its maximum or minimum. This is a local extremum on S. The Lagrange rule with λ₀=1 gives ∇φ(x₀)=μ∇f(x₀) for a real μ (the multiplier of the rule is −μ). Compute ∇φ=(y,x+z,y). So y=2μx, x+z=2μy and y=2μz. The point also satisfies x²+y²+z²=1.
Case y=0. The first and third equations give 2μx=0 and 2μz=0. If μ≠0, then x=z=0 and the constraint fails (the point would be 0). So μ=0, and the middle equation gives x+z=0. Then φ=y(x+z)=0.
Case y≠0. The first and third equations give 2μx=y=2μz, so μ≠0 and x=z=y/(2μ). The middle equation becomes y/μ=2μy, so μ²=1/2 and μ=±1/√2.
For μ=1/√2: x=z=y/√2. The constraint gives y²/2+y²+y²/2=2y²=1, so y=±1/√2 and x=z=y/√2=±1/2. At (1/2,1/√2,1/2) we get φ=y(x+z)=(1/√2)(1)=√2/2. The opposite point gives the same value.
For μ=−1/√2: x=z=−y/√2. The constraint again gives y=±1/√2. At (−1/2,1/√2,−1/2) we get φ=(1/√2)(−1)=−√2/2. The opposite point gives the same value.

The critical values are 0, √2/2 and −√2/2. By compactness the largest and smallest critical values are the global extrema. This agrees with the eigenvalues 0, ±1/√2 of the symmetric matrix [[0,1/2,0],[1/2,0,1/2],[0,1/2,0]] of the form xy+yz.

worked_application.result: The maximum of xy+yz on the unit sphere is √2/2, at ±(1/2,1/√2,1/2). The minimum is −√2/2, at ±(−1/2,1/√2,−1/2).

limitations: The rule is a necessary condition. A critical point need not be an extremum.
Without independent constraint gradients, λ₀ may be 0. Example: constraint x²=0 in one variable gives ∇f(0)=0.
C¹ regularity matters at x₀. For merely differentiable data the inverse function step can fail.
Inequality constraints need the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions, which this entry does not prove.

results.name: Gauss's lemma and the reduction modulo p irreducibility test
results.statement: A polynomial in ℤ[x] is primitive if the gcd of its coefficients is 1. (1) The product of two primitive polynomials in ℤ[x] is primitive. (2) Let f∈ℤ[x] be primitive. Then f is irreducible in ℤ[x] if and only if f is irreducible in ℚ[x]. (3) If f is monic with integer coefficients and its reduction modulo a prime p is irreducible in 𝔽ₚ[x], then f is irreducible in ℚ[x].
hypotheses: Statements (1) and (2) hold for primitive f,g∈ℤ[x]. A primitive polynomial is nonzero.
Statement (3) needs f monic. The reduction map ℤ[x]→𝔽ₚ[x] must keep the degree of f, which holds because the leading coefficient 1 stays nonzero modulo p.

definitions.name: primitive polynomial

definitions.name: content

definitions.name: irreducible in a ring
definitions.text: A non-unit nonzero element is irreducible if each factorization into two factors has a unit factor.

steps.text: Let p be a prime. Suppose p divides every coefficient of fg, with f and g primitive. Reduce modulo p. The ring 𝔽ₚ[x] is an integral domain, and f̄ḡ=0, so f̄=0 or ḡ=0. Then p divides all coefficients of f or of g. This contradicts primitivity. So fg is primitive. This proves (1).

Prove (2), direction "ℤ irreducible ⇒ ℚ irreducible". Let f be primitive and irreducible in ℤ[x]. Then deg f≥1, since a constant primitive polynomial is ±1, a unit. Suppose f=GH in ℚ[x] with deg G≥1 and deg H≥1.
Clear denominators. Write G=(a/b)G₁ and H=(c/d)H₁, where G₁,H₁∈ℤ[x] are primitive and a/b, c/d are nonzero rationals. Then f=(ac/bd)G₁H₁ with G₁H₁ primitive by (1).

The polynomial f is primitive, and G₁H₁ is primitive. The rational r=ac/bd must have f=rG₁H₁ with integer coefficients. Write r=u/v in lowest terms. Then v divides every coefficient of uG₁H₁ and gcd(v,u)=1, so v divides all coefficients of G₁H₁. Hence v=±1. Also u divides all coefficients of f. Hence u=±1. So r=±1 and f=±G₁H₁ in ℤ[x].
Both G₁ and H₁ have degree at least 1, so neither is a unit of ℤ[x]. This contradicts the irreducibility of f in ℤ[x]. So f is irreducible in ℚ[x].

Prove (2), direction "ℚ irreducible ⇒ ℤ irreducible". Let f be primitive and irreducible in ℚ[x]. Then deg f≥1, so f is not a unit of ℤ[x]. Suppose f=gh in ℤ[x]. In ℚ[x] one factor is a unit, say g=c is a nonzero constant. The integer c divides every coefficient of f. Since f is primitive, c=±1, and g is a unit of ℤ[x]. So f is irreducible in ℤ[x].

Prove (3). Let f be monic with f̄ irreducible in 𝔽ₚ[x]. Then f is primitive, because its leading coefficient is 1. By (2) it is enough to show f is irreducible in ℤ[x]. Suppose f=gh in ℤ[x] with g,h non-units. The leading coefficients multiply to 1, so both equal 1 or both equal −1. Replace (g,h) by (−g,−h) if needed, so g and h are monic.

Both g and h have degree at least 1, since a monic non-unit constant does not exist. Reduce modulo p. We get f̄=ḡh̄ with deg ḡ=deg g≥1 and deg h̄=deg h≥1, because the leading coefficient 1 survives. This is a proper factorization of f̄ in 𝔽ₚ[x]. It contradicts the irreducibility of f̄. So f is irreducible in ℤ[x], and by (2) in ℚ[x].

worked_application.title: Irreducibility of x³−3x−1 and x⁴+6x²+x+3 over ℚ
worked_application.goal: Show that f=x³−3x−1 and h=x⁴+6x²+x+3 are irreducible in ℚ[x] by reduction modulo 2.
hypotheses: f and h are monic with integer coefficients.
Both reduce to polynomials of the same degree in 𝔽₂[x].
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Statement (3) turns a question about ℚ[x] into a finite check in 𝔽₂[x]. A cubic over a field is irreducible if and only if it has no root. A quartic is irreducible if and only if it has no root and no quadratic factor.

steps.text: Reduce f modulo 2. We get f̄=x³+x+1, because −3≡1 and −1≡1 modulo 2.
The field 𝔽₂ has two elements. f̄(0)=1 and f̄(1)=1+1+1=1. So f̄ has no root.
A cubic with a proper factorization has a factor of degree 1, so it has a root. Thus f̄ is irreducible in 𝔽₂[x].
Statement (3) with p=2 shows that f is irreducible in ℚ[x]. So ℚ(α) has degree 3 over ℚ for each root α.
Reduce h modulo 2. We get h̄=x⁴+x+1, because 6≡0 and 3≡1. Then h̄(0)=1 and h̄(1)=1+1+1=1, so h̄ has no root.
The only irreducible monic quadratic over 𝔽₂ is x²+x+1, because x², x²+1=(x+1)² and x²+x=x(x+1) are reducible. Its square is x⁴+x²+1, which is not h̄.
A proper factorization of h̄ has a factor of degree 1, or two factors of degree 2. Both cases are excluded. So h̄ is irreducible in 𝔽₂[x].

Statement (3) with p=2 shows that h is irreducible in ℚ[x]. Note that h has no rational root, by the rational root test, and no quadratic factor over ℚ, although we never checked these cases directly.

worked_application.result: Both x³−3x−1 and x⁴+6x²+x+3 are irreducible over ℚ. The proof for h avoids a case analysis over ℤ.

limitations: Statement (3) is only a sufficient test. A polynomial may be irreducible over ℚ and reducible modulo every prime. Example: x⁴+1, which is reducible modulo every prime.
Statement (2) needs f primitive. The polynomial 2x is irreducible in ℚ[x] but not in ℤ[x].
Eisenstein style tests are not proven in this entry.

results.name: Möbius inversion on divisors
results.statement: Let μ(n)=(−1)^k if n is a product of k distinct primes, and μ(n)=0 if some square greater than 1 divides n. Let R be a commutative ring and f,g:ℕ_{>0}→R. Then g(n)=∑_{d|n} f(d) for all n≥1 if and only if f(n)=∑_{d|n} μ(d) g(n/d) for all n≥1. The same holds when R is only an abelian group, with μ(d)g(n/d) read as an integer multiple.
hypotheses: The sums run over positive divisors d of n.
f and g take values in a commutative ring or an abelian group. No other condition holds.
Both equivalent statements must hold for every n≥1.

/-- Möbius inversion for functions to a `Ring`. -/

/-- Möbius inversion for functions to an `AddCommGroup`. -/
theorem sum_eq_iff_sum_smul_moebius_eq [AddCommGroup R] {f g : ℕ → R} :
    (∀ n > 0, ∑ i ∈ n.divisors, f i = g n) ↔
      ∀ n > 0, ∑ x ∈ n.divisorsAntidiagonal, μ x.fst • g x.snd = f n := by
  let f' : ArithmeticFunction R := ⟨fun x => if x = 0 then 0 else f x, ite_eq_left rfl⟩
  let g' : ArithmeticFunction R := ⟨fun x => if x = 0 then 0 else g x, ite_eq_left rfl⟩
  trans (ζ : ArithmeticFunction ℤ) • f' = g'
  · rw [ArithmeticFunction.ext_iff]
    apply forall_congr'
    intro n
    cases n with
    | zero => simp
    | succ n =>
      rw [coe_zeta_smul_apply]
      simp only [forall_prop_of_true, succ_pos', f', g', coe_mk, succ_ne_zero, ite_false]
      rw [sum_congr rfl fun x hx => ite_eq_right (pos_of_mem_divisors hx).ne']
  trans μ • g' = f'
  · constructor <;> intro h <;>
      simp only [← h, ← mul_smul, moebius_mul_coe_zeta, coe_zeta_mul_moebius, one_smul]
  · rw [ArithmeticFunction.ext_iff]
    apply forall_congr'
    intro n
    cases n with
    | zero => simp
    | succ n =>
      simp only [forall_prop_of_true, succ_pos', smul_apply, f', g', coe_mk, succ_ne_zero,
        ite_false]
      rw [sum_congr rfl fun x hx => ?_]
      rw [ite_eq_right (pos_of_mem_divisors (snd_mem_divisors_of_mem_antidiagonal hx)).ne']

steps.text: Key lemma: ∑_{d|n} μ(d)=1 if n=1, and 0 if n>1. For n=1 the sum is μ(1)=1. For n>1 write n=p₁^{a₁}…p_k^{a_k} with k≥1. Only divisors d that are products of distinct primes among p₁,…,p_k give nonzero terms. There are C(k,j) such d with j primes, and each has μ(d)=(−1)^j. So the sum is ∑_{j=0}^k C(k,j)(−1)^j=(1−1)^k=0.
Forward direction. Assume g(n)=∑_{e|n} f(e) for all n. Then for fixed n, ∑_{d|n} μ(d) g(n/d)=∑_{d|n} μ(d) ∑_{e|n/d} f(e).
The pairs (d,e) with d|n and e|(n/d) are exactly the pairs with e|n and d|(n/e). Both conditions say that de divides n. So we can swap the order of summation: ∑_{e|n} f(e) ∑_{d|n/e} μ(d).
By the key lemma the inner sum is 1 when n/e=1 and 0 otherwise. Only e=n survives, so the total is f(n).
Converse direction. Assume f(n)=∑_{d|n} μ(d) g(n/d) for all n. Then ∑_{d|n} f(d)=∑_{d|n} ∑_{e|d} μ(e) g(d/e). Put m=d/e. The pairs (d,e) with e|d|n correspond to pairs (m,e) with me|n.
Swap the sums: ∑_{m|n} g(m) ∑_{e|n/m} μ(e). By the key lemma the inner sum is 1 only for m=n. So the total is g(n). Both directions are proved.
Over an abelian group, the same computation holds. Each term μ(d)g(n/d) is an integer multiple of a group element, and the sums are finite, so rearrangement is valid.

worked_application.title: Counting binary Lyndon words of length 6 and 12
worked_application.goal: A word is primitive if it is not a power u^a with a≥2. A Lyndon word is the least word in a conjugacy class of a primitive word. Count the Lyndon words of length n over {0,1}.
hypotheses: Words have length n≥1 over a 2 letter alphabet.
Two words are conjugate if one is a cyclic rotation of the other.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Let P(d) be the number of primitive words of length d. We show ∑_{d|n}P(d)=2ⁿ for all n. Then the forward and converse directions of the theorem give P(n) in terms of powers of 2.

steps.text: Each word w of length n is a power u^{n/d} of a primitive word u of length d, with d|n. We claim d is unique. Suppose w=u^{n/d}=v^{n/e} with u,v primitive and |u|=d, |v|=e. Then w is invariant under the cyclic rotation by d and by e positions, hence by the subgroup of ℤ/n generated by them, which is generated by g=gcd(d,e).
A word invariant under rotation by g, with g|n, is the power z^{n/g} of its prefix z of length g. Since g|d, u=z^{d/g}. Primitivity of u forces d=g. In the same way e=g. So d=e, and u=v.
Hence the map w↦(d,u) is a bijection between words of length n and pairs (d,u) with d|n and u primitive of length d. So 2ⁿ=∑_{d|n}P(d).
Apply Möbius inversion with g(n)=2ⁿ and f=P: P(n)=∑_{d|n} μ(d) 2^{n/d}.

A primitive word of length n has n distinct rotations. If two rotations by i<j agree, then the word is invariant under rotation by j−i, which would force a proper period dividing n (as in the claim above). So each conjugacy class of a primitive word has n elements, and the Lyndon count is L(n)=P(n)/n.
Check n=6 by hand: the 9 Lyndon words are 000001, 000011, 000101, 000111, 001011, 001101, 001111, 010111, 011111. This confirms the count.

worked_application.result: There are 9 binary Lyndon words of length 6 and 335 of length 12. In general L(n)=(1/n)∑_{d|n}μ(d)2^{n/d}.

limitations: Inversion needs the relation for every n, not only for some n. Sections over divisor-closed sets need the variants for finite divisor-closed sets.
A different weighting needs a different inverse. For sums over multiples (g(n)=∑_{n|m}f(m)) the same μ gives an inverse, but the sums are infinite and need convergence.
The Lyndon count formula is a count of necklaces without symmetry. It is not a count of all necklaces.

steps.text: Reduction formula. For m≥0, integrate by parts with u=sin^{m+1}x and dv=sin x dx. We get I_{m+2}=(m+1)∫ sinᵐx cos²x dx=(m+1)(I_m−I_{m+2}). Hence I_{m+2}=(m+1)/(m+2)·I_m. The boundary terms vanish at 0 and π/2.
Iterate from I₀=π/2 and I₁=1. We get I_{2n}=(π/2)∏_{k=1}^n (2k−1)/(2k) and I_{2n+1}=∏_{k=1}^n (2k)/(2k+1). Both are positive.
On [0,π/2] we have 0≤sin x≤1, so sin^{2n+2}x≤sin^{2n+1}x≤sin^{2n}x. Integrating gives I_{2n+2}≤I_{2n+1}≤I_{2n}.
By the reduction formula, I_{2n+2}=(2n+1)/(2n+2)·I_{2n}. Divide the chain by I_{2n}: (2n+1)/(2n+2)≤I_{2n+1}/I_{2n}≤1.
Multiply by π/2 and use step 3: (2n+1)/(2n+2)·(π/2)≤W_n≤π/2. The left bound tends to π/2, so W_n→π/2 by the squeeze theorem.
For the asymptotics, note that (m+1)·I_{m+1}·I_m is constant in m. Indeed, by the reduction formula (m+2)I_{m+2}I_{m+1}=(m+1)I_mI_{m+1}. At m=0 the constant is I₁I₀=π/2. So I_mI_{m+1}=π/(2(m+1)).
Set m=2n. Then I_{2n}I_{2n+1}=π/(2(2n+1)). By the squeeze in step 5, I_{2n+1}/I_{2n}→1. So I_{2n}²·(I_{2n+1}/I_{2n})=π/(2(2n+1)), and I_{2n}²∼π/(4n).
By step 2, I_{2n}=(π/2)·∏(2k−1)/(2k)=(π/2)·C(2n,n)/4ⁿ. Thus ((π/2)C(2n,n)/4ⁿ)²∼π/(4n), which gives C(2n,n)²∼4^{2n}/(πn). Take square roots (both sides are positive) to get C(2n,n)√(πn)/4ⁿ→1.

results.name: Finite subgroups of the multiplicative group of a field are cyclic
results.statement: Let K be a field and G a finite subgroup of the multiplicative group K^×. Then G is cyclic. In particular, K^× is cyclic if K is finite, and (ℤ/p)^× is cyclic of order p−1 for each prime p. A generator of (ℤ/p)^× is called a primitive root mod p. There are φ(p−1) primitive roots, where φ is Euler's totient function.
hypotheses: K is a field, or more generally an integral domain.
G is a finite subgroup of K^×. Infinite subgroups need not be cyclic: ℚ^× is not cyclic.

steps.text: Let m=|G|. For each divisor d of m let ψ(d) be the number of elements of G of order d. Every element has an order that divides m, so ∑_{d|m} ψ(d)=m.
Root bound. For each d≥1 the polynomial X^d−1 has at most d roots in the field K. So at most d elements x of G satisfy x^d=1.

Claim: ψ(d)≤φ(d) for each d|m. If ψ(d)=0 this is clear. Otherwise pick x∈G of order d. The d powers 1,x,…,x^{d−1} are distinct and satisfy y^d=1. By the root bound they are all of the roots of X^d−1 in K.

Any element y of order d satisfies y^d=1, so y is a power x^k. The order of x^k is d/gcd(k,d). So y has order d if and only if gcd(k,d)=1. There are exactly φ(d) such k in 1..d. Thus ψ(d)=φ(d) in this case.

Identity: ∑_{d|m} φ(d)=m. Sort the m fractions k/m for k=1..m by their reduced denominator d. The fractions with reduced denominator d are a/d with gcd(a,d)=1 and 1≤a≤d. There are φ(d) of them. Every divisor d of m occurs.
Compare: ∑ψ(d)=m=∑φ(d), and ψ(d)≤φ(d) for each d by step 3. So ψ(d)=φ(d) for all d|m. In particular ψ(m)=φ(m)≥1. An element of order m=|G| generates G, so G is cyclic.
For (ℤ/p)^×, apply the result with K=𝔽ₚ and G=K^×, which has order p−1. The number of generators of a cyclic group of order p−1 is φ(p−1), by step 4.

worked_application.title: Primitive roots mod 17 and solving x⁴≡13
worked_application.goal: Find all primitive roots mod 17. Then solve x⁴≡13 (mod 17) with a discrete logarithm table.
hypotheses: p=17, so (ℤ/17)^× has order 16.
13 is a unit mod 17.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The theorem says (ℤ/17)^× is cyclic of order 16. So one primitive root g exists, and every unit is gᵏ for a unique k mod 16.

steps.text: Test g=3. Powers: 3²=9, 3⁴=81≡13, 3⁸=169≡16≡−1. So 3⁸≠1 and 3 has order 16, not 8. Because the order divides 16 and does not divide 8, it is 16. So 3 is a primitive root.
Every primitive root is 3ᵏ with gcd(k,16)=1, i.e. k odd, by the order formula in step 4. This gives φ(16)=8 primitive roots.
The other units have orders dividing 16 but less than 16. For example 2⁸=256≡1, so 2 has order 8 (since 2⁴=16≢1).
Discrete logarithm: write 13=3⁴. Let x=3ᵏ. Then x⁴≡13 means 4k≡4 (mod 16). This gives k≡1 (mod 4), so k∈{1,5,9,13}.
Compute x=3ᵏ: 3¹=3, 3⁵=5, 3⁹=14, 3¹³=12. Check 5⁴=625=17·36+13. So x⁴≡13 has exactly the solutions 3, 5, 12 and 14.
General rule: in a cyclic group of order n, the equation x^e=a has either 0 or gcd(e,n) solutions. Here gcd(4,16)=4 solutions exist.

worked_application.result: There are 8 primitive roots mod 17: 3, 5, 6, 7, 10, 11, 12, 14. The equation x⁴≡13 (mod 17) has the 4 solutions 3, 5, 12, 14.

/-- If `G` is a `p`-group acting on a finite set `α`, then the number of fixed points
  of the action is congruent mod `p` to the cardinality of `α` -/
theorem card_modEq_card_fixedPoints : Nat.card α ≡ Nat.card (fixedPoints G α) [MOD p] := by
  have := Fintype.ofFinite α
  have := Fintype.ofFinite (fixedPoints G α)
  rw [Nat.card_eq_fintype_card, Nat.card_eq_fintype_card]
  classical
    calc
      card α = card (Σ y : Quotient (orbitRel G α), { x // Quotient.mk'' x = y }) :=
        card_congr (Equiv.sigmaFiberEquiv (@Quotient.mk'' _ (orbitRel G α))).symm
      _ = ∑ a : Quotient (orbitRel G α), card { x // Quotient.mk'' x = a } := card_sigma
      _ ≡ ∑ _a : fixedPoints G α, 1 [MOD p] := ?_
      _ = _ := by simp
    rw [← ZMod.natCast_eq_natCast_iff _ _ p, Nat.cast_sum, Nat.cast_sum]
    have key :
      ∀ x,
        card { y // (Quotient.mk'' y : Quotient (orbitRel G α)) = Quotient.mk'' x } =
          card (orbit G x) :=
      fun x => by simp only [Quotient.eq'']; congr
    refine
      Eq.symm
        (Finset.sum_bij_ne_zero (fun a _ _ => Quotient.mk'' a.1) (fun _ _ _ => Finset.mem_univ _)
          (fun a₁ _ _ a₂ _ _ h =>
            Subtype.ext (mem_fixedPoints'.mp a₂.2 a₁.1 (Quotient.exact' h)))
          (fun b => Quotient.inductionOn' b fun b _ hb => ?_) fun a ha _ => by
          rw [key, mem_fixedPoints_iff_card_orbit_eq_one.mp a.2])
    obtain ⟨k, hk⟩ := hG.card_orbit b
    rw [Nat.card_eq_fintype_card] at hk
    have : k = 0 := by
      contrapose! hb
      simp [key, hk, hb]
    exact
      ⟨⟨b, mem_fixedPoints_iff_card_orbit_eq_one.2 <| by rw [hk, this, pow_zero]⟩,
        Finset.mem_univ _, ne_of_eq_of_ne Nat.cast_one one_ne_zero, rfl⟩

steps.text: Orbit-stabilizer count. Fix x in X and let P_x be its stabilizer. The map gP_x ↦ g·x is a well defined bijection from the left cosets of P_x onto the orbit of x. It is well defined and injective because g·x = h·x if and only if h⁻¹g fixes x. So |orbit of x|·|P_x| = |P|.
Orbit sizes. By step 1 the size of each orbit divides |P| = p^n. So each orbit size is a power of p. An orbit has size 1 if and only if its point is fixed. Every other orbit has size divisible by p.
Partition X into orbits. The orbits of size 1 are the points of X^P. The other orbits have sizes divisible by p. Add the sizes: |X| = |X^P| + (a sum of multiples of p). Hence |X| ≡ |X^P| (mod p).
Center. Let P act on the set X = P by conjugation, g·x = gxg⁻¹. A point x is fixed if and only if gxg⁻¹ = x for all g. That means x lies in Z(P). So X^P = Z(P).
Apply step 3 to this action. We get |P| ≡ |Z(P)| (mod p). Because n≥1, we have p | |P|. So p | |Z(P)|.
The identity element lies in Z(P), so |Z(P)| ≥ 1. A positive multiple of p is at least p. So |Z(P)| ≥ p ≥ 2, and Z(P) is not trivial.

Remark. Grouping the conjugation action by orbits (conjugacy classes) gives the class equation |P| = |Z(P)| + ∑ [P : C(x)] over class representatives x outside the center. Step 2 shows that each term of the sum is divisible by p.

worked_application.title: Cauchy theorem from the fixed point congruence
worked_application.goal: Prove that a finite group G with a prime p dividing |G| has an element of order p. Check the count for S₃ and S₄. Also check the center of the dihedral group of order 8.
hypotheses: G is a finite group and p is a prime that divides |G|.
Let X be the set of p-tuples (g₁,…,g_p) in G^p with g₁g₂⋯g_p = e.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The cyclic group C_p of order p is a p-group. It acts on X by rotating the entries. The theorem then counts the fixed points of this action modulo p.

steps.text: Size of X. Here X is the set of p-tuples (g₁,…,g_p) in G^p with g₁g₂⋯g_p = e. Choose g₁,…,g_{p−1} freely in G. Then g_p = (g₁⋯g_{p−1})⁻¹ is forced. So |X| = |G|^{p−1}.
Rotation keeps X. If g₁⋯g_p = e, then g₂⋯g_p g₁ = g₁⁻¹(g₁⋯g_p)g₁ = e. So the rotation (g₁,…,g_p) ↦ (g₂,…,g_p,g₁) maps X to X. It generates an action of C_p.

A tuple is fixed by the rotation if and only if all its entries are equal. The fixed tuples are (g,…,g) with g^p = e. Let N be the number of g in G with g^p = e. The theorem for C_p gives |G|^{p−1} ≡ N (mod p).

Because p divides |G| and p−1 ≥ 1, the left side is divisible by p. So p divides N. The identity satisfies e^p = e, so N ≥ 1. Because p | N, we get N ≥ p ≥ 2. So some g ≠ e has g^p = e. The order of g divides p and is not 1, so it is p.
Check with G = S₃ and p = 3. Here |X| = 6² = 36. The solutions of g³ = e are the identity and the two 3-cycles, so N = 3. Both 36 and 3 are divisible by 3.
Check with G = S₃ and p = 2. Here |X| = 6. The solutions of g² = e are the identity and the three transpositions, so N = 4. Then 6 ≡ 4 ≡ 0 (mod 2).

Check with G = S₄ and p = 3. Here |X| = 24² = 576. The solutions of g³ = e are the identity and the eight 3-cycles, so N = 9. Both 576 = 3·192 and 9 are divisible by 3. A computer enumeration of all tuples agrees with these counts.

Center of the dihedral group D₄ of order 8, acting on the square. Its conjugacy classes have sizes 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, and 1+1+2+2+2 = 8. The center has order 2, which is a multiple of 2. This agrees with the theorem.
The action of D₄ on the four vertices has no fixed vertex. The theorem predicts 4 ≡ 0 (mod 2), which holds.

worked_application.result: Every prime divisor of |G| is the order of some element of G. For S₃ and S₄ the counts N = 3, 4 and 9 match the congruence |G|^{p−1} ≡ N (mod p). The center of D₄ has order 2.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: The congruence needs a p-group. For S₃ acting on three points, no point is fixed and 3 is not 0 mod 2, while the group has order 6.
The congruence gives only a residue mod p. It does not say how many fixed points exist. It shows that X^P is not empty when p does not divide |X|.
Nontrivial center does not mean abelian. The group D₄ of order 8 has center of order 2 and is not abelian.

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: G is a p-group, because |G| = p². By the fixed point congruence its center Z has order divisible by p. So |Z| is p or p², by Lagrange.
If |Z| = p², then Z = G and G is abelian. We now show that |Z| = p is impossible. Suppose |Z| = p.
Then |G/Z| = p²/p = p. A group of prime order is cyclic. Indeed any non identity element has an order that divides p, so it has order p and generates the group. So G/Z is cyclic.
Lemma. If G/Z is cyclic for Z = Z(G), then G is abelian. Let gZ generate G/Z. Every x in G has the form x = gⁱz with z in Z, because xZ = (gZ)ⁱ = gⁱZ.

Take x = gⁱz and y = gʲz′ with z, z′ in Z. Then xy = gⁱ z gʲ z′ = gⁱ⁺ʲ z z′, because z commutes with everything. In the same way yx = gʲ⁺ⁱ z′ z. Since z z′ = z′ z and i+j = j+i, we get xy = yx. So G is abelian.
By the lemma, |Z| = p gives G abelian. Then Z = G, so |Z| = p². This contradicts |Z| = p. So the case |Z| = p does not occur, and Z = G.
Classification. Suppose G has an element a of order p². Then G = ⟨a⟩ has p² elements, so G ≅ ℤ/p². Otherwise each non identity element has order p. Pick a ≠ e and b outside ⟨a⟩.

The map (i,j) ↦ aⁱbʲ from ℤ/p × ℤ/p to G is a homomorphism, because G is abelian. It is injective. If aⁱbʲ = e with j ≢ 0 mod p, then b would be a power of a, because j has an inverse mod p and b = b^{jj′} for some j′ with jj′ ≡ 1 (mod p). This contradicts b ∉ ⟨a⟩. So j ≡ 0 and then aⁱ = e gives i ≡ 0. Both groups have p² elements, so the map is an isomorphism.

steps.text: By the theorem, any group of order 49 is abelian, and it is ℤ/49 or ℤ/7 × ℤ/7.
These two groups are not isomorphic. The group ℤ/49 has an element of order 49, namely 1. In ℤ/7 × ℤ/7, every element (a,b) satisfies 7(a,b) = (0,0), so no element has order 49.
Count elements of order 7. In ℤ/49 these are the multiples of 7 other than 0. There are 6 of them (7, 14, 21, 28, 35, 42). In ℤ/7 × ℤ/7 all 48 non zero elements have order 7.

Count subgroups of order 7. Each such subgroup has 6 elements of order 7 and each element of order 7 lies in exactly one such subgroup. In ℤ/49 there is 1 subgroup, namely ⟨7⟩. In ℤ/7 × ℤ/7 there are 48/6 = 8 subgroups.
The same count for order 25 gives 24 non zero elements in ℤ/5 × ℤ/5 and 24/4 = 6 subgroups of order 5. For ℤ/25 there is 1 subgroup of order 5.

/-- Euler's Criterion: a nonzero `a : ZMod p` is a square if and only if `x ^ (p / 2) = 1`. -/
theorem euler_criterion {a : ZMod p} (ha : a ≠ 0) : IsSquare (a : ZMod p) ↔ a ^ (p / 2) = 1 := by
  apply (iff_congr _ (by simp [Units.ext_iff])).mp (euler_criterion_units p (Units.mk0 a ha))
  simp only [Units.ext_iff, sq, Units.val_mk0, Units.val_mul]
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨y, hy⟩; exact ⟨y, hy.symm⟩
  · rintro ⟨y, rfl⟩
    have hy : y ≠ 0 := by
      rintro rfl
      simp [mul_zero, ne_eq] at ha
    refine ⟨Units.mk0 y hy, ?_⟩; simp

theorem euler_criterion_units (x : (ZMod p)ˣ) : (∃ y : (ZMod p)ˣ, y ^ 2 = x) ↔ x ^ (p / 2) = 1 := by
  by_cases hc : p = 2
  · subst hc
    simp only [eq_iff_true_of_subsingleton, exists_const]
  · have h₀ := FiniteField.unit_isSquare_iff (by rwa [ringChar_zmod_n]) x
    have hs : (∃ y : (ZMod p)ˣ, y ^ 2 = x) ↔ IsSquare x := by
      rw [isSquare_iff_exists_sq x]
      simp_rw [eq_comm]
    rw [hs]
    rwa [card p] at h₀

steps.text: Work in the field F = ℤ/p. Because p is odd, for non zero x we have x ≠ −x. Also x² = y² implies (x−y)(x+y) = 0, so y = x or y = −x, because F has no zero divisors.
So the squaring map on F^× is exactly 2 to 1. The set S of non zero squares has (p−1)/2 elements.
Each s in S has the form s = x². Then s^{(p−1)/2} = x^{p−1} = 1 by Fermat little theorem.

So all (p−1)/2 elements of S are roots of the polynomial f = X^{(p−1)/2} − 1. This polynomial has degree (p−1)/2. By the root bound it has at most (p−1)/2 roots. So the roots of f are exactly the elements of S.
Therefore a non zero a is a square if and only if a^{(p−1)/2} = 1. This is the criterion.
For any non zero a put b = a^{(p−1)/2}. Then b² = a^{p−1} = 1 by Fermat. So (b−1)(b+1) = 0 in the field F, and b = 1 or b = −1. For a non square, b ≠ 1, so b = −1.
Square roots for p ≡ 3 (mod 4). Then (p+1)/4 is an integer. If a is a square, a^{(p−1)/2} = 1. Put r = a^{(p+1)/4}. Then r² = a^{(p+1)/2} = a·a^{(p−1)/2} = a.
Remark. For a = −1 we have (−1)^{(p−1)/2} = 1 if and only if (p−1)/2 is even. So −1 is a square modulo p if and only if p ≡ 1 (mod 4).

worked_application.title: Squares modulo 23 and modulo 10007
worked_application.goal: Decide which numbers are squares modulo 23 and modulo 10007 with one modular power each. Compute a square root when p ≡ 3 (mod 4).
hypotheses: q = 10007 is prime, and 10007 ≡ 3 (mod 4).
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Both primes are odd and the numbers tested are not divisible by them. So the criterion applies.

steps.text: List the squares modulo 23 by squaring 1,…,22. The set is {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12, 13, 16, 18}. It has 11 = (23−1)/2 elements, as the theorem says.
Compute a^{11} mod 23. For a = 2 and a = 3 the result is 1. For a = 5, 7 and 10 the result is 22 ≡ −1. This agrees with the list: 2 and 3 are squares, and 5, 7 and 10 are not.
Square root of 2 modulo 23. Here (p+1)/4 = 6. So r = 2⁶ = 64 ≡ 18 (mod 23). Check 18² = 324 = 14·23 + 2 ≡ 2.

For the large prime q = 10007 compute a^{5003} mod q. For a = 2, 3 and 6 the result is 1. For a = 5, 7 and 10 the result is 10006 ≡ −1. So 2, 3 and 6 are squares and 5, 7 and 10 are not. No search over 5003 candidates is needed.
Square root of 2 modulo 10007. Here (q+1)/4 = 2502. A modular power gives r = 2^{2502} ≡ 2641. Check 2641² = 6974881 ≡ 2 (mod 10007).
As q ≡ 3 (mod 4), −1 is not a square modulo 10007. This also follows from (−1)^{5003} = −1.

theorem prod_cyclotomic_eq_X_pow_sub_one {n : ℕ} (hpos : 0 < n) (R : Type*) [CommRing R] :

steps.text: Roots of Xⁿ−1. The n numbers e^{2πik/n}, for k = 0,…,n−1, are distinct and each is a root of Xⁿ−1. A polynomial of degree n has at most n roots. So Xⁿ−1 = ∏_{k=0}^{n−1}(X − e^{2πik/n}), because it is monic.

Order of a root. Let ζ be a root of Xⁿ−1. Its multiplicative order d divides n, because the set of m with ζ^m = 1 is a subgroup of ℤ containing n. Then ζ is a primitive d-th root of unity. Each root has exactly one order.

Group the n linear factors by the order d of the root. For fixed d | n, the roots of order d are exactly the primitive d-th roots of unity. Every primitive d-th root with d | n is a root of Xⁿ−1. So Xⁿ − 1 = ∏_{d|n} ∏_{ζ of order d}(X − ζ) = ∏_{d|n} Φ_d. This proves (1).
Degree. The primitive n-th roots are e^{2πik/n}, where k is in {1,…,n} and gcd(k,n) = 1. Indeed e^{2πik/n} has order n/gcd(k,n). So there are φ(n) of them, and Φ_n has degree φ(n). This proves (2).
Counting degrees in (1): n = ∑_{d|n} φ(d). This proves (4).

Integer coefficients by strong induction on n. Φ_1 = X − 1. Assume that Φ_d is monic with integer coefficients for all d<n. Let g = ∏_{d|n, d<n} Φ_d. This product is monic with integer coefficients, and Xⁿ−1 = g·Φ_n by (1).

Divide Xⁿ−1 by the monic g with remainder in ℤ[X]. We get Xⁿ − 1 = g·q + r with q, r in ℤ[X] and deg r < deg g. Division with remainder by a monic polynomial stays inside ℤ[X]. Also Xⁿ−1 = g·Φ_n, so g(Φ_n − q) = r in ℂ[X]. If Φ_n ≠ q, the left side has degree at least deg g, but deg r < deg g. So r = 0 and Φ_n = q lies in ℤ[X] and is monic. This proves (3).

Multiply Φ₁Φ₃ = X³ − 1. Then (X³ − 1)Φ₅ = X⁷ + X⁶ + X⁵ − X² − X − 1.

For n = 105 = 3·5·7, an exact computation gives φ(105) = 48. The polynomial Φ₁₀₅ has degree 48 and its smallest coefficient is −2. So cyclotomic polynomials can have coefficients other than 0, 1 and −1.
