source_references.alignment: The source relates the Fourier coefficient of f on an interval to that of f′ and the boundary values. It is the integration by parts in step 1.

results.proof_status: source declaration inspected; authored proof awaits inference review; no local Lean check

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Coefficients of the derivative. Fix n≠0. On each piece, integration by parts gives ∫_{x_{k−1}}^{x_k}f′(x)e^{−inx}dx=[f(x)e^{−inx}]_{x_{k−1}}^{x_k}+in∫_{x_{k−1}}^{x_k}f(x)e^{−inx}dx. Sum over k. The boundary terms telescope because f is continuous. The remaining terms f(2π)e^{−2πin}−f(0) cancel because f is periodic. So c_n(f′)=in c_n.
Parseval for f′. The function f′ is piecewise continuous and bounded, so it is square integrable. Parseval gives ∑_{n∈ℤ}|c_n(f′)|²=(1/2π)∫|f′|²=σ². By step 1, c_n(f′)=in c_n, so ∑n²|c_n|²=σ².

Cauchy-Schwarz. For M≥1, ∑_{0<|n|≤M}|c_n|=∑(1/|n|)(|n||c_n|)≤(∑_{0<|n|≤M}n⁻²)^{1/2}(∑n²|c_n|²)^{1/2}. The first factor is at most (2ζ(2))^{1/2}=(π²/3)^{1/2}, because ζ(2)=π²/6. The second is at most σ by step 2. Let M→∞ to get ∑_{n≠0}|c_n|≤(π/√3)σ.
Uniform convergence. The terms c_ne^{inx} have modulus |c_n|, and ∑|c_n| is finite by step 3. The Weierstrass M-test shows that the partial sums S_N converge uniformly to a continuous function g.

Identification g=f. Uniform convergence allows termwise integration, so c_n(g)=c_n(f) for all n. The function f−g is continuous with all Fourier coefficients 0. Parseval gives (1/2π)∫|f−g|²=∑|c_n(f−g)|²=0. A continuous function with zero integral of |f−g|² is 0, so f=g.
The tail bound. For N≥1 and every x, |f(x)−S_Nf(x)|≤∑_{|n|>N}|c_n|. As in step 3, this is at most (2∑_{n>N}n⁻²)^{1/2}σ. Since ∑_{n>N}n⁻²<∑_{n>N}1/(n(n−1))=1/N, the bound is σ√(2/N).

worked_application.title: The function f(x)=|x| on [−π,π]
worked_application.goal: Verify the bound on ∑|c_n|, the value f(π), and the tail estimate for N=10.
hypotheses: f(x)=|x| for x in [−π,π], extended 2π-periodically. It is continuous, with break points at 0 and ±π.
f′=±1 off the break points, so σ²=(1/2π)∫_{−π}^{π}1dx=1.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The function is continuous, periodic and C¹ on [−π,0] and [0,π]. All hypotheses hold with σ=1.

steps.text: Coefficients. c₀=π/2. For n≠0, c_n=(1/π)∫₀^π x cos(nx)dx=((−1)ⁿ−1)/(πn²). So c_n=−2/(πn²) for odd n and c_n=0 for even n≠0.
Sum of moduli. ∑_{n≠0}|c_n|=2∑_{n odd, n>0}2/(πn²)=(4/π)(π²/8)=π/2=1.570796. A sum of 100000 odd terms gives 1.570793.
The bound of the theorem is (π/√3)σ=1.813799. The value 1.570796 is below it.
Value at π. The series at x=π is c₀+∑c_n(−1)ⁿ=π/2+π/2=π. This equals f(π)=π, as the theorem states.
Tail for N=10. S₁₀(π)=π/2+∑_{n odd≤9}(4/(πn²))=3.078140. The error at x=π is π−3.078140=0.063453. The bound σ√(2/N)=0.447214 holds.

worked_application.result: The series for |x| converges absolutely with ∑|c_n|=π/2, below the bound 1.8138. At N=10 the error 0.0635 at x=π is below the bound 0.4472.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: A discontinuous f is excluded. For a function with a jump, c_n is of size 1/n, and the series ∑|c_n| diverges.
The rate σ√(2/N) is not sharp for smoother f. If f has two derivatives in L², the error is of order N^{−3/2}.
The theorem needs a derivative in L². A merely continuous function can have a Fourier series that is not absolutely convergent.

results.name: Existence and uniqueness for a nonlinear boundary value problem by Green function and contraction
results.statement: Let f:[0,1]×ℝ→ℝ be continuous and let |f(x,u)−f(x,v)|≤L|u−v| for all x,u,v with a constant L<8. Then the problem y″=f(x,y), y(0)=y(1)=0 has exactly one solution y∈C²[0,1]. Let y₀ be any continuous function and y_{k+1}=Ty_k, where (Ty)(x)=−∫₀¹G(x,t)f(t,y(t))dt, and G(x,t)=x(1−t) for x≤t and G(x,t)=t(1−x) for x≥t. Then ‖y_k−y‖_∞≤(L/8)^k(1−L/8)⁻¹‖y₁−y₀‖_∞.
hypotheses: The Lipschitz constant L is global in the second variable. A local Lipschitz condition gives only local existence.
The bound L<8 is a bound for the interval [0,1] and Dirichlet conditions. It is 8 because max_x∫|G(x,t)|dt=1/8.

The condition L<8 is sufficient, not necessary. For f(x,u)=10u, L=10, and the problem has only the solution y=0. If y″=10y and y(0)=y(1)=0, then multiply by y and integrate by parts. This gives ∫y′²+10∫y²=0, so y=0. Also, for f(x,u)=−π²u, L=π² is above 8, and y=sin(πx) and y=0 both solve the problem. So uniqueness can fail when L is large.

definitions.name: Green function of y″ with Dirichlet conditions
definitions.text: The function G(x,t) on [0,1]² with G=x(1−t) for x≤t and G=t(1−x) for x≥t. For continuous g, the function u=−∫G(·,t)g(t)dt solves u″=g with u(0)=u(1)=0.

definitions.name: contraction mapping
definitions.text: A map T on a metric space with d(Tx,Ty)≤q d(x,y) for a constant q<1. In a complete space it has exactly one fixed point.

definitions.name: sup norm
definitions.text: ‖y‖_∞=max over x in [0,1] of |y(x)|. The space C[0,1] with this norm is a Banach space.

steps.text: The solution formula for the linear problem. For continuous g put u(x)=−(1−x)∫₀^x t g(t)dt−x∫_x^1(1−t)g(t)dt. Differentiate: u′(x)=∫₀^x t g(t)dt−∫_x^1(1−t)g(t)dt, because the terms with g(x) cancel. Differentiate again: u″(x)=xg(x)+(1−x)g(x)=g(x). Also u(0)=0 and u(1)=0 from the formula. So u∈C² solves u″=g with u(0)=u(1)=0.
Uniqueness for the linear problem. If u₁ and u₂ both solve it, then w=u₁−u₂ has w″=0 and w(0)=w(1)=0. So w is affine with two zeros, and w=0. Hence u is the only solution, and u=−∫G g.

Equivalence. By steps 1 and 2, y∈C² solves the BVP if and only if y is continuous and y=Ty. Indeed, if y solves the BVP, then g=f(·,y) is continuous and y=−∫G g=Ty. If y=Ty with y continuous, then y∈C² by step 1 and y″=f(·,y).
The kernel integral. For x in [0,1], ∫₀¹|G(x,t)|dt=∫₀^x t(1−x)dt+∫_x^1 x(1−t)dt=(1−x)x²/2+x(1−x)²/2=x(1−x)/2≤1/8.

Contraction. T maps C[0,1] into itself, because the integral of a continuous function against the continuous kernel is continuous. For y,z in C[0,1], |(Ty−Tz)(x)|≤∫|G(x,t)|L|y(t)−z(t)|dt≤L‖y−z‖_∞x(1−x)/2≤(L/8)‖y−z‖_∞. So ‖Ty−Tz‖_∞≤q‖y−z‖_∞ with q=L/8<1.

Apply the Banach fixed-point theorem. The space (C[0,1],‖·‖_∞) is complete, and T is a contraction. So T has exactly one fixed point y, and y_k→y for every y₀. By step 3, y is the unique C² solution of the BVP. The a priori bound ‖y_k−y‖≤q^k(1−q)⁻¹‖y₁−y₀‖ is the standard estimate of the fixed-point theorem.

worked_application.title: The problem y″=½sin y+x with y(0)=y(1)=0
worked_application.goal: Run the iteration from y₀=0 and compare the error with the a priori bound.
hypotheses: f(x,u)=½sin u+x. Then |f(x,u)−f(x,v)|≤½|u−v|, so L=½ and q=1/16.
Quantity: y_k at x=½. The iteration starts at y₀=0.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The function f is continuous and Lipschitz in u with L=½<8. All hypotheses hold.

steps.text: First iterate. y₁(x)=−∫G(x,t)t dt=−x(1−x²)/6. Its sup norm is at x=1/√3 and equals 1/(9√3)=0.064150. So ‖y₁−y₀‖=0.064150 and y₁(½)=−0.062500.
Iteration with 2000 trapezoid cells for the kernel integral. y₂(½)=−0.059247, y₃(½)=−0.059412, y₄(½)=−0.059403, y₅(½)=−0.0594037 and y₆(½)=−0.05940371.
The sup norms of successive differences are 0.064150, 0.003259, 0.000165, 8.36×10⁻⁶, 4.2×10⁻⁷ and 2.1×10⁻⁸. Each ratio is about 0.051, which is below q=0.0625.
A priori bound for k=3. q³(1−q)⁻¹‖y₁−y₀‖=(1/4096)(16/15)(0.064150)=1.67×10⁻⁵. The observed error at x=½ is |y₃−y₆|=7.95×10⁻⁶. It is below the bound.
Uniqueness. Any other solution would be another fixed point of T. The theorem excludes it. The fixed point value is y(½)=−0.059404.

worked_application.result: The iteration converges at the rate 1/16 per step. The unique solution has y(½)=−0.059404, and the a priori bound 1.67×10⁻⁵ holds after 3 steps.

limitations: The Lipschitz condition is global in u. For f=u² there is no global L, and the problem needs local arguments.
The condition L<8 is far from sharp for many f. The sharp threshold for linear f(u)=−λu is the first Dirichlet eigenvalue π².
The proof gives existence by iteration only for the Dirichlet problem on a bounded interval of length 1. A longer interval of length ℓ gives the condition L<8/ℓ².

results.name: Möbius function of a locally finite poset: two-sided inversion and the product rule
results.statement: Let (P,≤) be a poset in which every closed interval [a,b] = {x : a ≤ x ≤ b} is finite. Define μ(a,b) = 0 if a ≰ b, μ(a,a) = 1, and μ(a,b) = −∑_{a≤x<b} μ(a,x) if a < b. Then: (1) ∑_{a≤x≤b} μ(a,x) = δ_{ab} and ∑_{a≤x≤b} μ(x,b) = δ_{ab}. (2) If every set {a : a ≤ b} is finite, and g(b) = ∑_{a≤b} f(a) for all b, then f(b) = ∑_{a≤b} μ(a,b)·g(a). (3) If every set {b : b ≥ a} is finite, and g(a) = ∑_{b≥a} f(b) for all a, then f(a) = ∑_{b≥a} μ(a,b)·g(b). (4) For the product order on P×Q, μ((a,c),(b,d)) = μ_P(a,b)·μ_Q(c,d). (5) On the Boolean lattice of subsets, μ(A,B) = (−1)^{|B∖A|} for A ⊆ B. On the divisor lattice of ℕ, μ(d,m) equals the number-theoretic Möbius function of m/d.
hypotheses: P is a partial order. Every interval [a,b] is finite, so P is locally finite.
The functions f and g take values in an abelian group, and μ takes values in ℤ.
For (2), each principal down-set is finite. For (3), each principal up-set is finite. For a finite poset, both hold.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: The proof uses only associativity of finite sums and an induction on the size of intervals. No catalog theorem is cited.

definitions.name: incidence algebra
definitions.text: The set of functions h(a,b), defined for a ≤ b, with convolution (h*k)(a,b) = ∑_{a≤x≤b} h(a,x)·k(x,b). The unit is δ(a,b) = 1 if a = b and 0 otherwise.

definitions.name: zeta function
definitions.text: The element ζ of the incidence algebra with ζ(a,b) = 1 for all a ≤ b. Then (ζ*ζ)(a,b) = |[a,b]|.

definitions.name: Möbius function
definitions.text: The function μ defined by the recursion in the statement. By step 1 and step 2 it is the two-sided inverse of ζ in the incidence algebra.

definitions.name: product order
definitions.text: On P×Q, (a,c) ≤ (b,d) means a ≤ b and c ≤ d. Then [(a,c),(b,d)] = [a,b]×[c,d].

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Definition by recursion. For a < b every x with a ≤ x < b has [a,x] a proper subset of [a,b], so the interval [a,x] is smaller. Thus μ(a,b) is well defined by induction on |[a,b]|. For a = b the sum ∑_{a≤x≤b} μ(a,x) is μ(a,a) = 1. For a < b the recursion says ∑_{a≤x<b} μ(a,x) + μ(a,b) = 0. This proves the first identity in (1). In symbols, μ*ζ = δ.

Convolution is associative. Both (h*k)*l and h*(k*l) at (a,b) equal the sum of h(a,x)·k(x,y)·l(y,b) over all pairs x,y with a ≤ x ≤ y ≤ b. Also δ is a two-sided unit. These are finite sums, so the reindexing is valid.

Define μ′ by the dual recursion on the upper end: μ′(b,b) = 1 and μ′(a,b) = −∑_{a<x≤b} μ′(x,b) for a < b. The same induction shows that this is well defined. It gives ζ*μ′ = δ. Now μ = μ*δ = μ*(ζ*μ′) = (μ*ζ)*μ′ = δ*μ′ = μ′. Hence ∑_{a≤x≤b} μ(x,b) = δ_{ab}. This proves the second identity in (1).

Inversion from below, statement (2). Substitute g(a) = ∑_{c≤a} f(c) into ∑_{a≤b} μ(a,b)·g(a). The set of pairs (c,a) with c ≤ a ≤ b is finite, because {c : c ≤ b} is finite. Swap the sums to get ∑_{c≤b} f(c)·∑_{c≤a≤b} μ(a,b). By the second identity in (1), the inner sum is δ_{cb}. The whole sum is f(b).

Inversion from above, statement (3). Substitute g(b) = ∑_{c≥b} f(c) into ∑_{b≥a} μ(a,b)·g(b). Swap the finite sums to get ∑_{c≥a} f(c)·∑_{a≤b≤c} μ(a,b). By the first identity in (1), the inner sum is δ_{ac}. The whole sum is f(a).

Uniqueness of the recursion. Suppose a function h on pairs a ≤ b satisfies ∑_{a≤x≤b} h(a,x) = δ_{ab} for all a ≤ b. The case a = b gives h(a,a) = 1. The case a < b gives h(a,b) = −∑_{a≤x<b} h(a,x). By induction on |[a,b]|, h is equal to μ. So any such h is μ.

Product rule, statement (4). Put ν((a,c),(b,d)) = μ_P(a,b)·μ_Q(c,d). Since [(a,c),(b,d)] = [a,b]×[c,d], the sum of ν((a,c),(x,y)) over the interval factors as (∑_{a≤x≤b} μ_P(a,x))·(∑_{c≤y≤d} μ_Q(c,y)) = δ_{ab}·δ_{cd}. This is the unit of the product poset. By the uniqueness in step 6, ν = μ_{P×Q}.

Boolean lattice, statement (5). The chain 0 < 1 has μ(0,0) = μ(1,1) = 1 and μ(0,1) = −1. The subsets of an n-set form the product of n such chains, and the interval [A,B] is isomorphic to the product of |B∖A| copies of the chain. By step 7, μ(A,B) = (−1)^{|B∖A|}.

Divisor lattice, statement (5). The interval [d,m] of divisors is isomorphic to the product, over primes p, of the chains 0 < 1 < … < e_p with e_p = v_p(m/d). On a chain of length e, the recursion gives μ(i,i) = 1, μ(i,i+1) = −1 and μ(i,j) = −(1 − 1 + 0 + … + 0) = 0 for j ≥ i+2, by induction on j−i. By step 7, μ(d,m) is the product of these values. It is (−1)^k if m/d is a product of k distinct primes, and 0 otherwise. This is the number-theoretic Möbius function of m/d.

worked_application.title: Surjection count, divisor lattice of 360 and a poset that is not a product
worked_application.goal: Use the Möbius function of the Boolean lattice, of a divisor lattice and of a five-element poset to invert sums.
hypotheses: Part 1: f(S) counts the words of length 4 over {1,2,3} that use exactly the letters in S. Part 2: P is the lattice of divisors of 360 = 2³·3²·5.

Part 3: N is the poset with elements 0,a,b,c,1. Its order relations are the reflexive ones and 0<a, 0<b, 0<c, 0<1, a<c, a<1, b<1, c<1. The element b is incomparable with a and with c. So the covering relations are 0<a<c<1 and 0<b<1.
All posets are finite, so every hypothesis of the statement holds.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Each part is an instance of the statement. Part 1 uses the Boolean lattice. Part 2 uses the divisor lattice. Part 3 uses the recursion directly, because N is not a product of chains.

steps.text: Part 1. Every word over S uses some set T ⊆ S of letters. So g(S) = |S|⁴ = ∑_{T⊆S} f(T). Inversion from below with μ(T,S) = (−1)^{|S∖T|} gives f({1,2,3}) = ∑_T (−1)^{3−|T|}·|T|⁴ = 3⁴ − 3·2⁴ + 3·1⁴ − 0⁴ = 81 − 48 + 3 = 36. A direct count agrees: the surjections from a 4-set onto a 3-set number 3!·S(4,3) = 6·6 = 36.

Part 2. The divisors of 360 are 24 in number. The exponent chains of 2, 3 and 5 have lengths 3, 2 and 1. The product rule gives μ(1,360) = μ_chain3(0,3)·μ_chain2(0,2)·μ_chain1(0,1) = 0·0·(−1) = 0. Also μ(1,30) = (−1)³ = −1 and μ(1,6) = 1 and μ(1,12) = 0. A computer evaluation of the recursion on all 24 divisors gives these four values.

Part 3. Define the order of N. The elements are 0,a,b,c,1. The relations are x≤x for each x, and 0<a, 0<b, 0<c, 0<1, a<c, a<1, b<1, c<1. No other pair is related, so b is incomparable with a and with c. Use the recursion from the bottom element. μ(0,0) = 1. μ(0,a) = −1. μ(0,b) = −1. μ(0,c) = −(μ(0,0)+μ(0,a)) = −(1 − 1) = 0, because [0,c]={0,a,c}. μ(0,1) = −(1 − 1 − 1 + 0) = 1. For the upper end, [x,1] is a chain for x = a,b,c, so μ(c,1) = −1, μ(b,1) = −1 and μ(a,1) = 0.

Take f(0)=2, f(a)=3, f(b)=5, f(c)=7, f(1)=11. Define g(y)=∑_{x≤y}f(x). Since a<c and b is not below c, g(0)=2, g(a)=2+3=5, g(b)=2+5=7, g(c)=2+3+7=12 and g(1)=28. Inversion from below at the top element gives f(1) = μ(0,1)g(0) + μ(a,1)g(a) + μ(b,1)g(b) + μ(c,1)g(c) + μ(1,1)g(1) = 2 + 0 − 7 − 12 + 28 = 11. This is the original value.

worked_application.result: The word count is 36. The Möbius values of the divisor lattice of 360 are μ(1,360) = 0 and μ(1,30) = −1. In the poset N, μ(0,1) = 1, and the inversion formula returns f(1) = 11.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: The recursion for μ is easy to state, but the values can be hard to find. For the partition lattice or for the lattice of subspaces of a finite vector space, a product decomposition does not exist and other arguments are needed. This entry proves none of those values.

Inversion needs finiteness of the principal down-set or up-set. In an infinite poset such as the divisor lattice of ℕ, the formula for sums over divisors is fine, but sums over multiples need extra convergence.
The theorem inverts sums over order ideals. It does not invert sums over other families, for example over all subsets of a given size.

results.name: Stirling numbers of the second kind: falling factorial basis, set partitions and surjections
results.statement: Define S(0,0) = 1, S(n,0) = 0 for n ≥ 1, S(0,k) = 0 for k ≥ 1, and S(n+1,k+1) = (k+1)·S(n,k+1) + S(n,k). Write x^{\underline{k}} = x(x−1)⋯(x−k+1). Then: (1) In ℤ[x], x^n = ∑_{k=0}^n S(n,k)·x^{\underline{k}}, and the coefficients are unique. (2) S(n,k) is the number of partitions of an n-element set into k nonempty blocks. (3) The number of surjections from an n-set onto a k-set is k!·S(n,k) = ∑_{j=0}^k (−1)^{k−j}·C(k,j)·j^n. (4) For N ≥ 0 and k ≥ 0, ∑_{x=0}^{N−1} x^{\underline{k}} = N^{\underline{k+1}}/(k+1). Hence, for n ≥ 1, ∑_{x=0}^{N−1} x^n = ∑_{k=1}^n S(n,k)·N^{\underline{k+1}}/(k+1).
hypotheses: n and k are integers with n,k ≥ 0.
The identity (1) holds in the polynomial ring ℤ[x], so it holds for every integer x.
A block of a set partition is nonempty, and blocks are not ordered.

definitions.name: falling factorial
definitions.text: x^{\underline{k}} = x(x−1)⋯(x−k+1) with k factors, and x^{\underline{0}} = 1. For a natural number x it is the number of injections from a k-set to an x-set.

definitions.name: Stirling number of the second kind
definitions.text: The number S(n,k) of partitions of {1,…,n} into k nonempty unlabeled blocks. Step 4 shows that this number satisfies the recursion in the statement.

definitions.name: surjection
definitions.text: A map f : [n] → [k] such that every element of [k] has at least one preimage.

/-- Every power `n ^ k` is a linear combination of the descending factorials `n.descFactorial j`
with the Stirling numbers of the second kind `stirlingSecond k j` as coefficients. -/
theorem pow_eq_sum_stirlingSecond_mul_descFactorial (n k : ℕ) :
    n ^ k = ∑ j ∈ Finset.range (k + 1), stirlingSecond k j * n.descFactorial j := by
  induction k with
  | zero => simp
  | succ k ih =>
    have : ∑ j ∈ Finset.range (k + 1), stirlingSecond k j * (j * n.descFactorial j)
        = ∑ j ∈ Finset.range (k + 1),
            (j + 1) * (stirlingSecond k (j + 1) * n.descFactorial (j + 1)) := by
      rw [Finset.sum_range_succ' (fun j ↦ stirlingSecond k j * (j * n.descFactorial j)) k,
        Finset.sum_range_succ (fun j ↦ (j + 1) * (stirlingSecond k (j + 1) *
          n.descFactorial (j + 1))) k,
        stirlingSecond_eq_zero_of_lt k.lt_add_one]
      simp [mul_left_comm]
    rw [pow_succ, ih, Finset.sum_mul,
      Finset.sum_range_succ' (fun j ↦ stirlingSecond (k + 1) j * n.descFactorial j) (k + 1)]
    simp only [mul_assoc, descFactorial_mul_self, mul_add, Finset.sum_add_distrib, this,
      stirlingSecond_succ_succ, add_mul, stirlingSecond_succ_zero, zero_mul, add_zero]
    exact add_comm _ _

steps.text: Falling factorials form a basis. The polynomial x^{\underline{k}} is monic of degree k. Monic polynomials of distinct degrees are linearly independent, and they span ℤ[x] by induction on the degree. So every polynomial has a unique expansion ∑ c_k·x^{\underline{k}}.
Key identity. Since x = (x − k) + k, we have x·x^{\underline{k}} = (x − k)·x^{\underline{k}} + k·x^{\underline{k}} = x^{\underline{k+1}} + k·x^{\underline{k}}.

Proof of (1) by induction on n. For n = 0 we have x^0 = 1 = S(0,0)·x^{\underline{0}}. Assume x^n = ∑_k S(n,k)·x^{\underline{k}}. Multiply by x and use step 2. Then x^{n+1} = ∑_k S(n,k)·x^{\underline{k+1}} + ∑_k k·S(n,k)·x^{\underline{k}}. The coefficient of x^{\underline{j}} for j ≥ 1 is S(n,j−1) + j·S(n,j), which is S(n+1,j) by the recursion. The coefficient for j = 0 is 0·S(n,0) = 0 = S(n+1,0). Uniqueness comes from step 1.

Proof of (2). Let T(n,k) be the number of partitions of [n] into k nonempty blocks. T(0,0) = 1, and T(n,0) = 0 for n ≥ 1, and T(0,k) = 0 for k ≥ 1. Take a partition of [n+1] into k+1 blocks. If {n+1} is a block, removing it leaves a partition of [n] into k blocks, which gives T(n,k) partitions. Otherwise, removing n+1 leaves a partition of [n] into k+1 blocks, and n+1 was in one of its k+1 blocks. This gives (k+1)·T(n,k+1) partitions. So T satisfies the recursion of S with the same start values, hence T = S.

Surjections. A surjection f : [n] → [k] has fibers f⁻¹(1),…,f⁻¹(k). They form a partition of [n] into k blocks, together with an order of the blocks. Conversely, a partition into k blocks and one of the k! orders of the blocks gives exactly one surjection. So the number of surjections is k!·S(n,k).

Explicit sum. Let Sur(n,k) be the number of surjections. For a set M ⊆ [k] the number of maps [n] → [k] whose image misses M is (k−|M|)^n. A map is a surjection if it misses no value. By inclusion-exclusion over the missed set, Sur(n,k) = ∑_{M⊆[k]} (−1)^{|M|}·(k−|M|)^n = ∑_{j=0}^k (−1)^{k−j}·C(k,j)·j^n.

Proof of (4). The forward difference of a falling factorial is (x+1)^{\underline{k+1}} − x^{\underline{k+1}} = (x+1)·x^{\underline{k}} − x^{\underline{k}}·(x−k) = (k+1)·x^{\underline{k}}. Sum over x = 0,…,N−1. The left side telescopes to N^{\underline{k+1}} − 0^{\underline{k+1}} = N^{\underline{k+1}}. Divide by k+1.

Power sums. Sum the expansion (1) over x = 0,…,N−1 and use step 7 term by term. The term k = 0 gives x^{\underline{0}} = 1, but S(n,0) = 0 for n ≥ 1, so this term vanishes. This gives ∑_{x<N} x^n = ∑_{k=1}^n S(n,k)·N^{\underline{k+1}}/(k+1) for n ≥ 1.

worked_application.title: Sum of fourth powers and a count of surjections
worked_application.goal: Compute 1⁴ + 2⁴ + … + 10⁴ and the number of surjections from a 5-set onto a 3-set.
hypotheses: The Stirling numbers S(4,k) for k = 1,…,4 are 1, 7, 6, 1.
The surjection count uses n = 5 and k = 3.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The power sum is statement (4) with n = 4 and N = 11. The surjection count is statement (3).

steps.text: Build the row. S(1,1) = 1. S(2,k) = 1, 1 for k = 1,2. S(3,k) = 1, 3, 1. S(4,1) = 1·S(3,1) + 0 = 1. S(4,2) = 2·S(3,2) + S(3,1) = 6 + 1 = 7. S(4,3) = 3·S(3,3) + S(3,2) = 3 + 3 = 6. S(4,4) = 1. This matches a direct count of 7 partitions of a 4-set into 2 blocks (3 of type 2+2 and 4 of type 3+1).

Apply statement (4) with N = 11. The falling factorials are 11^{\underline{2}} = 110, 11^{\underline{3}} = 990, 11^{\underline{4}} = 7920 and 11^{\underline{5}} = 55440. The four terms are 1·110/2 = 55, 7·990/3 = 2310, 6·7920/4 = 11880 and 1·55440/5 = 11088.

Surjections from a 5-set onto a 3-set. By statement (3) with the inclusion-exclusion sum, the number is 3⁵ − 3·2⁵ + 3·1⁵ − 0⁵ = 243 − 96 + 3 = 150. The other formula gives 3!·S(5,3) = 6·25 = 150, because S(5,3) = 3·S(4,3) + S(4,2) = 18 + 7 = 25. A brute force count over all 243 maps gives 150.

worked_application.result: 1⁴ + … + 10⁴ = 25333. There are 150 surjections from a 5-set onto a 3-set, and S(5,3) = 25.

limitations: The proofs of (2) and (3) are authored here. The source does not define Stirling numbers as counts of set partitions.
Statement (1) is an identity of polynomials. It does not give a closed form for S(n,k) without the alternating sum in (3), which has heavy cancellation for large n.
Stirling numbers of the first kind give the inverse change of basis, from falling factorials to powers. This entry does not cover them.

results.name: Walk counting by powers of the adjacency matrix, with closed walks, triangles and eigenvalues
results.statement: Let G be a finite simple graph on n vertices with adjacency matrix A, so A_{uv} = 1 if u and v are adjacent and 0 otherwise. Then: (1) For k ≥ 0, (A^k)_{uv} is the number of walks of length k from u to v. (2) tr(A^k) is the number of closed walks of length k, counted with a marked start vertex. In particular tr A = 0, tr A² = 2|E|, and tr A³ = 6·t where t is the number of triangles. (3) A is real symmetric. If λ_1,…,λ_n are its eigenvalues with multiplicity, then tr(A^k) = ∑_i λ_i^k. (4) If u ≠ v, the distance from u to v is the least k with (A^k)_{uv} > 0. The graph has diameter at most D if and only if every entry of (I+A)^D is positive and the graph is connected.
hypotheses: G is finite, undirected, without loops and without multiple edges.
A walk of length k is a sequence of vertices v_0,…,v_k with v_{i−1} adjacent to v_i for each i. Vertices may repeat.
A triangle is a set of 3 pairwise adjacent vertices.

prerequisites.reason: Steps 4 of the proof and 1 of the application use the spectral theorem for real symmetric matrices to diagonalise the adjacency matrix.

definitions.name: walk
definitions.text: A sequence of vertices in which consecutive vertices are adjacent. Its length is the number of steps.

definitions.name: closed walk
definitions.text: A walk with v_k = v_0. A closed walk with a marked start vertex is counted once for each choice of start and direction.

definitions.name: adjacency matrix
definitions.text: The n×n matrix A with A_{uv} = 1 when u ~ v and 0 otherwise. It is symmetric with zero diagonal.

theorem adjMatrix_pow_apply_eq_card_walk [DecidableEq V] [Semiring α] (n : ℕ) (u v : V) :
    (G.adjMatrix α ^ n) u v = Fintype.card { p : G.Walk u v | p.length = n } := by
  rw [card_set_walk_length_eq]
  induction n generalizing u v with
  | zero => obtain rfl | h := eq_or_ne u v <;> simp [finsetWalkLength, *]
  | succ n ih =>
    simp only [pow_succ', finsetWalkLength, ih, adjMatrix_mul_apply]
    rw [Finset.card_biUnion]
    · norm_cast
      simp only [Nat.cast_sum, card_map, neighborFinset_def]
      apply Finset.sum_toFinset_eq_subtype
    -- Disjointness for card_bUnion
    · rintro ⟨x, hx⟩ - ⟨y, hy⟩ - hxy
      rw [Function.onFun, disjoint_iff_inf_le]
      intro p hp
      simp only [inf_eq_inter, mem_inter, mem_map] at hp
      obtain ⟨⟨px, _, rfl⟩, ⟨py, hpy, hp⟩⟩ := hp
      cases hp
      simp at hxy

source_references.alignment: The source proves that the trace of the adjacency matrix is zero. This is the case k = 1 of statement (2).

results.proof_status: source declaration inspected; authored proof awaits inference review; no local Lean check

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Proof of (1) by induction on k. For k = 0 the matrix A⁰ = I counts the walk of length 0 from u to u and no other walk. Assume the claim for k. A walk of length k+1 from u to v is a walk of length k from u to some w, followed by a step from w to v. This step exists exactly when A_{wv} = 1. So the number of such walks is ∑_w (A^k)_{uw}·A_{wv} = (A^{k+1})_{uv}.

Proof of (2). A closed walk of length k with start u is a walk of length k from u to u. By (1) their number is (A^k)_{uu}. Sum over u to get tr(A^k). For k = 1, a closed walk of length 1 is a loop, so tr A = 0. For k = 2, a closed walk is u,w,u with w adjacent to u. The count is ∑_u deg(u) = 2|E|.

Triangles. A closed walk u,v,w,u of length 3 has u ~ v, v ~ w and w ~ u. There are no loops, so u ≠ v, v ≠ w and w ≠ u. Hence {u,v,w} is a triangle. Conversely, each triangle gives 6 closed walks of length 3, one for each of the 3 choices of start and the 2 directions. So tr A³ = 6t.

Proof of (3). A is real and A_{uv} = A_{vu}, so A is real symmetric. By the spectral theorem there is an orthogonal matrix Q with A = Q·diag(λ_1,…,λ_n)·Qᵀ. Then A^k = Q·diag(λ_i^k)·Qᵀ, and the trace is invariant under conjugation: tr(A^k) = ∑_i λ_i^k.

Proof of (4). The distance from u to v is the length of a shortest walk from u to v. A shortest walk exists exactly when some k has a walk of length k, and the least such k is the distance. By (1) this is the least k with (A^k)_{uv} > 0.

Diameter. Expand (I+A)^D = ∑_{j=0}^D C(D,j)·A^j. All terms have nonnegative entries, and C(D,j) > 0. So an entry is positive exactly when some A^j with j ≤ D has a positive entry there. By (1) and (4) this holds for all pairs exactly when every pair is at distance at most D. The pairs with u = v are covered by j = 0.

worked_application.title: Triangles in K4, five-walks in the Petersen graph and the spectrum of C5
worked_application.goal: Count closed walks and walks by trace and by eigenvalues, and check the counts by direct enumeration.
hypotheses: K4 is the complete graph on 4 vertices, with eigenvalues 3, −1, −1, −1.
The Petersen graph has 10 vertices, 15 edges and eigenvalues 3 (once), 1 (five times), −2 (four times). Its vertices are the 2-subsets of {1,…,5}, and two are adjacent when disjoint.
The cycle C5 has eigenvalues 2cos(2πj/5) for j = 0,…,4.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: All three graphs are finite and simple. The theorem applies. Each count in the steps below is compared to a direct enumeration.

steps.text: K4. By (3), tr A³ = 3³ + 3·(−1)³ = 24. By (2) this equals 6t, so K4 has t = 4 triangles. This agrees with C(4,3) = 4.

Petersen graph, closed walks. By (3), tr A^k = 3^k + 5 + 4·(−2)^k. This gives 0, 30, 0, 150, 120, 990 for k = 1,…,6. The value for k = 2 is 2·15 = 30 and the value for k = 3 is 0, so the graph has no triangle. These traces agree with matrix powers computed by computer.

Closed 5-walks. The value tr A⁵ = 243 + 5 − 128 = 120 counts closed walks of length 5. In a triangle-free graph, a closed walk of odd length 5 that repeats a vertex splits into a closed walk of odd length at most 3, which must be a loop or a triangle. Neither exists. So each such walk is a 5-cycle, and each 5-cycle gives 5·2 = 10 closed walks. The Petersen graph has 120/10 = 12 five-cycles, and an exhaustive search finds exactly 12.

Walk counts from one vertex. Row sums of A⁵ are 3⁵ = 243, because each vertex has degree 3. For a fixed vertex u, (A⁵)_{uu} = 12, (A⁵)_{uv} = 33 for each of the 3 neighbours v, and (A⁵)_{uw} = 22 for each of the 6 vertices w at distance 2. The row sum is 12 + 3·33 + 6·22 = 243, as it must be. Distances: A² has entry 1 at every vertex not adjacent to u and different from u, so every pair is at distance at most 2 by (4), and (I+A)² is positive.

C5. By (3), tr A⁵ = ∑_{j=0}^4 (2cos(2πj/5))⁵ = 10. A direct count agrees: the 5-cycle gives 5 starts and 2 directions, and no other closed 5-walk exists, because C5 is triangle-free and has no shorter odd cycle.

worked_application.result: K4 has 4 triangles. The Petersen graph has no triangle, 120 closed 5-walks and 12 five-cycles, and it has diameter 2. The graph C5 has 10 closed 5-walks.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: The count in (2) treats a closed walk with different start vertices as different walks. To count cycles, divide by the start and direction symmetry only for cycles, and only when no shorter closed walk exists.
Statement (3) needs real symmetric matrices. For directed graphs the adjacency matrix is not symmetric, and the trace formula holds only with complex eigenvalues of A.
The formula tr A³ = 6t is special to three steps. For longer cycles, closed walks include degenerate walks, and a correction term is needed.

results.name: Finite projective planes: constant line size n+1 and n²+n+1 points and lines
results.statement: Let a finite projective plane be a finite set of points and a finite set of lines, with an incidence relation, such that: (A1) two distinct points lie on exactly one common line, (A2) two distinct lines meet in exactly one common point, (A3) there are four points, no three on a common line. Then there is an integer n ≥ 2, called the order, such that: (1) every line contains exactly n+1 points, (2) every point lies on exactly n+1 lines, (3) there are exactly n²+n+1 points and exactly n²+n+1 lines.
hypotheses: The point set and line set are finite.
Incidence is a relation between points and lines. A line is identified with its set of points.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: The proof uses only the axioms and elementary counting. No catalog theorem is cited.

definitions.name: collinear
definitions.text: Points are collinear if some line contains all of them.

definitions.name: order
definitions.text: The integer n = (number of points on a line) − 1. Step 5 shows that it does not depend on the line.

definitions.name: planar difference set
definitions.text: A set D of n+1 residues modulo n²+n+1 such that each nonzero residue occurs exactly once as a difference d−d′ with d,d′ ∈ D. The set {0,1,3} modulo 7 is one. The application uses such a set only as a source of an example.

theorem card_points [Fintype P] [Finite L] : Fintype.card P = order P L ^ 2 + order P L + 1 := by
  cases nonempty_fintype L
  obtain ⟨p, -⟩ := @exists_config P L _ _
  let ϕ : { q // q ≠ p } ≃ Σ l : { l : L // p ∈ l }, { q // q ∈ l.1 ∧ q ≠ p } :=
    { toFun := fun q => ⟨⟨mkLine q.2, (mkLine_ax q.2).2⟩, q, (mkLine_ax q.2).1, q.2⟩
      invFun := fun lq => ⟨lq.2, lq.2.2.2⟩
      right_inv := fun lq =>
        Sigma.subtype_ext
          (Subtype.ext
            ((eq_or_eq (mkLine_ax lq.2.2.2).1 (mkLine_ax lq.2.2.2).2 lq.2.2.1 lq.1.2).resolve_left
              lq.2.2.2))
          rfl }
  classical
    have h1 : Fintype.card { q // q ≠ p } + 1 = Fintype.card P := by
      apply (eq_tsub_iff_add_eq_of_le (Nat.succ_le_of_lt (Fintype.card_pos_iff.mpr ⟨p⟩))).mp
      convert (Fintype.card_subtype_compl _).trans (congr_arg _ (Fintype.card_subtype_eq p))
    have h2 : ∀ l : { l : L // p ∈ l }, Fintype.card { q // q ∈ l.1 ∧ q ≠ p } = order P L := by
      intro l
      rw [← Fintype.card_congr (Equiv.subtypeSubtypeEquivSubtypeInter (· ∈ l.val) (· ≠ p)),
        Fintype.card_subtype_compl fun x : Subtype (· ∈ l.val) => x.val = p, ←
        Nat.card_eq_fintype_card]
      refine tsub_eq_of_eq_add ((pointCount_eq P l.1).trans ?_)
      rw [← Fintype.card_subtype_eq (⟨p, l.2⟩ : { q : P // q ∈ l.1 })]
      simp_rw [Subtype.ext_iff]
    simp_rw [← h1, Fintype.card_congr ϕ, Fintype.card_sigma, h2, Finset.sum_const, Finset.card_univ]
    rw [← Nat.card_eq_fintype_card, ← lineCount, lineCount_eq, smul_eq_mul, Nat.succ_mul, sq]

steps.text: Line through a point and a line. Let ℓ be a line and P a point not on ℓ. Map each point Q on ℓ to the line PQ, which exists and is unique by (A1). This map from the points of ℓ to the lines through P is injective. If PQ = PQ′ = m for Q ≠ Q′ on ℓ, then m and ℓ share the two points Q and Q′, so m = ℓ by (A2). But P is on m and not on ℓ. This is a contradiction.

The same map is surjective. Let m be a line through P. By (A2), m meets ℓ in a point Q. Since P is not on ℓ, P ≠ Q, so m = PQ by (A1). Hence, if P is not on ℓ, then the number of points on ℓ equals the number of lines through P.

A point off two lines. Let ℓ ≠ m be lines with common point X. Suppose that every point is on ℓ or on m. Take four points a,b,c,d from (A3). A line holds at most two of them, so exactly two lie on ℓ and two on m. None is X, because X would count for both lines and then at most 3 distinct points would be covered. Say a,b ∈ ℓ and c,d ∈ m, and all four differ from X.

Continue step 3. Lines ac and bd meet at a point Y by (A2). Y lies on ℓ or on m. If Y ∈ ℓ and Y ≠ a, then line ac contains a and Y, so ac = ℓ and c ∈ ℓ ∩ m = {X}, a contradiction. If Y = a, then a,b,d lie on bd, which contradicts (A3). If Y ∈ m, the same argument with c in place of a gives a contradiction. So some point P lies on neither ℓ nor m.

All lines have the same size. For lines ℓ and m, pick P on neither, by step 4. By step 2, |ℓ| equals the number of lines through P, and so does |m|. Hence |ℓ| = |m|. Call the common value n+1. Every point lies off some line: if P lay on ab, cd, ac and bd, then P = a from ab ∩ ac and P ∉ cd, a contradiction. So by step 2, every point lies on exactly n+1 lines. This proves (1) and (2).
The number n is at least 2. The lines ab and cd meet at a point Z by (A2). Z is not a or b, since otherwise three of the four points would be collinear. So line ab contains a, b and Z, and n+1 ≥ 3.

Counting points. Fix a point P. Every other point lies on exactly one line through P, by (A1). There are n+1 lines through P, and each has n points other than P. So the number of points is 1 + (n+1)·n = n²+n+1.

Counting lines. Fix a line ℓ. Every other line meets ℓ in exactly one point, by (A2). Each of the n+1 points of ℓ lies on n lines other than ℓ. So the number of lines is 1 + (n+1)·n = n²+n+1. This proves (3).

worked_application.title: The plane of order 3 from the difference set {0,1,3,9} modulo 13
worked_application.goal: Build a projective plane of order 3 and check the counts of the theorem on it.
hypotheses: The difference set is D = {0,1,3,9} in ℤ/13. The points are the 13 residues, and the lines are the 13 translates D+s.
The order is n = 3, and n²+n+1 = 13.

A computer check of all 78 pairs of points finds exactly one line through each pair. A check of all 78 pairs of lines finds exactly one common point. The points 0,1,2,5 are four points with no three on a line, which gives (A3). One of the 234 such quadruples is 0,1,2,5.

results.name: Singleton, Hamming and Gilbert-Varshamov bounds for block codes
results.statement: Let A be an alphabet with q ≥ 2 symbols. Let C ⊆ A^n be a code with M ≥ 2 words and minimum Hamming distance d, where 1 ≤ d ≤ n. Put V_q(n,r) = ∑_{i=0}^r C(n,i)(q−1)^i and t = ⌊(d−1)/2⌋. Then: (1) Singleton bound: M ≤ q^{n−d+1}. (2) Hamming bound: M·V_q(n,t) ≤ q^n, with equality if and only if every word of A^n lies within distance t of exactly one codeword (a perfect code). (3) Gilbert-Varshamov bound: there is a code in A^n with minimum distance at least d and with at least q^n / V_q(n,d−1) words. (4) If C is linear over a field with q elements and has dimension k, then k ≤ n−d+1 and q^k·V_q(n,t) ≤ q^n.
hypotheses: q ≥ 2 is the size of the alphabet.
The Hamming distance of x and y is the number of coordinates in which they differ.
For (4), A is a finite field F_q, the code is a subspace of F_q^n, and M = q^k.

steps.text: Ball size. Take a word x. The words at distance exactly i from x are made by choosing i coordinates (C(n,i) ways) and replacing each by one of the q−1 other symbols. So |B(x,r)| = ∑_{i≤r} C(n,i)(q−1)^i = V_q(n,r), independent of x.

Singleton bound (1). Let π : A^n → A^{n−d+1} delete the last d−1 coordinates. If π(x) = π(y) for distinct codewords x and y, they differ only in the last d−1 coordinates, so d(x,y) ≤ d−1 < d. This contradicts the minimum distance. So π is injective on C, and M ≤ q^{n−d+1}.

Disjoint balls. Let x ≠ y be codewords and suppose z ∈ B(x,t) ∩ B(y,t). The triangle inequality gives d(x,y) ≤ d(x,z) + d(z,y) ≤ 2t ≤ d−1. This is less than d, a contradiction. So the balls B(c,t) with c ∈ C are pairwise disjoint.

Hamming bound (2). The M disjoint balls of size V_q(n,t) lie inside A^n, so M·V_q(n,t) ≤ q^n. Equality holds if and only if the disjoint balls cover A^n. This is the statement that each word lies in exactly one ball.

Gilbert-Varshamov bound (3). The family of codes with minimum distance at least d is finite and has a code of one word. Choose such a code C with the largest number of words. Take any word w ∈ A^n. If d(w,c) ≥ d for all c ∈ C, then C ∪ {w} is a larger code with minimum distance at least d, a contradiction. So every w lies in some ball B(c,d−1).
Count the cover. The balls B(c,d−1) with c ∈ C cover A^n. So q^n ≤ |C|·V_q(n,d−1). Hence |C| ≥ q^n / V_q(n,d−1).

Linear codes (4). A subspace of dimension k over F_q has M = q^k words. Its minimum distance is the least weight of a nonzero word. Apply (1) and (2). Taking logarithms base q in q^k ≤ q^{n−d+1} gives k ≤ n−d+1. The Hamming bound gives q^k·V_q(n,t) ≤ q^n directly.

worked_application.title: Perfect codes and the gap between the bounds for n = 8, d = 5
worked_application.goal: Check that the binary Hamming code and the binary Golay code meet the Hamming bound, and compare all three bounds for binary words of length 8 and distance 5.
hypotheses: The binary Hamming code is the kernel of the 3×7 matrix whose columns are the binary numbers 1 to 7. It has n = 7, M = 16, d = 3.
The binary Golay code is the cyclic code of length 23 generated by x¹¹+x¹⁰+x⁶+x⁵+x⁴+x²+1. It has 2¹² words and minimum weight 7, checked by computer.
For the comparison, q = 2, n = 8 and d = 5.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Each code is a binary code with a known number of words and minimum distance. The bounds then apply.

steps.text: Hamming code, n = 7, d = 3, t = 1. Here V_2(7,1) = 1 + 7 = 8. So M·V = 16·8 = 128 = 2⁷. The bound (2) is an equality, so the code is perfect. A computer check confirms that every one of the 128 words lies within distance 1 of exactly one of the 16 codewords.
Golay code, n = 23, d = 7, t = 3. Here V_2(23,3) = 1 + 23 + 253 + 1771 = 2048 = 2¹¹. So M·V = 2¹²·2¹¹ = 2²³. The bound (2) is an equality, so the code is perfect.

Comparison for q = 2, n = 8, d = 5, t = 2. Singleton gives M ≤ 2⁴ = 16. Hamming uses V_2(8,2) = 1 + 8 + 28 = 37, so M ≤ 256/37 < 6.92, hence M ≤ 6. Gilbert-Varshamov uses V_2(8,4) = 1 + 8 + 28 + 56 + 70 = 163, so a code exists with at least 256/163 > 1.57, hence at least 2 words.

An exhaustive search over all binary words of length 8 finds that the largest code with distance 5 has exactly 4 words. So the true value 4 lies between the lower bound 2 and the upper bound 6. The Hamming bound is much stronger than the Singleton bound here. This is the typical case for small alphabets.

worked_application.result: The binary Hamming code and the binary Golay code are perfect. For n = 8 and d = 5 over two symbols the bounds are 2 ≤ M ≤ 6, and the true maximum is 4.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: These are upper and lower bounds only. They do not construct optimal codes. The gap can be large, for example in the application.

Only the Hamming bound can be an equality for large t, and perfect codes are rare. Over a prime power alphabet, the only nontrivial perfect codes are the Hamming codes and the Golay codes. This entry does not prove this classification.
The Gilbert-Varshamov bound here is for arbitrary codes. For linear codes a similar bound holds with a slightly different proof, which this entry does not give.

steps.text: Lower bound on S. There are M(M−1) ordered pairs of distinct codewords. Each pair has distance at least d. So S ≥ M(M−1)d.
Split S by coordinate. The distance d(x,y) is the number of coordinates i with x_i ≠ y_i. So S = ∑_{i=1}^n S_i, where S_i is the number of ordered pairs (x,y) of codewords with x_i ≠ y_i.
Count S_i. Fix i. For each symbol a, let m_a be the number of codewords with symbol a at coordinate i. Then ∑_a m_a = M. The ordered pairs with x_i = y_i number ∑_a m_a². So S_i = M² − ∑_a m_a².
Bound ∑_a m_a² from below. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for the vectors (m_a) and (1,…,1) in R^q gives M² = (∑_a m_a)² ≤ q·∑_a m_a². So ∑_a m_a² ≥ M²/q.
Hence S_i ≤ M² − M²/q = θM² for every i. Summing over the n coordinates gives S ≤ θnM².
Combine the two bounds. M(M−1)d ≤ S ≤ θnM². Divide by M > 0 to get (M−1)d ≤ θnM. This is the same as M(d − θn) ≤ d.
Divide by d − θn > 0. This gives M ≤ d/(d − θn). Multiply the numerator and the denominator by q to get the second form.

results.name: Weighted partition generating function as an Euler product
results.statement: Let R be a commutative ring. Let f(i,m) ∈ R be given for all integers i ≥ 1 and m ≥ 0, with f(i,0) = 1. For a partition λ of n, let m_i(λ) be the number of parts of λ equal to i. Put W(λ) = ∏_{i≥1} f(i, m_i(λ)). Then in the power series ring R[[x]], ∑_{n≥0} (∑_{λ ⊢ n} W(λ)) x^n = ∏_{i≥1} (∑_{m≥0} f(i,m) x^{im}). The infinite product is defined by coefficients: the factor with index i equals 1 modulo x^{i}, so each coefficient is a finite product.
hypotheses: R is a commutative ring with identity.
f(i,0) = 1 for every i ≥ 1.
A partition of n is a multiset of positive integers with sum n. The only partition of 0 is the empty one, and it has weight 1.

steps.text: Well-defined product. Put F_i = ∑_{m≥0} f(i,m) x^{im}. Since f(i,0) = 1, F_i = 1 + (terms of degree at least i). So for each N, the factors F_i with i > N do not change the coefficients of x^0,…,x^N. The coefficient of x^N in the infinite product is, by definition, the coefficient of x^N in the finite product F_1···F_N.

Expand the finite product. Fix N. Multiplying out F_1···F_N gives the sum over all tuples (m_1,…,m_N) of non-negative integers of (∏_i f(i,m_i)) x^{∑ i·m_i}. This holds because x^{i·m_i} multiplies as x^{∑ i·m_i}.
Select the coefficient. The coefficient of x^N in F_1···F_N is ∑ ∏_{i=1}^N f(i,m_i), taken over all tuples (m_1,…,m_N) with ∑_{i=1}^N i·m_i = N.

Bijection with partitions. A partition λ of N has parts at most N. The map λ ↦ (m_1(λ),…,m_N(λ)) is injective, because a multiset is determined by its multiplicities. It is surjective onto the tuples with ∑ i·m_i = N, because the multiset with m_i copies of i is a partition of N. Its weight is ∏_{i=1}^N f(i,m_i), since m_i(λ) = 0 for i > N and f(i,0) = 1.
Conclude. The coefficient of x^N in the product equals ∑_{λ ⊢ N} W(λ). This holds for every N ≥ 0, so the two power series are equal.
Special case. For f ≡ 1, each F_i = ∑_{m≥0} x^{im} = 1/(1 − x^i) in R[[x]]. So ∑ p(n) x^n = ∏_{i≥1} 1/(1 − x^i).

results.name: Large Schröder paths: first-return recurrence, flat-step formula and generating function
results.statement: A large Schröder path of semilength n is a lattice path from (0,0) to (2n,0) with steps U = (1,1), D = (1,−1) and F = (2,0), which never goes below the x-axis. Let s_n be the number of such paths. Let D_m be the number of Dyck paths of semilength m, that is, paths with only U and D steps. Then: (1) s_0 = 1 and s_{n+1} = s_n + ∑_{i=0}^n s_i s_{n−i}. (2) s_n = ∑_{j=0}^n D_{n−j} · C(2n−j, j). (3) The series S(x) = ∑ s_n x^n satisfies x S² − (1−x) S + 1 = 0, and S(x) = (1 − x − √(1 − 6x + x²)) / (2x), where the square root is the series with constant term 1.

steps.text: Base case. Only the empty path has semilength 0, so s_0 = 1.
First-step split for (1). Take a path of semilength n+1. If its first step is F, the rest is any Schröder path of semilength n. This gives s_n paths.

First return for (1). If the first step is U, let D* be the first step that returns to the x-axis. The part between U and D* stays at height at least 1. After lowering it by 1, it is a Schröder path of some semilength i. The part after D* is a Schröder path of semilength k. The x-length gives 2 + 2i + 2k = 2n + 2, so k = n − i.

Count for (1). The map from the path to the triple (i, first part, last part) is a bijection onto the choices with 0 ≤ i ≤ n. This is because U and D* are determined by the path, and the two parts can be chosen freely. So there are ∑_{i=0}^n s_i s_{n−i} paths with first step U. Adding the two cases proves (1).

Flat-step formula (2). Take a Schröder path with j flat steps. Delete all flat steps. The result is a Dyck path of semilength n − j, because the remaining steps are U and D and their total x-length is 2(n−j).

Reverse map. A Dyck path of semilength n − j has 2(n − j) + 1 vertices. To rebuild a Schröder path with j flat steps, choose how many flat steps to insert at each vertex. This is a multiset of size j from 2(n − j) + 1 vertices. Inserting a flat step at a vertex at height h ≥ 0 keeps the height ≥ 0. Different multisets give different paths.

Count for (2). The number of multisets of size j from 2(n − j) + 1 elements is C(2(n − j) + j, j) = C(2n − j, j). So there are D_{n−j} · C(2n − j, j) paths with j flat steps. Summing over j = 0,…,n gives (2).

Generating function (3). Multiply (1) by x^{n+1} and sum over n ≥ 0. The left side is S − 1. The right side is x S + x S², because ∑_n (∑_{i} s_i s_{n−i}) x^n = S². So S = 1 + x S + x S², which is x S² − (1 − x) S + 1 = 0.

Closed form. Complete the square: 4x² S² − 4x(1−x) S + 4x = 0 becomes (2xS − (1−x))² = (1−x)² − 4x = 1 − 6x + x². The series 1 − 6x + x² has constant term 1, so it has exactly one square root Q with constant term 1. Then 2xS − (1−x) = ±Q. The constant term of the left side is −1, and that of Q is 1, so the sign is minus. Hence 2xS = 1 − x − Q, and S = (1 − x − Q)/(2x). The numerator has constant term 0, so the division by x is valid.

results.name: Gallai identities and the matching-cover inequalities for finite graphs
results.statement: Let G be a finite simple graph with n vertices. Let α be the largest size of an independent set. Let τ be the smallest size of a vertex cover. Let ν be the largest size of a matching. Let ρ be the smallest size of an edge cover, that is, a set of edges that touches every vertex. Then: (1) α + τ = n. (2) ν ≤ τ ≤ 2ν. (3) If G has no isolated vertex, then ρ exists and ρ + ν = n.
hypotheses: G is finite and simple.
A vertex cover is a set of vertices that contains an end of every edge.
A matching is a set of edges with no common end.

steps.text: Proof of (1), first half. Let I be an independent set. Take any edge uv. Not both u and v lie in I. So at least one lies in V \ I, and V \ I is a vertex cover.

Proof of (1), second half. Let C be a vertex cover. If u and v both lie in V \ C and uv is an edge, then C misses both ends of uv. This is a contradiction. So V \ C is independent. Hence I ↦ V \ I is a bijection between independent sets and vertex covers, and it sends size k to size n − k.

Conclusion of (1). The largest independent set has size α. Its complement is a vertex cover of size n − α, so τ ≤ n − α. The complement of a smallest cover is an independent set of size n − τ, so α ≥ n − τ. Together, α + τ = n.

Proof of ν ≤ τ. Let M be a matching of size ν and C a vertex cover. Each edge of M has an end in C. The edges of M share no ends, so these ends are distinct. Hence |C| ≥ |M|. Taking C of size τ gives τ ≥ ν.

Proof of τ ≤ 2ν. Let M be a matching with ν edges and let V(M) be the set of its 2ν ends. Suppose an edge uv has both ends outside V(M). Then M ∪ {uv} is a matching with ν + 1 edges, which is impossible. So every edge has an end in V(M), and V(M) is a vertex cover. Hence τ ≤ 2ν.

Proof of ρ ≤ n − ν in (3). Take a matching M with ν edges. The 2ν ends of M are covered by M. Each of the other n − 2ν vertices lies on an edge, because G has no isolated vertex. Choose one such edge for each. The set M together with the chosen edges covers all vertices and has at most ν + (n − 2ν) = n − ν edges.

Proof of ρ ≥ n − ν, step 1. Let F be an edge cover with the least number of edges. Every edge e = uv of F has an end of degree 1 in F. If both ends had degree at least 2 in F, then F \ {e} would still cover u and v, and it would be a smaller edge cover.

Proof of ρ ≥ n − ν, step 2. A cycle in F would contain an edge whose two ends both have degree at least 2. So F has no cycle and is a forest. Every vertex lies on an edge of F. If F has c components, then |F| = n − c, because a forest on n vertices with c components has n − c edges.

Proof of ρ ≥ n − ν, step 3. Pick one edge from each component of F. Edges from different components share no end, so they form a matching of size c. So c ≤ ν, and ρ = |F| = n − c ≥ n − ν. With the previous bound, ρ = n − ν.

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Proof of (1), pair map. Take a proper colouring c of G with χ colours and a proper colouring c′ of G^c with χ^c colours. Define Φ(v) = (c(v), c′(v)). The image lies in a set of χ · χ^c pairs.

Φ is injective. Suppose u ≠ v and Φ(u) = Φ(v). Then c(u) = c(v), so u and v are not adjacent in G, because c is proper. Also c′(u) = c′(v), so u and v are not adjacent in G^c. But two distinct vertices are adjacent in G or in G^c. This is a contradiction. Hence n ≤ χ · χ^c.
Sum bound in (1). By the inequality of arithmetic and geometric means, χ + χ^c ≥ 2√(χ · χ^c) ≥ 2√n.
Proof of (2), set-up. We use induction on n. For n = 1, both χ and χ^c equal 1, so the sum is 2 = n + 1. Take n ≥ 2 and assume (2) for graphs with n − 1 vertices.

Remove a vertex. Pick a vertex v and let H = G − v. Then H^c = G^c − v. Let d be the degree of v in G. Its degree in G^c is n − 1 − d. Colouring H with χ(H) colours and giving v a new colour shows χ(G) ≤ χ(H) + 1. In the same way χ^c ≤ χ(H^c) + 1.
Case A. If one of these two inequalities is strict, then χ + χ^c ≤ χ(H) + χ(H^c) + 1. By the induction hypothesis this is at most (n − 1 + 1) + 1 = n + 1.

Case B, degree bound. Assume χ = χ(H) + 1. We claim d ≥ χ(H). Suppose d < χ(H). In an optimal colouring of H, the d neighbours of v use at most d colours, so one of the χ(H) colours is free for v. Then χ(G) ≤ χ(H), a contradiction. In the same way, if χ^c = χ(H^c) + 1, then n − 1 − d ≥ χ(H^c).
Case B, sum. Adding the two bounds gives n − 1 ≥ χ(H) + χ(H^c). Hence χ + χ^c = χ(H) + χ(H^c) + 2 ≤ n + 1. This proves (2).
Proof of (3). By the inequality of arithmetic and geometric means, χ · χ^c ≤ ((χ + χ^c)/2)². By (2), χ + χ^c ≤ n + 1, so χ · χ^c ≤ ((n+1)/2)².

results.name: Commuting pairs equal the class number times the group order, and the bound 5/8
results.statement: Let G be a finite group. Let k(G) be the number of conjugacy classes of G. Let C be the set of ordered pairs (x,y) in G×G with xy = yx. Then |C| = k(G)·|G|. So the probability that two random elements commute is k(G)/|G|. If G is not abelian, then k(G)/|G| ≤ 5/8.
hypotheses: G is a finite group.
The bound 5/8 needs G to be non abelian. For an abelian group the probability is 1.
The bound is sharp. The dihedral group of order 8 and the quaternion group of order 8 reach it.

theorem card_comm_eq_card_conjClasses_mul_card (G : Type*) [Group G] :
    Nat.card { p : G × G // Commute p.1 p.2 } = Nat.card (ConjClasses G) * Nat.card G := by
  classical
  rcases fintypeOrInfinite G; swap
  · rw [mul_comm, Nat.card_eq_zero_of_infinite, Nat.card_eq_zero_of_infinite, zero_mul]
  simp only [Nat.card_eq_fintype_card]
  calc card { p : G × G // Commute p.1 p.2 }
      _ = card ((a : G) × { b // Commute a b }) :=
            card_congr (Equiv.subtypeProdEquivSigmaSubtype Commute)
      _ = ∑ i, card { b // Commute i b } := card_sigma
      _ = ∑ x, card (MulAction.fixedBy G x) :=
            sum_equiv ConjAct.toConjAct.toEquiv (fun a ↦ card { b // Commute a b })
              (fun g ↦ card (MulAction.fixedBy G g))
              fun g ↦ card_congr' <| congr_arg _ <| funext fun h ↦ mul_inv_eq_iff_eq_mul.symm.eq
      _ = card (Quotient (MulAction.orbitRel (ConjAct G) G)) * card (ConjAct G) :=
             MulAction.sum_card_fixedBy_eq_card_orbits_mul_card_group _ _
      _ = card (ConjClasses G) * card G := by
             congr 1; apply card_congr'; congr; ext
             exact (Setoid.comm' _).trans isConj_iff.symm

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Count the pairs by the first entry. For each x in G, the number of y with xy = yx is |C_G(x)|. So |C| = ∑_{x in G} |C_G(x)|.

Orbit-stabilizer. Let G act on itself by conjugation. The orbit of x is its class cl(x). The stabilizer of x is C_G(x). The map gC_G(x) ↦ gxg⁻¹ is a bijection from the cosets of C_G(x) onto cl(x). So |cl(x)|·|C_G(x)| = |G|.

Substitute step 2 into step 1. We get |C| = ∑_{x in G} |G|/|cl(x)|. Group the sum by classes. A class K contains |K| elements, and each of them contributes |G|/|K|. So the class K contributes |K|·|G|/|K| = |G|.
There are k(G) classes. So |C| = k(G)·|G|. This is the first claim. Dividing by |G|² gives the probability k(G)/|G|.

Class sizes. Let z = |Z(G)|. A class of size 1 is the class of a central element, so there are exactly z classes of size 1. Every other class has size at least 2. If k = k(G), there are k − z other classes, and they contain |G| − z elements. So 2(k − z) ≤ |G| − z, that is k ≤ (|G| + z)/2.

Cyclic quotient lemma. Suppose G/Z(G) is cyclic with generator gZ. Every element has the form gⁱc with c central. Two such elements gⁱc and gʲc′ commute, because c and c′ are central and gⁱgʲ = gʲgⁱ. So G is abelian.
Now let G be non abelian. By step 6 the quotient G/Z(G) is not cyclic. A group of order 1, 2 or 3 is cyclic. So |G/Z(G)| ≥ 4, which gives z ≤ |G|/4.
Combine steps 5 and 7. We get k/|G| ≤ 1/2 + z/(2|G|) ≤ 1/2 + 1/8 = 5/8.

Sharpness. The dihedral group D₄ of order 8 has center of order 2 and 5 classes: {1}, {r²}, {r,r³}, {s,sr²}, {sr,sr³}. Here z = 2 = |G|/4 and k = 5 = (8+2)/2. Both inequalities in steps 5 and 7 are equalities, and k/|G| = 5/8.

results.name: Neumann lemma: a finite union of cosets covering a group has a subgroup of small finite index
results.statement: Let G be a group. Let G = g_1H_1 ∪ … ∪ g_nH_n be a covering by n left cosets of subgroups H_1,…,H_n. Then (a) at least one H_i has finite index in G. (b) The cosets g_iH_i with [G:H_i] finite already cover G. (c) ∑ over i with [G:H_i] finite of 1/[G:H_i] ≥ 1. (d) At least one H_i has [G:H_i] ≤ n.
hypotheses: G is any group. It may be infinite and non abelian.
The family of cosets is finite, with n ≥ 1 members. Repeated subgroups are allowed.
The theorem is also true for the additive form: cosets a_i + H_i of subgroups of an abelian group.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: The proof is self contained. It uses only that left cosets of one subgroup are equal or disjoint, and counts cosets of a finite index subgroup. No catalog theorem is cited.

definitions.name: left coset gH
definitions.text: gH = {gh : h in H}. Two left cosets of the same subgroup are equal or disjoint. The number of left cosets is the index [G:H].

definitions.name: finite index
definitions.text: A subgroup H has finite index if G is a finite union of cosets of H. The intersection of finitely many subgroups of finite index has finite index.

definitions.name: covering system
definitions.text: A covering system is a finite family of residue classes a_i + m_iℤ whose union is ℤ. It is the additive case G = ℤ and H_i = m_iℤ.

theorem exists_index_le_card_of_leftCoset_cover :
    ∃ i ∈ s, (H i).FiniteIndex ∧ (H i).index ≤ s.card := by
  by_contra! h
  apply (one_le_sum_inv_index_of_leftCoset_cover hcovers).not_gt
  cases s.eq_empty_or_nonempty with
  | inl hs => simp only [hs, Finset.sum_empty, zero_lt_one]
  | inr hs =>
  have hs' : 0 < s.card := hs.card_pos
  have hlt : ∀ i ∈ s, ((H i).index : ℚ)⁻¹ < (s.card : ℚ)⁻¹ := fun i hi ↦ by
    cases eq_or_ne (H i).index 0 with
    | inl hindex =>
      rwa [hindex, Nat.cast_zero, inv_zero, inv_pos, Nat.cast_pos]
    | inr hindex =>
      exact inv_strictAnti₀ (by exact_mod_cast hs') (by exact_mod_cast h i hi ⟨hindex⟩)
  apply (Finset.sum_lt_sum_of_nonempty hs hlt).trans_eq
  rw [Finset.sum_const, nsmul_eq_mul, mul_inv_cancel₀ (Nat.cast_ne_zero.mpr hs'.ne')]

end

steps.text: Part (a), set up. Say that a covering is a finite family of cosets with union G. We prove by induction on m: if a covering uses at most m distinct subgroups, then one of these subgroups has finite index. This holds for every group G. The case m = 0 holds because an empty family has an empty union, and G is not empty.

Induction step. Fix a covering that uses m ≥ 1 distinct subgroups, and fix a member subgroup H. Let S be the cosets of the family that use H. If the cosets in S cover G, then G is a finite union of cosets of H. Then H has finite index, and we are done.

Otherwise, there is an element x such that xH is not a member of S. The cosets xH and g H for the members gH of S are different cosets of H, so they are disjoint. So no member of S contains any element of xH.

Take any y in G and any z in yH. Then w = xy⁻¹z lies in xH, because y⁻¹z is in H. The covering contains w in some member g_iH_i. This member is not in S. So H_i ≠ H. Now z = yx⁻¹w lies in (yx⁻¹g_i)H_i.

So every coset yH is contained in the union of the cosets (yx⁻¹g_i)H_i with H_i ≠ H. Replace each member gH of S by these cosets. The result is a covering of G that uses at most m − 1 distinct subgroups. By the induction hypothesis, one of the subgroups H_i ≠ H has finite index. This proves (a).

Part (b). Let F be the set of indices i with [G:H_i] finite. By (a), F is not empty. Let D be the intersection of the H_i with i in F. Then D has finite index in G, and D ⊆ H_i for i in F. Each H_i with i in F is a union of [H_i:D] cosets of D, so each g_iH_i with i in F is a union of cosets of D.

Replace every member with i in F by these cosets of D. We get a new covering of G. Its subgroups are D and the H_i with i outside F. The subgroup D has finite index, and the others have infinite index, so D differs from them.

Apply the argument of steps 2 to 5 to the new covering with H = D. If the cosets of D did not cover G, step 5 would give a covering of G by cosets of the subgroups H_i with i outside F. By (a), one of these would have finite index. This is false. So the cosets of D cover G, and these cosets come from the members with i in F. This proves (b).
Part (c). G has [G:D] cosets of D. By (b), every coset of D lies in one of the members g_iH_i with i in F. The member g_iH_i contains exactly [H_i:D] cosets of D. So [G:D] ≤ ∑_{i in F} [H_i:D].

Divide by [G:D]. Because [G:D] = [G:H_i]·[H_i:D], we get 1 ≤ ∑_{i in F} 1/[G:H_i]. The terms with i outside F are zero when we read 1/∞ as 0, so the sum over all i has the same value. This proves (c).

Part (d). Suppose [G:H_i] > n for every i with finite index. Then 1/[G:H_i] < 1/n for those i, and the terms of the other i are 0 < 1/n. Since n ≥ 1, the sum of n terms is less than n·(1/n) = 1. This contradicts (c). So some H_i has finite index at most n.

worked_application.title: A covering system of the integers with five classes
worked_application.goal: Check that the five classes 0 mod 2, 0 mod 3, 1 mod 4, 5 mod 6 and 7 mod 12 cover ℤ. Then check the density sum and the index bound.
hypotheses: G = ℤ. The five cosets are 0+2ℤ, 0+3ℤ, 1+4ℤ, 5+6ℤ and 7+12ℤ.
The indices are 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: These are cosets of subgroups of ℤ. The lemma applies if they cover ℤ, and it also gives constraints for other families.

steps.text: The common period is lcm(2,3,4,6,12) = 12. The five classes repeat with period 12, so it is enough to check the residues 0 to 11.

Class 0 mod 2 covers 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. Class 0 mod 3 adds 3 and 9. Class 1 mod 4 adds 1 and 5 (9 is already covered). Class 5 mod 6 adds 11 (5 is already covered). Class 7 mod 12 adds 7. All 12 residues are covered.

Density sum. 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 + 1/6 + 1/12 = 6/12 + 4/12 + 3/12 + 2/12 + 1/12 = 16/12 = 4/3. This is at least 1, as part (c) requires. The excess 1/3 is the overlap: residues 0, 6 are covered twice, 9 twice, 5 twice.
Index bound. Here n = 5, and the smallest index is 2 ≤ 5. This agrees with part (d).

The covering is irredundant. Without 7 mod 12 the residue 7 is not covered. Without 5 mod 6 the residue 11 is not covered. Without 1 mod 4 the residue 1 is not covered. Without 0 mod 3 the residue 3 is not covered. Without 0 mod 2 the residue 2 is not covered.
A consequence of (d). No three classes with moduli 4, 5 and 6 can cover ℤ. Here n = 3 and all indices exceed 3. Also 1/4 + 1/5 + 1/6 = 37/60 < 1, which agrees with (c).

worked_application.result: The five classes cover ℤ with density sum 4/3. The minimum modulus 2 is at most 5. Three classes with moduli 4, 5 and 6 cannot cover ℤ.

limitations: The lemma does not say that the covering exists. It gives necessary conditions only.
The bound (d) can be sharp. The two classes 0 mod 2 and 1 mod 2 cover ℤ, and the smallest index is 2 = n. In the five class example the bound 5 is far from the smallest index 2.
Part (c) does not give disjointness in general. The sum can be above 1 when the cosets overlap, as in the example.

results.name: Finite nilpotent groups: normalizer growth, normal Sylow subgroups, and direct products of p-groups
results.statement: Let G be a finite group. The following five statements are equivalent. (1) G is nilpotent: the upper central series reaches G. (2) Normalizer condition: every proper subgroup H of G is properly contained in its normalizer N_G(H). (3) Every maximal subgroup of G is normal. (4) Every Sylow subgroup of G is normal. (5) G is the internal direct product of its Sylow subgroups, one for each prime that divides |G|.
hypotheses: G is a finite group.
In (5), each Sylow subgroup is unique by (4), so the direct product is well defined.
A maximal subgroup is a proper subgroup that is not contained in any other proper subgroup.

prerequisites.reason: Step 4 and 5 apply the Frattini argument to a normal maximal subgroup and its Sylow subgroup.
Step 11 uses that the center of a nontrivial finite p-group is not trivial.

definitions.name: upper central series
definitions.text: Z_0 = 1. Z_{i+1} is the set of x in G such that xZ_i is in the center of G/Z_i. Equivalently [x,g] is in Z_i for all g. G is nilpotent if Z_c = G for some c.

definitions.name: normalizer N_G(H)
definitions.text: N_G(H) = {g : gHg⁻¹ = H}. It is the largest subgroup in which H is normal.

definitions.name: internal direct product
definitions.text: G is the internal direct product of normal subgroups P_1,…,P_r if every element is a unique product x_1⋯x_r with x_i in P_i. Then elements of different P_i commute.

/-- A finite group is nilpotent iff the normalizer condition holds, and iff all maximal groups are
normal and iff all Sylow groups are normal and iff the group is the direct product of its Sylow
groups. -/
theorem Group.isNilpotent_of_finite_tfae :
    List.TFAE
      [IsNilpotent G, NormalizerCondition G, ∀ H : Subgroup G, IsCoatom H → H.Normal,
        ∀ (p : ℕ) (_hp : Fact p.Prime) (P : Sylow p G), (↑P : Subgroup G).Normal,
        Nonempty
          ((∀ p : (Nat.card G).primeFactors, ∀ P : Sylow p G, (↑P : Subgroup G)) ≃* G)] := by
  tfae_have 1 → 2 := @normalizerCondition_of_isNilpotent _ _
  tfae_have 2 → 3
  | h, H => NormalizerCondition.normal_of_coatom H h
  tfae_have 3 → 4
  | h, p, _, P => Sylow.normal_of_all_max_subgroups_normal h _
  tfae_have 4 → 5
  | h => Nonempty.intro (Sylow.directProductOfNormal fun {p hp hP} => h p hp hP)
  tfae_have 5 → 1
  | ⟨e⟩ => isNilpotent_of_product_of_sylow_group e
  tfae_finish

theorem Group.isNilpotent_of_product_of_sylow_group
    (e : (∀ p : (Nat.card G).primeFactors, ∀ P : Sylow p G, (↑P : Subgroup G)) ≃* G) :

  let ps := (Nat.card G).primeFactors

    intro p P
    have : Fact (Nat.Prime ↑p) := Fact.mk <| Nat.prime_of_mem_primeFactors p.2
    exact P.isPGroup'.isNilpotent
  exact nilpotent_of_mulEquiv e

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: (1) ⇒ (2). Let Z_0 ≤ Z_1 ≤ … ≤ Z_c = G be the upper central series. Let H be a proper subgroup. Let i be the largest index with Z_i ≤ H. Then i < c, and Z_{i+1} is not contained in H. Choose z in Z_{i+1} with z not in H.

Let h be in H. By the definition of Z_{i+1}, the commutator zhz⁻¹h⁻¹ is in Z_i. Also Z_i ≤ H. So zhz⁻¹ = (zhz⁻¹h⁻¹)h is in H. Thus z normalizes H. So z is in N_G(H) but not in H, and H is properly contained in N_G(H).
(2) ⇒ (3). Let M be a maximal subgroup. By (2), M is properly contained in N_G(M). Because M is maximal, N_G(M) = G. So M is normal.

(3) ⇒ (4). Suppose a Sylow p-subgroup P is not normal. Then N_G(P) ≠ G. Because G is finite, N_G(P) lies in a maximal subgroup M. By (3), M is normal in G. The group P lies in N_G(P), so P lies in M, and P is a Sylow p-subgroup of M, since its order is the largest power of p that divides |G|.
By the Frattini argument for the normal subgroup M and its Sylow subgroup P, G = M·N_G(P). But N_G(P) ≤ M, so G = M. This contradicts that M is proper. So every Sylow subgroup is normal.

(4) ⇒ (5). Let p_1,…,p_r be the primes that divide |G|. By (4) and the Sylow conjugacy theorem, each prime p has exactly one Sylow subgroup P_p, and it is normal. For p ≠ q, the groups P_p and P_q have coprime orders, so P_p ∩ P_q = 1.
Elements of different P_p commute. If a is in P_p and b is in P_q, the commutator aba⁻¹b⁻¹ is in P_q, since P_q is normal, and in P_p, since P_p is normal. So it lies in P_p ∩ P_q = 1.

Define f : P_{p_1}×…×P_{p_r} → G by f(x_1,…,x_r) = x_1⋯x_r. By step 7, f is a homomorphism. Suppose f(x_1,…,x_r) = 1. Fix j. Then x_j = (∏_{i≠j} x_i)⁻¹. The order of the right side divides the product of the orders of the x_i with i ≠ j, because these elements commute. That product is coprime to p_j. The order of x_j is a power of p_j. So x_j = 1, and f is injective.
The order of the domain is ∏|P_{p_i}| = ∏ p_i^{a_i} = |G|. So f is a bijection, and G is the internal direct product of the P_p. This proves (5).

(5) ⇒ (1). First, every finite p-group P is nilpotent. We use induction on |P|. If |P| = 1 this is clear. If |P| > 1, the center Z(P) is not trivial by the fixed point congruence. The quotient P/Z(P) is a smaller p-group. By induction its upper central series reaches P/Z(P). The preimage of Z_i(P/Z(P)) is Z_{i+1}(P). So the upper central series of P reaches P.

Next, a direct product of two nilpotent groups is nilpotent. For A × B we have Z_i(A×B) = Z_i(A)×Z_i(B), by induction on i, because (a,b) commutes with (a′,b′) modulo Z_i(A)×Z_i(B) if and only if each coordinate does. If Z_c(A) = A and Z_d(B) = B, then Z_{max(c,d)}(A×B) = A×B.
In (5), G is isomorphic to the direct product of the P_p. Each P_p is a p-group, so it is nilpotent by step 10. By step 11, G is nilpotent. This completes the cycle (1) ⇒ (2) ⇒ (3) ⇒ (4) ⇒ (5) ⇒ (1).

worked_application.title: Which small groups are nilpotent
worked_application.goal: Decide nilpotency of D₄, S₃, A₄, S₄, ℤ₃×ℤ₄ and S₃×ℤ₂ by the upper central series, the Sylow counts and the normalizer condition.
hypotheses: D₄ is the dihedral group of order 8. A₄ and S₄ are the alternating and symmetric groups.
The groups ℤ₃×ℤ₄ and S₃×ℤ₂ have order 12.
A computer calculation lists the upper central series orders, the number of Sylow subgroups, and the proper subgroups equal to their own normalizer.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: All six groups are finite, so the five conditions are equivalent. One failed or one valid condition decides each group.

steps.text: D₄. The upper central series has orders 1, 2, 8. It reaches D₄ in two steps, so D₄ is nilpotent of class 2. It has one Sylow 2-subgroup, itself. No proper subgroup equals its own normalizer.

ℤ₃×ℤ₄. This group is abelian, so Z_1 = G and the series has orders 1, 12. It has one Sylow 2-subgroup and one Sylow 3-subgroup. Both are normal, and the group is the product ℤ₄×ℤ₃ of them. So it is nilpotent.
S₃. The upper central series stays at order 1, so S₃ is not nilpotent. It has 3 Sylow 2-subgroups, so a Sylow subgroup is not normal. Each of the 3 subgroups of order 2 equals its own normalizer.

A₄. The center is trivial and the series stays at order 1. A₄ has 4 Sylow 3-subgroups, so they are not normal. The 4 subgroups of order 3 are self normalizing. The Sylow 2-subgroup is the normal Klein group of order 4, but one normal Sylow subgroup is not enough.
S₄. The center is trivial. S₄ has 3 Sylow 2-subgroups and 4 Sylow 3-subgroups. Seven proper subgroups, of orders 6 and 8, equal their own normalizers. So S₄ is not nilpotent.

S₃×ℤ₂. The upper central series has orders 1, 2, 2 and stops at order 2 ≠ 12. It has 3 Sylow 2-subgroups. So this group of order 12 is not nilpotent, even though its center is not trivial. A nontrivial center does not give nilpotency.

worked_application.result: D₄ and ℤ₃×ℤ₄ are nilpotent. S₃, A₄, S₄ and S₃×ℤ₂ are not. In every case the five conditions give the same answer.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: The theorem is for finite groups. An infinite nilpotent group need not have a normal Sylow subgroup structure, and the normalizer condition does not imply nilpotency for infinite groups.
Condition (5) uses all primes of |G|. A group with one normal Sylow subgroup need not be nilpotent, as A₄ shows.
The theorem gives no bound on the nilpotency class. It only tells whether the class is finite.

results.name: Symmetric groups of degree at least 5 are not solvable, because the alternating group is perfect
results.statement: Let X be a set with at least 5 elements. For finite X with n elements, the alternating group A_n equals its own commutator subgroup, so the derived series of S_n is S_n > A_n = A_n = … and never reaches 1. Hence S_n and A_n are not solvable for n ≥ 5. For any set X with at least 5 elements, the group of all permutations of X is not solvable.

steps.text: A_n is generated by 3-cycles for n ≥ 3. Every element of A_n is a product of an even number of transpositions. Group the transpositions in pairs. We show that each pair is a product of 3-cycles.

Pairs of transpositions. (a b)(a b) = 1. (a b)(b c) is a 3-cycle on {a,b,c} for distinct a, b, c. For disjoint transpositions, (a b)(c d) = (a b)(b c)·(b c)(c d), because (b c)(b c) = 1. This is a product of two 3-cycles. So every element of A_n is a product of 3-cycles.

Every 3-cycle is a commutator in A_n for n ≥ 5. Let ρ = (a b c). Choose two other points d, e, which exist because n ≥ 5. Put σ = (b c)(d e). Then σ is a product of two transpositions, so σ is in A_n. Also ρ is in A_n.
Conjugation by σ swaps b and c and fixes a. So σρσ⁻¹ = (a c b) = ρ⁻¹. Then the commutator is σρσ⁻¹ρ⁻¹ = ρ⁻¹ρ⁻¹ = ρ⁻² = ρ, because ρ³ = 1. So ρ = [σ,ρ] lies in [A_n,A_n].
By steps 1 to 4, every generator of A_n lies in [A_n,A_n]. So A_n ≤ [A_n,A_n]. The other inclusion is clear, so A_n = [A_n,A_n] for n ≥ 5.

The commutator subgroup of S_n. The sign map S_n → {±1} is a homomorphism to an abelian group, so its kernel A_n contains all commutators. So [S_n,S_n] ≤ A_n. Also A_n = [A_n,A_n] ≤ [S_n,S_n]. So [S_n,S_n] = A_n.

Derived series. S_n^(1) = A_n. By step 5, A_n^(k) = A_n for all k ≥ 0. So S_n^(k) = A_n for all k ≥ 1. The group A_n is not trivial, because it contains the 3-cycle (1 2 3). So the series never reaches 1, and S_n and A_n are not solvable.

Arbitrary sets. Let X have at least 5 elements and let Sym(X) be the group of all permutations of X. Choose 5 points of X. The permutations that fix every other point form a subgroup isomorphic to S_5.
A subgroup of a solvable group is solvable, because H^(k) ≤ G^(k) for all k. If Sym(X) were solvable, then S_5 would be solvable. This contradicts step 7. So Sym(X) is not solvable.

results.name: Iwasawa criterion for the simplicity of a perfect primitive permutation group
results.statement: Let G be a group that acts faithfully on a set X with at least 2 points. Assume the action is primitive: it is transitive and the only blocks are the singletons and X. Assume that for each x in X there is an abelian subgroup T(x) of G with T(gx) = gT(x)g⁻¹ for all g in G and x in X, and that the subgroups T(x) generate G. Then every normal subgroup N of G that acts non trivially on X contains the commutator subgroup [G,G]. If G is also perfect, G = [G,G], then G is simple.
hypotheses: G acts faithfully: only the identity fixes every point of X.
|X| ≥ 2, so G is not trivial.
A block is a subset B of X such that, for every g in G, the sets gB and B are equal or disjoint.
The groups T(x) are abelian. They need not lie in the stabilizer of x.

definitions.name: primitive action
definitions.text: A transitive action is primitive if every block is a singleton or all of X. Equivalently the point stabilizers are maximal subgroups.

definitions.name: perfect group
definitions.text: G is perfect if G = [G,G], that is, if G has no non trivial abelian quotient.

definitions.name: Iwasawa family
definitions.text: A family (T(x)) of abelian subgroups with T(gx) = gT(x)g⁻¹, that generate G. It lets the action detect the commutator subgroup.

/-- The Iwasawa criterion for simplicity -/
theorem isSimpleGroup [Nontrivial M] (is_perfect : commutator M = ⊤)
    [IsQuasiPreprimitive M α] (IwaS : IwasawaStructure M α) (is_faithful : FaithfulSMul M α) :
    IsSimpleGroup M := by
  apply IsSimpleGroup.mk
  intro N nN
  cases or_iff_not_imp_left.mpr (IwaS.commutator_le N) with
  | inl h =>
    refine Or.inl (N.eq_bot_iff_forall.mpr fun n hn => ?_)
    apply is_faithful.eq_of_smul_eq_smul
    intro x
    rw [one_smul]
    exact Set.eq_univ_iff_forall.mp h x ⟨n, hn⟩
  | inr h => exact Or.inr (top_le_iff.mp (le_trans (ge_of_eq is_perfect) h))

/-- The Iwasawa criterion : If a quasiprimitive action of a group G on X
  has an Iwasawa structure, then any normal subgroup that acts nontrivially
  contains the group of commutators. -/
theorem commutator_le (IwaS : IwasawaStructure M α) [IsQuasiPreprimitive M α]
    (N : Subgroup M) [nN : N.Normal] (hNX : MulAction.fixedPoints N α ≠ .univ) :
    commutator M ≤ N := by
  have is_transN := IsQuasiPreprimitive.isPretransitive_of_normal hNX
  have ntα : Nontrivial α := nontrivial_of_fixedPoints_ne_univ hNX
  obtain a : α := Nontrivial.to_nonempty.some
  apply nN.commutator_le_of_self_sup_commutative_eq_top ?_ (IwaS.is_comm a)
  -- We have to prove that N ⊔ IwaS.T x = ⊤
  rw [eq_top_iff, ← IwaS.is_generator, iSup_le_iff]
  intro x
  obtain ⟨g, rfl⟩ := MulAction.exists_smul_eq N a x
  rw [Subgroup.smul_def, IwaS.is_conj g a]
  rintro _ ⟨k, hk, rfl⟩
  have hg' : ↑g ∈ N ⊔ IwaS.T a := Subgroup.mem_sup_left (Subtype.mem g)
  have hk' : k ∈ N ⊔ IwaS.T a := Subgroup.mem_sup_right hk
  exact (N ⊔ IwaS.T a).mul_mem ((N ⊔ IwaS.T a).mul_mem hg' hk') ((N ⊔ IwaS.T a).inv_mem hg')
