proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Let N be a normal subgroup of G. Look at the orbits of N on X. For g in G and x in X we have g(Nx) = (gNg⁻¹)(gx) = N(gx). So g maps the N-orbit of x onto the N-orbit of gx. Thus any two sets g(Nx) and Nx are equal or disjoint, because orbits of N are equal or disjoint. So each N-orbit is a block.

By primitivity each N-orbit is a singleton or X. Suppose some N-orbit Nx is a singleton. For any point y = gx and any n in N, we have n(gx) = g(g⁻¹ng)x = gx, because g⁻¹ng is in N and fixes x. Here we used that G is transitive. So N fixes every point.

Because the action is faithful, N = 1 in the case of step 2. Otherwise, all N-orbits are equal to X. So N acts non trivially exactly when N is transitive. From now on assume N acts non trivially, so N is transitive on X.
Fix a in X. Put K = N·T(a). Because N is normal, K is a subgroup of G. Let x be any point of X. By transitivity of N there is n in N with x = na. Then T(x) = nT(a)n⁻¹.
Each element nkn⁻¹ with k in T(a) lies in K. Indeed n and n⁻¹ lie in N ≤ K, and k lies in T(a) ≤ K. The set K is a subgroup, so it contains the product nkn⁻¹. So T(x) ≤ K for every x.

The groups T(x) generate G. So K = G, which means G = N·T(a). Then G/N is the image of T(a), because every coset gN has the form tN with t in T(a). So G/N is a quotient of the abelian group T(a), and G/N is abelian.
A quotient G/N is abelian if and only if [G,G] ≤ N. So [G,G] ≤ N. This is the first claim.

Now assume G is perfect. Let N be a normal subgroup. Either N acts trivially, and then N = 1 by faithfulness, or N acts non trivially, and then N ≥ [G,G] = G, so N = G. Because G is not trivial, G is simple.

worked_application.title: A₅ is simple by the Iwasawa criterion
worked_application.goal: Take G = A₅ acting on X = {1,2,3,4,5}. For each x, let T(x) be the Klein group of the double transpositions that fix x. Check all hypotheses and conclude that A₅ is simple.
hypotheses: A₅ is the group of even permutations of 5 points. It has order 60.
T(x) = {1} together with the 3 double transpositions that fix x. It has order 4.
A computer enumeration checks the hypotheses.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Each hypothesis of the criterion can be checked on this finite group. Then simplicity follows without a list of conjugacy classes.

steps.text: Faithful and primitive. A₅ acts faithfully, because a permutation that fixes 5 points is the identity. The action is transitive, since A₅ contains the 3-cycles on every triple. A block has a size that divides 5. So a block has size 1 or 5. The action is primitive.
Abelian. T(x) is the Klein four group on the 4 points other than x, so it is abelian. There are 5 such groups, each of order 4.

Conjugation. For g in A₅, the conjugate gT(x)g⁻¹ consists of double transpositions that fix gx. The conjugate has 4 elements, and so does T(gx). So gT(x)g⁻¹ = T(gx). A computer check confirms this for all 60 elements g and all 5 points.

Generation. The double transpositions (a b)(c d) fix the fifth point e, so they lie in T(e). A₅ has 15 double transpositions, and they all lie in the union of the T(x). The group they generate has order 60 by a computer count. The product (a b)(c d)·(a b)(c e) = (c d)(c e) is a 3-cycle on {c,d,e}. So all 3-cycles are in the group, and 3-cycles generate A₅.
Perfect. The commutator subgroup of A₅ has order 60 (the full group). Every element of A₅ is a commutator. This is the statement that A₅ is perfect.
By the criterion, a normal subgroup N of A₅ is trivial or equal to A₅. A computer check agrees: the normal closure of every non identity element has order 60. So A₅ is simple of order 60.
Failure of a hypothesis. For S₅ the same groups T(x) generate A₅ only, of order 60, not S₅. Also S₅ is not perfect. The criterion does not apply, and S₅ has the normal subgroup A₅.

worked_application.result: The five Klein groups T(x) satisfy the criterion. The group A₅ is simple. For S₅ the generation hypothesis and the perfectness hypothesis fail, and S₅ is not simple.

limitations: The criterion needs abelian subgroups T(x) that generate G. For A_6 acting on 6 points there is no such family, so the criterion does not prove A_6 simple on this action.
The proof gives simplicity only with perfectness. Perfectness must be checked separately.
The source formulates quasi-primitivity, which is weaker than primitivity. This entry uses primitivity and so states a special case.

results.name: Engel theorem: ad-nilpotent Lie algebras are nilpotent
results.statement: Let F be a field. Let V be a non zero finite-dimensional F-vector space. Let L be a Lie subalgebra of gl(V) such that every x in L is a nilpotent endomorphism of V. Then there is a non zero v in V with xv = 0 for all x in L. Also V has a basis in which every x in L is strictly upper triangular, and the product of any dim V elements of L is 0. Consequently, a finite-dimensional Lie algebra g is nilpotent if and only if ad(x) is a nilpotent endomorphism of g for every x in g.
hypotheses: F is any field. No assumption on the characteristic is needed.
V is finite-dimensional and non zero.
The bracket on L is the commutator [x,y] = xy - yx.
For the last claim, g is a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over F.

/-- *Engel's theorem*.

Note that this implies all traditional forms of Engel's theorem via
`LieModule.nontrivial_max_triv_of_isNilpotent`, `LieModule.isNilpotent_iff_forall`,
`LieAlgebra.isNilpotent_iff_forall`. -/
theorem LieAlgebra.isEngelian_of_isNoetherian [IsNoetherian R L] : LieAlgebra.IsEngelian R L := by
  intro M _i1 _i2 _i3 _i4 h
  rw [← isNilpotent_range_toEnd_iff R]
  let L' := (toEnd R L M).range
  replace h : ∀ y : L', IsNilpotent (y : Module.End R M) := by
    rintro ⟨-, ⟨y, rfl⟩⟩
    simp [h]
  change LieModule.IsNilpotent L' M
  let s := {K : LieSubalgebra R L' | LieAlgebra.IsEngelian R K}
  have hs : s.Nonempty := ⟨⊥, LieAlgebra.isEngelian_of_subsingleton⟩
  suffices ⊤ ∈ s by
    rw [← isNilpotent_of_top_iff (R := R)]
    apply this M
    simp [LieSubalgebra.toEnd_eq, h]
  have : ∀ K ∈ s, K ≠ ⊤ → ∃ K' ∈ s, K < K' := by
    rintro K (hK₁ : LieAlgebra.IsEngelian R K) hK₂
    apply LieAlgebra.exists_engelian_lieSubalgebra_of_lt_normalizer hK₁
    apply lt_of_le_of_ne K.le_normalizer
    rw [Ne, eq_comm, K.normalizer_eq_self_iff, ← Ne, ←
      LieSubmodule.nontrivial_iff_ne_bot R K]
    have : Nontrivial (L' ⧸ K.toLieSubmodule) := Submodule.Quotient.nontrivial_iff.2 <| by simpa
    have : LieModule.IsNilpotent K (L' ⧸ K.toLieSubmodule) := by
      refine hK₁ _ fun x => ?_
      have hx := LieAlgebra.isNilpotent_ad_of_isNilpotent (h x)
      apply Module.End.IsNilpotent.mapQ ?_ hx
      intro X HX
      simp only [LieSubalgebra.coe_toLieSubmodule, LieSubalgebra.mem_toSubmodule] at HX
      simp only [LieSubalgebra.coe_toLieSubmodule, Submodule.mem_comap, ad_apply,
        LieSubalgebra.mem_toSubmodule]
      exact LieSubalgebra.lie_mem K x.prop HX
    exact nontrivial_max_triv_of_isNilpotent R K (L' ⧸ K.toLieSubmodule)
  have _i5 : IsNoetherian R L' := by
    refine isNoetherian_of_surjective (LieHom.rangeRestrict (toEnd R L M)).toLinearMap ?_
    simp only [LinearMap.range_eq_top]
    exact LieHom.surjective_rangeRestrict (toEnd R L M)
  obtain ⟨K, hK₁, hK₂⟩ := (LieSubalgebra.wellFoundedGT_of_noetherian R L').has_min s hs
  obtain rfl : K = ⊤ := by grind
  exact hK₁

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Part 1, common kernel vector. We use induction on dim L. If L = 0, any non zero v works. Now let dim L ≥ 1, and assume the claim for all Lie algebras of smaller dimension that satisfy the hypothesis, for every non zero space.

Let K be a maximal proper subalgebra of L. It exists because the zero subalgebra is proper and L is finite-dimensional. For x in K, define λx and ρx on End(V) by λx(a) = xa and ρx(a) = ax. These commute, and both are nilpotent because x is nilpotent. So ad(x) = λx - ρx is nilpotent on End(V), by the binomial formula for commuting nilpotent maps.

The map ad(x) sends L to L and K to K when x is in K. So it induces a nilpotent endomorphism of the quotient space L/K. Thus K acts on L/K by nilpotent operators. The image of K in gl(L/K) is a Lie subalgebra of dimension at most dim K, which is less than dim L. The space L/K is non zero.

By the induction hypothesis there is a non zero class y + K in L/K with [x,y] in K for all x in K. So y is in the normalizer N(K) of K in L, and y is not in K. Now N(K) is a subalgebra, and it strictly contains K. By maximality, N(K) = L. So K is an ideal of L.

The quotient L/K has dimension 1. To see this, take any 1-dimensional subspace of L/K and let S be its preimage in L. Because K is an ideal, [S,S] lies in K, so S is a subalgebra. It strictly contains K. So S = L by maximality. Hence L/K is 1-dimensional. Write L = K + Fz.

Let W = {v in V : xv = 0 for all x in K}. Because dim K < dim L, the induction hypothesis shows W is non zero. For x in K and w in W we have x(zw) = z(xw) + [x,z]w = 0, because [x,z] is in K. So zW lies in W.

The element z is nilpotent, so its restriction to the non zero space W is nilpotent. A nilpotent endomorphism of a non zero space has a non zero kernel vector. So there is a non zero w in W with zw = 0. Then xw = 0 for all x in K and for z. Hence xw = 0 for all x in L. This proves Part 1.

Part 2, flag and nilpotent action. We use induction on dim V. Let V1 be the non zero space of common kernel vectors from Part 1. If V1 = V, then all x in L are 0 and the claim is clear. Otherwise L acts on V/V1 by nilpotent operators, and the image of L in gl(V/V1) is a Lie subalgebra. The induction hypothesis gives a basis of V/V1 in which L is strictly upper triangular.

Lift this basis of V/V1 and put a basis of V1 in front of it. Every x in L kills V1, and maps each lifted vector into the span of V1 and the earlier lifted vectors. So x is strictly upper triangular in this basis. A product of n = dim V strictly upper triangular n×n matrices is 0.
Part 3, the criterion for g. Suppose g is nilpotent, so C^k g = 0 for some k. Then ad(x)^(k-1)(y) lies in C^k g = 0 for all y, so ad(x) is nilpotent.

Conversely, suppose ad(x) is nilpotent for every x in g. Then ad(g) is a Lie subalgebra of gl(g) consisting of nilpotent endomorphisms. By Part 2, any product of n = dim g operators ad(x1)...ad(xn) is 0. Now C^(n+1) g is spanned by the elements [x1,[x2,[...,[xn,y]]]], and each of these equals ad(x1)...ad(xn)(y) = 0. So C^(n+1) g = 0, and g is nilpotent.

worked_application.title: Engel theorem for the Heisenberg algebra and for sl2
worked_application.goal: Compare n₃, the strictly upper triangular 3×3 matrices, with the algebra spanned by e, f in sl₂. Find a common kernel vector in the first case and show that none exists in the second.
hypotheses: n₃ has basis x = E12, y = E23, z = E13.
e = E12 and f = E21 in 2×2 matrices.
The field is Q.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The theorem predicts a common kernel vector exactly when the algebra consists of nilpotent matrices. Direct checks on small algebras show both outcomes.

steps.text: The bracket of n₃. We have [x,y] = E12E23 - E23E12 = E13 = z. Also [x,z] = 0 and [y,z] = 0. So C¹ = n₃ has dimension 3, C² = span(z) has dimension 1 and C³ = 0. Thus n₃ is nilpotent.
Nilpotent elements. A general element is a·x + b·y + c·z. It is strictly upper triangular, so its cube is 0. So the hypothesis of the theorem holds for n₃ in gl₃.

Common kernel. We have x e2 = e1, x e1 = x e3 = 0, y e3 = e2, y e1 = y e2 = 0, and z e3 = e1, z e1 = z e2 = 0. Only e1 and its multiples are killed by x, y and z together. The theorem is satisfied with v = e1. The flag span(e1) ⊂ span(e1,e2) ⊂ Q³ gives strictly upper triangular form.

The algebra generated by e and f. Both e = E12 and f = E21 are nilpotent. But e + f is the matrix with rows (0,1) and (1,0), whose square is the identity. So e + f is not nilpotent, and the algebra generated by e and f in gl₂ is sl₂ with a non nilpotent element. The hypothesis fails.
No common kernel. The kernel of e is span(e1) and the kernel of f is span(e2). They meet only in 0. So there is no common kernel vector, as expected.

The criterion for ad. In the 2-dimensional algebra with [h,e] = e, ad(h) has e as eigenvector with eigenvalue 1, so ad(h) is not nilpotent. The algebra is not nilpotent, because C^k g = span(e) for all k ≥ 2. This agrees with Part 3.

worked_application.result: The Heisenberg algebra has nilpotency class 2 and a common kernel vector. The algebra with e + f has no common kernel vector. The 2-dimensional non abelian algebra is not nilpotent, and ad(h) is not nilpotent.

limitations: The statement is for finite-dimensional spaces. The source proves a more general version for Noetherian modules over a commutative ring.
The theorem fails when the algebra is only solvable. The algebra with [h,e] = e is solvable but not nilpotent.
The theorem needs every element of L to be nilpotent, not only the generators. The sum of two nilpotent matrices can be invertible.

results.name: Normal form theorem for free groups by confluence of cancellation
results.statement: Let S be a set. A word on S is a finite list of letters s or s⁻¹ with s in S. Let F(S) be the quotient of the set of words by the equivalence relation generated by inserting or deleting a pair s s⁻¹ or s⁻¹ s. Then every class in F(S) contains exactly one reduced word, that is, a word with no adjacent pair s s⁻¹ or s⁻¹ s. The product of two classes is the class of the reduced form of the concatenation of any representatives. In particular a word represents the identity if and only if it reduces to the empty word. If |S| = k is finite, the number of reduced words of length n ≥ 1 is 2k(2k-1)^(n-1).
hypotheses: S is any set, finite or infinite.
Words are finite lists. The empty word is allowed.
F(S) is the free group on S. The inverse of a class is the class of the reversed word with each letter inverted.
The count formula needs k = |S| finite and n ≥ 1.

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Termination. Each cancellation step lowers the length by 2. So every chain of steps from a word w is finite, and it ends at a reduced word. This shows that every word w can be reduced to at least one reduced word.

Local confluence. Let w → u and w → v be two single steps at positions i and j. If the two deleted pairs do not overlap, then deleting both gives one word t, and u → t and v → t. This is the case |i - j| ≥ 2.

Overlap. If j = i + 1, the three letters at positions i, i+1, i+2 have the form x x⁻¹ x, for a letter x. Deleting the first two leaves x. Deleting the last two also leaves x. So u = v. Thus in all cases u and v have a common descendant.

Uniqueness of the reduced form. We show by induction on the length of w that all maximal chains from w end in the same reduced word. If w is reduced, the only chain is the empty chain. Otherwise let two chains start with steps w → u and w → v. By step 2 and step 3 there is t with u →* t and v →* t. Let r be a reduced word reached from t.

The word u is shorter than w. By induction, every maximal chain from u ends at the same reduced word. The chain u →* t →* r is maximal, so every chain from u ends at r. In the same way every chain from v ends at r. So every chain from w ends at r.

Invariance on classes. Call this unique word red(w). If w → w′ by one step, then red(w) = red(w′), because the chain from w′ extends to a chain from w. The equivalence relation is generated by steps and their reverse. So red is constant on each class.

Each class contains a reduced word, namely red(w). Two reduced words in one class have equal red values. But red of a reduced word is the word itself. So the two words are equal. Thus each class contains exactly one reduced word.

Product and identity. The product of classes is defined by concatenation of representatives. So the product has the reduced representative red(uv). A word w represents the identity class if and only if red(w) = red(empty) = empty.

Counting. A reduced word of length n on k letters and their inverses is a sequence x1,...,xn from 2k symbols with x(i+1) not equal to the inverse of xi. There are 2k choices for x1 and then 2k - 1 choices for each later letter. So the count is 2k(2k-1)^(n-1).

worked_application.goal: Find reduced forms of products in F(a,b), show that the commutator [a,b] is not the identity, and count reduced words.

worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The normal form turns questions about equality in F(a,b) into questions about a word that has no cancellation.

steps.text: The commutator is reduced. The word a b a⁻¹ b⁻¹ has no adjacent inverse pair. So it is its own normal form, and it is not the empty word. Hence c is not the identity, so a and b do not commute in F(a,b).
The square. The word c c = a b a⁻¹ b⁻¹ a b a⁻¹ b⁻¹ has the junction b⁻¹ a, which is not an inverse pair. So c² is reduced and has length 8. Likewise c³ has reduced length 12.
The inverse. The word c · c⁻¹ = a b a⁻¹ b⁻¹ · b a b⁻¹ a⁻¹ cancels step by step to the empty word. The reduction of the product is empty, so c⁻¹ is the inverse of c.
A word problem. Take w = a b b⁻¹ a a⁻¹ a⁻¹. Delete b b⁻¹ and then a a⁻¹. We get a a⁻¹ and then the empty word. So w represents the identity.
Counting. With k = 2 the formula gives 4, 12, 36, 108, 324 reduced words for n = 1,...,5. An exhaustive enumeration of all 4^n words for n ≤ 5 gives the same numbers.

worked_application.result: The commutator [a,b] has reduced length 4 and is not the identity. The powers c², c³ have reduced lengths 8 and 12. There are 4·3^(n-1) reduced words of length n.

steps.text: Setup. Choose a transversal t1,...,tn for the cosets of Z. For g in G, left multiplication by g permutes the cosets. Write g·ti = t(σg(i))·zi(g) with σg a permutation of {1,...,n} and zi(g) in Z.

The transfer is a homomorphism. Compute gh·ti = g·t(σh(i))·zi(h) = t(σg σh (i))·z(σh(i))(g)·zi(h). Since Z is central, the Z-part is a product in Z. So zi(gh) = z(σh(i))(g)·zi(h). Now take the product over i. As σh is a permutation, we get V(gh) = V(g)·V(h), where V(g) = ∏ zi(g). The target Z is abelian, so the order of the product does not matter.

V(g) equals gⁿ. Split {1,...,n} into cycles of σg. Take a cycle (i1 → i2 → ... → im) of length m. Apply g repeatedly: gᵐ·t(i1) = t(i1)·z(i1)(g)·z(i2)(g)···z(im)(g). The element z(i1)···z(im) is central. So gᵐ = t(i1)·(z product)·t(i1)⁻¹ = z(i1)(g)···z(im)(g).

Multiply over all cycles c with lengths mc. We get V(g) = ∏ g^(mc). The lengths add up to n. All the factors are powers of g, so they commute. Hence V(g) = g^(Σ mc) = gⁿ. This proves that g ↦ gⁿ is a homomorphism G → Z.
The exponent. The target Z is abelian, so G' lies in the kernel of the homomorphism V. Thus gⁿ = 1 for all g in G'.

Few commutators. For central elements z, w we have [xz, yw] = [x,y]. So [x,y] depends only on the cosets xZ and yZ. There are at most n² such pairs of cosets. So the set C of all commutators has at most n² elements, and G' is generated by C. The set C is closed under inverses, because [x,y]⁻¹ = [y,x].
The group G' is finitely generated, by at most n² elements. The subgroup G'∩Z is the kernel of the map G' → G/Z. Thus G'/(G'∩Z) embeds in G/Z, so the index of G'∩Z in G' is at most n.

By the Schreier lemma, G'∩Z is generated by at most n·n² = n³ elements. It is abelian, and each of its elements has order dividing n by step 5. A finite generating set of r elements in an abelian group of exponent dividing n gives at most nʳ elements. So G'∩Z is finite.
Finally |G'| = [G' : G'∩Z]·|G'∩Z| ≤ n·nʳ, which is finite. This proves the theorem.

Check of the bound. The proof gives |G'| ≤ n·nʳ, which is a weak bound. The true value 3 is much smaller. The element orders in G are 1 (once), 2 (once), 3 (twice), 4 (six times) and 6 (twice).

results.name: Conjugacy classes of the symmetric group by cycle type, with class sizes
results.statement: Let n ≥ 1. Two permutations in Sₙ are conjugate if and only if they have the same cycle type, that is, the same multiset of cycle lengths when fixed points are counted as cycles of length 1. So the conjugacy classes of Sₙ correspond to the partitions of n. If a permutation σ has mₖ cycles of length k, then its centralizer has order ∏ k^(mₖ)·mₖ!, and its conjugacy class has n!/∏ k^(mₖ)·mₖ! elements.
hypotheses: n is a positive integer.
Sₙ is the group of all permutations of {1,...,n}.
The cycle type of σ lists the lengths of all cycles of σ, with the fixed points as 1-cycles. The lengths add up to n.
mₖ is the number of cycles of length k, and Σ k·mₖ = n.

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Conjugation relabels. Let σ have a cycle (a1 a2 ... ak). For g in Sₙ, we have gσg⁻¹(g(ai)) = g(σ(ai)) = g(a(i+1)). So gσg⁻¹ has the cycle (g(a1) ... g(ak)). Thus gσg⁻¹ has the same cycle lengths as σ, and conjugate permutations have the same cycle type.

Same type implies conjugate. Let σ and τ have the same cycle type. Write σ and τ as products of disjoint cycles, with the fixed points as 1-cycles. For each length k, pair the cycles of length k in σ with those in τ by any bijection. Write each pair as (a1...ak) and (b1...bk).

Define g(ai) = bi for all such pairs. Since the cycles of σ cover {1,...,n} exactly once, and the same holds for τ, the map g is a well defined bijection. By step 1, gσg⁻¹ has the cycles (b1...bk) of τ. So gσg⁻¹ = τ, and σ and τ are conjugate.

Count of the centralizer. Let σ have cycles of lengths with multiplicities mₖ. Let g commute with σ, so gσg⁻¹ = σ. By step 1, g maps each cycle of σ onto a cycle of σ of the same length. So g determines a bijection from the cycles of length k to themselves, for each k, and there are mₖ! of these.

Given the cycle bijection, g also sends the first point of each cycle of length k to one of the k points of the image cycle. This gives k choices for each of the mₖ cycles. After these choices the rest of g is fixed, because g(σʲ(a)) = σʲ(g(a)). Every such choice commutes with σ. Hence |C(σ)| = ∏ k^(mₖ)·mₖ!.

Class size. Sₙ acts on itself by conjugation. The stabilizer of σ is C(σ), and the orbit of σ is its conjugacy class. By the orbit-stabilizer theorem, the class has n!/|C(σ)| = n!/∏ k^(mₖ)·mₖ! elements.

Number of classes. By steps 1 to 3, the classes of Sₙ correspond one to one to the cycle types. A cycle type is a multiset of positive integers that add up to n. That is a partition of n. So the number of classes is p(n), the number of partitions of n.

steps.text: Types in S₅. There are 7 partitions of 5. They are 1⁵, 2·1³, 2²·1, 3·1², 3·2, 4·1 and 5.
Centralizer orders. For 1⁵ the order is 5! = 120. For 2·1³ it is 2·3! = 12. For 2²·1 it is 2²·2!·1 = 8. For 3·1² it is 3·2! = 6. For 3·2 it is 3·2 = 6. For 4·1 it is 4. For 5 it is 5.
Class sizes. Divide 120 by each centralizer order. We get 1, 10, 15, 20, 20, 30 and 24. The sum is 1 + 10 + 15 + 20 + 20 + 30 + 24 = 120, as the class equation requires.

Number of classes. S₅ has p(5) = 7 classes. S₆ has p(6) = 11 classes. The enumeration of the 720 permutations of S₆ also gives 11 types, and all class sizes agree with the formula.
A consequence. The number of commuting pairs in S₅ is k(S₅)·|S₅| = 7·120 = 840, by the standard count of commuting pairs.

results.name: A nondegenerate Killing form excludes all non zero solvable ideals
results.statement: Let g be a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over a field F. Let κ(x,y) = tr(ad(x) ad(y)) be its Killing form. If κ is nondegenerate, then every solvable ideal of g is 0, and in particular every abelian ideal of g is 0.
hypotheses: g is finite-dimensional over a field F of any characteristic.
κ is nondegenerate if κ(x,y) = 0 for all y in g forces x = 0.
An ideal I of g is solvable if its derived series I ⊇ [I,I] ⊇ [[I,I],[I,I]] ⊇ ... reaches 0.

results.proof_status: source declaration inspected; authored proof awaits inference review; no local Lean check

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Assume κ is nondegenerate and let I be a solvable ideal of g with I ≠ 0. We seek a contradiction. Because I is solvable, its derived series reaches 0. Let k be the largest index with I⁽ᵏ⁾ ≠ 0, so that I⁽ᵏ⁺¹⁾ = 0. Put J = I⁽ᵏ⁾.

J is an ideal of g. We show by induction that each I⁽ʲ⁾ is an ideal of g. For j = 0 this is the assumption. If a, b are in I⁽ʲ⁾ and x is in g, the Jacobi identity gives [x,[a,b]] = [[x,a],b] + [a,[x,b]]. Both terms are in [I⁽ʲ⁾, I⁽ʲ⁾] because [x,a] and [x,b] are in I⁽ʲ⁾. So I⁽ʲ⁺¹⁾ is an ideal.
J is abelian, because [J,J] = I⁽ᵏ⁺¹⁾ = 0. Also J ≠ 0 by the choice of k.
Let x be in J and y be in g. Look at the composite φ = ad(x) ad(y) acting on g. For any z in g, we have ad(y)(z) in g, and ad(x) sends g into J because J is an ideal. So φ maps g into J.

Apply φ twice. The second application of φ starts with an element w = φ(z) of J. Then ad(y) w lies in J because J is an ideal. Then ad(x)(ad(y) w) = [x, ad(y) w] = 0 because J is abelian and both x and ad(y) w are in J. So φ² = 0.
A nilpotent endomorphism has trace 0. This holds over any field, because its characteristic polynomial is a power of t. So κ(x,y) = tr(φ) = 0.
Thus κ(x,y) = 0 for all y in g. By nondegeneracy, x = 0. This holds for every x in J, so J = 0. This contradicts J ≠ 0. Hence I = 0.
An abelian ideal is solvable, because its derived series is I ⊇ 0. So an abelian ideal is also 0.

worked_application.title: Killing forms of sl₂, its Borel subalgebra and the Heisenberg algebra
worked_application.goal: Compute κ for sl₂, for the Borel subalgebra b = span(h,e), and for the Heisenberg algebra. See when κ is nondegenerate and which abelian ideals appear.
hypotheses: The field is Q.
sl₂ has basis e, h, f with [h,e] = 2e, [h,f] = -2f, [e,f] = h.
b has basis h, e with [h,e] = 2e.
The Heisenberg algebra has basis x, y, z with [x,y] = z and z central.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The theorem predicts that a degenerate κ is the only way to hide a non zero abelian ideal. The three examples show both situations.

steps.text: The Killing form of sl₂. We have ad(h) = diag(2, 0, -2) on (e, h, f), so κ(h,h) = 4 + 0 + 4 = 8. The product ad(e)ad(f) sends e to 2e, h to 2h, f to 0, so κ(e,f) = 4. We also have κ(e,e) = κ(f,f) = κ(h,e) = κ(h,f) = 0.
Determinant. In the basis (e,h,f) the matrix of κ has rows (0,0,4), (0,8,0), (4,0,0). Its determinant is -128, which is not 0 over Q. So κ is nondegenerate.
Consequence for sl₂. By the theorem, sl₂ has no non zero solvable ideal. In particular no abelian ideal exists. For example span(e) is not an ideal, because [f,e] = -h.

The Borel subalgebra. For b = span(h,e), ad(h) has eigenvalues 0 and 2, so κ(h,h) = 4. Next ad(e) is nilpotent and sends h to -2e and e to 0, so ad(e)ad(y) = 0 for y in b. Thus κ(e,y) = 0 for all y in b. The matrix of κ has rows (4,0) and (0,0), and it is degenerate.
The hidden ideal. The kernel of κ is span(e). It is an abelian ideal, since [h,e] = 2e. This is the ideal J of the proof, the last non zero term of the derived series of b.

The Heisenberg algebra. Each ad(w) sends x and y into span(z) and sends z to 0. So ad(w)ad(w′) maps g into span(z) and kills z. Its square is 0, so its trace is 0. Thus κ is identically 0. The center span(z) is an abelian ideal, as the theorem allows.

worked_application.result: The Killing form of sl₂ has determinant -128, so it is nondegenerate and sl₂ has no non zero solvable ideal. The Borel subalgebra and the Heisenberg algebra have a degenerate form with a non zero abelian ideal.

limitations: Only one direction is proved. The converse, that a Lie algebra with trivial radical has nondegenerate Killing form, needs characteristic 0 and the Cartan criterion. It is not proved here and it fails in positive characteristic.
The theorem is for finite-dimensional algebras, because the trace must exist.
The proof gives only that J = 0, so that I = 0. It does not describe the structure of g.

results.name: Multivariate division algorithm for a monomial order
results.statement: Let R be a nonzero commutative ring and let ≼ be a monomial order on the monomials x^a of R[x_1,…,x_n]. Let b_1,…,b_s be polynomials whose leading coefficients are units of R. Then for every f in R[x_1,…,x_n] there are polynomials g_1,…,g_s and r with f = g_1 b_1 + … + g_s b_s + r. Also deg(g_i b_i) ≼ deg f for every i with g_i b_i ≠ 0, and no monomial of r is divisible by the leading monomial of any b_i. Here deg means the largest exponent vector under ≼.
hypotheses: R is a commutative ring with 1 ≠ 0.
≼ is a total order on exponent vectors a in ℕ^n. It satisfies a ≼ b ⇒ a+c ≼ b+c, and 0 ≼ a for all a.
Each b_i is nonzero and its leading coefficient is a unit of R.
The result gives existence only. It does not give uniqueness of g_i or r.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: The proof uses only the compatibility and positivity of the monomial order and a self contained Dickson argument. No catalog theorem is cited.
concepts: degree, leading monomial and leading coefficient

definitions.name: monomial order
definitions.text: A total order ≼ on exponent vectors in ℕ^n such that a ≼ b implies a+c ≼ b+c, and such that 0 ≼ a for all a.

definitions.name: degree, leading monomial and leading coefficient
definitions.text: For a nonzero polynomial f, deg f is the largest exponent vector in its support under ≼. The leading coefficient is the coefficient of x^{deg f}.

definitions.name: divisibility of monomials
definitions.text: x^a divides x^c if a ≤ c in every coordinate. Then x^c = x^a·x^{c−a}.

definitions.name: remainder
definitions.text: The polynomial r in the division. None of its monomials is divisible by the leading monomial of a divisor b_i.

/-- Division by a family of multivariate polynomials
whose leading coefficients are invertible with respect to a monomial order -/
theorem div {ι : Type*} {b : ι → MvPolynomial σ R}
    (hb : ∀ i, IsUnit (m.leadingCoeff (b i))) (f : MvPolynomial σ R) :
    ∃ (g : ι →₀ (MvPolynomial σ R)) (r : MvPolynomial σ R),
      f = Finsupp.linearCombination _ b g + r ∧
        (∀ i, m.degree (b i * (g i)) ≼[m] m.degree f) ∧
        (∀ c ∈ r.support, ∀ i, ¬ (m.degree (b i) ≤ c)) := by
  by_cases! hb' : ∃ i, m.degree (b i) = 0
  · obtain ⟨i, hb0⟩ := hb'
    use Finsupp.single i ((hb i).unit⁻¹ • f), 0
    constructor
    · simp only [Finsupp.linearCombination_single, smul_eq_mul, add_zero]
      simp only [smul_mul_assoc, ← smul_eq_iff_eq_inv_smul, Units.smul_isUnit]
      nth_rewrite 2 [eq_C_of_degree_eq_zero hb0]
      rw [mul_comm, smul_eq_C_mul]
    constructor
    · intro j
      by_cases hj : j = i
      · apply le_trans degree_mul_le
        simp only [hj, hb0, Finsupp.single_eq_same, zero_add]
        apply le_of_eq
        simp only [EmbeddingLike.apply_eq_iff_eq]
        apply degree_smul_of_isRegular (Units.isRegular _)
      · simp only [Finsupp.single_eq_of_ne hj, mul_zero, degree_zero, map_zero]
        apply bot_le
    · simp
  by_cases hf0 : f = 0
  · refine ⟨0, 0, by simp [hf0], ?_, by simp⟩
    intro b
    simp only [Finsupp.coe_zero, Pi.zero_apply, mul_zero, degree_zero, map_zero]
    exact bot_le
  by_cases! hf : ∃ i, m.degree (b i) ≤ m.degree f
  · obtain ⟨i, hf⟩ := hf
    have deg_reduce : m.degree (m.reduce (hb i) f) ≺[m] m.degree f := by
      apply degree_reduce_lt (hb i) hf
      intro hf0'
      apply hb' i
      simpa [hf0'] using hf
    obtain ⟨g', r', H'⟩ := div hb (m.reduce (hb i) f)
    use g' +
      Finsupp.single i (monomial (m.degree f - m.degree (b i)) ((hb i).unit⁻¹ * m.leadingCoeff f))
    use r'
    constructor
    · rw [map_add, add_assoc, add_comm _ r', ← add_assoc, ← H'.1]
      simp [reduce]
    constructor
    · rintro j
      simp only [Finsupp.coe_add, Pi.add_apply]
      rw [mul_add]
      apply le_trans degree_add_le
      simp only [sup_le_iff]
      constructor
      · exact le_trans (H'.2.1 _) (le_of_lt deg_reduce)
      · classical
        rw [Finsupp.single_apply]
        split_ifs with hc
        · subst j
          grw [degree_mul_le, map_add, degree_monomial_le, ← map_add, add_tsub_cancel_of_le hf]
        · simp only [mul_zero, degree_zero, map_zero]
          exact bot_le
    · exact H'.2.2
  · suffices ∃ (g' : ι →₀ MvPolynomial σ R), ∃ r',
        (m.subLTerm f = Finsupp.linearCombination (MvPolynomial σ R) b g' + r') ∧
        (∀ i, m.degree ((b i) * (g' i)) ≼[m] m.degree (m.subLTerm f)) ∧
        (∀ c ∈ r'.support, ∀ i, ¬ m.degree (b i) ≤ c) by
      obtain ⟨g', r', H'⟩ := this
      use g', r' + monomial (m.degree f) (m.leadingCoeff f)
      constructor
      · simp [← add_assoc, ← H'.1, subLTerm]
      constructor
      · exact fun b ↦ le_trans (H'.2.1 b) (degree_sub_LTerm_le f)
      · intro c hc i
        by_cases hc' : c ∈ r'.support
        · exact H'.2.2 c hc' i
        · convert hf i
          classical
          have := MvPolynomial.support_add hc
          rw [Finset.mem_union, Classical.or_iff_not_imp_left] at this
          simpa only [Finset.mem_singleton] using support_monomial_subset (this hc')
    by_cases hf'0 : m.subLTerm f = 0
    · refine ⟨0, 0, by simp [hf'0], ?_, by simp⟩
      intro b
      simp only [Finsupp.coe_zero, Pi.zero_apply, mul_zero, degree_zero, map_zero]
      exact bot_le
    · exact (div hb) (m.subLTerm f)
termination_by WellFounded.wrap m.wellFoundedLT_syn (m.toSyn (m.degree f))
decreasing_by
  · exact deg_reduce
  · apply degree_sub_LTerm_lt
    intro hf0
    apply hf'0
    simp only [subLTerm, sub_eq_zero]
    nth_rewrite 1 [eq_C_of_degree_eq_zero hf0, hf0]
    simp

steps.text: Lemma A: the monomial order is a well order. First show that every infinite sequence a^1, a^2, … in ℕ^n has indices i < j with a^i ≤ a^j in every coordinate. Take a subsequence that does not decrease in coordinate 1. This exists because every sequence in ℕ has a non decreasing subsequence, since ℕ is well ordered and we can pick the minimum of the tail repeatedly. In this subsequence take a further subsequence that does not decrease in coordinate 2, and so on to coordinate n. The last subsequence does not decrease in any coordinate.

Now suppose a^1 ≻ a^2 ≻ … is a strictly decreasing sequence for ≼. By step 1 there are i < j with a^i ≤ a^j in every coordinate. Then a^j = a^i + c with c in ℕ^n. Since 0 ≼ c, adding a^i gives a^i ≼ a^j. This contradicts a^j ≺ a^i. So no infinite strictly decreasing sequence exists. A total order with this property is a well order, so every non empty set of exponent vectors has a least element and induction on the degree is allowed.

Setup of the induction. We prove the claim by induction on deg f, for f ≠ 0. The case f = 0 is trivial with all g_i = 0 and r = 0. Let f ≠ 0 with d = deg f and leading coefficient c. Assume the claim for every nonzero polynomial whose degree is ≺ d. The claim is also true for the zero polynomial.

Case 1: some b_i has deg b_i ≤ d in every coordinate. Put e = d − deg b_i, ℓ = lc(b_i) and u = c·ℓ⁻¹·x^e. Every monomial of b_i is ≼ deg b_i. By compatibility with addition, every monomial of u·b_i is ≼ deg b_i + e = d. The coefficient of x^d in u·b_i is c·ℓ⁻¹·ℓ = c. Put f′ = f − u·b_i. All monomials of f′ are ≼ d, and the coefficient of x^d in f′ is c − c = 0. So f′ = 0 or deg f′ ≺ d.

Apply the induction hypothesis to f′. We get f′ = Σ_j g′_j b_j + r′ with deg(g′_j b_j) ≼ deg f′ ≺ d and with r′ free of monomials divisible by any deg b_j. Put g_i = g′_i + u, g_j = g′_j for j ≠ i, and r = r′. Then f = Σ g_j b_j + r. The monomials of g_i b_i = g′_i b_i + u b_i are all ≼ d. For j ≠ i the bound deg(g_j b_j) ≼ d holds already. The remainder r = r′ has the required property.

Case 2: no b_i has deg b_i ≤ d. Write f = c·x^d + f_1, where f_1 = 0 or deg f_1 ≺ d. Apply the induction hypothesis to f_1. We get f_1 = Σ_j g_j b_j + r_1 with deg(g_j b_j) ≼ deg f_1 ≺ d = deg f, and r_1 free of divisible monomials. Put r = r_1 + c·x^d. Then f = Σ g_j b_j + r.

In Case 2 the monomials of r are those of r_1 and possibly x^d. The monomial x^d is not divisible by any deg b_i, because Case 2 assumes deg b_i ≤ d fails for all i. The monomials of r_1 have the property by hypothesis. So no monomial of r is divisible by any leading monomial of a b_i. This completes the induction.

Final bound. The induction proves deg(g_i b_i) ≼ deg f whenever g_i b_i ≠ 0. Each step lowers the degree of the working polynomial strictly in the well order of step 2. So the process ends. Each step of the process is the algorithm: subtract a multiple of some b_i that cancels the leading term, or move the leading term to the remainder.

worked_application.title: Divide x²y + xy² + y² by xy − 1 and y² − 1
worked_application.goal: Use the lex order x > y on ℚ[x,y]. Divide f = x²y + xy² + y² by (b_1, b_2) = (xy − 1, y² − 1) and then by (b_2, b_1). Compare the two remainders and decide ideal membership with a Gröbner basis.
hypotheses: R = ℚ, so all nonzero leading coefficients are units.
The leading monomials are xy for b_1 and y² for b_2.
deg f = (2,1), the monomial x²y.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Both divisors have leading coefficient 1, which is a unit of ℚ. So the theorem gives a division for every order of the divisors.

steps.text: Order (b_1, b_2). The leading monomial x²y of f is divisible by xy. Step by step: f − x·(xy−1) = xy² + y² + x. Then subtract y·(xy−1) to get y² + x + y. Then subtract (y²−1) to get x + y + 1. So the quotients are g_1 = x + y and g_2 = 1, and the remainder is r = x + y + 1.

Check the identity: (x+y)(xy−1) + (y²−1) = x²y − x + xy² − y + y² − 1. Adding x + y + 1 gives x²y + xy² + y² = f. The degrees are deg(g_1 b_1) = (2,1) ≼ (2,1) and deg(g_2 b_2) = (0,2) ≺ (2,1), as the theorem says.
The remainder x + y + 1 has monomials x, y and 1. None is divisible by xy or y². So r satisfies the remainder condition.

Order (b_2, b_1). The leading monomial x²y is not divisible by y², so the algorithm uses b_1 first and subtracts x·(xy−1) to get xy² + y² + x. The leading monomial xy² is divisible by y², so it subtracts x·(y²−1), then (y²−1) again, and ends with 2x + 1. Hence f = (x+1)(y²−1) + x(xy−1) + 2x + 1. Check: (x+1)(y²−1) = xy² − x + y² − 1 and x(xy−1) = x²y − x. The sum plus 2x + 1 equals f. A computer algebra system returns the same quotients (x+1, x) and remainder 2x + 1.

The two remainders differ: x + y + 1 and 2x + 1. Their difference y − x lies in the ideal (b_1, b_2), because the reduced lex Gröbner basis of this ideal is {x − y, y² − 1}. So the remainder depends on the order of the divisors here, and {b_1, b_2} is not a Gröbner basis.

Divide f by the Gröbner basis {x − y, y² − 1}. Replace x by y to get 2y³ + y². Reduce y³ = y(y²−1) + y to get 2y + 1. The remainder 2y + 1 is not zero, so f is not in the ideal. The division by (b_1, b_2) could not prove this, because a non zero remainder there says nothing.

worked_application.result: The division gives f = (x+y)(xy−1) + (y²−1) + (x+y+1) and also f = (x+1)(y²−1) + x(xy−1) + (2x+1). The ideal membership test with the Gröbner basis shows f is not in (xy−1, y²−1), with remainder 2y + 1.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: The remainder and the quotients are not unique in general. The example shows two different remainders for two divisor orders.
A zero remainder proves membership in the ideal. A non zero remainder proves non membership only if the divisors form a Gröbner basis.
The leading coefficients must be units. Over ℤ, dividing x by 2x gives no quotient with a remainder free of divisible monomials.
The proof needs a monomial order, so 0 ≼ a for all a. A non well ordered term order, such as one that prefers negative exponents, makes the process loop.

results.name: Resultant: Bezout identity, common factors and elimination
results.statement: Let R be a commutative ring. Let f and g be polynomials in R[y] with deg f ≤ m and deg g ≤ n, where m+n ≥ 1. Let Res_{m,n}(f,g) be the determinant of the Sylvester matrix. (a) There are p and q in R[y] with deg p < n, deg q < m and f·p + g·q = Res_{m,n}(f,g). (b) If R = K is a field and f, g are nonzero with m = deg f and n = deg g, then Res(f,g) = 0 if and only if f and g have a common factor of positive degree. (c) Let A be a commutative ring, let f, g be in A[y] with y-degrees exactly m and n, and let a be a point where A maps to a field K and the leading coefficients of f and g in y do not vanish. Then Res_y(f,g)(a) = 0 if and only if f(a,y) and g(a,y) have a common root in an algebraic closure of K. Also every common zero of f and g satisfies Res_y(f,g) = 0.
hypotheses: R is a commutative ring. The polynomials are in one variable y with coefficients in R.
In (a) the degrees satisfy deg f ≤ m and deg g ≤ n, and m+n ≥ 1.
In (b) the base is a field and the exact degrees are used. Both f and g are nonzero.
In (c) the leading coefficients of f and g in y must not vanish at the chosen point.

definitions.name: Sylvester matrix and resultant
definitions.text: Let f = Σ_{i≤m} f_i y^i and g = Σ_{j≤n} g_j y^j. The Sylvester matrix is the (m+n)×(m+n) matrix whose first n rows are the shifts of the coefficient row (f_m,…,f_0) and whose last m rows are the shifts of (g_n,…,g_0), with the highest power first. Res_{m,n}(f,g) is its determinant.

definitions.name: the map Φ
definitions.text: Φ sends a pair (p,q) with deg p < n and deg q < m to f·p + g·q, which has degree < m+n. Its matrix in the monomial bases is the transpose of the Sylvester matrix. So det Φ = Res_{m,n}(f,g).

definitions.name: adjugate
definitions.text: For a square matrix M, adj(M) satisfies adj(M)·M = M·adj(M) = det(M)·I. It exists over any commutative ring.

definitions.name: elimination
definitions.text: A polynomial in A that lies in the ideal (f,g) of A[y] is zero at every common zero of f and g. The resultant is such a polynomial.

/-- Note that if `n = m = 0` then `resultant = 1` but `f` and `g` aren't necessarily coprime. -/
lemma exists_mul_add_mul_eq_C_resultant
    (f g : R[X]) (hf : f.natDegree ≤ m) (hg : g.natDegree ≤ n) (H : m ≠ 0 ∨ n ≠ 0) :
    ∃ p q, p.degree < ↑n ∧ q.degree < ↑m ∧ f * p + g * q = C (f.resultant g m n) := by
  nontriviality R
  let X := adjSylvester f g ⟨1, by simpa [Polynomial.mem_degreeLT,
    ← Nat.cast_add, Nat.pos_iff_ne_zero, not_and_or, -not_and] using H⟩
  have : ((sylvesterMap f g hf hg X)).1 = _ :=
    congr(($(sylvesterMap_comp_adjSylvester f g hf hg) _).1)
  refine ⟨X.2, X.1, by simpa [-SetLike.coe_mem] using X.2.2,
    by simpa [-SetLike.coe_mem] using X.1.2, by simpa [Algebra.smul_def] using this⟩

lemma resultant_eq_zero_iff {K : Type*} [Field K] {f g : K[X]} :
    resultant f g = 0 ↔ (f ≠ 0 ∨ g ≠ 0) ∧ ¬ IsCoprime f g := by
  obtain rfl | hf := eq_or_ne f 0
  · obtain rfl | hg := eq_or_ne g 0; · simp
    simpa [isCoprime_zero_left, isUnit_iff, hg, natDegree_eq_zero] using
      show (∀ x, C x ≠ g) ↔ ∀ x ≠ 0, C x ≠ g by aesop
  have H : (C f.leadingCoeff⁻¹ * f).Monic := by
    rw [Monic, ← coeff_natDegree, natDegree_C_mul (by simpa), coeff_C_mul]; simp [hf]
  have := isUnit_resultant_iff_isCoprime (f := C f.leadingCoeff⁻¹ * f) (g := g) H
  rw [resultant_C_mul_left, IsUnit.mul_iff, natDegree_C_mul (by simp [hf]),
    isCoprime_mul_unit_left_left (isUnit_C.mpr (by simp [hf]))] at this
  simp [← this, hf]

steps.text: Part (a). Let N = m+n ≥ 1 and let M be the matrix of Φ in the monomial bases. Let e be the coordinate vector of the constant polynomial 1, which is a basis vector of the target. Put v = adj(M)·e. Then M·v = M·adj(M)·e = det(M)·e. Let (p,q) be the pair with coordinate vector v. Then deg p < n, deg q < m, and f·p + g·q is the polynomial with coordinate vector det(M)·e. This polynomial is the constant Res_{m,n}(f,g).

Part (b), direction ⇐. Let h be a common factor of positive degree, f = h·f_1 and g = h·g_1. Then deg f_1 < m and deg g_1 < n. Take p = g_1 and q = −f_1. Both are nonzero. Then f·p + g·q = h f_1 g_1 − h g_1 f_1 = 0. So Φ has a non zero vector in its kernel, and det Φ = 0 because Φ is a square matrix over a field. Hence Res(f,g) = 0.

Part (b), direction ⇒. Suppose Res(f,g) = 0. Over a field a square matrix with zero determinant has a non zero kernel vector. So there is a pair (p,q) ≠ (0,0) with deg p < n, deg q < m and f·p = −g·q. If p = 0, then g·q = 0 and q = 0 because g ≠ 0 and K[y] has no zero divisors. This is false, so p ≠ 0. In the same way q ≠ 0.

Let d = gcd(f,g) in K[y]. Write f = d·f_1 and g = d·g_1 with f_1 and g_1 coprime. From f·p = −g·q we get f_1·p = −g_1·q after cancelling d. So g_1 divides f_1·p. Because g_1 and f_1 are coprime, g_1 divides p. Since p ≠ 0, we get deg g_1 ≤ deg p < n = deg g.
Therefore deg d = deg g − deg g_1 > 0. So f and g have the common factor d of positive degree. This proves (b).

Part (c). The determinant commutes with ring homomorphisms, so the resultant of the specialised polynomials f(a,y), g(a,y) with the formal degrees m and n equals Res_y(f,g)(a). By assumption the leading coefficients stay nonzero, so the specialised degrees are exactly m and n. Both specialised polynomials are nonzero. Apply (b) over the algebraic closure K̄. The resultant vanishes if and only if there is a common factor of positive degree in K̄[y]. Over K̄ a factor of positive degree has a root, and a common root gives a common linear factor. So the resultant vanishes if and only if there is a common root.

Elimination. By part (a) applied with R = A, there are p and q in A[y] with f·p + g·q = Res_y(f,g), which lies in A. If (a,b) is a common zero of f and g, evaluate the identity at (a,b). The left side is 0·p(a,b) + 0·q(a,b) = 0. So Res_y(f,g)(a) = 0.

worked_application.title: Intersect the circle with the hyperbola, and implicitize a nodal cubic
worked_application.goal: Eliminate y from x²+y²−1 = 0 and xy−1 = 0. Show an explicit Bezout identity. Show a resultant of integers that detects a common root modulo 3. Find the equation of the curve x = t²−1, y = t³−t.
hypotheses: A = ℚ[x] and f = y² + (x²−1) with m = 2, g = x·y − 1 with n = 1.
The integer polynomials f_2 = y²−3y+2 and g_4 = y²−5y+7.
The pair F = x−t²+1 and G = y−t³+t in ℚ[x,y][t].
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: In each case the polynomials are in one variable (y or t) over a commutative ring. The leading coefficients are checked in each step before part (c) is used.

steps.text: The Sylvester matrix has rows (1, 0, x²−1), (x, −1, 0), (0, x, −1). Its determinant is 1·1 + (x²−1)·x² = x⁴ − x² + 1. So Res_y(f,g) = x⁴ − x² + 1. A computer algebra system returns the same value.

Bezout identity from part (a): p = x², q = −xy − 1. Check: x²(y²+x²−1) − (xy+1)(xy−1) = x²y² + x⁴ − x² − x²y² + 1 = x⁴ − x² + 1. The degrees are deg p = 0 < 1 and deg q = 1 < 2. So the elimination ideal contains x⁴−x²+1.

Common zeros. If x is a root of x⁴−x²+1, then x ≠ 0 because the value at 0 is 1. The leading coefficients 1 and x are nonzero at this point. By part (c) the polynomials have a common root, namely y = 1/x, since f(x,1/x) = (x⁴−x²+1)/x² = 0. The polynomial x⁴−x²+1 is the cyclotomic polynomial Φ₁₂, so x is a primitive 12th root of unity. It has no real root, which agrees with x² + 1/x² ≥ 2 > 1 for real x.

Integers. Res(y²−3y+2, y²−5y+7) = 3, again by a determinant of the 4×4 Sylvester matrix. It is not zero, so the two polynomials are coprime over ℚ. Modulo 3 the resultant is 0. Indeed y = 1 is a root of both: 1−3+2 = 0 and 1−5+7 = 3 ≡ 0. So the polynomials share the factor y−1 over F₃. The primes dividing the resultant are the only primes where a common factor can appear.
For comparison, Res(y²−3y+2, y²−5y+6) = 0, and the gcd is y−2. Also Res(y²−3y+2, y²−5y+4) = 0, and the gcd is y−1. These agree with part (b).

Implicitization. Take F = x−t²+1 and G = y−t³+t, with leading coefficients −1 and −1 in t. They never vanish, so part (c) applies at every point (x,y) in ℂ². A computer algebra system gives Res_t(F,G) = x³ + x² − y². So (x,y) lies on the image of the map t ↦ (t²−1, t³−t) if and only if y² = x³ + x². A direct check: t² = x+1 gives y = t(t²−1) = t·x, so y² = (x+1)·x².

results.statement: Let R be a commutative ring. Let P_1,…,P_n be prime ideals and let I be an ideal with I ⊆ P_1 ∪ … ∪ P_n. Then I ⊆ P_j for some j. Equivalently, if I is not contained in any P_j, then I contains an element that lies in none of the P_j.

n ≥ 1 and every P_j is a prime ideal.

definitions.name: prime ideal

/-- Prime avoidance. Atiyah-Macdonald 1.11, Eisenbud 3.3, Matsumura Ex.1.6. -/
@[stacks 00DS]
theorem subset_union_prime {R : Type u} [CommRing R] {s : Finset ι} {f : ι → Ideal R} (a b : ι)
    (hp : ∀ i ∈ s, i ≠ a → i ≠ b → IsPrime (f i)) {I : Ideal R} :
    ((I : Set R) ⊆ ⋃ i ∈ (↑s : Set ι), f i) ↔ ∃ i ∈ s, I ≤ f i :=
  suffices ((I : Set R) ⊆ ⋃ i ∈ (↑s : Set ι), f i) → ∃ i, i ∈ s ∧ I ≤ f i by
    have aux := fun h => (bex_def.2 <| this h)
    simp_rw [exists_prop] at aux
    refine ⟨aux, fun ⟨i, his, hi⟩ ↦ Set.Subset.trans hi ?_⟩
    apply Set.subset_biUnion_of_mem (show i ∈ (↑s : Set ι) from his)
  fun h : (I : Set R) ⊆ ⋃ i ∈ (↑s : Set ι), f i => by
  classical
    by_cases has : a ∈ s
    · obtain ⟨t, hat, rfl⟩ : ∃ t, a ∉ t ∧ insert a t = s :=
        ⟨s.erase a, Finset.notMem_erase a s, Finset.insert_erase has⟩
      by_cases hbt : b ∈ t
      · obtain ⟨u, hbu, rfl⟩ : ∃ u, b ∉ u ∧ insert b u = t :=
          ⟨t.erase b, Finset.notMem_erase b t, Finset.insert_erase hbt⟩
        have hp' : ∀ i ∈ u, IsPrime (f i) := by
          intro i hiu
          refine hp i (Finset.mem_insert_of_mem (Finset.mem_insert_of_mem hiu)) ?_ ?_ <;>
              rintro rfl <;>
            solve_by_elim only [Finset.mem_insert_of_mem, *]
        rw [Finset.coe_insert, Finset.coe_insert, Set.biUnion_insert, Set.biUnion_insert, ←
          Set.union_assoc, subset_union_prime' hp'] at h
        rwa [Finset.exists_mem_insert, Finset.exists_mem_insert]
      · have hp' : ∀ j ∈ t, IsPrime (f j) := by
          intro j hj
          refine hp j (Finset.mem_insert_of_mem hj) ?_ ?_ <;> rintro rfl <;>
            solve_by_elim only [Finset.mem_insert_of_mem, *]
        rw [Finset.coe_insert, Set.biUnion_insert, ← Set.union_self (f a : Set R),
          subset_union_prime' hp', ← or_assoc, or_self_iff] at h
        rwa [Finset.exists_mem_insert]
    · by_cases hbs : b ∈ s
      · obtain ⟨t, hbt, rfl⟩ : ∃ t, b ∉ t ∧ insert b t = s :=
          ⟨s.erase b, Finset.notMem_erase b s, Finset.insert_erase hbs⟩
        have hp' : ∀ j ∈ t, IsPrime (f j) := by
          intro j hj
          refine hp j (Finset.mem_insert_of_mem hj) ?_ ?_ <;> rintro rfl <;>
            solve_by_elim only [Finset.mem_insert_of_mem, *]
        rw [Finset.coe_insert, Set.biUnion_insert, ← Set.union_self (f b : Set R),
          subset_union_prime' hp', ← or_assoc, or_self_iff] at h
        rwa [Finset.exists_mem_insert]
      rcases s.eq_empty_or_nonempty with rfl | hsne
      · rw [Finset.coe_empty, Set.biUnion_empty] at h
        exact (h I.zero_mem).elim
      · obtain ⟨i, his⟩ := hsne
        obtain ⟨t, _, rfl⟩ : ∃ t, i ∉ t ∧ insert i t = s :=
          ⟨s.erase i, Finset.notMem_erase i s, Finset.insert_erase his⟩
        have hp' : ∀ j ∈ t, IsPrime (f j) := by
          intro j hj
          refine hp j (Finset.mem_insert_of_mem hj) ?_ ?_ <;> rintro rfl <;>
            solve_by_elim only [Finset.mem_insert_of_mem, *]
        rw [Finset.coe_insert, Set.biUnion_insert, ← Set.union_self (f i : Set R),
          subset_union_prime' hp', ← or_assoc, or_self_iff] at h
        rwa [Finset.exists_mem_insert]

steps.text: Induction on n. For n = 1 the claim is the hypothesis. Let n ≥ 2 and assume the claim for n−1 primes. Suppose I ⊆ P_1 ∪ … ∪ P_n and I is not contained in any single P_j. We look for a contradiction.

Reduction. If I were contained in the union of the n−1 primes P_j with j ≠ i for some i, the induction hypothesis would give I ⊆ P_j for some j. This is excluded. So for every i there is an element x_i in I that lies in no P_j with j ≠ i. Because I lies in the union, x_i lies in P_i. So x_i ∈ P_i and x_i ∉ P_j for j ≠ i.

Case n = 2. Consider x_1 + x_2, which lies in I. If x_1 + x_2 ∈ P_1, then x_2 = (x_1 + x_2) − x_1 ∈ P_1. This contradicts x_2 ∉ P_1. If x_1 + x_2 ∈ P_2, then x_1 ∈ P_2, which contradicts x_1 ∉ P_2. So x_1 + x_2 is in neither prime. This contradicts I ⊆ P_1 ∪ P_2.

Case n ≥ 3. Put y = x_1 + x_2 x_3 ⋯ x_n, which lies in I because I is an ideal. The product x_2 ⋯ x_n lies in every P_j with j ≥ 2, because each P_j contains the factor x_j. It does not lie in P_1, because every x_i with i ≥ 2 lies outside the prime P_1 and a product of elements outside a prime is outside it.

The element y is not in P_1. Otherwise x_2 ⋯ x_n = y − x_1 would lie in P_1 because x_1 ∈ P_1. The element y is not in P_j for j ≥ 2. Otherwise x_1 = y − x_2 ⋯ x_n would lie in P_j because the product does. This contradicts x_1 ∉ P_j.
So y is an element of I outside all P_j. This contradicts I ⊆ P_1 ∪ … ∪ P_n. The assumption that I lies in no single P_j is false, which completes the induction.
Equivalent form. The contrapositive says: if I ⊄ P_j for every j, then I ⊄ P_1 ∪ … ∪ P_n. That is, some element of I lies outside every P_j.

worked_application.title: Avoid three primes in F₂[x,y] and in ℤ[x]
worked_application.goal: Find an element of the maximal ideal (x,y) of F₂[x,y] that lies in none of the primes (x), (y), (x+y). Then find an element of (6,x) in ℤ[x] outside (2), (3), (x). Show that the theorem fails for three non prime ideals.
hypotheses: R₃ = F₂[x,y]/(x²,xy,y²).
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: All ideals P_j and Q_j are prime, because the quotients F₂[y], F₂[x], ℤ/2[x], ℤ/3[x] and ℤ[x]/(x) ≅ ℤ are domains. The ideals I and J are not contained in any single one of them.

steps.text: The ideal I contains x, y and x+y, so it is not contained in (x), (y) or (x+y). Every linear form over F₂ is 0, x, y or x+y, so each nonzero linear form lies in one of the three primes. The theorem still says that I contains an element outside all three. Such an element has degree at least 2.

Take z = x² + xy + y². Set x = 0 in z to get y² ≠ 0, so z ∉ (x). Set y = 0 to get x² ≠ 0, so z ∉ (y). Set y = x to get x² + x² + x² = 3x² = x² ≠ 0 in characteristic 2, so z ∉ (x+y). The element z lies in I. This is the element the theorem predicts.

In ℤ[x], the ideal J = (6,x) is not contained in (2), because x ∉ (2). It is not in (3), because x ∉ (3). It is not in (x), because 6 ∉ (x). So the theorem gives an element of J outside all three primes. Take w = x + 6. Its constant term 6 is not zero, so w ∉ (x). Its coefficients 1 and 6 are not all even, so w ∉ (2). They are not all divisible by 3, so w ∉ (3).

Failure for non prime ideals. In R₃ the ideals (x) = {0,x}, (y) = {0,y} and (x+y) = {0,x+y} are each of order 2. The maximal ideal m = {0, x, y, x+y} has 4 elements and equals their union. But m is not contained in any one of them. None of the three ideals is prime, because for example R₃/(x) ≅ F₂[y]/(y²) has the zero divisor y.

Count check in R₃. The three ideals have 2 elements each and any two of them meet only in {0}. Their union has 3 nonzero elements plus 0, so it has 4 elements. This equals the order of m. So m is the union of the three ideals, and m is not inside any one of them.

worked_application.result: The element x² + xy + y² of (x,y) avoids the primes (x), (y) and (x+y). The element x + 6 of (6,x) avoids (2), (3) and (x). The three non prime ideals (x), (y), (x+y) of F₂[x,y]/(x²,xy,y²) cover the maximal ideal and none contains it.

limitations: The proof uses induction on the number of primes. It does not apply to an infinite union of primes.
At most two of the ideals may be non prime. The example in F₂[x,y]/(x²,xy,y²) has three non prime ideals and fails. The entry proves only the case with all primes.
The result is about containment, not about equality. It does not say that a union of ideals is an ideal.
Prime avoidance gives no bound on the degree or size of the avoiding element. The example shows that such an element can need a higher degree than the generators.

results.name: Basic opens of the prime spectrum and quasi-compactness
results.statement: Let R be a commutative ring and D(f) = {P prime : f ∉ P} the basic open set of f in Spec R. (a) D(f) is empty if and only if f is nilpotent. D(f) = Spec R if and only if f is a unit. (b) For any family (f_i), D(f) ⊆ ⋃ D(f_i) if and only if f lies in the radical of the ideal (f_i). In that case there are a finite set F and N ≥ 1 with f^N ∈ (f_i : i ∈ F), so D(f) ⊆ ⋃_{i∈F} D(f_i). (c) Every basic open set D(f) is quasi-compact. Spec R is quasi-compact. Every open cover of Spec R has a finite subcover.
hypotheses: R is a commutative ring with 1. If R = 0, then Spec R is empty and all statements hold.
Spec R carries the Zariski topology, whose closed sets are V(I) = {P : I ⊆ P}.
The result does not say that every open set is quasi-compact. The limitations show a counterexample.

prerequisites.reason: Parts (a) and (b) use that the nilradical of a ring is the intersection of its prime ideals. It is applied to R and to R/I.
Part (a) uses that every proper ideal lies in a maximal ideal, which is prime.

definitions.name: basic open set D(f)
definitions.text: D(f) = Spec R ∖ V(f). The sets D(f) form a basis of the Zariski topology, because every closed set is V(I) = ⋂_{f∈I} V(f).

definitions.name: radical of an ideal
definitions.text: √I = {f : f^N ∈ I for some N ≥ 1}. It equals the intersection of all primes that contain I.

definitions.name: quasi-compact
definitions.text: A space is quasi-compact if every open cover has a finite subcover. It needs no separation axiom.

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Part (a), first claim. D(f) is empty if and only if f lies in every prime ideal. The intersection of all prime ideals is the nilradical. So D(f) = ∅ if and only if f is nilpotent.

Part (a), second claim. If f is a unit, no proper ideal contains f, so D(f) = Spec R. Conversely let f be a non unit. Then (f) is a proper ideal. A proper ideal is contained in a maximal ideal, which is prime and contains f. So D(f) ≠ Spec R.

Part (b), set up. Let I be the ideal generated by all f_i. A prime P lies outside ⋃ D(f_i) if and only if every f_i is in P, that is, if and only if P ∈ V(I). A prime P lies outside D(f) if and only if f ∈ P. Taking complements, D(f) ⊆ ⋃ D(f_i) is equivalent to V(I) ⊆ V(f).

Now V(I) ⊆ V(f) means that f lies in every prime that contains I. Apply the nilradical theorem to R/I. The primes of R/I are the primes of R that contain I. So the intersection of the primes containing I is the radical √I. Hence the inclusion holds if and only if f ∈ √I.

Finite subcover in (b). If f ∈ √I, then f^N ∈ I for some N ≥ 1. An element of I is a finite combination f^N = Σ_{i∈F} a_i f_i with F finite. Then f^N lies in the ideal (f_i : i ∈ F). Apply the equivalence of the previous steps to this finite family. We get D(f) ⊆ ⋃_{i∈F} D(f_i).

Part (c), basic opens. Let D(f) be covered by open sets U_j. Every point P of D(f) has a basic neighbourhood D(g) ⊆ U_j for some j, because the sets D(g) form a basis. Let (D(g_k)) be all basic open sets in D(f) that lie in some U_j. These cover D(f). By (b) a finite subfamily covers D(f). Each member lies in some U_j. So finitely many U_j cover D(f).
Part (c), Spec R. Spec R = D(1). So Spec R is quasi-compact by the previous step. Every open cover of Spec R has a finite subcover.

worked_application.title: Basic opens in Spec ℤ, Spec ℤ/12 and Spec ℤ[x]

hypotheses: Spec ℤ/12 has two points, (2) and (3).
The family D(p), over all primes p, covers Spec ℤ.
The family D(x), D(x−1) in ℤ[x].
The inclusion D(xy) ⊆ D(x²) ∪ D(y²) in ℚ[x,y].

steps.text: In ℤ/12, 6² = 36 = 0, so 6 is nilpotent. By (a) D(6) = ∅. Indeed 6 lies in (2) and in (3). Also 5·5 = 25 = 1, so 5 is a unit, and D(5) = Spec. Indeed 5 is in neither (2) nor (3).

In ℤ/12, D(2) = {(3)} because 2 ∈ (2) and 2 ∉ (3). Also D(4) = {(3)}, which agrees with D(2²) = D(2). The sets D(2) and D(3) = {(2)} cover Spec ℤ/12. By (b) this must correspond to 1 ∈ (2,3). Indeed 3 − 2 = 1.

Spec ℤ has the points (0) and (q) for primes q. The sets D(q) for all primes q cover it. Every prime ideal (q) misses D(q), but it lies in D(p) for any prime p ≠ q, and (0) lies in all of them. By (c) finitely many suffice. The sets D(2) and D(3) work because 1 = 3 − 2. A prime (q) contains both 2 and 3 only if q divides both, which is impossible.

In ℤ[x], the sets D(x) and D(x−1) cover Spec ℤ[x], because x − (x−1) = 1. So no prime ideal of ℤ[x] contains both x and x−1. The sets D(2x) and D(3x−3) do not cover Spec ℤ[x]. Evaluation at x = 1 is a ring map ℤ[x] → ℤ. It sends 2x to 2 and 3x−3 to 0. So it maps the ideal (2x, 3x−3) into (2), and the ideal cannot contain 1. By (b) with f = 1, the two basic open sets do not cover.

In ℚ[x,y], take f = xy, f_1 = x², f_2 = y². Then f² = x²y² = y²·f_1, so f² ∈ (f_1, f_2) with N = 2. By (b) D(xy) ⊆ D(x²) ∪ D(y²). Also f itself is not in (x², y²), since all monomials of the ideal have x-degree ≥ 2 or y-degree ≥ 2. So N = 1 is not enough.

results.name: Minimal primes of a Noetherian ring and the irreducible components of V(I)
results.statement: Let R be a Noetherian commutative ring and I an ideal of R. (a) The set of minimal prime ideals over I is finite, say {P_1,…,P_r}, and √I = P_1 ∩ … ∩ P_r. No P_i contains another P_j. (b) V(I) = V(P_1) ∪ … ∪ V(P_r), and the sets V(P_i) are exactly the irreducible components of the closed set V(I) in Spec R. (c) For any ideal J, the closed set V(J) is irreducible if and only if √J is prime. The case I = R has r = 0.
hypotheses: R is Noetherian: every ascending chain of ideals stops.
V(I) has the Zariski topology as a subspace of Spec R.
An irreducible set is non empty and is not the union of two proper closed subsets. An irreducible component is a maximal irreducible subset.

steps.text: Existence of a finite prime decomposition of the radical. Let 𝒮 be the set of ideals I such that √I is not a finite intersection of prime ideals. The empty intersection is R. Suppose 𝒮 is not empty. Since R is Noetherian, 𝒮 has a maximal element I. We show this is impossible.

The ideal I is not R, because √R = R is the empty intersection. The ideal I is not prime, because then √I = I would be a one-term intersection. So there are a, b ∉ I with ab ∈ I. The ideals I + (a) and I + (b) are strictly larger than I. By maximality they are not in 𝒮. So √(I+(a)) and √(I+(b)) are finite intersections of primes.

Claim: √I = √(I+(a)) ∩ √(I+(b)). The inclusion ⊆ is clear. Let x lie in both radicals. Then x^k ∈ I + (a) and x^l ∈ I + (b) for some k, l. So x^{k+l} ∈ (I+(a))(I+(b)) ⊆ I + (ab) = I. Hence x ∈ √I. So √I is a finite intersection of primes, a contradiction. Thus 𝒮 is empty.

Irredundant form. Write √I = Q_1 ∩ … ∩ Q_s with primes Q_j. If Q_j ⊆ Q_k for some j ≠ k, remove Q_k. The intersection does not change. Repeat until no prime contains another. We get √I = P_1 ∩ … ∩ P_r with P_i ⊄ P_j for i ≠ j. If I = R, then r = 0.

Every prime Q ⊇ I contains some P_i. Suppose not. Choose x_i ∈ P_i ∖ Q for each i. Then x_1 ⋯ x_r lies in ∩ P_i = √I ⊆ Q, because Q ⊇ I and Q is radical. But Q is prime and no x_i is in Q, so x_1 ⋯ x_r ∉ Q. This is a contradiction.

The P_i are exactly the minimal primes over I. Each P_i contains √I ⊇ I. If Q is prime with I ⊆ Q ⊆ P_i, then Q contains some P_j. So P_j ⊆ Q ⊆ P_i, and the antichain condition gives j = i and Q = P_i. So P_i is minimal. Conversely, a minimal prime Q over I contains some P_i, which is a prime over I. Minimality gives Q = P_i. This proves (a).

Part (c). Let V(J) be irreducible. It is not empty, so J ≠ R and √J ≠ R. Let ab ∈ √J. Then V(J) ⊆ V(ab) = V(a) ∪ V(b). So V(J) = (V(J) ∩ V(a)) ∪ (V(J) ∩ V(b)), a union of two closed sets. By irreducibility V(J) ⊆ V(a), say. So a lies in every prime that contains J. By the nilradical theorem applied to R/J, a ∈ √J. Hence √J is prime.

Part (c), converse. Let √J = P be prime. Then V(J) = V(P) ≠ ∅. Suppose V(P) = V(J_1) ∪ V(J_2). Then P ∈ V(J_1) ∪ V(J_2), say P ∈ V(J_1), so J_1 ⊆ P. Every prime in V(P) contains P, hence contains J_1. So V(P) ⊆ V(J_1). Thus V(P) = V(J_1), and V(P) is irreducible.

Part (b). A prime Q lies in V(I) if and only if Q ⊇ I, if and only if Q contains some P_i. So V(I) = ∪ V(P_i). Each V(P_i) is irreducible by part (c). Next, V(P_i) ⊆ V(P_j) if and only if P_j ⊆ P_i, which happens only for i = j. So no V(P_i) lies in another V(P_j).

Let Z ⊆ V(I) be any irreducible subset. Its closure is irreducible and closed, so it equals V(J) with √J prime by part (c). Since V(J) ⊆ V(I), we get I ⊆ √J. The prime √J contains some P_i by the earlier step. Hence Z ⊆ V(J) ⊆ V(P_i). So every irreducible subset lies in some V(P_i), and no V(P_i) lies in another. Therefore the V(P_i) are exactly the maximal irreducible subsets of V(I).

worked_application.title: Components of V(xz, yz), of Spec ℤ/360 and of V(x², xy)
worked_application.goal: Find the minimal primes and the irreducible components for three ideals. Show a non Noetherian ring with infinitely many minimal primes.
hypotheses: R₁ = ℚ[x,y,z] and I₁ = (xz, yz).
R₂ = ℤ/360 and I₂ = (0).
R₃ = ℚ[x,y] and I₃ = (x², xy).
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The first three rings are quotients of polynomial rings or ℤ, so they are Noetherian. The fourth ring is not Noetherian, and it shows that the hypothesis is needed.

steps.text: For I₁, we claim (xz, yz) = (z) ∩ (x,y). The inclusion ⊆ is clear. If f = z·h lies in (x,y), then h ∈ (x,y) because z ∉ (x,y) and (x,y) is prime. So f ∈ z·(x,y) = (xz, yz). Both (z) and (x,y) are prime and neither contains the other.

So I₁ is radical, and its minimal primes are P_1 = (z) and P_2 = (x,y). By the theorem V(I₁) has two irreducible components. They are the plane {z = 0} of dimension 2 and the line {x = y = 0} of dimension 1. The line is not contained in the plane, because z ∉ (x,y) means the point set of the line has points with z ≠ 0.

For R₂ = ℤ/360, 360 = 2³·3²·5. The ideal √(0) is the ideal generated by 30. It equals (2) ∩ (3) ∩ (5) in ℤ/360. The minimal primes over (0) are (2), (3), (5). The space Spec R₂ has three points. They are closed, and they are its three irreducible components.

For I₃ = (x², xy), x² ∈ I₃ gives x ∈ √I₃, and I₃ ⊆ (x). So √I₃ = (x), which is prime. The only minimal prime is (x). V(I₃) is the line {x = 0}, irreducible. The ideal I₃ equals (x) ∩ (x², y), and the prime (x,y) = √(x²,y) is embedded. It does not appear among the minimal primes.

For R₄, a prime Q contains x_i x_j = 0 for all i ≠ j. So for each pair, x_i ∈ Q or x_j ∈ Q. Hence all but at most one x_i lie in Q. So Q ⊇ P_i = (x_j : j ≠ i) for some i. Each P_i is prime, since R₄/P_i ≅ k[x_i]. The P_i are pairwise incomparable, because x_i ∈ P_j ∖ P_i for j ≠ i. So R₄ has infinitely many minimal primes, which the theorem forbids for a Noetherian ring.

worked_application.result: The ideal (xz, yz) has the minimal primes (z) and (x,y). Spec ℤ/360 has three components. The ideal (x², xy) has one minimal prime (x) and one embedded prime (x,y). The ring k[x_1,x_2,…]/(x_i x_j : i ≠ j) has infinitely many minimal primes.

limitations: The decomposition √I = ∩ P_i forgets the multiplicity and the embedded primes. The ideal I is not the intersection of the P_i unless I is radical.
The Noetherian hypothesis is needed. The ring k[x_1,x_2,…]/(x_i x_j : i ≠ j) has infinitely many minimal primes.
Irreducible components are a statement about the topological space Spec R. They need not be disjoint, as the plane and the line in the example show.

results.name: Artinian rings: primes are maximal, there are finitely many, and the radical is nilpotent
results.statement: Let R be a commutative ring that satisfies the descending chain condition on ideals. (a) Every prime ideal of R is maximal. (b) R has only finitely many maximal ideals, so Spec R is a finite discrete space. (c) The Jacobson radical J, which is the intersection of the maximal ideals, equals the nilradical. There is k ≥ 1 with J^k = 0.
hypotheses: R is commutative with 1.
Every descending chain of ideals I_1 ⊇ I_2 ⊇ … stops.
The result does not assume that R is Noetherian.

prerequisites.reason: Parts (b) and (c) use that the nilradical is the intersection of all prime ideals.

definitions.name: Artinian ring
definitions.text: A ring in which every descending chain of ideals becomes constant.

definitions.name: Jacobson radical
definitions.text: The intersection J of all maximal ideals. An element j lies in J if and only if 1 − rj is a unit for all r in R.

definitions.name: nilpotent ideal
definitions.text: An ideal J with J^k = 0 for some k. The product J^k is the ideal generated by all products of k elements of J.

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Part (a). Let P be prime. The ring D = R/P is an Artinian domain, because ideals of D correspond to ideals of R that contain P. Take a ≠ 0 in D. The chain (a) ⊇ (a²) ⊇ (a³) ⊇ … stops, so a^n = a^{n+1} b for some n and some b. Then a^n (1 − ab) = 0. Since D is a domain and a^n ≠ 0, we get ab = 1. So every non zero element is a unit and D is a field. Hence P is maximal.
Part (b). Suppose there are infinitely many maximal ideals. Pick distinct maximal ideals m_1, m_2, … . The chain m_1 ⊇ m_1 ∩ m_2 ⊇ m_1 ∩ m_2 ∩ m_3 ⊇ … stops. So for some n, m_1 ∩ … ∩ m_n ⊆ m_{n+1}.

The prime m_{n+1} contains the product m_1 ⋯ m_n, since a product lies in the intersection. If m_{n+1} contained none of the m_i with i ≤ n, we could pick x_i ∈ m_i ∖ m_{n+1}. Then x_1 ⋯ x_n ∈ m_{n+1} contradicts primality. So m_i ⊆ m_{n+1} for some i ≤ n. Both are maximal, so m_i = m_{n+1}. This contradicts the choice of distinct ideals. So the number of maximal ideals is finite.

By part (a) the prime ideals and the maximal ideals are the same. By part (b) there are finitely many. Every point of Spec R is closed, because a maximal ideal m has V(m) = {m}. A finite space with all points closed is discrete.
Part (c), equality. The nilradical is the intersection of all primes. By part (a) the primes are the maximal ideals. So the nilradical equals the intersection of the maximal ideals, which is J.

Part (c), nilpotence. The chain J ⊇ J² ⊇ J³ ⊇ … stops. So there is n with I := J^n = J^{n+1}. We claim I = 0. Suppose I ≠ 0. The set of ideals K with K·I ≠ 0 is not empty, because R·I = I ≠ 0. By the descending chain condition it has a minimal element K.

Choose x in K with x·I ≠ 0. Then (x)·I = xI ≠ 0 and (x) ⊆ K. By minimality of K, (x) = K. Now consider xJ, an ideal contained in (x) = K. We have (xJ)·I = x·J·J^n = x·J^{n+1} = x·I ≠ 0. By minimality, xJ = K = (x).

So x ∈ xJ, that is, x = xj for some j in J. Then x(1 − j) = 0. The element 1 − j is a unit, because j lies in every maximal ideal, so 1 − j lies in no maximal ideal. Hence x = 0, which contradicts xI ≠ 0. So I = J^n = 0.

worked_application.title: The rings ℤ/360, ℤ/720 and ℚ[x]/(x²(x−1)⁵)
worked_application.goal: Find the maximal ideals, the radical J and the nilpotency index in three Artinian rings. Check that ℤ and ℚ[x] fail.
hypotheses: R₃ = ℚ[x]/(x²(x−1)⁵).
Non example: R = ℤ with the prime (0).
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The three rings are finite or finite dimensional over a field. A descending chain of ideals gives a descending chain of subspaces or subgroups of a finite set, so it stops.

steps.text: In R₁ = ℤ/360, 360 = 2³·3²·5. The prime ideals are (2), (3), (5), all maximal. So there are 3 of them. The radical is J = (30). The theorem says J is nilpotent.
Compute the powers of 30 modulo 360: 30¹ = 30, 30² = 900 ≡ 180, 30³ = 27000 = 75·360 ≡ 0. So J² ≠ 0 and J³ = 0. The nilpotency index is 3, which equals the largest exponent in 2³·3²·5.
In R₂ = ℤ/720, 720 = 2⁴·3²·5. The powers of 30 modulo 720 are 30, 180, 360, 0. So J³ ≠ 0 and J⁴ = 0. The index is 4, the largest exponent of a prime in 720.

In R₃ = ℚ[x]/(x²(x−1)⁵), the maximal ideals are (x) and (x−1), and J = (x(x−1)). Then J^k = (x^k (x−1)^k) is zero in R₃ if and only if x²(x−1)⁵ divides x^k (x−1)^k. This holds if and only if k ≥ 2 and k ≥ 5. So the index is 5.

The ring ℤ is not Artinian. The prime (0) is not maximal, and the chain (2) ⊋ (4) ⊋ (8) ⊋ … does not stop. The same holds for ℚ[x], with the chain (x) ⊋ (x²) ⊋ … . This shows that part (a) needs the descending chain condition.

worked_application.result: ℤ/360 has 3 maximal ideals and J = (30) with J³ = 0 and J² ≠ 0. ℤ/720 has the same radical with nilpotency index 4. ℚ[x]/(x²(x−1)⁵) has nilpotency index 5. The rings ℤ and ℚ[x] have non maximal primes and are not Artinian.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: The ring must be Artinian. A Noetherian domain such as ℤ has the prime (0), which is not maximal.
The nilpotency index J^k = 0 can be large. The index is not bounded by the number of maximal ideals. In ℚ[x]/(x²(x−1)⁵) there are 2 maximal ideals and the index is 5.
The theorem does not say that R is a product of local rings. That structure result uses the Chinese remainder theorem and idempotent lifting in addition.

results.name: Integral extensions: incomparability and the correspondence of maximal primes
results.statement: Let R ⊆ S be commutative rings with S integral over R. (a) Let Q ⊊ Q′ be prime ideals of S. Then Q ∩ R ⊊ Q′ ∩ R. (b) A prime ideal Q of S is maximal if and only if Q ∩ R is maximal in R. (c) Every strict chain of prime ideals of S of length n contracts to a strict chain of prime ideals of R of length n. So the Krull dimension of S is at most the Krull dimension of R.
hypotheses: R is a subring of S with the same identity.
Every element of S is a root of a monic polynomial with coefficients in R.
Krull dimension is the supremum of the lengths of strict chains of prime ideals.

definitions.name: Krull dimension

steps.text: Step 0, reduction. Let Q be a prime of S and let p = Q ∩ R. The map R/p → S/Q is injective, and S/Q is a domain that is integral over the image of R/p. Reducing a monic equation modulo Q gives a monic equation over R/p. So we may study an extension of domains R̄ ⊆ S̄ with S̄ integral over R̄.

Step 1, key lemma. Let R̄ ⊆ S̄ be domains with S̄ integral over R̄. Let x ≠ 0 be an element of S̄. Then there is a monic equation x^n + a_{n−1}x^{n−1} + … + a_0 = 0 with a_i in R̄ and a_0 ≠ 0. To see this, take a monic equation of the smallest degree n. If a_0 = 0, then x(x^{n−1} + … + a_1) = 0. Since S̄ is a domain and x ≠ 0, the second factor is zero. If n = 1 this says 1 = 0, which is false. If n > 1 it is a monic equation of smaller degree. Both cases are impossible, so a_0 ≠ 0. Also a_0 = −x(x^{n−1} + … + a_1) lies in xS̄.

Step 2, proof of (a). Let Q ⊊ Q′ be primes of S and suppose Q ∩ R = Q′ ∩ R = p. Choose x in Q′ ∖ Q. Work in S̄ = S/Q and R̄ = R/p. The image x̄ of x is non zero and lies in Q̄′ = Q′/Q. By Step 1, a_0 ≠ 0 in R̄ and a_0 ∈ x̄S̄ ⊆ Q̄′. Lift a_0 to a ∈ R. Then a ∈ Q′ ∩ R = p and so a_0 = 0 in R̄. This contradicts a_0 ≠ 0. So Q ∩ R ≠ Q′ ∩ R. Also Q ∩ R ⊆ Q′ ∩ R, hence the inclusion is strict.

Step 3, proof of (b), direction Q∩R maximal implies Q maximal. Let p = Q ∩ R be maximal. Then R̄ = R/p is a field. Take x ≠ 0 in S̄ = S/Q. By Step 1, a_0 ≠ 0 and a_0 = −x·y with y = x^{n−1} + … + a_1 in S̄. The element a_0 is a unit of the field R̄. So x·(−y a_0^{−1}) = 1. Hence S̄ is a field and Q is maximal.

Step 4, proof of (b), direction Q maximal implies Q∩R maximal. Let S̄ = S/Q be a field. Take a ≠ 0 in R̄ = R/p. Then a^{−1} lies in S̄. It is integral over R̄, so a^{−m} + c_{m−1}a^{−m+1} + … + c_0 = 0 with c_i in R̄. Multiply by a^{m−1}. We get a^{−1} = −(c_{m−1} + c_{m−2}a + … + c_0 a^{m−1}), which lies in R̄. So every non zero element of R̄ is a unit. Also R̄ is not the zero ring because p ≠ R, as 1 ∉ Q. Thus p is maximal.

Step 5, proof of (c). Let Q_0 ⊊ Q_1 ⊊ … ⊊ Q_n be primes of S. By part (a), the primes Q_i ∩ R form a strict chain. Each contraction is a prime ideal of R. So R has a strict chain of length n. Taking the supremum over all chains gives dim S ≤ dim R.

worked_application.title: The extension ℤ ⊆ ℤ[i] and the non integral extension ℚ[x] ⊆ ℚ[x,y]
worked_application.goal: Use incomparability to read off the primes of ℤ[i] that lie over 5. Then show that both conclusions fail for non integral extensions.
hypotheses: R = ℤ and S = ℤ[i] with i² = −1. Every element a + bi is a root of t² − 2at + (a² + b²).
R′ = ℚ[x] ⊆ S′ = ℚ[x,y], where y is not integral over ℚ[x].
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The polynomial t² − 2at + (a² + b²) is monic with coefficients in ℤ. So ℤ[i] is integral over ℤ and the theorem applies to it.

steps.text: Since 5 = (2 + i)(2 − i), the ideals (2 + i) and (2 − i) of ℤ[i] contain 5. The quotient ℤ[i]/(2 + i) has 5 elements, because the norm of 2 + i is 5. So it is the field with 5 elements. Hence (2 + i) is maximal. The same holds for (2 − i).

Both ideals contract to (5) in ℤ. By part (a), neither contains the other, because a strict inclusion would give a strict inclusion of contractions. We can check this directly. By step 1, both (2 + i) and (2 − i) are maximal. Suppose (2 − i) ⊆ (2 + i). The ideal (2 + i) is proper and the ideal (2 − i) is maximal. So the two ideals are equal. Then 2 + i divides 2 − i in ℤ[i]. But the quotient (2 − i)/(2 + i) = (3 − 4i)/5 is not in ℤ[i]. This is a contradiction. The inclusion (2 + i) ⊆ (2 − i) fails in the same way, because (2 − i) is proper and (2 + i) is maximal. So the two ideals are distinct maximal ideals and neither contains the other.

Only two primes lie over 5. Let Q be a prime of ℤ[i] with Q ∩ ℤ = (5). The prime (5) is maximal in ℤ. By part (b), Q is maximal. Also 5 ∈ Q, so Q corresponds to a maximal ideal of ℤ[i]/(5). We have ℤ[i]/(5) ≅ 𝔽₅[x]/(x²+1). Modulo 5, x²+1 = (x−2)(x+2) with distinct roots 2 and −2. By the Chinese remainder theorem, ℤ[i]/(5) ≅ 𝔽₅ × 𝔽₅. This ring has exactly two maximal ideals. So exactly two primes lie over 5. They are (2 + i) and (2 − i), because i ↦ −2 and i ↦ 2 give the two maps to 𝔽₅.

Part (b) holds in this example. The zero ideal of ℤ[i] is not maximal, and it contracts to the zero ideal of ℤ, which is not maximal. The ideal (2 + i) is maximal, and it contracts to the maximal ideal (5).
Part (c) gives dim ℤ[i] ≤ dim ℤ = 1. The chain (0) ⊊ (2 + i) of length 1 shows that dim ℤ[i] = 1.

Now use R′ = ℚ[x] and S′ = ℚ[x,y]. The ideals (0) ⊊ (xy − 1) are primes with Q ⊊ Q′. A non zero polynomial in x alone has y degree 0. A multiple of xy − 1 that is non zero has y degree at least 1. So (xy − 1) ∩ ℚ[x] = 0. Both primes contract to (0). Part (a) fails, because y is not integral over ℚ[x].
For part (b), take the field K = ℚ(x) over R′ = ℚ[x]. The zero ideal of K is maximal. It contracts to the zero ideal of ℚ[x], which is not maximal. So part (b) fails for this non integral extension.

results.name: Noetherian modules in a short exact sequence, and finitely generated modules over a Noetherian ring
results.statement: Let R be a ring and let 0 → M′ → M → M″ → 0 be a short exact sequence of R-modules, with maps f and g. (a) M is Noetherian if and only if M′ and M″ are Noetherian. (b) If R is a Noetherian ring, every finitely generated R-module is Noetherian. Here a module is Noetherian when every ascending chain of submodules becomes constant.
hypotheses: f is injective, g is surjective and the image of f equals the kernel of g.
Part (b) takes R as a left Noetherian ring and uses left modules.

definitions.name: Noetherian module
definitions.text: A module in which every ascending chain of submodules is eventually constant. This is the same as saying that every submodule is finitely generated.

definitions.name: short exact sequence
definitions.text: A sequence 0 → M′ → M → M″ → 0 with f injective, g surjective and im f = ker g.
