/-- Main theorem of this section: if both `f` and `x ↦ ‖x‖ * ‖f x‖` are integrable, then the
Fourier transform of `f` has a Fréchet derivative (everywhere in its domain) and its derivative is
the Fourier transform of `smulRight L f`. -/
theorem hasFDerivAt_fourierIntegral
    [MeasurableSpace V] [BorelSpace V] [SecondCountableTopology V] {μ : Measure V}
    (hf : Integrable f μ) (hf' : Integrable (fun v : V ↦ ‖v‖ * ‖f v‖) μ) (w : W) :
    HasFDerivAt (fourierIntegral 𝐞 μ L.toLinearMap₁₂ f)
      (fourierIntegral 𝐞 μ L.toLinearMap₁₂ (fourierSMulRight L f) w) w := by
  let F : W → V → E := fun w' v ↦ 𝐞 (-L v w') • f v
  let F' : W → V → W →L[ℝ] E := fun w' v ↦ 𝐞 (-L v w') • fourierSMulRight L f v
  let B : V → ℝ := fun v ↦ 2 * π * ‖L‖ * ‖v‖ * ‖f v‖
  have h0 (w' : W) : Integrable (F w') μ :=
    (fourierIntegral_convergent_iff continuous_fourierChar
      (by apply L.continuous₂ : Continuous (fun p : V × W ↦ L.toLinearMap₁₂ p.1 p.2)) w').2 hf
  have h1 : ∀ᶠ w' in 𝓝 w, AEStronglyMeasurable (F w') μ :=
    Eventually.of_forall (fun w' ↦ (h0 w').aestronglyMeasurable)
  have h3 : AEStronglyMeasurable (F' w) μ := by
    refine .fun_smul ?_ hf.1.fourierSMulRight
    refine (continuous_fourierChar.comp ?_).aestronglyMeasurable
    fun_prop
  have h4 : (∀ᵐ v ∂μ, ∀ (w' : W), w' ∈ Metric.ball w 1 → ‖F' w' v‖ ≤ B v) := by
    filter_upwards with v w' _
    rw [Circle.norm_smul _ (fourierSMulRight L f v)]
    exact norm_fourierSMulRight_le L f v
  have h5 : Integrable B μ := by simpa only [← mul_assoc] using hf'.const_mul (2 * π * ‖L‖)
  have h6 : ∀ᵐ v ∂μ, ∀ w', w' ∈ Metric.ball w 1 → HasFDerivAt (fun x ↦ F x v) (F' w' v) w' :=
    ae_of_all _ (fun v w' _ ↦ hasFDerivAt_fourierChar_smul L f v w')
  exact hasFDerivAt_integral_of_dominated_of_fderiv_le (Metric.ball_mem_nhds _ one_pos) h1 (h0 w)
    h3 h4 h5 h6

steps.text: Boundary values. Let g∈C¹ with g,g′∈L¹. Then g(x)=g(0)+∫₀ˣg′ has limits at ±∞, because g′ is integrable. Since g is integrable, both limits are 0. Apply this to g=f^{(j)} for j<m: f^{(j)}(x)→0 as |x|→∞.

Integration by parts. For j<m and R>0, ∫_{−R}^{R}f^{(j+1)}(x)e^{−2πixξ}dx=[f^{(j)}(x)e^{−2πixξ}]_{−R}^{R}+2πiξ∫_{−R}^{R}f^{(j)}(x)e^{−2πixξ}dx. Let R→∞. The boundary term tends to 0 by step 1. So (f^{(j+1)})^(ξ)=2πiξ(f^{(j)})^(ξ). By induction, (f^{(j)})^(ξ)=(2πiξ)ʲf̂(ξ).
Decay. By step 2, |2πξ|ᵐ|f̂(ξ)|=|(f^{(m)})^(ξ)|≤‖f^{(m)}‖₁. This is the bound in (A). Since f^{(m)}∈L¹, the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma gives (f^{(m)})^(ξ)→0. So |2πξ|ᵐ|f̂(ξ)|→0.

Differentiation under the integral, one step. Let xf∈L¹. For h≠0, (f̂(ξ+h)−f̂(ξ))/h=∫f(x)e^{−2πixξ}(e^{−2πixh}−1)/h dx. The integrand tends to −2πix f(x)e^{−2πixξ} pointwise. Also |e^{−2πixh}−1|≤2π|x||h|, so the integrand is bounded by 2π|x||f(x)|, which is integrable. By dominated convergence, f̂′(ξ)=∫(−2πix)f(x)e^{−2πixξ}dx.

Induction for (B). The function (−2πix)ʲf is integrable for j≤m. Apply step 4 to it repeatedly. This gives f̂^{(j)} for j≤m. Each f̂^{(j)} is continuous, as a Fourier transform of an L¹ function, again by dominated convergence. So f̂∈Cᵐ.

worked_application.title: Gaussian decay bounds against the exact transform
worked_application.goal: Compare |f̂(ξ)| with the bounds of part (A) for f(x)=e^{−πx²}, which has f̂=f.
hypotheses: For f(x)=e^{−πx²} one has f′(x)=−2πxf(x) and f″(x)=(4π²x²−2π)f(x).
The integrals ‖f′‖₁ and ‖f″‖₁ are exact, and decimals come from 30 digit arithmetic.
The bound for m=1 is ‖f′‖₁/(2π|ξ|) and the bound for m=2 is ‖f″‖₁/(4π²ξ²).
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The bounds hold at every test point, and the true transform decays much faster than either bound.

steps.text: ‖f′‖₁=2f(0)=2, because f′ has one sign change at 0 and f vanishes at infinity.
‖f″‖₁=4|f′(x₀)| with x₀=1/√(2π), the point where f″ changes sign. This equals 4√(2π)e^{−1/2}=6.0813876.
At ξ=1 the true value is f̂(1)=e^{−π}=0.0432139. The m=1 bound is 0.318310 and the m=2 bound is 0.154043.

All bounds hold. The higher m gives the faster decay of the bound for large ξ, but the true decay is Gaussian. A smooth function in the class of part (B) gives the same speed on the other side: f has all moments, so f̂ is C^∞.

worked_application.result: The bound |f̂(ξ)|≤‖f″‖₁/(4π²ξ²) holds at ξ=0.5, 1, 2 and 3. The true values fall from 0.456 to 5.3·10⁻¹³, far below the polynomial bound.

limitations: Part (A) needs f^{(j)}∈L¹ for every j≤m. Integrability of f^{(m)} alone does not give the bound.
Part (B) needs moments xʲf∈L¹. Exponential decay of f gives analyticity of f̂ in a strip, which this entry does not prove.
The bound is one-sided. The true decay can be much faster, as for the Gaussian.
The statement is on ℝ. The same proof works on ℝⁿ with multi-indices, but the notation changes.

results.name: Lyapunov interpolation inequality for Lp norms
results.statement: Let (Ω,μ) be a measure space and let 0<p<r<q≤∞. Define θ∈(0,1) by 1/r=(1−θ)/p+θ/q. Then every measurable f satisfies ‖f‖_r ≤ ‖f‖_p^{1−θ}‖f‖_q^θ. Hence L^p∩L^q⊂L^r. Also the function 1/s↦log‖f‖_s is convex on the set of 1/s with f∈L^s.
hypotheses: The exponents satisfy p<r<q with q finite or infinite.
The norm may be infinite. Then the right side is infinite or the left side is covered by the finite factors.
If q=∞ then θ=1−p/r.

theorem lintegral_Lp_mul_le_Lq_mul_Lr {α} [MeasurableSpace α] {p q r : ℝ} (hp0_lt : 0 < p)
    (hpq : p < q) (hpqr : 1 / p = 1 / q + 1 / r) (μ : Measure α) {f g : α → ℝ≥0∞}
    (hf : AEMeasurable f μ) (hg : AEMeasurable g μ) :
    (∫⁻ a, (f * g) a ^ p ∂μ) ^ (1 / p) ≤
      (∫⁻ a, f a ^ q ∂μ) ^ (1 / q) * (∫⁻ a, g a ^ r ∂μ) ^ (1 / r) := by
  have hp0_ne : p ≠ 0 := (ne_of_lt hp0_lt).symm
  have hp0 : 0 ≤ p := le_of_lt hp0_lt
  have hq0_lt : 0 < q := lt_of_le_of_lt hp0 hpq
  have hq0_ne : q ≠ 0 := (ne_of_lt hq0_lt).symm
  have h_one_div_r : 1 / r = 1 / p - 1 / q := by rw [hpqr]; simp
  let p2 := q / p
  let q2 := p2.conjExponent
  have hp2q2 : p2.HolderConjugate q2 :=
    .conjExponent (by simp [p2, _root_.lt_div_iff₀, hpq, hp0_lt])
  calc
    (∫⁻ a : α, (f * g) a ^ p ∂μ) ^ (1 / p) = (∫⁻ a : α, f a ^ p * g a ^ p ∂μ) ^ (1 / p) := by
      simp_rw [Pi.mul_apply, ENNReal.mul_rpow_of_nonneg _ _ hp0]
    _ ≤ ((∫⁻ a, f a ^ (p * p2) ∂μ) ^ (1 / p2) *
        (∫⁻ a, g a ^ (p * q2) ∂μ) ^ (1 / q2)) ^ (1 / p) := by
      gcongr
      simp_rw [ENNReal.rpow_mul]
      exact ENNReal.lintegral_mul_le_Lp_mul_Lq μ hp2q2 (hf.pow_const _) (hg.pow_const _)
    _ = (∫⁻ a : α, f a ^ q ∂μ) ^ (1 / q) * (∫⁻ a : α, g a ^ r ∂μ) ^ (1 / r) := by
      rw [@ENNReal.mul_rpow_of_nonneg _ _ (1 / p) (by simp [hp0]), ← ENNReal.rpow_mul, ←
        ENNReal.rpow_mul]
      have hpp2 : p * p2 = q := by
        symm
        rw [mul_comm, ← div_eq_iff hp0_ne]
      have hpq2 : p * q2 = r := by
        rw [← inv_inv r, ← one_div, ← one_div, h_one_div_r]
        simp [field, p2, q2, Real.conjExponent]
      simp_rw [div_mul_div_comm, mul_one, mul_comm p2, mul_comm q2, hpp2, hpq2]

steps.text: Exponents. For q<∞, put s=r(1−θ)/p and t=rθ/q. The relation 1/r=(1−θ)/p+θ/q gives s+t=1, with s,t∈(0,1). Put P=1/s and Q=1/t. Then P,Q>1 and 1/P+1/Q=1.

Hölder with the split of |f|^r. Write |f|^r=|f|^{(1−θ)r}·|f|^{θr}. Hölder gives ∫|f|^r ≤ (∫|f|^{(1−θ)rP})^{1/P}(∫|f|^{θrQ})^{1/Q}. Now (1−θ)rP=p and θrQ=q, because P=p/((1−θ)r) and Q=q/(θr). So ∫|f|^r ≤ (∫|f|^p)^{(1−θ)r/p}(∫|f|^q)^{θr/q}.

Take the r-th root. The exponents become (1−θ)/p·p=1−θ and θ/q·q=θ after the root: ‖f‖_r ≤ ‖f‖_p^{1−θ}‖f‖_q^θ. If one of the norms on the right is infinite the inequality is trivial, so assume both are finite.
The case q=∞. Here |f|^r ≤ |f|^p‖f‖_∞^{r−p} almost everywhere. So ‖f‖_r^r ≤ ‖f‖_p^p‖f‖_∞^{r−p}. Take the r-th root. The exponents are p/r=1−θ and 1−p/r=θ.

Inclusion and convexity. If f∈L^p∩L^q then the right side is finite, so f∈L^r and ‖f‖_r≤max(‖f‖_p,‖f‖_q). Put t=1/s. The identity 1/r=(1−θ)/p+θ/q says t_r=(1−θ)t_p+θt_q. So the inequality says log‖f‖_{1/t} is a convex function of t on its domain.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Integration by parts. Since |f|²=f f̄ has derivative 2Re(f′ f̄), and x|f|²→0 at infinity, ∫|f|² dx=[x|f|²]_{−∞}^{∞}−∫x(|f|²)′dx=−2Re∫x f′ f̄ dx.
Cauchy–Schwarz. Then ‖f‖₂²=−2Re∫(xf̄)f′ ≤ 2|∫(xf̄)f′| ≤ 2‖xf‖₂‖f′‖₂.
Plancherel. The transform of f′ is 2πiξf̂(ξ), by the derivative rule. By Plancherel, ‖f′‖₂=‖(f′)^‖₂=2π‖ξf̂‖₂. Put this into step 2: ‖f‖₂² ≤ 2‖xf‖₂·2π‖ξf̂‖₂=4π‖xf‖₂‖ξf̂‖₂.

Equality, necessity. Equality needs equality in both inequalities of step 2. Equality in Cauchy–Schwarz gives f′=λxf almost everywhere for some λ∈ℂ. Then ∫x f′ f̄=λ∫x²|f|², which must be real and negative. So λ=−2a with a>0. Solving f′=−2axf gives f=Ce^{−ax²}.

Equality, sufficiency. For f=e^{−ax²} one has ∫x f′ f̄=−2a∫x²e^{−2ax²}dx and ‖f‖₂²=−2Re∫x f′ f̄ by step 1. Both Cauchy–Schwarz and the real part step are equalities, because f′=−2axf is a real multiple of xf. So equality holds.

results.name: Polya theorem: convergence of quadrature rules via Banach–Steinhaus
results.statement: Let Qₙ(f)=∑_{i=1}^{mₙ}w_{n,i}f(x_{n,i}) be quadrature rules on C[a,b], with distinct nodes x_{n,i}∈[a,b] in each rule. Then Qₙ(f)→∫ₐᵇf for every f∈C[a,b] if and only if (i) Qₙ(p)→∫ₐᵇp for every polynomial p, and (ii) supₙ∑ᵢ|w_{n,i}|<∞. In particular, if all weights are positive and the rules are exact on constants, condition (ii) holds with value b−a, and convergence for polynomials implies convergence for every continuous function.
hypotheses: Each rule has distinct nodes, so that ‖Qₙ‖ can be computed exactly.
C[a,b] has the sup norm and is complete.
Condition (i) can be checked on the monomials 1,x,x²,….

prerequisites.reason: Step 2 applies the uniform boundedness principle to the sequence of rules.
Step 4 approximates a continuous function by a polynomial.

definitions.name: quadrature rule
definitions.text: A linear functional Qₙ(f)=∑w_{n,i}f(x_{n,i}) on C[a,b], with nodes x_{n,i} and weights w_{n,i}.

source.excerpt:
/-- This is the standard Banach-Steinhaus theorem, or Uniform Boundedness Principle.
If a family of continuous linear maps from a Banach space into a normed space is pointwise
bounded, then the norms of these linear maps are uniformly bounded.

See also `WithSeminorms.banach_steinhaus` for the general statement in barrelled spaces. -/
theorem banach_steinhaus {ι : Type*} [CompleteSpace E] {g : ι → E →SL[σ₁₂] F}
    (h : ∀ x, ∃ C, ∀ i, ‖g i x‖ ≤ C) : ∃ C', ∀ i, ‖g i‖ ≤ C' := by
  rw [show (∃ C, ∀ i, ‖g i‖ ≤ C) ↔ _ from (NormedSpace.equicontinuous_TFAE g).out 6 3]
  refine (norm_withSeminorms 𝕜₂ F).banach_steinhaus (fun _ x ↦ ?_)
  simpa [bddAbove_def, forall_mem_range] using h x

source.alignment: Mathlib proves the uniform boundedness principle for families of continuous linear maps from a Banach space. It is the engine of the necessity of (ii). Mathlib does not prove the quadrature theorem.

results.proof_status: source declaration inspected; authored proof awaits inference review; no local Lean check

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Norm of a rule. For f with ‖f‖_∞≤1, |Qₙ(f)|≤∑|w_{n,i}|. For the converse, let f be the piecewise linear function that interpolates the values sgn(w_{n,i}) at the distinct nodes and is constant outside them. Then ‖f‖_∞=1 and Qₙ(f)=∑|w_{n,i}|. So ‖Qₙ‖=∑ᵢ|w_{n,i}|.

Necessity of (ii). Suppose Qₙ(f)→∫f for each f. Then (Qₙ(f))ₙ is bounded for each f, because convergent sequences are bounded. C[a,b] is a Banach space. By the Banach–Steinhaus theorem, supₙ‖Qₙ‖<∞. By step 1 this is (ii).
Necessity of (i). Polynomials are continuous functions, so convergence for all f includes convergence for polynomials.

Sufficiency, approximation. Assume (i) and (ii) and put M=supₙ‖Qₙ‖. Let f∈C[a,b] and ε>0. By the Weierstrass theorem there is a polynomial p with ‖f−p‖_∞<ε. Then |Qₙ(f)−∫f| ≤ |Qₙ(f−p)|+|Qₙ(p)−∫p|+|∫(p−f)| ≤ Mε+|Qₙ(p)−∫p|+(b−a)ε.
Sufficiency, conclusion. By (i), the middle term is below ε for n large. So the error is below (M+1+b−a)ε for large n. Since ε is arbitrary, Qₙ(f)→∫f.
Positive weights. If wᵢ>0 and Qₙ(1)=b−a for all n, then ∑|w_{n,i}|=∑w_{n,i}=Qₙ(1)=b−a. So (ii) holds with value b−a.

worked_application.title: Newton–Cotes rules fail on the Runge function while Gauss rules converge
worked_application.goal: Compute ∑|w| and the quadrature error for equispaced Newton–Cotes rules of several orders on [−1,1] and test them on f(x)=1/(1+25x²). Compare with Gauss–Legendre rules.
hypotheses: The exact integral is (2/5)arctan 5=0.5493603.
The Newton–Cotes rule of order n uses n+1 equispaced nodes −1+2i/n and is exact for polynomials of degree n. Weights are computed in exact rational arithmetic.
Gauss–Legendre rules have positive weights and are exact on polynomials. They are computed in double precision.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The weight norm ∑|w| is 2 for n=1 to 7 and for n=9. It is above 2 for n=8, 10 and every larger tested n, and it is large for n=12 and above. The quadrature error grows with it. For Gauss rules ∑|w|=2 for every size.

steps.text: Weight sums. ∑|w| is 2 for n=1 to 7 and for n=9 (all weights are positive). It is 2.9024 for n=8, 6.1296 for n=10, 3.1788 for n=11, 15.063 for n=12, 116.91 for n=16 and 1088.4 for n=20. Every Newton–Cotes weight sums to 2, so the sums above 2 come from negative weights.

For n=8 the weights are 989/14175, 5888/14175, −928/14175, 10496/14175, −908/2835, and the same values in reverse order. For n=20 the smallest weight is −1684005984173647/9355030915230, which is −1.684·10¹⁵/9.355·10¹²=−180.01.
Errors for the Runge function. The error Qₙ(f)−0.5493603 is −0.07456 for n=4, −0.24926 for n=8, −0.61195 for n=12, −1.79765 for n=16 and −5.91927 for n=20.
Gauss–Legendre rules. ∑|w|=2 for every size, so (ii) holds. The errors are 0.15759 for 5 nodes, −0.018988 for 10 nodes and −0.000363 for 20 nodes, and they tend to 0.

Reading by the theorem. A uniformly bounded ∑|w| and exactness on polynomials give convergence for all continuous f. For the Newton–Cotes sequence, the computed sums grow without sign of a bound up to n=20. If ∑|w| tends to infinity along the full sequence, the theorem gives a continuous function with divergent Qₙ(f). This computation does not prove that.

worked_application.result: Gauss–Legendre errors fall from 0.158 to 0.00036 as the size grows from 5 to 20. Newton–Cotes errors grow from 0.075 to 5.9 on the same function.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: Distinct nodes are assumed so that the norm of a rule equals ∑|w|. With repeated nodes, first combine the weights.
The theorem concerns convergence for every continuous function. A single function such as an analytic one can be integrated well by rules with unbounded ∑|w|.
The proof of the divergence for a specific rule sequence needs the growth of ∑|w| for that sequence. This is known for Newton–Cotes rules but is not proved here.
The theorem does not give rates of convergence. For rates one needs smoothness of f.

results.name: Fourier transform turns the convolution of integrable functions into a product
results.statement: Let f,g be integrable functions on ℝⁿ with Lebesgue measure. Put 𝓕f(ξ)=∫f(x)e^{−2πi⟨x,ξ⟩}dx. Then: (i) for almost every x the integral (f∗g)(x)=∫f(y)g(x−y)dy converges absolutely. (ii) The function f∗g is integrable and ‖f∗g‖₁≤‖f‖₁‖g‖₁. (iii) f∗g=g∗f almost everywhere. (iv) 𝓕(f∗g)(ξ)=𝓕f(ξ)·𝓕g(ξ) for every ξ∈ℝⁿ.
hypotheses: The functions f and g are measurable and ∫|f|<∞ and ∫|g|<∞.
The measure is Lebesgue measure, which is invariant under translation and under x↦−x.
The values are complex numbers.

prerequisites.reason: Tonelli and Fubini give integrability of the double integral and the exchange of the order of integration.

definitions.name: convolution

definitions.text: 𝓕f(ξ)=∫f(x)e^{−2πi⟨x,ξ⟩}dx. It is defined for every ξ because |e^{iθ}|=1.

/-- The Fourier transform of the convolution is given by the multiplication of the Fourier transform
of the individual functions.

Version for multiplication. -/
theorem fourier_mul_convolution_eq {f₁ : E → R} {f₂ : E → R}

    𝓕 (f₁ ⋆[mul ℂ R] f₂) ξ = (𝓕 f₁ ξ) * (𝓕 f₂ ξ) :=
  fourier_bilin_convolution_eq (mul ℂ R) hf₁ hf₂ ξ

source_references.alignment: Mathlib proves that the convolution of two integrable functions is integrable. This is part (ii).

results.proof_status: source declaration inspected; authored proof awaits inference review; no local Lean check

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Measurability. The map (x,y)↦(y,x−y) is a linear bijection of ℝ²ⁿ with determinant ±1. It preserves Lebesgue measure. So (x,y)↦f(y)g(x−y) is measurable on ℝⁿ×ℝⁿ.
Tonelli bound. By Tonelli, ∫∫|f(y)||g(x−y)|dy dx=∫|f(y)|(∫|g(x−y)|dx)dy. Translation invariance gives ∫|g(x−y)|dx=‖g‖₁. So the double integral equals ‖f‖₁‖g‖₁<∞.

Existence and norm. Since the double integral is finite, the inner integral ∫|f(y)||g(x−y)|dy is finite for almost every x. This is (i). Then |(f∗g)(x)|≤∫|f(y)||g(x−y)|dy, and integration in x gives ‖f∗g‖₁≤‖f‖₁‖g‖₁. This is (ii).
Commutativity. For fixed x, substitute y↦x−y. This map preserves Lebesgue measure. So ∫f(y)g(x−y)dy=∫f(x−y)g(y)dy at each x where one side converges absolutely. This is (iii).

Swap of integrals. Fix ξ. Write 𝓕(f∗g)(ξ)=∫(∫f(y)g(x−y)dy)e^{−2πi⟨x,ξ⟩}dx. The integrand has absolute value |f(y)||g(x−y)|, which is integrable on ℝ²ⁿ by step 2. So Fubini allows the swap: the value is ∫f(y)(∫g(x−y)e^{−2πi⟨x,ξ⟩}dx)dy.

Factorisation. In the inner integral put x=y+w. Then e^{−2πi⟨y+w,ξ⟩}=e^{−2πi⟨y,ξ⟩}e^{−2πi⟨w,ξ⟩}. So the inner integral is e^{−2πi⟨y,ξ⟩}𝓕g(ξ). The outer integral gives 𝓕g(ξ)∫f(y)e^{−2πi⟨y,ξ⟩}dy=𝓕f(ξ)𝓕g(ξ). This is (iv).

worked_application.title: A triangle function as the convolution of two boxes
worked_application.goal: Check part (iv) for f=g=1_{[0,1]} on ℝ at ξ=0.7.
hypotheses: f=g is the indicator of [0,1]. It is integrable with ‖f‖₁=1.
The convolution is the triangle function with peak 1 at x=1 and support [0,2].
The numbers come from numerical quadrature in double precision.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The two functions are bounded with compact support, so they are integrable. The theorem applies at once.

steps.text: Convolution. For 0≤x≤1 the product f(y)g(x−y) is nonzero when 0≤y≤x, so (f∗f)(x)=x. For 1≤x≤2 it is nonzero when x−1≤y≤1, so (f∗f)(x)=2−x. The integral of the triangle is 1, which equals ‖f‖₁‖f‖₁. Equality holds because f≥0.
Transform of the box. 𝓕f(ξ)=∫₀¹e^{−2πixξ}dx=(1−e^{−2πiξ})/(2πiξ). At ξ=0.7 the square of this number is −0.041822+0.128714i, and its modulus is 0.135338.
Transform of the triangle. Numerical integration of ∫₀²(f∗f)(x)e^{−2πix·0.7}dx gives −0.041822+0.128714i.
The two complex numbers agree to six digits. This confirms 𝓕(f∗f)(0.7)=(𝓕f(0.7))².

worked_application.result: The Fourier transform of the triangle equals the square of the Fourier transform of the box. The value at ξ=0.7 is −0.041822+0.128714i.

limitations: Part (iv) needs both functions in L¹. For L² functions the transform is defined by extension, and the product rule holds only after that extension.
For two functions in L² the convolution need not be integrable, and the product of transforms is then not the transform of an integrable function.
The proof does not say that 𝓕f𝓕g is a transform of an integrable function for every pair of integrable functions with an integrable product.

results.name: Poincare lemma: a closed one-form on an open convex set is exact
results.statement: Let U⊂ℝⁿ be open and convex. Let ω=(ω₁,…,ωₙ):U→ℝⁿ be a C¹ map with ∂_kω_i=∂_iω_k on U for all i,k. Then there is a C² function f:U→ℝ with ∇f=ω on U. The function f is unique up to an additive constant.
hypotheses: The set U is open and convex, so it is star-shaped about each of its points.
The components of ω are C¹. The closedness condition holds at every point of U.

definitions.name: closed one-form
definitions.text: The form ω=Σω_i dx_i is closed if ∂_kω_i=∂_iω_k for all i,k. Equivalently, the derivative matrix of ω is symmetric.

definitions.name: exact one-form
definitions.text: The form ω is exact if ω=df for some function f. Then f is a primitive of ω.

source.excerpt:
/-- If `ω` is a closed `1`-form on an open convex set `s`, then it admits a primitive,
a version stated in terms of `fderiv`. -/
theorem exists_forall_hasFDerivAt_of_fderiv_symmetric (hs : Convex ℝ s) (hso : IsOpen s)
    (hω : DifferentiableOn ℝ ω s) (hdω : ∀ a ∈ s, ∀ x y, fderiv ℝ ω a x y = fderiv ℝ ω a y x) :
    ∃ f, ∀ a ∈ s, HasFDerivAt f (ω a) a := by
  obtain ⟨f, hf⟩ : ∃ f, ∀ a ∈ s, HasFDerivWithinAt f (ω a) s a := by
    refine hs.exists_forall_hasFDerivWithinAt_of_fderivWithin_symmetric hω fun a ha x _ y _ ↦ ?_
    rw [fderivWithin_eq_fderiv, hdω a ha]
    exacts [hso.uniqueDiffOn a ha, hω.differentiableAt (hso.mem_nhds ha)]
  exact ⟨f, fun a ha ↦ (hf a ha).hasFDerivAt (hso.mem_nhds ha)⟩

source.alignment: Mathlib proves the same primitive existence on an open convex set. It assumes only differentiability of ω and symmetry of its derivative.

results.proof_status: source declaration inspected; authored proof awaits inference review; no local Lean check

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Reduction. A translation of coordinates puts 0 in U. Convexity gives tx∈U for all x∈U and t∈[0,1]. The map (t,x)↦ω(tx) is C¹ on a neighbourhood of [0,1]×U.

Definition of f. Put f(x)=∫₀¹Σ_iω_i(tx)x_i dt. The integrand is C¹ in x and continuous with its x-derivatives in (t,x) on [0,1]×U. So f is C¹ and its derivatives can be computed under the integral sign.
Derivative. For each k, ∂_kf(x)=∫₀¹[ω_k(tx)+tΣ_ix_i(∂_kω_i)(tx)]dt. The first term comes from differentiating x_i, and the second from the chain rule for ω_i(tx).
Use of closedness. Replace ∂_kω_i by ∂_iω_k. Then tΣ_ix_i(∂_iω_k)(tx)=t·(d/dt)[ω_k(tx)], by the chain rule applied to t↦ω_k(tx).
Fundamental theorem. The integrand now equals (d/dt)[tω_k(tx)]. So ∂_kf(x)=[tω_k(tx)] from t=0 to t=1, which is ω_k(x). Hence ∇f=ω. Since ω is C¹, f is C².
Uniqueness. If ∇f₁=∇f₂ on the connected open set U, then f₁−f₂ has zero gradient. So it is constant. Closedness is also necessary, since mixed second derivatives of a C² function are equal.

worked_application.goal: Compute a primitive of ω=(2xy+cos x)dx+(x²+3y²)dy by the integral formula, then show that convexity cannot be removed.
hypotheses: The domain is ℝ², which is open and convex.
The form is ω=(2xy+cos x)dx+(x²+3y²)dy.
The second form is θ=(−y dx+x dy)/(x²+y²) on ℝ²∖{0}.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: On ℝ² the components are smooth and ∂_y(2xy+cos x)=2x=∂_x(x²+3y²). So the theorem applies.

steps.text: Closedness. ∂_y(2xy+cos x)=2x and ∂_x(x²+3y²)=2x. The two agree.
Integral formula at (1,2). f(1,2)=∫₀¹[ω₁(t,2t)·1+ω₂(t,2t)·2]dt. Numerical quadrature gives 10.841471.
Closed form guess. The function F=x²y+sin x+y³ has ∇F=ω. Its value is F(1,2)−F(0,0)=2+sin 1+8=10.841471. This matches the integral.

Convexity is needed. The form θ is closed on ℝ²∖{0}, which is not convex. On the unit circle (cos s,sin s), ∫₀^{2π}(sin²s+cos²s)ds=6.283185=2π. An exact form has zero circulation on a closed loop, so θ is not exact there.

results.name: Discrete Fourier transform on Z/N: inversion, Plancherel, cyclic convolution and circulant matrices
results.statement: Let N≥1 and e(s)=e^{2πis}. For Φ:ℤ/N→ℂ put 𝓕Φ(k)=Σ_je(−jk/N)Φ(j). Then: (i) Σ_ke(jk/N)=N if j≡0 and 0 otherwise. (ii) Inversion: Φ(j)=(1/N)Σ_ke(jk/N)𝓕Φ(k). Then the vector v_k(j)=e(jk/N) satisfies Cv_k=𝓕c(k)v_k. So C has the N eigenvalues 𝓕c(0),…,𝓕c(N−1) and det C=Π_k𝓕c(k).

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Geometric sum. Put ζ=e(1/N). If j≢0 then ζʲ≠1 and Σ_{k=0}^{N−1}ζ^{jk}=(ζ^{jN}−1)/(ζʲ−1)=0. If j≡0 each term is 1. This is (i).
Inversion. Σ_ke(jk/N)𝓕Φ(k)=Σ_mΦ(m)Σ_ke((j−m)k/N). By step 1 the inner sum is N when m=j and 0 otherwise. So the total is NΦ(j). This is (ii). In Mathlib form, 𝓕(𝓕Φ)(j)=NΦ(−j).
Plancherel. Σ_k|𝓕Φ(k)|²=Σ_{m,m′}Φ(m)conj(Φ(m′))Σ_ke(−(m−m′)k/N). By step 1 only m=m′ survives, with weight N. So the sum is NΣ|Φ(m)|². This is (iii).
Convolution. 𝓕(Φ∗Ψ)(k)=Σ_mΣ_jΦ(j)Ψ(m−j)e(−mk/N). Put m=j+l. The sums are finite, so they can be reordered. The term becomes Φ(j)e(−jk/N)·Ψ(l)e(−lk/N). So the total is 𝓕Φ(k)𝓕Ψ(k). This is (iv).
Eigenvectors. (Cv_k)(m)=Σ_jc(m−j)e(jk/N). Put l=m−j. Then the sum is e(mk/N)Σ_lc(l)e(−lk/N)=𝓕c(k)v_k(m). So Cv_k=𝓕c(k)v_k.

Basis and determinant. By step 1 the vectors v_0,…,v_{N−1} are pairwise orthogonal and nonzero. So they form a basis, and C is diagonal in this basis with entries 𝓕c(k). Hence det C=Π𝓕c(k). Also C is invertible exactly when no 𝓕c(k) is zero, and then the solution of Cx=b is x=𝓕⁻¹(𝓕b/𝓕c).

results.name: Characters of a finite abelian group: orthogonality in both directions, Fourier expansion and Plancherel
results.statement: Let G be a finite abelian group (written additively). Let Ĝ be the set of characters ψ:G→S¹, that is, homomorphisms into the unit circle. Put ⟨f,h⟩=(1/|G|)Σ_xf(x)conj(h(x)). Then: (i) ⟨ψ₁,ψ₂⟩=1 if ψ₁=ψ₂ and 0 otherwise. (ii) |Ĝ|=|G|. (iii) Σ_{ψ∈Ĝ}ψ(a)=|G| if a=0 and 0 if a≠0. (iv) Every f:G→ℂ satisfies f=Σ_ψf̂(ψ)ψ with f̂(ψ)=⟨f,ψ⟩, and Σ_ψ|f̂(ψ)|²=(1/|G|)Σ_x|f(x)|².
hypotheses: G is finite and abelian.
Characters take values in the unit circle in ℂ.
Part (iii) is the orthogonality of characters in the group variable. It is also called dual orthogonality.

steps.text: Orthogonality in ψ. Let ψ=ψ₁·conj(ψ₂), which is a character. If ψ=1 then ⟨ψ₁,ψ₂⟩=1. If ψ≠1 pick y with ψ(y)≠1. Then Σ_xψ(x)=Σ_xψ(x+y)=ψ(y)Σ_xψ(x). So Σ_xψ(x)=0. This is (i).

Counting characters. By the structure theorem, G≅⊕_iℤ/n_i. Each character ψ has ψ(e_i)^{n_i}=1, where e_i is the i-th generator. So ψ(x)=Π_ie(a_ix_i/n_i) for unique a_i∈ℤ/n_i. Conversely each tuple gives a character. So |Ĝ|=Πn_i=|G|. This is (ii).
Separation of points. If a≠0, some coordinate a_i is nonzero modulo n_i. The character ψ₀(x)=e(x_i/n_i) has ψ₀(a)=e(a_i/n_i)≠1.

Dual orthogonality. Let a≠0 and ψ₀ be as in step 3. The map ψ↦ψ₀ψ is a bijection of Ĝ. So Σ_ψψ(a)=Σ_ψ(ψ₀ψ)(a)=ψ₀(a)Σ_ψψ(a). Since ψ₀(a)≠1 the sum is 0. For a=0 each term is 1, and the sum is |Ĝ|=|G|. This is (iii).

Expansion. By steps 1 and 2 the family Ĝ is an orthonormal family of |G| vectors in the |G|-dimensional space ℂ^G. So it is an orthonormal basis. For an orthonormal basis, f=Σ⟨f,ψ⟩ψ and ⟨f,f⟩=Σ|⟨f,ψ⟩|². This is (iv).

results.statement: Let 1≤p,q,r<∞ with 1/p+1/q=1+1/r. Let f∈Lᵖ(ℝⁿ) and g∈L^q(ℝⁿ). Then for almost every x the integral ∫|f(y)||g(x−y)|dy is finite, the function f∗g lies in Lʳ, and ‖f∗g‖_r≤‖f‖_p‖g‖_q.

source_references.alignment: Mathlib proves the endpoint case r=∞, where p and q are Hölder conjugate. It is the only case in Mathlib. The case r<∞ is proved here.

steps.text: Exponents. Define s and t by 1/s=1/p−1/r and 1/t=1/q−1/r. From 1/p=1+1/r−1/q≥1/r we get 1/s≥0, and likewise 1/t≥0. Also 1/r+1/s+1/t=1/p+1/q−1/r=1.
Reduction. Since |f∗g|≤|f|∗|g|, it is enough to treat F=|f| and G=|g|, which are nonnegative.

Splitting the integrand. Write F(y)G(x−y)=[F(y)ᵖG(x−y)^q]^{1/r}·F(y)^{p/s}·G(x−y)^{q/t}. The exponent of F is p/r+p/s=p(1/r+1/s)=p·(1/p)=1. The exponent of G is checked in the same way. If 1/s=0 the factor F^{p/s} is 1.

Hölder with three exponents. Apply the three-exponent Hölder inequality with exponents r, s, t. This gives (F∗G)(x)≤(∫F(y)ᵖG(x−y)^qdy)^{1/r}·(∫Fᵖ)^{1/s}·(∫G^q)^{1/t}. Here (F^{p/s})^s=Fᵖ, and the same holds for G.
Integrate in x. Raise the bound to the power r and integrate in x. By Tonelli and translation invariance, ∫∫F(y)ᵖG(x−y)^qdy dx=‖F‖ₚᵖ‖G‖_q^q. Hence ‖F∗G‖_r^r≤‖F‖ₚᵖ‖G‖_q^q·‖F‖ₚ^{pr/s}‖G‖_q^{qr/t}.

Exponent count. The power of ‖F‖_p is p+pr/s=p(1+r(1/p−1/r))=r. The power of ‖G‖_q is r in the same way. So ‖F∗G‖_r^r≤(‖F‖_p‖G‖_q)ʳ. Take the r-th root. Finiteness of ‖F∗G‖_r shows that F∗G(x) is finite almost everywhere.

/--
Companion theorem to the Poisson Integral Formula: Upper estimate for the real part of the
Herglotz-Riesz kernel.

theorem re_herglotzRieszKernel_le {c z : ℂ} (hz : z ∈ sphere c R) (hw : w ∈ ball c R) :
    ((z - c + (w - c)) / ((z - c) - (w - c))).re ≤ (R + ‖w - c‖) / (R - ‖w - c‖) := by
  obtain ⟨η₀, rfl, η₂⟩ : 0 < R ∧ R = ‖z - c‖ ∧ z - c ≠ 0 := by
    grind [ball_eq_empty, mem_sphere, dist_eq_norm, norm_pos_iff]
  by_cases h₁w : ‖w - c‖ = 0
  · aesop
  simpa using re_herglotzRieszKernel_le_aux (w - c).arg (z - c).arg ‖w - c‖ ‖z - c‖
    (by simpa using h₁w) (mem_ball_iff_norm.1 hw)

steps.text: Poisson formula. For harmonic u near the closed disc, u(w)=(1/2π)∫₀^{2π}u(c+Re^{iθ})P(θ)dθ with P as above.
Closed form of the kernel. With ζ=Re^{iθ} and η=w−c, Re((ζ+η)(conj ζ−conj η))=|ζ|²−|η|²+Re(η conj ζ−ζ conj η). The last term is purely imaginary, so its real part is 0. Hence P(θ)=(R²−ρ²)/|ζ−η|².
Kernel bounds. The triangle inequality gives R−ρ≤|ζ−η|≤R+ρ. So (R−ρ)/(R+ρ)≤P(θ)≤(R+ρ)/(R−ρ) for all θ.
Two sided estimate. Since u≥0 on the circle, multiplying by the bounds keeps the inequalities. So (R−ρ)/(R+ρ)·avg(u)≤u(w)≤(R+ρ)/(R−ρ)·avg(u), where avg(u) is the circle average.
Mean value. For harmonic u, the circle average equals u(c). Put this in step 4 to obtain the Harnack inequality.
Liouville. Let u≥0 be harmonic on ℂ and fix c and w. For every R>|w−c| the Harnack inequality holds. Let R→∞. Then (R−ρ)/(R+ρ)→1 and (R+ρ)/(R−ρ)→1, so u(w)=u(c). Hence u is constant.

results.statement: For t>0 put G_t(x)=(4πt)^{−1/2}e^{−x²/(4t)} and 𝓕g(ξ)=∫g(x)e^{−2πixξ}dx. Then: (i) 𝓕G_t(ξ)=e^{−4π²tξ²}. (ii) G_s∗G_t=G_{s+t} for s,t>0. (iii) Let f∈L¹(ℝ) and u(t,x)=(G_t∗f)(x) for t>0. Then u is C^∞ on (0,∞)×ℝ, u_t=u_xx, 𝓕u(t,·)=e^{−4π²tξ²}𝓕f, ‖u(t,·)‖₁≤‖f‖₁ and ∫u(t,x)dx=∫f.

source.alignment: Mathlib proves the transform of the Gaussian e^{−πb x²}. It gives part (i) after scaling. The convolution theorem is in the entry on the convolution of integrable functions.

results.proof_status: source declaration inspected; authored proof awaits inference review; no local Lean check

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Transform of the standard Gaussian. Let H(ξ)=∫e^{−πx²}e^{−2πixξ}dx. Differentiate under the integral. −2πix e^{−πx²}=i(e^{−πx²})′. Integration by parts, which is the rule for the transform of a derivative, gives H′(ξ)=−2πξH(ξ). Also H(0)=1. So H(ξ)=e^{−πξ²}.
Scaling. Let a=(4πt)^{−1/2}. Then x²/(4t)=π(ax)², so G_t(x)=a·e^{−π(ax)²}. Dilation gives 𝓕G_t(ξ)=H(ξ/a)=e^{−πξ²/a²}=e^{−4π²tξ²}. This is (i).

Semigroup. G_t is the density of a normal law with variance 2t. The convolution of normal laws adds variances. So G_s∗G_t is the density with variance 2(s+t), which is G_{s+t}. This is (ii). It also agrees with the product e^{−4π²sξ²}e^{−4π²tξ²}.
Equation for the kernel. ∂_xG_t=−(x/2t)G_t, so ∂ₓ²G_t=(−1/(2t)+x²/(4t²))G_t. Also ∂_tG_t=(−1/(2t)+x²/(4t²))G_t. So ∂_tG_t=∂ₓ²G_t.

Differentiation under the integral. For t in [a,b]⊂(0,∞) every derivative of G_t(z) in (t,z) is bounded by a constant C independent of z. So |f(y)∂G_t(x−y)|≤C|f(y)|, which is integrable. Dominated convergence shows that u is smooth, and u_t=f∗∂_tG_t=f∗∂ₓ²G_t=u_xx.
Transform and norm. The convolution theorem for L¹ gives 𝓕u(t)=𝓕G_t·𝓕f. Since G_t>0 and ∫G_t=1, ‖u(t)‖₁≤‖f‖₁‖G_t‖₁=‖f‖₁ and ∫u=∫f·∫G_t=∫f.

results.name: A finite measure on R^d is determined by its characteristic function
results.statement: Let μ,ν be finite Borel measures on ℝᵈ. Put μ̂(t)=∫e^{i⟨x,t⟩}dμ(x). (i) If μ̂(t)=ν̂(t) for all t∈ℝᵈ, then μ=ν. (ii) For the convolution of finite measures, (μ∗ν)^(t)=μ̂(t)ν̂(t).

/-- If the characteristic functions `charFun` of two finite measures `μ` and `ν` on
a complete second-countable inner product space coincide, then `μ = ν`. -/
theorem Measure.ext_of_charFun [CompleteSpace E]
    [IsFiniteMeasure μ] [IsFiniteMeasure ν] (h : charFun μ = charFun ν) :
    μ = ν := by
  simp_rw [funext_iff, charFun_eq_integral_innerProbChar] at h
  refine ext_of_integral_char_eq continuous_probChar probChar_ne_one (L := innerₗ E)
    ?_ ?_ h
  · exact fun v hv ↦ DFunLike.ne_iff.mpr ⟨v, inner_self_ne_zero.mpr hv⟩
  · exact continuous_inner

/-- The characteristic function of a convolution of measures
is the product of the respective characteristic functions. -/
lemma charFun_conv [IsFiniteMeasure μ] [IsFiniteMeasure ν] (t : E) :
    charFun (μ ∗ ν) t = charFun μ t * charFun ν t := by
  simp_rw [charFun_apply]
  rw [integral_conv]
  · simp [inner_add_left, add_mul, Complex.exp_add, integral_const_mul, integral_mul_const]
  · exact (integrable_const (1 : ℝ)).mono (by fun_prop) (by simp)

source_references.alignment: Mathlib proves that the characteristic function of a convolution is the product. This is part (ii).

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Gaussian identity. For ε>0, e^{−ε²|z|²/2}=(2π)^{−d/2}ε^{−d}∫e^{i⟨z,t⟩}e^{−|t|²/(2ε²)}dt. This is the transform of a Gaussian.

Smoothing by Fubini. Put z=x−y and integrate in μ. The integrand is bounded by e^{−|t|²/(2ε²)} times the finite mass of μ, which is integrable. So Fubini gives ∫e^{−ε²|x−y|²/2}dμ(x)=(2π)^{−d/2}ε^{−d}∫e^{−|t|²/(2ε²)}e^{−i⟨y,t⟩}μ̂(t)dt.
Equal smoothings. The right side depends on μ only through μ̂. So if μ̂=ν̂, then ∫k_ε(x−y)dμ(x)=∫k_ε(x−y)dν(x) for every y and every ε>0.
Test functions. Let φ be continuous with compact support. Integrate step 3 against φ(y)dy and use Fubini. Since k_ε is even, ∫(k_ε∗φ)dμ=∫(k_ε∗φ)dν.
Limit. The functions k_ε∗φ converge to φ uniformly as ε→∞, because φ is uniformly continuous. They are bounded by sup|φ|. The measures are finite. By dominated convergence ∫φ dμ=∫φ dν.
Conclusion for (i). Two finite Borel measures on ℝᵈ that agree on all continuous functions of compact support are equal, by uniqueness in the Riesz–Markov representation. So μ=ν.
Convolution. (μ∗ν)^(t)=∫∫e^{i⟨x+y,t⟩}dμ(x)dν(y). The integrand has modulus 1 and the measures are finite, so Fubini applies. The integral splits into μ̂(t)ν̂(t). This is (ii).

worked_application.title: The mean of Cauchy variables is again Cauchy
worked_application.goal: Use the theorem to show that the mean of n independent standard Cauchy variables has the standard Cauchy law.
hypotheses: The standard Cauchy law has characteristic function e^{−|t|}.
X₁,…,Xₙ are independent with this law.
The check uses a seeded simulation (seed 7) with 10⁶ samples for each n.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The characteristic function of the mean is a product by part (ii). Part (i) then identifies the law.

steps.text: Product. The characteristic function of (X₁+…+Xₙ)/n at t is (e^{−|t|/n})ⁿ=e^{−|t|}.
Identification. This equals the characteristic function of one Cauchy variable. By part (i) the mean has the standard Cauchy law.
Exact probability. P(|X|<3)=(2/π)arctan 3=0.795167.

Simulation. The frequencies of |mean|<3 are 0.794493 for n=1, 0.795278 for n=2, and 0.795029 for n=5. The frequencies of |mean|<1 are 0.499235, 0.499489 and 0.500018, and the exact value is 0.5. The standard error is 0.0005, so all values agree.

worked_application.result: The mean of n Cauchy variables has the same law as one variable. Averaging does not reduce the spread, so the law of large numbers fails.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: The measures must be finite. For Lebesgue measure the integral μ̂ is not defined.
The proof is not an inversion formula. It does not recover the density or the distribution function from μ̂.
The entry does not prove Lévy continuity, which links convergence of laws to convergence of μ̂.

results.name: Riesz-Thorin interpolation for matrices by the three lines theorem
results.statement: Let T be a complex matrix with index sets J (columns) and I (rows). Let 1≤p₀,p₁<∞ and 1<q₀,q₁<∞. Let M_i be the norm of T from ℓ^{p_i}(J) to ℓ^{q_i}(I). For 0<t<1 define p and q by 1/p=(1−t)/p₀+t/p₁ and 1/q=(1−t)/q₀+t/q₁. Then ‖Tf‖_q≤M₀^{1−t}M₁ᵗ‖f‖_p for every f.
hypotheses: The sets I and J are finite and carry counting measure.
Scalars are complex. This is needed for the complex three lines theorem.
The exponents satisfy p_i<∞ and q_i>1. Then the conjugate exponents q_i′ are finite.

prerequisites.reason: The three lines theorem is the analytic step of the proof.
Hölder duality gives the norm as a supremum and the bound on the edges.

/-- **Hadamard three-line theorem** on `re ⁻¹' [0, 1]` (Variant in simpler terms): Let `f` be a
bounded function, continuous on the closed strip `re ⁻¹' [0, 1]` and differentiable on open strip
`re ⁻¹' (0, 1)`. If, for all `z.re = 0`, `‖f z‖ ≤ a` for some `a ∈ ℝ` and, similarly, for all
`z.re = 1`, `‖f z‖ ≤ b` for some `b ∈ ℝ` then for all `z` in the closed strip
`re ⁻¹' [0, 1]` the inequality `‖f(z)‖ ≤ a ^ (1 - z.re) * b ^ z.re` holds. -/
lemma norm_le_interp_of_mem_verticalClosedStrip₀₁' (f : ℂ → E) {z : ℂ} {a b : ℝ}
    (hz : z ∈ verticalClosedStrip 0 1) (hd : DiffContOnCl ℂ f (verticalStrip 0 1))
    (hB : BddAbove ((norm ∘ f) '' verticalClosedStrip 0 1))
    (ha : ∀ z ∈ re ⁻¹' {0}, ‖f z‖ ≤ a) (hb : ∀ z ∈ re ⁻¹' {1}, ‖f z‖ ≤ b) :
    ‖f z‖ ≤ a ^ (1 - z.re) * b ^ z.re := by
  have : ‖interpStrip f z‖ ≤ sSupNormIm f 0 ^ (1 - z.re) * sSupNormIm f 1 ^ z.re := by
    by_cases! h : sSupNormIm f 0 = 0 ∨ sSupNormIm f 1 = 0
    · rw [interpStrip_eq_of_zero f z h, norm_zero, mul_nonneg_iff]
      left
      exact ⟨Real.rpow_nonneg (sSupNormIm_nonneg f _) _,
        Real.rpow_nonneg (sSupNormIm_nonneg f _) _ ⟩
    · rcases h with ⟨h0, h1⟩
      rw [ne_comm] at h0 h1
      simp_rw [interpStrip_eq_of_pos f _ (lt_of_le_of_ne (sSupNormIm_nonneg f 0) h0)
        (lt_of_le_of_ne (sSupNormIm_nonneg f 1) h1)]
      simp only [norm_mul]
      rw [norm_cpow_eq_rpow_re_of_pos ((Ne.le_iff_lt h0).mp (sSupNormIm_nonneg f _)) _]
      rw [norm_cpow_eq_rpow_re_of_pos ((Ne.le_iff_lt h1).mp (sSupNormIm_nonneg f _)) _]
      simp only [sub_re, one_re, le_refl]
  apply (norm_le_interpStrip_of_mem_verticalClosedStrip₀₁ f hz hd hB).trans (this.trans _)
  apply mul_le_mul_of_nonneg _ _ (Real.rpow_nonneg (sSupNormIm_nonneg f _) _)
  · apply (Real.rpow_nonneg _ _)
    specialize hb 1
    simp only [mem_preimage, one_re, mem_singleton_iff, forall_true_left] at hb
    exact (norm_nonneg _).trans hb
  · gcongr
    · exact sSupNormIm_nonneg f _
    · exact sub_nonneg.mpr hz.2
    rw [sSupNormIm]
    apply csSup_le _
    · simpa [comp_apply, mem_image, forall_exists_index,
        and_imp, forall_apply_eq_imp_iff₂] using ha
    · use ‖(f 0)‖, 0
      simp
  · apply Real.rpow_le_rpow (sSupNormIm_nonneg f _) _ hz.1
    rw [sSupNormIm]
    apply csSup_le _
    · simpa [comp_apply, mem_image, forall_exists_index, and_imp, forall_apply_eq_imp_iff₂] using hb
    · use ‖(f 1)‖, 1
      simp

source.alignment: Mathlib proves the three lines theorem on the strip 0≤Re z≤1 for bounded functions that are continuous on the closed strip and holomorphic inside. It is step 5. Mathlib has no Riesz-Thorin theorem.

results.proof_status: source declaration inspected; authored proof awaits inference review; no local Lean check

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Duality. For 1<q<∞, ‖h‖_q=sup{|Σ_ih_ig_i| : ‖g‖_{q′}=1}. So it suffices to prove |Σ_i(Tf)_ig_i|≤M₀^{1−t}M₁ᵗ for ‖f‖_p=1 and ‖g‖_{q′}=1. If M₀ or M₁ is 0 then T=0 and the claim is trivial.
Exponent maps. Note 1/q′=(1−t)/q₀′+t/q₁′. For Re z in [0,1] put a(z)=p((1−z)/p₀+z/p₁) and b(z)=q′((1−z)/q₀′+z/q₁′). Then a(t)=b(t)=1.

Analytic family. Put f_z(j)=(f_j/|f_j|)|f_j|^{a(z)} and g_z(i)=(g_i/|g_i|)|g_i|^{b(z)}, with value 0 where the entry is 0. Let Φ(z)=Σ_{i,j}T_{ij}f_z(j)g_z(i). Each term is a constant times an exponential of a linear function of z. So Φ is entire. It is bounded on the strip 0≤Re z≤1, since |f_z(j)|=|f_j|^{Re a(z)} and Re a(z) lies in a bounded interval. Also Φ(t)=Σ_i(Tf)_ig_i.
Edge Re z=0. |f_{iy}(j)|=|f_j|^{p/p₀}, so ‖f_{iy}‖_{p₀}^{p₀}=Σ|f_j|ᵖ=1. Likewise ‖g_{iy}‖_{q₀′}=1. By Hölder and the definition of M₀, |Φ(iy)|≤‖Tf_{iy}‖_{q₀}‖g_{iy}‖_{q₀′}≤M₀.

Edge Re z=1. The same argument with p₁,q₁ gives |Φ(1+iy)|≤M₁. Apply the Hadamard three lines theorem to Φ on the strip. It gives |Φ(z)|≤M₀^{1−Re z}M₁^{Re z} for all z in the strip. At z=t this is |Φ(t)|≤M₀^{1−t}M₁ᵗ.
Conclusion. By step 3 Φ(t)=Σ_i(Tf)_ig_i. Take the supremum over g and use step 1 and Hölder duality: ‖Tf‖_q≤M₀^{1−t}M₁ᵗ for ‖f‖_p=1. The general case follows by homogeneity.

/-- When the reference set is dense, the embedding map is an isometry on its image. -/
theorem embeddingOfSubset_isometry (H : DenseRange x) : Isometry (embeddingOfSubset x) := by
  refine Isometry.of_dist_eq fun a b => ?_
  refine (embeddingOfSubset_dist_le x a b).antisymm (le_of_forall_pos_le_add fun e epos => ?_)
  -- First step: find n with dist a (x n) < e
  rcases Metric.mem_closure_range_iff.1 (H a) (e / 2) (half_pos epos) with ⟨n, hn⟩
  -- Second step: use the norm control at index n to conclude
  have C : dist b (x n) - dist a (x n) = embeddingOfSubset x b n - embeddingOfSubset x a n := by
    simp only [embeddingOfSubset_coe, sub_sub_sub_cancel_right]
  have :=
    calc
      dist a b ≤ dist a (x n) + dist (x n) b := dist_triangle _ _ _
      _ = 2 * dist a (x n) + (dist b (x n) - dist a (x n)) := by simp [dist_comm]; ring
      _ ≤ 2 * dist a (x n) + |dist b (x n) - dist a (x n)| := by grw [← le_abs_self]
      _ ≤ 2 * (e / 2) + |embeddingOfSubset x b n - embeddingOfSubset x a n| := by
        rw [C]
        gcongr
      _ ≤ 2 * (e / 2) + dist (embeddingOfSubset x b) (embeddingOfSubset x a) := by
        gcongr
        simp only [dist_eq_norm]
        exact lp.norm_apply_le_norm ENNReal.top_ne_zero
          (embeddingOfSubset x b - embeddingOfSubset x a) n
      _ = dist (embeddingOfSubset x b) (embeddingOfSubset x a) + e := by ring
  simpa [dist_comm] using this

/-- Every separable metric space embeds isometrically in `ℓ^∞(ℕ)`. -/
theorem exists_isometric_embedding (α : Type u) [MetricSpace α] [SeparableSpace α] :
    ∃ f : α → ℓ^∞(ℕ, ℝ), Isometry f := by
  rcases (univ : Set α).eq_empty_or_nonempty with h | h
  · use fun _ => 0; intro x; exact absurd h (Nonempty.ne_empty ⟨x, mem_univ x⟩)
  · -- We construct a map x : ℕ → α with dense image
    rcases h with ⟨basepoint⟩
    have : Inhabited α := ⟨basepoint⟩
    have : ∃ s : Set α, s.Countable ∧ Dense s := exists_countable_dense α
    rcases this with ⟨S, ⟨S_countable, S_dense⟩⟩
    rcases Set.countable_iff_exists_subset_range.1 S_countable with ⟨x, x_range⟩
    -- Use embeddingOfSubset to construct the desired isometry
    exact ⟨embeddingOfSubset x, embeddingOfSubset_isometry x (S_dense.mono x_range)⟩

steps.text: Boundedness. By the triangle inequality, |d(a,x_n)−d(x_0,x_n)|≤d(a,x_0) for every n. So F(a) lies in ℓ^∞(ℕ) and ‖F(a)‖_∞≤d(a,x_0).

Upper bound. The x_0 terms cancel in a difference: F(a)_n−F(b)_n=d(a,x_n)−d(b,x_n). The triangle inequality gives |d(a,x_n)−d(b,x_n)|≤d(a,b) for every n. Take the supremum over n to get ‖F(a)−F(b)‖_∞≤d(a,b).
Lower bound, set up. Fix a,b∈X and ε>0. By density choose n with d(a,x_n)<ε/2.

Lower bound, estimate. Write d(a,b)≤d(a,x_n)+d(x_n,b). Rewrite the right side as 2d(a,x_n)+(d(b,x_n)−d(a,x_n)). The first term is less than ε. The second term is F(b)_n−F(a)_n, which is at most ‖F(b)−F(a)‖_∞.
Hence d(a,b)<ε+‖F(b)−F(a)‖_∞ for every ε>0. Let ε→0 to get d(a,b)≤‖F(a)−F(b)‖_∞. With step 2 this gives equality, so F is an isometric embedding.

Existence of the sequence. A separable space has a countable dense set S. If S is finite or countably infinite, list it as a sequence that may repeat points. Its range is S, which is dense. Then apply the construction above.

/-- In a compact T₂ space, the connected component of a point equals the intersection of all
its clopen neighbourhoods. -/
theorem connectedComponent_eq_iInter_isClopen [T2Space X] [CompactSpace X] (x : X) :
    connectedComponent x = ⋂ s : { s : Set X // IsClopen s ∧ x ∈ s }, s := by
  apply Subset.antisymm connectedComponent_subset_iInter_isClopen
  -- Reduce to showing that the clopen intersection is connected.
  refine IsPreconnected.subset_connectedComponent ?_ (mem_iInter.2 fun s => s.2.2)
  -- We do this by showing that any disjoint cover by two closed sets implies
  -- that one of these closed sets must contain our whole thing.
  -- To reduce to the case where the cover is disjoint on all of `X` we need that `s` is closed
  have hs : @IsClosed X _ (⋂ s : { s : Set X // IsClopen s ∧ x ∈ s }, s) :=
    isClosed_iInter fun s => s.2.1.1
  rw [isPreconnected_iff_subset_of_fully_disjoint_closed hs]
  intro a b ha hb hab ab_disj
  -- Since our space is normal, we get two larger disjoint open sets containing the disjoint
  -- closed sets. If we can show that our intersection is a subset of any of these we can then
  -- "descend" this to show that it is a subset of either a or b.
  rcases normal_separation ha hb ab_disj with ⟨u, v, hu, hv, hau, hbv, huv⟩
  obtain ⟨s, H⟩ : ∃ s : Set X, IsClopen s ∧ x ∈ s ∧ s ⊆ u ∪ v := by
    /- Now we find a clopen set `s` around `x`, contained in `u ∪ v`. We utilize the fact that
    `X \ u ∪ v` will be compact, so there must be some finite intersection of clopen neighbourhoods
    of `X` disjoint to it, but a finite intersection of clopen sets is clopen,
    so we let this be our `s`. -/
    have H1 := (hu.union hv).isClosed_compl.isCompact.inter_iInter_nonempty
      (fun s : { s : Set X // IsClopen s ∧ x ∈ s } => s) fun s => s.2.1.1
    rw [← not_disjoint_iff_nonempty_inter, imp_not_comm, not_forall] at H1
    obtain ⟨si, H2⟩ :=
      H1 (disjoint_compl_left_iff_subset.2 <| hab.trans <| union_subset_union hau hbv)
    refine ⟨⋂ U ∈ si, Subtype.val U, ?_, ?_, ?_⟩
    · exact isClopen_biInter_finset fun s _ => s.2.1
    · exact mem_iInter₂.2 fun s _ => s.2.2

        ← not_nonempty_iff_eq_empty]

  -- clopen neighbourhoods will then lie in whichever of u or v x lies in and hence will be a subset
  -- of either a or b.
  · have H1 := isClopen_inter_of_disjoint_cover_clopen H.1 H.2.2 hu hv huv
    rw [union_comm] at H

    by_cases hxu : x ∈ u <;> [left; right]

    · suffices ⋂ s : { s : Set X // IsClopen s ∧ x ∈ s }, ↑s ⊆ u
        from Disjoint.left_le_of_le_sup_right hab (huv.mono this hbv)
      · apply Subset.trans _ s.inter_subset_right
        exact iInter_subset (fun s : { s : Set X // IsClopen s ∧ x ∈ s } => s.1)

    · have h1 : x ∈ v :=

        from (huv.symm.mono this hau).left_le_of_le_sup_left hab
      · refine Subset.trans ?_ s.inter_subset_right
        exact iInter_subset (fun s : { s : Set X // IsClopen s ∧ x ∈ s } => s.1)
          ⟨s ∩ v, H2, mem_inter H.2.1 h1⟩

steps.text: Easy inclusion C(x)⊆Q(x). Let K be clopen with x∈K. The set C(x)∩K is clopen in C(x) and nonempty. Since C(x) is connected, C(x)∩K=C(x), so C(x)⊆K. Take the intersection over all such K.
Q(x) is closed, because it is an intersection of closed sets. Hence Q(x) is compact. It contains x.
Main claim: Q=Q(x) is connected. Suppose not. Then Q=A∪B, where A and B are disjoint, nonempty and closed in Q, and x∈A. Both are closed in X because Q is closed in X.

The closed sets A and B are compact and disjoint. In a Hausdorff space, disjoint compact sets have disjoint open neighbourhoods. To see this, separate each pair of points by open sets, then use compactness twice. So there are disjoint open sets U⊇A and V⊇B. The set Q lies in U∪V. Hence the compact set Z=X∖(U∪V) is disjoint from Q.

Every point of Z lies outside some clopen set that contains x, because Q is the intersection of those sets. So the open sets X∖K, for clopen K∋x, cover Z. By compactness finitely many K_1,…,K_m satisfy Z∩K_1∩…∩K_m=∅. Put K=K_1∩…∩K_m. It is clopen, contains x, and lies in U∪V.
Because K⊆U∪V and U∩V=∅, we have K∩U=K∖V. The first set is open and the second is closed. So K∩U is clopen, and it contains x since x∈A⊆U.
By the definition of Q, Q⊆K∩U. Then B⊆Q∩V⊆U∩V=∅. This contradicts B≠∅. So Q is connected.
Q is a connected set that contains x, so Q⊆C(x). Together with step 1, C(x)=Q(x).

Consequences. Every Q(x) is closed, so every component is closed. If clopen sets separate points, then Q(x)={x}, so C(x)={x} and X is totally disconnected. If X is totally disconnected then Q(x)=C(x)={x}, so for y≠x some clopen set contains x and not y.

worked_application.title: The component of a point in a convergent sequence times an interval
worked_application.goal: Let X=({0}∪{1/k : k≥1})×[0,1]. Find the component of (0,0) by clopen sets.
hypotheses: X is a closed bounded subset of ℝ², so it is compact Hausdorff.
The points 1/k are isolated in S={0}∪{1/k : k≥1}.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The theorem applies to X. It says that the component equals the intersection of clopen sets, so we can compute the component without testing connectedness of unknown sets.

steps.text: For N≥1 put K_N=({0}∪{1/k : k≥N})×[0,1]. Its complement in X is the finite union of the segments {1/k}×[0,1] for k<N. Each of these is open and closed in X, because 1/k is isolated in S. So K_N is clopen and contains (0,0).
The intersection of all K_N is {0}×[0,1]. A point (1/k,t) is missing from K_{k+1}. So Q((0,0))={0}×[0,1].
By the theorem C((0,0))=Q((0,0))={0}×[0,1]. The segment {0}×[0,1] is connected, so it is the whole component.
Check the size of a neighbourhood. For ε=1/100 the set K_101 is clopen, contains (0,0) and has all first coordinates below 1/100, since 1/101<1/100. It removes the 100 segments with k=1,…,100.
Every other component is a segment {1/k}×[0,1]. There are countably many components. The quotient space of components is S, which is homeomorphic to {0}∪{1/k}.

worked_application.result: The component of (0,0) is the segment {0}×[0,1]. All other components are the segments {1/k}×[0,1].

limitations: Compactness is essential. Remove the point (0,1/2) from the space of the application. The result is locally compact Hausdorff. A clopen set that contains (0,0) must contain the whole segments {1/k}×[0,1] for large k, so it contains (0,1) by closedness. Hence (0,1) lies in Q((0,0)). But the component of (0,0) lies in {0}×[0,1/2), so the two sets differ.

The statement is about components in X. It does not say that the quotient space of components is Hausdorff or has a nice basis. The quotient space is compact Hausdorff and totally disconnected, but the proof here does not show this.
The result does not say that a compact connected set is a point or an interval. It only compares two descriptions of the component.

results.name: Proper maps: closed with compact fibres, universally closed, and ultrafilter lifting
results.statement: Let f:X→Y be a continuous map of topological spaces. The following three statements are equivalent. (a) f is a closed map and every fibre f⁻¹(y) is compact. (b) For every topological space Z, the map f×id:X×Z→Y×Z is closed. (c) For every ultrafilter 𝒰 on X and every y∈Y such that f(𝒰) converges to y, there is a point x∈X with f(x)=y and 𝒰 converging to x. A map with these properties is called proper.
hypotheses: f is continuous. No separation axiom is assumed on X or Y.
In (c), 𝒰 converges to x means that every neighbourhood of x belongs to 𝒰.
In (b), Z ranges over all topological spaces.

/-- A map `f : X → Y` is proper if and only if it is continuous and **universally closed**, in the
sense that for any topological space `Z`, the map `Prod.map f id : X × Z → Y × Z` is closed. Note
that `Z` lives in the same universe as `X` here, but `IsProperMap.universally_closed` does not
have this restriction.

This is taken as the definition of properness in
[N. Bourbaki, *General Topology*][bourbaki1966]. -/
theorem isProperMap_iff_universally_closed {X : Type u} {Y : Type v} [TopologicalSpace X]
    [TopologicalSpace Y] {f : X → Y} :
    IsProperMap f ↔ Continuous f ∧ ∀ (Z : Type u) [TopologicalSpace Z],
      IsClosedMap (Prod.map f id : X × Z → Y × Z) := by
  constructor <;> intro H
  · exact ⟨H.continuous, fun Z ↦ H.universally_closed _⟩
  · rw [isProperMap_iff_isClosedMap_ultrafilter]
    exact ⟨H.1, H.2 _⟩

/-- A map `f : X → Y` is proper if and only if it is continuous and the map
`(Prod.map f id : X × Ultrafilter X → Y × Ultrafilter X)` is closed. This is stronger than
`isProperMap_iff_universally_closed` since it shows that there's only one space to check to get
properness, but in most cases it doesn't matter. -/
theorem isProperMap_iff_isClosedMap_ultrafilter {X : Type u} {Y : Type v} [TopologicalSpace X]
    [TopologicalSpace Y] {f : X → Y} :
    IsProperMap f ↔ Continuous f ∧ IsClosedMap
      (Prod.map f id : X × Ultrafilter X → Y × Ultrafilter X) := by
  -- The proof is basically the same as above.
  constructor <;> intro H
  · exact ⟨H.continuous, H.universally_closed _⟩
  · rw [isProperMap_iff_ultrafilter]
    refine ⟨H.1, fun 𝒰 y hy ↦ ?_⟩
    let F : Set (X × Ultrafilter X) := closure {xℱ | xℱ.2 = pure xℱ.1}
    have := H.2 F isClosed_closure
    have : (y, 𝒰) ∈ Prod.map f id '' F :=
      this.mem_of_tendsto (hy.prodMk_nhds (Ultrafilter.tendsto_pure_self 𝒰))
        (Eventually.of_forall fun x ↦ ⟨⟨x, pure x⟩, subset_closure rfl, rfl⟩)
    rcases this with ⟨⟨x, _⟩, hx, ⟨_, _⟩⟩
    refine ⟨x, rfl, fun U hU ↦ Ultrafilter.compl_notMem_iff.mp fun hUc ↦ ?_⟩
    rw [mem_closure_iff_nhds] at hx
    rcases hx (U ×ˢ {𝒢 | Uᶜ ∈ 𝒢}) (prod_mem_nhds hU ((ultrafilter_isOpen_basic _).mem_nhds hUc))
      with ⟨⟨y, 𝒢⟩, ⟨⟨hy : y ∈ U, hy' : Uᶜ ∈ 𝒢⟩, rfl : 𝒢 = pure y⟩⟩
    exact hy' hy

steps.text: Plan: prove (a)⇒(c)⇒(b)⇒(c)⇒(a). Fact used in several steps: if C is a closed set that belongs to an ultrafilter 𝒰 and 𝒰 converges to x, then x∈C. Otherwise X∖C is a neighbourhood of x, so X∖C∈𝒰, which is impossible.

(a)⇒(c). Let f(𝒰)→y and F=f⁻¹(y). Suppose no x∈F has 𝒰 converging to x. Because 𝒰 is an ultrafilter, each x∈F has an open set U_x∋x with U_x∉𝒰. F is compact, so F⊆U=U_{x_1}∪…∪U_{x_m}. A finite union of sets outside an ultrafilter is outside it, so U∉𝒰.

Continue (a)⇒(c). Since f is closed, f(X∖U) is closed. It does not contain y, because F⊆U. So V=Y∖f(X∖U) is an open neighbourhood of y with f⁻¹(V)⊆U. Since f(𝒰)→y, f⁻¹(V)∈𝒰, hence U∈𝒰. This contradicts step 2. So some x∈F has 𝒰 converging to x, and f(x)=y.

(c)⇒(b). Let Z be any space, C⊆X×Z closed, and (y,z) in the closure of (f×id)(C). The sets C∩(f×id)⁻¹(N), for N a neighbourhood of (y,z), are nonempty and closed under finite intersection. Extend the filter they generate to an ultrafilter 𝒲. Then (f×id)(𝒲)→(y,z) and C∈𝒲.

Continue (c)⇒(b). The first projection of 𝒲 is an ultrafilter 𝒰 on X, and f(𝒰)→y. By (c) there is x with f(x)=y and 𝒰→x. The second projection of 𝒲 converges to z. A filter whose two projections converge converges to the pair, because the product neighbourhoods U×V contain p₁⁻¹(U)∩p₂⁻¹(V). So 𝒲→(x,z). By the fact in step 1, (x,z)∈C, and (y,z)=(f×id)(x,z).

(b)⇒(c). Let Z be the set of ultrafilters on X with the topology whose basic open sets are Â={𝒢 : A∈𝒢}, for A⊆X. Let D={(x,pure x)}⊆X×Z and C its closure. By (b), (f×id)(C) is closed. Take 𝒰 with f(𝒰)→y.

Continue (b)⇒(c). A basic neighbourhood of (y,𝒰) is U×Â with U open, y∈U and A∈𝒰. Since f⁻¹(U)∈𝒰, the set f⁻¹(U)∩A is nonempty. A point x in it gives (f(x),pure x)∈U×Â. So (y,𝒰) lies in the closure of (f×id)(D), hence in (f×id)(C). So there is x with f(x)=y and (x,𝒰)∈C.

Finally, show 𝒰→x. Let U be open with x∈U and suppose U∉𝒰. Then X∖U∈𝒰, so U×(X∖U)^ is a neighbourhood of (x,𝒰). It meets D in a point (z,pure z) with z∈U and X∖U∈pure z, so z∉U. This is a contradiction. Hence every open U∋x is in 𝒰, and 𝒰→x.

(c)⇒(a), closedness. Let C be closed and y in the closure of f(C). As in step 4, build an ultrafilter 𝒰 that contains C and satisfies f(𝒰)→y. By (c) there is x with f(x)=y and 𝒰→x. By the fact in step 1, x∈C. So y∈f(C), and f(C) is closed.

(c)⇒(a), compact fibres. Let F=f⁻¹(y) and let 𝒱 be an ultrafilter on F. Its image 𝒰 in X is an ultrafilter that contains F, and f(𝒰)=pure y→y. By (c) there is x with f(x)=y and 𝒰→x. Then x∈F, and 𝒱 converges to x in the subspace F. So F is compact.

worked_application.title: Which real maps are proper
worked_application.goal: Test three maps on ℝ with the criteria: f(x)=x³−3x, g(x)=x/(1+x²), and the map ℝ→{pt}.
hypotheses: All three maps are continuous.
ℝ has the usual topology. It is Hausdorff and the compact sets are the closed bounded sets.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The theorem gives three equivalent tests. We use the ultrafilter test (c) for f and g, and the universal closedness test (b) for the constant map.

steps.text: f(x)=x³−3x satisfies |f(x)|→∞ as |x|→∞. Let f(𝒰)→y. Then |f| is below |y|+1 on a set of 𝒰. That set lies in a closed bounded interval, which is compact. So 𝒰 converges to some x. By continuity and uniqueness of limits in ℝ, f(x)=y. Hence f is proper.
By the theorem f is closed with compact fibres. The fibre over 2 solves x³−3x−2=(x−2)(x+1)²=0, so it is {2,−1}. The fibre over 0 is {0,√3,−√3}. Both are finite, hence compact.

g(x)=x/(1+x²). The derivative (1−x²)/(1+x²)² is at most 0 on [1,∞). So g decreases there from g(1)=1/2 through g(2)=2/5 and g(10)=10/101 toward 0. The closed set [1,∞) has image (0,1/2], which is not closed. So g is not closed and not proper.
Ultrafilter view for g. Let 𝒰 be an ultrafilter that contains every set [n,∞). Then g(𝒰)→0. But no x has 𝒰→x, since 𝒰 contains [|x|+1,∞), which misses a neighbourhood of x. So (c) fails.

The map ℝ→{pt}. Take Z=ℝ and C={(x,z) : xz=1}, a closed subset of ℝ×ℝ. The map f×id is the projection to Z. The image of C is ℝ∖{0}, which is not closed. So (b) fails and the map is not proper. This matches the fact that ℝ is not compact.

worked_application.result: f(x)=x³−3x is proper. g(x)=x/(1+x²) and the map ℝ→{pt} are not proper.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: The statement uses the Bourbaki definition of proper map. Some authors only ask for a closed map with compact fibres in the Hausdorff setting. Here (a) is equivalent in full generality.

Compact fibres alone are not enough. The inclusion (0,1)→ℝ has singleton fibres but is not closed, so it is not proper. Closedness alone is not enough either. The map ℝ→{pt} is closed but its fibre ℝ is not compact.
The test space Z in (b) must be arbitrary. A map can be closed without being universally closed.

results.name: Partitions of unity subordinate to an open cover of a paracompact normal space
results.statement: Let X be a paracompact T₄ space, which means a normal T₁ space in which every open cover has a locally finite open refinement. Let s⊆X be closed. Let (U_i)_{i∈I} be open sets with s⊆⋃U_i. Then there are continuous functions f_i:X→[0,1] such that: (1) the family of supports (supp f_i) is locally finite, (2) the closure of {f_i≠0} lies in U_i for every i, (3) ∑_i f_i(x)=1 for x∈s, (4) ∑_i f_i(x)≤1 for all x∈X.
hypotheses: X is T₁, normal and paracompact. Metrizable spaces and compact Hausdorff spaces are examples.
The index set I is arbitrary. The sum in (3) and (4) is locally finite, so it is a finite sum near each point.
Mathlib proves the result without the T₁ assumption. This statement keeps T₁ to make the proof short.

/-- If `X` is a paracompact normal topological space and `U` is an open covering of a closed set
`s`, then there exists a `BumpCovering ι X s` that is subordinate to `U`. This version assumes that
`p : (X → ℝ) → Prop` is a predicate that satisfies Urysohn's lemma, and provides a
`BumpCovering` such that each function of the covering satisfies `p`. -/
theorem exists_isSubordinate_of_prop [NormalSpace X] [ParacompactSpace X] (p : (X → ℝ) → Prop)
    (h01 : ∀ s t, IsClosed s → IsClosed t → Disjoint s t →
      ∃ f : C(X, ℝ), p f ∧ EqOn f 0 s ∧ EqOn f 1 t ∧ ∀ x, f x ∈ Icc (0 : ℝ) 1)
    (hs : IsClosed s) (U : ι → Set X) (ho : ∀ i, IsOpen (U i)) (hU : s ⊆ ⋃ i, U i) :
    ∃ f : BumpCovering ι X s, (∀ i, p (f i)) ∧ f.IsSubordinate U := by
  rcases precise_refinement_set hs _ ho hU with ⟨V, hVo, hsV, hVf, hVU⟩
  rcases exists_isSubordinate_of_locallyFinite_of_prop p h01 hs V hVo hVf hsV with ⟨f, hfp, hf⟩
  exact ⟨f, hfp, hf.mono hVU⟩

steps.text: Cover. Add the open set X∖s to the family (U_i). The new family covers X. Paracompactness gives a locally finite open refinement (V_j)_{j∈J}. For each j choose an index φ(j)∈I∪{∗} with V_j⊆U_{φ(j)}, where U_∗=X∖s.

Shrinking lemma, one step. Let (V_j) be a locally finite open cover. Then there is a locally finite open cover (W_j) with closure(W_j)⊆V_j for all j. Proof: a T₁ normal space is regular. So each x has an open N_x with closure(N_x)⊆V_j for some j. Take a locally finite open refinement (M_k) of (N_x), and choose j(k) with closure(M_k)⊆V_{j(k)}. Put W_j=⋃{M_k : j(k)=j}.

Check the shrinking lemma. The family (W_j) is an open cover. It is locally finite: a neighbourhood that meets only finitely many M_k meets only finitely many W_j. The closure of a locally finite union is the union of the closures, so closure(W_j)=⋃ closure(M_k)⊆V_j.
Apply the shrinking lemma twice. We get locally finite open covers (W_j) and (W′_j) with closure(W′_j)⊆W_j and closure(W_j)⊆V_j.

Urysohn step. The closed sets closure(W′_j) and X∖W_j are disjoint. By Urysohn lemma for normal spaces there is a continuous g_j:X→[0,1] equal to 1 on closure(W′_j) and 0 on X∖W_j. Then supp g_j⊆closure(W_j)⊆V_j.

Normalise. The family (supp g_j) is locally finite, so G=∑_j g_j is a locally finite sum and is continuous. Because the sets W′_j cover X, G≥1 everywhere. Put h_j=g_j/G. Then h_j is continuous, ∑_j h_j=1, and supp h_j=supp g_j⊆V_j.

Group the functions. For i∈I put f_i=∑_{φ(j)=i} h_j. The supports of the h_j with φ(j)=i form a locally finite family, so f_i is continuous and the closure of {f_i≠0} lies in the union of the closures of those V_j, which lies in U_i. This gives (1) and (2).
Sums. We have ∑_{i∈I} f_i=∑_{φ(j)≠∗} h_j≤∑_j h_j=1, which is (4). For x∈s, every V_j with φ(j)=∗ lies in X∖s, so h_j(x)=0 for those j. Hence ∑_i f_i(x)=∑_j h_j(x)=1, which is (3).

worked_application.title: Gluing two local functions on the real line
worked_application.goal: Cover ℝ by U₁=(−∞,2) and U₂=(0,∞). Build a partition of unity by hand and use it to glue the local functions g₁=0 on U₁ and g₂(x)=x on U₂.
hypotheses: ℝ is metrizable, hence paracompact and normal.
s=ℝ. The cover has two sets.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: ℝ satisfies the hypotheses. The theorem gives continuous f₁,f₂ with the properties (1) to (4). The functions below are one explicit choice.

steps.text: Put f₂(x)=min(1,max(0,x−1/2)) and f₁=1−f₂. Then f₂=0 for x≤1/2 and f₂=1 for x≥3/2. Both functions are continuous and take values in [0,1], and f₁+f₂=1.
Supports. {f₂≠0}=(1/2,∞) has closure [1/2,∞)⊆(0,∞)=U₂. {f₁≠0}=(−∞,3/2) has closure (−∞,3/2]⊆(−∞,2)=U₁. So (2) holds.

Glue. Define g=f₁g₁+f₂g₂=f₂(x)·x, using g₁=0 on U₁ and g₂(x)=x on U₂. The product f₁g₁ is defined on all of ℝ by 0 outside U₁, and f₂g₂ by 0 outside U₂. Both are continuous because the supports lie inside the domains.
Convexity check. At x=1 the weights are f₁=f₂=1/2, so g(1)=(1/2)·0+(1/2)·1=1/2. The glued value is a convex combination of the two local values, as expected.

worked_application.result: g(x)=min(1,max(0,x−1/2))·x is continuous on ℝ. It equals 0 for x≤1/2 and x for x≥3/2, and g(1)=1/2, g(5/4)=15/16.

Smooth partitions of unity on manifolds need extra bump function arguments. This statement gives only continuous functions.
The functions f_i are not unique. They depend on the choices of the refinement and the Urysohn functions.

results.name: Chain homotopic maps induce the same map on homology
results.statement: Let C and D be chain complexes of modules over a ring R, with differentials d. Let f,g:C→D be chain maps. Suppose there are R-linear maps h_n:C_n→D_{n+1} with f_n−g_n=d h_n+h_{n−1} d for all n. Then H_n(f)=H_n(g) for all n. Consequently a chain homotopy equivalence induces isomorphisms on all homology groups, and a complex whose identity map is homotopic to zero has zero homology.
hypotheses: C and D are chain complexes of R-modules. Chain maps commute with d.
The maps h_n are only R-linear. They need not commute with d.
The relation holds in every degree n, with h_{−1}=0.

definitions.name: chain homotopy equivalence

steps.text: Well defined action. A chain map sends cycles to cycles and boundaries to boundaries. So H_n(f)[z]=[f(z)] for every cycle z.
Take a cycle z∈C_n. Then dz=0, so the homotopy relation gives f(z)−g(z)=d h(z)+h(dz)=d h(z).
Hence f(z)−g(z) is a boundary in D, so [f(z)]=[g(z)]. This holds for every cycle, so H_n(f)=H_n(g).
Equivalences. If vu is homotopic to id_C and uv is homotopic to id_D, apply steps 1 to 3 and functoriality: H_n(v)H_n(u)=H_n(vu)=id and H_n(u)H_n(v)=id. So H_n(u) is an isomorphism.
Contractible complexes. If id_C is homotopic to 0, then H_n(id)=H_n(0). The left side is the identity and the right side is zero, so H_n(C)=0 for every n.

worked_application.goal: Let C_1=ℚ², C_0=ℚ, with d(x,y)=x+y. Let K be the complex with K_1=ℚ and K_0=0. Show that C and K are chain homotopy equivalent and read off the homology.

C_n=0 for n≠0,1 and K_n=0 for n≠1.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The theorem applies to C and to the maps u:K→C and v:C→K defined below, together with the homotopy h.

steps.text: Define u(a)=(a,−a) in degree 1 and v(x,y)=(x−y)/2 in degree 1. Both are zero in degree 0. They are chain maps because du(a)=a−a=0 and K_0=0. Then vu(a)=(a+a)/2=a, so vu=id_K.
Define h_0:C_0→C_1 by h_0(t)=(t/2,t/2) and h_1=0. Then compute uv(x,y)=((x−y)/2,−(x−y)/2) and h_0 d(x,y)=((x+y)/2,(x+y)/2).
Check degree 1: (uv+hd)(x,y)=(((x−y)+(x+y))/2, (−(x−y)+(x+y))/2)=(x,y). So id−uv=hd there. For (x,y)=(3,1) this is (1,−1)+(2,2)=(3,1).
Check degree 0: uv=0 and d h_0(t)=t/2+t/2=t. So id−uv=dh in degree 0. Hence id_C is homotopic to uv, and C is homotopy equivalent to K.

By the theorem H_n(u) is an isomorphism for all n. For K, H_1(K)=ℚ and all other groups are zero. So H_1(C)=ℚ and H_0(C)=0. This agrees with a direct count: ker d is spanned by (1,−1) and d is onto ℚ.

results.name: Cohomology of a finite cyclic group from the periodic resolution
results.statement: Let G be a cyclic group of order m with generator g. Let A be a G-module. Put N=1+g+…+g^{m−1} acting on A. Then H⁰(G,A)=ker(g−1). For every odd n, Hⁿ(G,A)=ker N/(g−1)A. For every even n≥2, Hⁿ(G,A)=ker(g−1)/N A.
hypotheses: G is finite cyclic with a fixed generator g.
A is a left module over ℤ[G]. The action of g on A is an additive automorphism of order dividing m.
Hⁿ(G,A) means Ext^n over ℤ[G] from the trivial module ℤ to A.

prerequisites.reason: The independence of group cohomology from the chosen resolution uses chain homotopy invariance of cohomology.

definitions.name: group cohomology

definitions.name: norm element
definitions.text: N=∑_{i=0}^{m−1} g^i in ℤ[G]. It satisfies (g−1)N=0=N(g−1).

definitions.name: periodic resolution
definitions.text: The complex … → ℤ[G] →(N) ℤ[G] →(g−1) ℤ[G] →ε ℤ, where ε is the augmentation.

source.excerpt:
/-- Given a finite cyclic group `G` generated by `g` and `A : Rep k G`, `Hⁱ(G, A)` is isomorphic
to the homology of the short complex of `k`-modules `A --N--> A --(ρ(g) - 𝟙)--> A` when `i` is
nonzero and even. -/
noncomputable def groupCohomologyIsoEven (i : ℕ) [h₀ : NeZero i] (hi : Even i) :
    groupCohomology A i ≅ (normHomCompSub A g).homology :=
  groupCohomologyIso A i (resolution k g hg) ≪≫
  (HomologicalComplex.homologyMapIso (homResolutionIso A g hg) i) ≪≫
  HomologicalComplex.alternatingConstHomologyIsoEven (ModuleCat.of k A.V) (by ext; simp [sub_hom])
    (by ext; simp [sub_hom]) (by simp)
    (by induction i generalizing h₀ with | zero => exact (NeZero.ne 0 rfl).elim | succ n _ => simp)
    (by simp) hi

steps.text: Write R=ℤ[G]. Let P_n=R for n≥0 with differentials d_1=g−1, d_2=N, d_3=g−1, d_4=N, and so on. Let ε:P_0→ℤ be the augmentation ε(∑a_i g^i)=∑a_i. Because (g−1)N=N(g−1)=g^m−1=0, this is a complex.
Exactness at the right end. ε is onto. Its kernel is the set of ∑a_i g^i with ∑a_i=0. Such an element equals ∑a_i(g^i−1), and g^i−1=(g−1)(1+g+…+g^{i−1}). So ker ε=(g−1)R=im d_1.
Exactness at the places where the next map is g−1. Let a=∑a_i g^i with (g−1)a=0. Then a_{i−1}=a_i for all i modulo m, so all coefficients are equal and a=cN. Hence ker(g−1)=ℤN=im(N).
Exactness at the places where the next map is N. Let a=∑a_i g^i with Na=0. Since N·g^i=N, Na=(∑a_i)N, so ∑a_i=0. By step 2, a∈(g−1)R. So ker N=(g−1)R=im(g−1).
Each P_n is a free R-module, so (P,ε) is a projective resolution of ℤ.

Independence of the resolution. Any two projective resolutions of ℤ are chain homotopy equivalent. Applying Hom_G(−,A) keeps the homotopy, and chain homotopic maps give equal maps on cohomology. So Hⁿ(G,A) can be computed from P.

Apply Hom_G(−,A). Since P_n=R is free of rank one, Hom_G(R,A)≅A by evaluation at 1. A map φ composed with multiplication by g−1 or N corresponds to multiplication by g−1 or N on A, because R is commutative. We get the cochain complex A →(g−1) A →(N) A →(g−1) A →(N) …

Read off cohomology. In degree 0, H⁰=ker(g−1). In odd degree n, the incoming map is g−1 and the outgoing map is N, so Hⁿ=ker N/im(g−1). In even degree n≥2 the incoming map is N and the outgoing map is g−1, so Hⁿ=ker(g−1)/im N.

results.name: Completeness of the Hausdorff metric on closed sets
results.statement: Let (X,d) be a complete metric space. For nonempty bounded closed sets S,T put H(S,T)=max(sup_{s∈S} d(s,T), sup_{t∈T} d(t,S)). Then H is a metric on the set of nonempty bounded closed subsets of X, and this metric space is complete. If (S_n) satisfies H(S_n,S_{n+1})<2^{−n}, then (S_n) converges to T=⋂_n closure(⋃_{m≥n} S_m) with H(S_n,T)≤3·2^{−n}.
hypotheses: X is a complete metric space.
The sets are nonempty, bounded and closed, so H is finite.
Mathlib proves the same for all closed sets with the extended Hausdorff distance, which may take the value ∞.

definitions.name: Hausdorff distance
definitions.text: H(S,T) is the least r such that every point of S is within r of T and every point of T is within r of S, taken as a supremum.

definitions.name: Cauchy criterion with a subsequence
definitions.text: A Cauchy sequence converges if some subsequence converges. A Cauchy sequence has a subsequence with H(S_{n},S_{n+1})<2^{−n}.

definitions.name: limit set
definitions.text: T=⋂_n closure(⋃_{m≥n}S_m). It is the set of limits of sequences x_{k_j}∈S_{k_j}.

source.excerpt:
/-- In a complete space, the type of closed subsets is complete for the Hausdorff edistance. -/
instance instCompleteSpace [CompleteSpace α] : CompleteSpace (Closeds α) := by
  /- We will show that, if a sequence of sets `s n` satisfies
    `edist (s n) (s (n+1)) < 2^{-n}`, then it converges. This is enough to guarantee
    completeness, by a standard completeness criterion.
    We use the shorthand `B n = 2^{-n}` in ennreal. -/
  let B : ℕ → ℝ≥0∞ := fun n => 2⁻¹ ^ n
  have B_pos : ∀ n, (0 : ℝ≥0∞) < B n := by simp [B, ENNReal.pow_pos]
  have B_ne_top : ∀ n, B n ≠ ⊤ := by finiteness
  /- Consider a sequence of closed sets `s n` with `edist (s n) (s (n+1)) < B n`.
    We will show that it converges. The limit set is `t0 = ⋂n, closure (⋃m≥n, s m)`.
    We will have to show that a point in `s n` is close to a point in `t0`, and a point
    in `t0` is close to a point in `s n`. The completeness then follows from a
    standard criterion. -/
  refine EMetric.complete_of_convergent_controlled_sequences B B_pos fun s hs => ?_
  let t0 := ⋂ n, closure (⋃ m ≥ n, s m : Set α)
  let t : Closeds α := ⟨t0, isClosed_iInter fun _ => isClosed_closure⟩
  use t
  -- The inequality is written this way to agree with `edist_le_of_edist_le_geometric_of_tendsto₀`
  have I1 : ∀ n, ∀ x ∈ s n, ∃ y ∈ t0, edist x y ≤ 2 * B n := by
    /- This is the main difficulty of the proof. Starting from `x ∈ s n`, we want
           to find a point in `t0` which is close to `x`. Define inductively a sequence of
           points `z m` with `z n = x` and `z m ∈ s m` and `edist (z m) (z (m+1)) ≤ B m`. This is
           possible since the Hausdorff distance between `s m` and `s (m+1)` is at most `B m`.
           This sequence is a Cauchy sequence, therefore converging as the space is complete, to
           a limit which satisfies the required properties. -/
    intro n x hx
    obtain ⟨z, hz₀, hz⟩ :
      ∃ z : ∀ l, s (n + l), (z 0 : α) = x ∧ ∀ k, edist (z k : α) (z (k + 1) : α) ≤ B n / 2 ^ k := by
      -- We prove existence of the sequence by induction.
      have : ∀ (l) (z : s (n + l)), ∃ z' : s (n + l + 1), edist (z : α) z' ≤ B n / 2 ^ l := by
        intro l z
        obtain ⟨z', z'_mem, hz'⟩ : ∃ z' ∈ s (n + l + 1), edist (z : α) z' < B n / 2 ^ l := by
          refine exists_edist_lt_of_hausdorffEDist_lt (s := s (n + l)) z.2 ?_
          simp only [ENNReal.inv_pow, div_eq_mul_inv]
          rw [← pow_add]
          apply hs <;> simp
        exact ⟨⟨z', z'_mem⟩, le_of_lt hz'⟩
      use fun k => Nat.recOn k ⟨x, hx⟩ fun l z => (this l z).choose
      simp only [Nat.add_zero, Nat.rec_zero, true_and]
      exact fun k => (this k _).choose_spec
    -- it follows from the previous bound that `z` is a Cauchy sequence
    have : CauchySeq fun k => (z k : α) := cauchySeq_of_edist_le_geometric_two (B n) (B_ne_top n) hz
    -- therefore, it converges
    rcases cauchySeq_tendsto_of_complete this with ⟨y, y_lim⟩
    use y
    -- the limit point `y` will be the desired point, in `t0` and close to our initial point `x`.
    -- First, we check it belongs to `t0`.
    have : y ∈ t0 :=
      mem_iInter.2 fun k =>
        mem_closure_of_tendsto y_lim
          (by
            simp only [exists_prop, Set.mem_iUnion, Filter.eventually_atTop]
            exact ⟨k, fun m hm => ⟨n + m, by lia, (z m).2⟩⟩)
    use this
    -- Then, we check that `y` is close to `x = z n`. This follows from the fact that `y`
    -- is the limit of `z k`, and the distance between `z n` and `z k` has already been estimated.
    rw [← hz₀]
    exact edist_le_of_edist_le_geometric_two_of_tendsto₀ (B n) hz y_lim
  have I2 : ∀ n, ∀ x ∈ t0, ∃ y ∈ s n, edist x y ≤ 2 * B n := by
    /- For the (much easier) reverse inequality, we start from a point `x ∈ t0` and we want
            to find a point `y ∈ s n` which is close to `x`.
            `x` belongs to `t0`, the intersection of the closures. In particular, it is well
            approximated by a point `z` in `⋃m≥n, s m`, say in `s m`. Since `s m` and
            `s n` are close, this point is itself well approximated by a point `y` in `s n`,
            as required. -/
    intro n x xt0
    have : x ∈ closure (⋃ m ≥ n, s m : Set α) := by apply mem_iInter.1 xt0 n
    obtain ⟨z : α, hz, Dxz : edist x z < B n⟩ := EMetric.mem_closure_iff.1 this (B n) (B_pos n)
    simp only [exists_prop, Set.mem_iUnion] at hz
    obtain ⟨m : ℕ, m_ge_n : m ≥ n, hm : z ∈ (s m : Set α)⟩ := hz
    have : hausdorffEDist (s m : Set α) (s n) < B n := hs n m n m_ge_n (le_refl n)
    obtain ⟨y : α, hy : y ∈ (s n : Set α), Dzy : edist z y < B n⟩ :=
      exists_edist_lt_of_hausdorffEDist_lt hm this
    exact
      ⟨y, hy,
        calc
          edist x y ≤ edist x z + edist z y := edist_triangle _ _ _
          _ ≤ B n + B n := by gcongr
          _ = 2 * B n := (two_mul _).symm
          ⟩
  -- Deduce from the above inequalities that the distance between `s n` and `t0` is at most `2 B n`.
  have main : ∀ n : ℕ, edist (s n) t ≤ 2 * B n := fun n =>
    hausdorffEDist_le_of_mem_edist (I1 n) (I2 n)
  -- from this, the convergence of `s n` to `t0` follows.
  refine EMetric.tendsto_atTop.2 fun ε εpos => ?_
  have : Tendsto (fun n => 2 * B n) atTop (𝓝 (2 * 0)) :=
    ENNReal.Tendsto.const_mul (ENNReal.tendsto_pow_atTop_nhds_zero_of_lt_one <|
      by simp) (Or.inr <| by simp)
  rw [mul_zero] at this
  obtain ⟨N, hN⟩ : ∃ N, ∀ b ≥ N, ε > 2 * B b :=
    ((tendsto_order.1 this).2 ε εpos).exists_forall_of_atTop
  exact ⟨N, fun n hn => lt_of_le_of_lt (main n) (hN n hn)⟩

steps.text: Reduction. Let (S_k) be H-Cauchy. Choose a subsequence with H(S_{k_n},S_{k_{n+1}})<2^{−n}. A Cauchy sequence with a convergent subsequence converges. So it is enough to prove convergence for a sequence with H(S_n,S_{n+1})<2^{−n}.
Define T=⋂_n closure(⋃_{m≥n}S_m). It is closed as an intersection of closed sets.

Points of S_n are near T. Let x∈S_n. Put x_n=x. Given x_k∈S_k, pick x_{k+1}∈S_{k+1} with d(x_k,x_{k+1})<2^{−k}, which is possible since H(S_k,S_{k+1})<2^{−k}. The sequence (x_k) is Cauchy, since d(x_k,x_l)<2^{1−k} for l>k.
Let y=lim x_k. It exists because X is complete. For each j, x_k∈S_k for k≥j, so y lies in closure(⋃_{m≥j}S_m). Hence y∈T. Also d(x,y)≤∑_{k≥n}2^{−k}=2^{1−n}. In particular T is nonempty.
Points of T are near S_n. Let x∈T. Then x lies in closure(⋃_{m≥n}S_m). Choose z∈S_m with m≥n and d(x,z)<2^{−n}.

Chain z back to S_n. Because H(S_{k+1},S_k)<2^{−k}, there is z_k∈S_k with d(z_{k+1},z_k)<2^{−k}. Starting at z_m=z, we get z_n∈S_n with d(z,z_n)<∑_{k=n}^{m−1}2^{−k}<2^{1−n}. So d(x,S_n)<2^{−n}+2^{1−n}=3·2^{−n}.
Boundedness and the limit. Steps 3 to 6 give sup_{x∈S_n}d(x,T)≤2^{1−n} and sup_{x∈T}d(x,S_n)≤3·2^{−n}. So H(S_n,T)≤3·2^{−n}. Since S_n is bounded, T is bounded. Hence T is in the space and S_n→T.

H is a metric. It is symmetric by definition. H(S,T)=0 forces every point of S to lie in the closure of T, which is T, and the reverse, so S=T. The triangle inequality follows from d(s,U)≤d(s,t)+d(t,U) after taking suprema.

Check one more stage. H(C_1,C_2)=1/18, and the tail ∑_{k≥1}3^{−(k+1)}/2=1/12 bounds H(C_1,T). The true value is 1/18.

/-- This technique to witness `HasSeparatingCover` in regular Lindelöf topological spaces
will be used to prove regular Lindelöf spaces are normal. -/
lemma IsClosed.HasSeparatingCover {s t : Set X} [LindelofSpace X] [RegularSpace X]
    (s_cl : IsClosed s) (t_cl : IsClosed t) (st_dis : Disjoint s t) : HasSeparatingCover s t := by
  -- `IsLindelof.indexed_countable_subcover` requires the space be Nonempty
  rcases isEmpty_or_nonempty X with empty_X | nonempty_X
  · rw [subset_eq_empty (t := s) (fun ⦃_⦄ _ ↦ trivial) (univ_eq_empty_iff.mpr empty_X)]
    exact hasSeparatingCovers_iff_separatedNhds.mpr (SeparatedNhds.empty_left t) |>.1
  -- This is almost `HasSeparatingCover`, but is not countable. We define for all `a : X` for use
  -- with `IsLindelof.indexed_countable_subcover` momentarily.
  have (a : X) : ∃ n : Set X, IsOpen n ∧ Disjoint (closure n) t ∧ (a ∈ s → a ∈ n) := by
    wlog ains : a ∈ s
    · exact ⟨∅, isOpen_empty, SeparatedNhds.empty_left t |>.disjoint_closure_left, fun a ↦ ains a⟩
    obtain ⟨n, nna, ncl, nsubkc⟩ := ((regularSpace_TFAE X).out 1 4 :).mp ‹RegularSpace X› a tᶜ <|
      t_cl.compl_mem_nhds (disjoint_left.mp st_dis ains)
    exact
      ⟨interior n,
       isOpen_interior,
       disjoint_left.mpr fun ⦃_⦄ ain ↦
         nsubkc <| (IsClosed.closure_subset_iff ncl).mpr interior_subset ain,
       fun _ ↦ mem_interior_iff_mem_nhds.mpr nna⟩
  -- By Lindelöf, we may obtain a countable subcover witnessing `HasSeparatingCover`
  choose u u_open u_dis u_nhds using this
  obtain ⟨f, f_cov⟩ := s_cl.isLindelof.indexed_countable_subcover
    u u_open (fun a ainh ↦ mem_iUnion.mpr ⟨a, u_nhds a ainh⟩)
  exact ⟨u ∘ f, f_cov, fun n ↦ ⟨u_open (f n), u_dis (f n)⟩⟩
