steps.text: Let A and B be disjoint closed sets. For each a∈A, regularity gives an open U_a∋a with closure(U_a)∩B=∅. The sets U_a together with X∖A form an open cover of X.
By the Lindelof property there is a countable subcover. So there are open sets U_0,U_1,… (possibly finitely many) with A⊆⋃U_n and closure(U_n)∩B=∅ for all n. Drop X∖A, which does not meet A.
In the same way there are open sets V_0,V_1,… with B⊆⋃V_n and closure(V_n)∩A=∅ for all n.
Trim the sets. Put U′_n=U_n∖⋃_{k≤n}closure(V_k) and V′_n=V_n∖⋃_{k≤n}closure(U_k). These are open, because a finite union of closed sets is closed.
Put U=⋃U′_n and V=⋃V′_n. Then A⊆U: a point a∈A lies in some U_n, and it lies in no closure(V_k) because closure(V_k)∩A=∅. So a∈U′_n. In the same way B⊆V.

The sets U and V are disjoint. Suppose x∈U′_n∩V′_m. If n≤m, then x∈U_n⊆closure(U_n), but V′_m excludes closure(U_k) for all k≤m, including k=n. This is a contradiction. If m≤n, the roles are swapped and U′_n excludes closure(V_m). So U∩V=∅.

Second countable spaces. If X has a countable base 𝔅 and 𝒰 is an open cover, choose for each B∈𝔅 contained in some member of 𝒰 one such member. The chosen members are countable, and they cover X because every point lies in a basic set inside some member of 𝒰. So X is Lindelof.

results.name: Open subsets of Polish spaces are Polish
results.statement: Let X be a separable complete metric space with metric d. Let U≠X be an open subset and put δ(x)=inf{d(x,z): z∉U}. For x,y in U define d′(x,y)=d(x,y)+|1/δ(x)−1/δ(y)|. Then d′ is a metric on U that induces the subspace topology, and (U,d′) is complete. Hence U is separable and completely metrizable, that is, U is Polish. (If U=X there is nothing to prove.)
hypotheses: X is a separable complete metric space.
U is open and U≠X, so the complement of U is closed and nonempty.
The new metric d′ is different from d. The old metric d on U is not complete in general.

/--
A metric space structure on a subset `s` of a metric space, designed to make it complete
if `s` is open. It is given by `dist' x y = dist x y + |1 / dist x sᶜ - 1 / dist y sᶜ|`, where the
second term blows up close to the boundary to ensure that Cauchy sequences for `dist'` remain well
inside `s`.

This definition ensures the `TopologicalSpace` structure on
`TopologicalSpace.Opens.CompleteCopy s` is definitionally equal to the original one.
-/
instance instMetricSpace : MetricSpace (CompleteCopy s) := by
  refine @MetricSpace.ofT0PseudoMetricSpace (CompleteCopy s)
    (.ofDistTopology dist (fun _ ↦ ?_) (fun _ _ ↦ ?_) (fun x y z ↦ ?_) fun t ↦ ?_) _
  · simp only [dist_eq, dist_self, one_div, sub_self, abs_zero, add_zero]
  · simp only [dist_eq, dist_comm, abs_sub_comm]
  · calc
      dist x z = dist x.1 z.1 + |1 / infDist x.1 sᶜ - 1 / infDist z.1 sᶜ| := rfl
      _ ≤ dist x.1 y.1 + dist y.1 z.1 + (|1 / infDist x.1 sᶜ - 1 / infDist y.1 sᶜ| +
            |1 / infDist y.1 sᶜ - 1 / infDist z.1 sᶜ|) :=
        add_le_add (dist_triangle _ _ _) (dist_triangle (1 / infDist _ _) _ _)
      _ = dist x y + dist y z := add_add_add_comm ..
  · refine ⟨fun h x hx ↦ ?_, fun h ↦ isOpen_iff_mem_nhds.2 fun x hx ↦ ?_⟩
    · rcases (Metric.isOpen_iff (α := s)).1 h x hx with ⟨ε, ε0, hε⟩
      exact ⟨ε, ε0, fun y hy ↦ hε <| (dist_comm _ _).trans_lt <| (dist_val_le_dist _ _).trans_lt hy⟩
    · rcases h x hx with ⟨ε, ε0, hε⟩
      simp only [dist_eq, one_div] at hε
      have : Tendsto (fun y : s ↦ dist x.1 y.1 + |(infDist x.1 sᶜ)⁻¹ - (infDist y.1 sᶜ)⁻¹|)
          (𝓝 x) (𝓝 (dist x.1 x.1 + |(infDist x.1 sᶜ)⁻¹ - (infDist x.1 sᶜ)⁻¹|)) := by
        refine (tendsto_const_nhds.dist continuous_subtype_val.continuousAt).add
          (tendsto_const_nhds.sub <| ?_).abs
        refine (continuousAt_inv_infDist_pt ?_).comp continuous_subtype_val.continuousAt
        rw [s.isOpen.isClosed_compl.closure_eq, mem_compl_iff, not_not]
        exact x.2
      simp only [dist_self, sub_self, abs_zero, zero_add] at this
      exact mem_of_superset (this <| gt_mem_nhds ε0) hε

steps.text: d′ is a metric. For x,y in U we have δ(x)>0, so d′ is finite. It is symmetric. It satisfies the triangle inequality because d and (x,y)↦|1/δ(x)−1/δ(y)| both do. If d′(x,y)=0 then d(x,y)=0, so x=y.
The topologies agree, part one. Since d≤d′, every d-ball contains the d′-ball of the same radius. So every d-open set in U is d′-open.

The topologies agree, part two. Fix x in U and ε>0. The map y↦1/δ(y) is continuous at x for d, because δ is continuous and δ(x)>0. So there is r>0 such that d(x,y)<r implies |1/δ(x)−1/δ(y)|<ε/2. With r small, also d(x,y)<ε/2. Then d′(x,y)<ε. So every d′-open set is d-open.
Completeness. Let (x_n) be d′-Cauchy in U. Since d≤d′, it is d-Cauchy in X. By completeness of X it converges to some x in X.
The sequence (1/δ(x_n)) is Cauchy in ℝ, because |1/δ(x_n)−1/δ(x_m)|≤d′(x_n,x_m). So it is bounded by some C>0. Hence δ(x_n)≥1/C for all n.
The function δ is continuous on X, so δ(x)=lim δ(x_n)≥1/C>0. Because the complement of U is closed, δ(x)>0 gives x∈U. So the limit lies in U.
By step 3, x_n→x in d implies d′(x_n,x)→0. So (x_n) converges in (U,d′). Hence (U,d′) is complete.

Separability. A subspace of a separable metric space is separable. Take a countable dense set D in X and a countable base 𝔅 of balls with centres in D and rational radii. The sets B∩U that meet U give a countable base of U. One point from each gives a dense countable subset. The topology on U is the same for d and d′, so U is separable and completely metrizable.

For n≥1 we have x_n≤1/2, so δ(x_n)=x_n and 1/δ(x_n)=n+1.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The old metric on (0,1) is not complete, since x_n→0 leaves the interval. The new metric d′ blows up near the boundary and removes this defect.

steps.text: Compute d(x_n,x_{n+1})=1/(n+1)−1/(n+2)=1/((n+1)(n+2)). This tends to 0, and the sequence converges to 0 in ℝ, so it is d-Cauchy.
Compute the second term. |1/δ(x_n)−1/δ(x_{n+1})|=|(n+1)−(n+2)|=1. So d′(x_n,x_{n+1})=1/((n+1)(n+2))+1>1 for every n. For n=1 the value is 1/6+1=7/6.
So (x_n) is not d′-Cauchy. This is correct: it does not converge in (0,1), and completeness of d′ rules out any Cauchy sequence without a limit.
A numeric check of the metric: d′(1/2,1/4)=1/4+|2−4|=9/4. The points 1/2 and 1/4 are close in d (distance 1/4) but far in d′.
Conclusion: (0,1) with d′ is complete and has the usual topology. So (0,1) is Polish, as an open subset of ℝ.

results.name: Stereographic projection charts and the inversion transition
results.statement: Let E be a real inner product space and S the unit sphere. Let v be in S and put H=v^⊥. Define σ_v(x)=2(x−⟨x,v⟩v)/(1−⟨x,v⟩) on S∖{v}, and τ_v(w)=((|w|²−4)v+4w)/(|w|²+4) on H. Then σ_v is a homeomorphism from S∖{v} onto H with inverse τ_v. For the two charts σ_v and σ_{−v}, the transition map on H∖{0} is w↦4w/|w|². So the two charts form a smooth atlas of S.
hypotheses: E is a real inner product space.
v is a unit vector and H is its orthogonal complement.
The sphere has the subspace topology. For finite dimension n+1 the atlas shows that S is a smooth n-manifold. The statement for homeomorphism does not need finite dimension.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: The proof is a direct computation with inner products. No catalog theorem is cited.

definitions.name: stereographic projection
definitions.text: The map that sends x on the sphere to the point where the line from v through x meets the hyperplane H.

definitions.name: transition map
definitions.text: For two charts φ and ψ the map ψ∘φ^{-1} on the overlap of their domains.

definitions.name: smooth atlas
definitions.text: A cover by charts such that every transition map is smooth.

theorem stereo_left_inv (hv : ‖v‖ = 1) {x : sphere (0 : E) 1} (hx : (x : E) ≠ v) :
    stereoInvFun hv (stereoToFun v x) = x := by
  ext
  simp only [stereoToFun_apply, stereoInvFun_apply, smul_add]
  -- name two frequently-occurring quantities and write down their basic properties
  set a : ℝ := innerSL _ v x
  set y := (ℝ ∙ v)ᗮ.orthogonalProjectionOnto x
  have split : ↑x = a • v + ↑y := by
    rw [← ((ℝ ∙ v).starProjection_add_starProjection_orthogonal x),
      Submodule.starProjection_unit_singleton ℝ hv x]
    rfl
  have hvy : ⟪v, y⟫_ℝ = 0 := Submodule.mem_orthogonal_singleton_iff_inner_right.mp y.2
  have pythag : 1 = a ^ 2 + ‖y‖ ^ 2 := by
    have hvy' : ⟪a • v, y⟫_ℝ = 0 := by simp only [inner_smul_left, hvy, mul_zero]
    convert norm_add_sq_eq_norm_sq_add_norm_sq_of_inner_eq_zero _ _ hvy' using 2
    · simp [← split]
    · simp [norm_smul, hv, ← sq, sq_abs]
    · exact sq _
  -- a fact which will be helpful for clearing denominators in the main calculation
  have ha : 0 < 1 - a := by
    have : a < 1 := (inner_lt_one_iff_real_of_norm_eq_one hv (by simp)).mpr hx.symm
    linarith
  rw [split, Submodule.coe_smul_of_tower]
  simp only [norm_smul, norm_div, Real.norm_eq_abs, abs_of_nonneg ha.le]
  match_scalars
  · field_simp
    linear_combination 4 * pythag
  · field_simp
    linear_combination 4 * (a - 1) * pythag

/-- Stereographic projection from the unit sphere in `E`, centred at a unit vector `v` in `E`;
this is the version as an open partial homeomorphism. -/
def stereographic (hv : ‖v‖ = 1) : OpenPartialHomeomorph (sphere (0 : E) 1) (ℝ ∙ v)ᗮ where
  toFun := stereoToFun v ∘ (↑)
  invFun := stereoInvFun hv
  source := {⟨v, by simp [hv]⟩}ᶜ
  target := Set.univ
  map_source' := by simp
  map_target' {w} _ := fun h => (stereoInvFun_ne_north_pole hv w) (Set.eq_of_mem_singleton h)
  left_inv' x hx := stereo_left_inv hv fun h => hx (by
    rw [← h] at hv
    apply Subtype.ext
    dsimp
    exact h)
  right_inv' w _ := stereo_right_inv hv w
  open_source := isOpen_compl_singleton
  open_target := isOpen_univ
  continuousOn_toFun :=
    continuousOn_stereoToFun.comp continuous_subtype_val.continuousOn fun w h => by
      dsimp
      exact
        h ∘ Subtype.ext ∘ Eq.symm ∘ (inner_eq_one_iff_of_norm_eq_one hv (by simp)).mp
  continuousOn_invFun := (continuous_stereoInvFun hv).continuousOn

steps.text: Image of τ_v lies in S∖{v}. Write t=(|w|²−4)/(|w|²+4) and u=4/(|w|²+4). Then τ_v(w)=tv+uw and w⊥v. So |τ_v(w)|²=t²+u²|w|²=((|w|²−4)²+16|w|²)/(|w|²+4)²=1. The v-coefficient is t<1, so τ_v(w)≠v.
σ_v∘τ_v=id on H. We have ⟨τ_v(w),v⟩=t, and 1−t=8/(|w|²+4). The component of τ_v(w) in H is uw. So σ_v(τ_v(w))=2·uw/(1−t)=2·(4/(|w|²+4))·((|w|²+4)/8)·w=w.

τ_v∘σ_v=id on S∖{v}. Let x be in S∖{v}, a=⟨x,v⟩<1, and w=σ_v(x)=2(x−av)/(1−a). Since |x|=1, |x−av|²=1−a². So |w|²=4(1−a²)/(1−a)²=4(1+a)/(1−a). Then |w|²+4=8/(1−a) and |w|²−4=8a/(1−a). Hence t=a and u=(1−a)/2.
Continue: τ_v(w)=av+((1−a)/2)·2(x−av)/(1−a)=av+x−av=x. So τ_v is the inverse of σ_v.

Continuity. Both σ_v and τ_v are given by formulas built from inner products, norms, sums and quotients, with denominators 1−⟨x,v⟩>0 and |w|²+4>0. So they are continuous. Hence σ_v is a homeomorphism onto H.

The transition. The same holds for −v. Since the formulas for −v use ⟨x,v⟩ with the opposite sign, σ_{−v}(x)=2(x−av)/(1+a). The overlap is S∖{v,−v}, and σ_v maps it onto H∖{0}, because τ_v(0)=−v and τ_v(w)≠v.
Let x=τ_v(w) with w≠0. Then a=t, and 1+t=2|w|²/(|w|²+4). The H-component of x is 4w/(|w|²+4). So σ_{−v}(x)=2·(4w/(|w|²+4))·((|w|²+4)/(2|w|²))=4w/|w|².
The map w↦4w/|w|² is smooth on H∖{0} and is its own inverse. So all transition maps are smooth, and the two charts form a smooth atlas.

results.name: Exponential law for the compact-open topology
results.statement: Let X, Y and Z be topological spaces and give C(Y,Z) the compact-open topology. (a) For every Y: if F:X×Y→Z is continuous, then x↦F(x,·) is a continuous map X→C(Y,Z). (b) If Y is locally compact: if f:X→C(Y,Z) is continuous, then (x,y)↦f(x)(y) is continuous on X×Y. So for locally compact Y, continuous maps X×Y→Z correspond to continuous maps X→C(Y,Z).
hypotheses: X, Y, Z are topological spaces.
Part (a) needs no assumption.
Part (b) needs Y locally compact: every point has a compact neighbourhood inside each of its neighbourhoods.

steps.text: It suffices to check preimages of subbasic sets. The topology is generated by V(K,U), so f is continuous if each f^{-1}(V(K,U)) is open.
Part (a). Let f(x)=F(x,·). Then f^{-1}(V(K,U))={x: F({x}×K)⊆U}. Let x₀ be in this set. The set W=F^{-1}(U) is open and contains {x₀}×K.
Tube lemma. For each k in K choose an open box A_k×B_k with (x₀,k) in A_k×B_k⊆W. Finitely many B_k cover K, say B_{k_1},…,B_{k_m}. Put A=A_{k_1}∩…∩A_{k_m}. Then A×K⊆W (if K is empty take A=X).
So A⊆f^{-1}(V(K,U)), and the preimage is open. This proves part (a).
Part (b), first the evaluation map. Let ev(g,y)=g(y) on C(Y,Z)×Y. Fix (g₀,y₀) and an open U∋g₀(y₀). The set g₀^{-1}(U) is an open neighbourhood of y₀.
By local compactness there is a compact K with y₀ in the interior of K and K⊆g₀^{-1}(U). Then V(K,U) is open and contains g₀, and int K is open and contains y₀.
For (g,y) in V(K,U)×int K we get g(y)∈g(K)⊆U. So ev is continuous at (g₀,y₀).
Now F(x,y)=f(x)(y)=ev(f(x),y)=ev∘(f×id)(x,y). The map f×id is continuous and ev is continuous. So F is continuous. This proves part (b).

steps.text: For fixed t in [0,1], the function y²+ty on [−1,1] has minimum −t²/4 at y=−t/2, because |t/2|≤1/2. Its maximum is 1+t at y=1.

So f^{-1}(V(K,U))=[0,1). This is open in [0,1]. It agrees with the theorem.
Tube lemma check at t₀=0. The set {0}×[−1,1] maps into [0,1]⊆(−1,2). The open set A=[0,1) works, and F([0,1)×[−1,1])⊆[−1/4,2) lies in (−1,2).
Part (b) in reverse: f is a path in C(ℝ,ℝ), and the uncurried map F is continuous on [0,1]×ℝ. This is a homotopy from y² to y²+y.

results.name: One-point compactification of a locally compact Hausdorff space
results.statement: Let X be a locally compact Hausdorff space and X*=X∪{∞}. Declare a set open if it is an open subset of X, or if it has the form X*∖K with K closed and compact in X. Then this is a topology, X is an open subspace of X*, the space X* is compact and Hausdorff, and the neighbourhoods of ∞ are the sets that contain some X*∖K. A sequence or filter converges to ∞ exactly when it eventually leaves every compact closed subset of X.
hypotheses: X is Hausdorff.
X is locally compact: each point has a compact neighbourhood.
If X is compact, ∞ is an isolated point and the statement still holds.

steps.text: Topology axioms, finite intersections. If A and B are open subsets of X, then A∩B is open. If A=X*∖K and B=X*∖L, then A∩B=X*∖(K∪L), and K∪L is closed and compact. If A is open in X and B=X*∖K, then A∩B=A∖K=A∩(X∖K), which is open in X because K is closed.

Unions. A union of open subsets of X is open. A union of sets X*∖K_i is X*∖⋂K_i, and ⋂K_i is closed and lies in a compact K_i, so it is compact. For A open in X and B=X*∖K, A∪B=X*∖(K∖A). The set K∖A=K∩(X∖A) is closed and contained in the compact K, so it is compact. Mixed unions follow. The empty set and X* are open.

Open embedding. The inclusion i:X→X* is injective. The preimage of an open subset of X is itself. The preimage of X*∖K is X∖K, open since K is closed. So i is continuous. Its image X is open in X*, and open sets of X are open in X*. So i is an open embedding.

Compactness. Let 𝒞 be an open cover of X*. Some member C₀ contains ∞, so C₀=X*∖K with K compact. The other members cover K. Their traces on X are open in X, so finitely many cover K. With C₀ this gives a finite subcover.
Hausdorff, two points of X. They have disjoint open neighbourhoods in X, because X is Hausdorff. These sets are open in X*, since X is open in X*.

Hausdorff, a point x of X and ∞. Local compactness gives a compact neighbourhood N of x. Let V be the interior of N. Then V is open, N is closed because X is Hausdorff, and V⊆N. The sets V and X*∖N are open, contain x and ∞ respectively, and are disjoint.

Neighbourhoods and convergence. Any open set containing ∞ has the form X*∖K. So the sets X*∖K form a base of neighbourhoods of ∞. A filter or sequence converges to ∞ exactly when it is eventually in each X*∖K.

worked_application.title: The natural numbers and the real line
worked_application.goal: Describe ℕ* for ℕ with the discrete topology. Then describe convergence to ∞ in ℝ* for a sequence.
hypotheses: ℕ is discrete, so it is locally compact Hausdorff.
The compact subsets of ℕ are the finite sets.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: In ℕ*, closed compact sets are finite sets. Neighbourhoods of ∞ are cofinite sets together with ∞.

steps.text: Map ℕ* to the set {0}∪{1/(n+1): n in ℕ} by n↦1/(n+1) and ∞↦0. A neighbourhood of 0 in this set contains all but finitely many points 1/(n+1). So it pulls back to a set containing ∞ and all but finitely many n. This is a neighbourhood of ∞ in ℕ*.

Conversely a neighbourhood of ∞ contains X*∖K with K finite. So it contains all n larger than max K. The image contains 0 and all 1/(n+1) below a threshold. This is a neighbourhood of 0. So the bijection is a homeomorphism.
Now take ℝ and the sequence x_n=(−1)^n n. Let K be closed and compact in ℝ. It lies in [−R,R] for some R. For n>R we have |x_n|>R, so x_n is outside K.
Take R=10. For n≥11 we have |x_n|=n>10. So x_n is outside [−10,10] from n=11 onward. Hence x_n→∞ in ℝ*, although x_n does not converge in ℝ.

The point ∞ is a limit of x_n and the neighbourhood basis shows ℝ* is compact. A compact Hausdorff space that contains ℝ as an open dense subset and has one extra point is the circle, but this entry does not prove that.

worked_application.result: ℕ* is homeomorphic to {0}∪{1/(n+1)}. The sequence (−1)^n n converges to ∞ in ℝ*, and it is outside [−10,10] from n=11.

results.name: Courant-Fischer min-max principle for Hermitian matrices
results.statement: Let A be an n×n Hermitian matrix with eigenvalues λ_1≥λ_2≥…≥λ_n, counted with multiplicity. For x≠0 put R(x)=x*Ax/(x*x). Then for every k with 1≤k≤n, λ_k = max over subspaces V of C^n with dim V=k of min over nonzero x in V of R(x), and also λ_k = min over subspaces W with dim W=n−k+1 of max over nonzero x in W of R(x). The outer maximum is attained at the span of k orthonormal eigenvectors for λ_1,…,λ_k. The outer minimum is attained at the span of eigenvectors for λ_k,…,λ_n. In particular λ_1=max R and λ_n=min R.
hypotheses: A=A*, with complex entries. The real symmetric case is the same, with real subspaces.
The eigenvalues are sorted in decreasing order and repeated by multiplicity.
The inner minimum and maximum exist because R is continuous on the compact unit sphere of the subspace.

prerequisites.reason: Step 1 uses an orthonormal eigenbasis of the Hermitian matrix.

definitions.name: Dimension formula for subspaces
definitions.text: For subspaces V and W of an n dimensional space, dim(V∩W)≥dim V+dim W−n. So two subspaces whose dimensions add to more than n share a nonzero vector.

definitions.text: If u_1,…,u_n is an orthonormal eigenbasis with Au_i=λ_iu_i, the flag is the chain span(u_1,…,u_k) for k=1,…,n.

finite-dimensional vector space is an eigenvalue for that operator. -/
theorem hasEigenvalue_iSup_of_finiteDimensional [Nontrivial E] (hT : T.IsSymmetric) :
    HasEigenvalue T (⨆ x : { x : E // x ≠ 0 }, RCLike.re ⟪T x, x⟫ / ‖(x : E)‖ ^ 2 : ℝ) := by
  have := FiniteDimensional.proper_rclike 𝕜 E
  let T' := hT.toSelfAdjoint
  obtain ⟨x, hx⟩ : ∃ x : E, x ≠ 0 := exists_ne 0
  have H₁ : IsCompact (sphere (0 : E) ‖x‖) := isCompact_sphere _ _

steps.text: Spectral decomposition. By the spectral theorem for Hermitian matrices, there is an orthonormal basis u_1,…,u_n of C^n with Au_i=λ_iu_i. For x=∑c_iu_i we get x*x=∑|c_i|² and x*Ax=∑λ_i|c_i|².

Tail and head bounds. Let x be a nonzero vector in span(u_k,…,u_n). Then x*Ax=∑_{i≥k}λ_i|c_i|²≤λ_k∑|c_i|², so R(x)≤λ_k. Let x be a nonzero vector in span(u_1,…,u_k). Then x*Ax=∑_{i≤k}λ_i|c_i|²≥λ_k∑|c_i|², so R(x)≥λ_k. Both bounds are equalities at x=u_k.

Lower bound for the max-min. Put V0=span(u_1,…,u_k), which has dimension k. By step 2, R(x)≥λ_k for all nonzero x in V0, and R(u_k)=λ_k. So the minimum of R on V0 is exactly λ_k. Hence the supremum over V of the minimum of R on V is at least λ_k.

Upper bound for the max-min. Let V be any subspace of dimension k. Put W0=span(u_k,…,u_n), which has dimension n−k+1. Since dim V+dim W0=n+1>n, the dimension formula gives a nonzero x in V∩W0. By step 2, R(x)≤λ_k. So the minimum of R on V is at most λ_k. With step 3 this proves that the max-min equals λ_k and is attained at V0.

The min-max. By step 2, the maximum of R on W0 is exactly λ_k. Now let W be any subspace of dimension n−k+1. Since dim W+dim V0=n+1>n, there is a nonzero x in W∩V0, and R(x)≥λ_k by step 2. So the maximum of R on W is at least λ_k. Hence the min-max equals λ_k and is attained at W0.

Special cases. For k=1 the subspaces V are lines, and R is constant on a line, so λ_1=max R. For k=n the subspace W is a line, and the second formula gives λ_n=min R. The inner extrema exist because a subspace has a compact unit sphere and R is continuous there.

worked_application.goal: Bound the second eigenvalue λ_2 of the 3×3 matrix A with 2 on the diagonal and −1 on the two off diagonals, using only coordinate subspaces, and then see that the upper bound is sharp.
hypotheses: A=[[2,−1,0],[−1,2,−1],[0,−1,2]], n=3 and k=2, so the subspaces V have dimension 2 and the subspaces W have dimension n−k+1=2.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: A is real symmetric, so the theorem applies. For k=2 both formulas use two dimensional subspaces.

steps.text: Exact spectrum. Write A=2I−T, where T is the adjacency matrix of the path on 3 vertices. T has eigenvalues √2, 0 and −√2. So the eigenvalues of A are 2+√2=3.4142, 2 and 2−√2=0.5858. Thus λ_2=2.

Lower bound. Take V=span(e_1,e_2). On V the quotient R is the Rayleigh quotient of the block [[2,−1],[−1,2]], which has eigenvalues 3 and 1. So the minimum of R on V is 1. The max-min formula gives λ_2≥1.
Upper bound. Take W=span(e_1,e_3). On W the matrix is diag(2,2), because A has zero entries at the positions (1,3) and (3,1). So R=2 on all of W and the maximum is 2. The min-max formula gives λ_2≤2.

Sharpness. The vector (1,0,−1) lies in W and satisfies A(1,0,−1)=2(1,0,−1). So W is an optimal subspace in the min-max formula and the bound 2 equals λ_2. The vector (1,−√2,1) satisfies A(1,−√2,1)=(2+√2)(1,−√2,1), so the optimal V is span((1,−√2,1),(1,0,−1)) and the minimum of R on it is 2.
Two easy coordinate subspaces gave 1≤λ_2≤2 with no eigenvalue computation. One of the two bounds is exact.

results.statement: Let A and B be n×n Hermitian matrices. Write λ_1(M)≥…≥λ_n(M) for the eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix M. Then (a) λ_{i+j−1}(A+B)≤λ_i(A)+λ_j(B) whenever i,j≥1 and i+j−1≤n. (d) |λ_k(A)−λ_k(B)|≤‖A−B‖ for all k, where ‖·‖ is the spectral norm, equal to the largest absolute value of an eigenvalue of A−B. (e) If B−A is positive semidefinite of rank at most r, then λ_k(B)≤λ_{k−r}(A) for k>r. So the eigenvalues of A and B interlace when r=1.
hypotheses: A and B are Hermitian of the same size n.
Eigenvalues are sorted in decreasing order and counted with multiplicity.

steps.text: Notation. Let a_1,…,a_n, b_1,…,b_n and c_1,…,c_n be orthonormal eigenbases of A, B and A+B, with the eigenvalues in decreasing order.
Spans. By the tail and head bounds in the proof of the Courant-Fischer principle, x*Ax≤λ_i(A)x*x for x in span(a_i,…,a_n) and x*(A+B)x≥λ_m(A+B)x*x for x in span(c_1,…,c_m).

Proof of (a). Put m=i+j−1≤n. The subspaces S1=span(a_i,…,a_n) and S2=span(b_j,…,b_n) have dimensions n−i+1 and n−j+1. So dim(S1∩S2)≥n−i−j+2≥1. The subspace S3=span(c_1,…,c_m) has dimension m=i+j−1. Then dim(S1∩S2∩S3)≥(n−i−j+2)+(i+j−1)−n=1. Take a unit vector x in this intersection. By step 2, x*Ax≤λ_i(A), x*Bx≤λ_j(B) and x*(A+B)x≥λ_m(A+B). So λ_m(A+B)≤x*(A+B)x=x*Ax+x*Bx≤λ_i(A)+λ_j(B).

Proof of (b). Apply (a) to the matrices −A and −B. Since λ_k(−M)=−λ_{n+1−k}(M), (a) with indices p and q gives −λ_{n+2−p−q}(A+B)≤−λ_{n+1−p}(A)−λ_{n+1−q}(B). Put i=n+1−p and j=n+1−q. The condition p+q−1≤n becomes i+j≥n+1, and the inequality becomes λ_{i+j−n}(A+B)≥λ_i(A)+λ_j(B).
Proof of (c). Write B=A+P with P positive semidefinite. All eigenvalues of P are at least 0. Apply (b) with the pair (A,P) and j=n. Then i+j−n=i, and we get λ_i(B)≥λ_i(A)+λ_n(P)≥λ_i(A).
Proof of (d). Let E=B−A and t=‖E‖. Then −tI≤E≤tI. So A−tI≤B≤A+tI in the Loewner order. By (c) and the eigenvalue shift, λ_k(A)−t≤λ_k(B)≤λ_k(A)+t.

Proof of (e). Let P=B−A be positive semidefinite of rank at most r. Then P has at most r nonzero eigenvalues, so λ_{r+1}(P)=0. Apply (a) to A and P with indices i=k−r and j=r+1. Then i+j−1=k and λ_k(B)≤λ_{k−r}(A)+λ_{r+1}(P)=λ_{k−r}(A). Together with (c), λ_k(A)≤λ_k(B)≤λ_{k−r}(A).

results.statement: Let A be an n×n Hermitian matrix with eigenvalues λ_1≥…≥λ_n and put s_k(A)=λ_1+…+λ_k. Then (a) s_k(A)=max{∑_{i=1}^k x_i*Ax_i : x_1,…,x_k orthonormal in C^n}. (c) Let d_1≥…≥d_n be the diagonal entries of A sorted in decreasing order. Then d_1+…+d_k≤s_k(A) for each k, with equality for k=n. That is, the diagonal of A is majorized by its vector of eigenvalues.

steps.text: Setup. Take an orthonormal eigenbasis u_1,…,u_n with Au_j=λ_ju_j. For orthonormal x_1,…,x_k put w_j=∑_{i=1}^k|u_j*x_i|². Expanding each x_i in the basis (u_j) gives x_i*Ax_i=∑_jλ_j|u_j*x_i|². So ∑_ix_i*Ax_i=∑_jλ_jw_j.
Weights. We have 0≤w_j≤1 by the Bessel inequality applied to the unit vector u_j. Also ∑_jw_j=∑_i∑_j|u_j*x_i|²=∑_i‖x_i‖²=k.

The bound. Compute ∑_jλ_jw_j−s_k(A)=∑_{j≤k}λ_j(w_j−1)+∑_{j>k}λ_jw_j. For j≤k we have w_j−1≤0 and λ_j≥λ_k, so λ_j(w_j−1)≤λ_k(w_j−1). For j>k we have w_j≥0 and λ_j≤λ_k, so λ_jw_j≤λ_kw_j. Sum these: the difference is at most λ_k(∑_jw_j−k)=0. So ∑_ix_i*Ax_i≤s_k(A).
Attainment. For x_i=u_i the sum is ∑_{i≤k}λ_i=s_k(A). This proves (a).

Proof of (b). For the same orthonormal x_1,…,x_k, ∑x_i*(A+B)x_i=∑x_i*Ax_i+∑x_i*Bx_i≤s_k(A)+s_k(B) by (a) for A and for B. Taking the maximum over x gives s_k(A+B)≤s_k(A)+s_k(B). Homogeneity for t≥0 is clear from (a). A positively homogeneous subadditive function is convex.

Proof of (c). For any set of k distinct indices i_1,…,i_k, the standard basis vectors e_{i_1},…,e_{i_k} are orthonormal and ∑_ae_{i_a}*Ae_{i_a}=a_{i_1i_1}+…+a_{i_ki_k}. By (a) this is at most s_k(A). Choose the indices of the k largest diagonal entries to get d_1+…+d_k≤s_k(A). For k=n both sides equal the trace of A, because the trace is the sum of the diagonal and the sum of the eigenvalues.

worked_application.title: Top two eigenvalue sums of a 3×3 matrix
worked_application.goal: Compute s_2 for A=[[3,1,1],[1,2,0],[1,0,1]], test it against two orthonormal vectors, and check subadditivity and the majorization of the diagonal.
hypotheses: A=[[3,1,1],[1,2,0],[1,0,1]] and B=diag(1,−1,0). Both are real symmetric. k=2.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Both matrices are Hermitian, so (a), (b) and (c) apply.

steps.text: Spectrum of A. The characteristic polynomial is λ³−6λ²+9λ−3. Put λ=2+μ to get μ³−3μ−1=0, so μ=2cos θ with cos 3θ=1/2. Thus the eigenvalues are 2+2cos20°=3.8794, 2+2cos100°=1.6527 and 2+2cos140°=0.4679. Then s_2(A)=4+2cos40°=5.5321.
Test pair. For x_1=e_1 and x_2=e_2, ∑x_i*Ax_i=3+2=5≤5.5321. The maximum is attained only by pairs that span the top two eigenvectors.
Majorization. The diagonal is (3,2,1). Its partial sums 3, 5 and 6 are at most the partial sums 3.8794, 5.5321 and 6 of the eigenvalues. The last pair is equal, since both are the trace 6.
Subadditivity. B has eigenvalues 1, 0 and −1, so s_2(B)=1. The matrix A+B=[[4,1,1],[1,1,0],[1,0,1]] has eigenvalues (5+√17)/2=4.5616, 1 and (5−√17)/2=0.4384. So s_2(A+B)=5.5616≤s_2(A)+s_2(B)=6.5321.

worked_application.result: For this matrix s_2(A)=4+2cos40°=5.5321. The coordinate pair gives 5, the diagonal is majorized by the spectrum, and s_2(A+B)=5.5616≤6.5321.

results.statement: Let I be an interval and f:I→R convex. Let x_1≥…≥x_n and y_1≥…≥y_n be points of I such that x_1+…+x_k≤y_1+…+y_k for k=1,…,n−1 and x_1+…+x_n=y_1+…+y_n. /-- If `f : 𝕜 → 𝕜` is convex, then for any three points `x < y < z` the slope of the secant line of
`f` on `[x, y]` is less than the slope of the secant line of `f` on `[y, z]`. -/
theorem ConvexOn.slope_mono_adjacent (hf : ConvexOn 𝕜 s f) {x y z : 𝕜} (hx : x ∈ s) (hz : z ∈ s)
    (hxy : x < y) (hyz : y < z) : (f y - f x) / (y - x) ≤ (f z - f y) / (z - y) := by
  have hxz := hxy.trans hyz
  rw [← sub_pos] at hxy hxz hyz
  have ha : 0 ≤ (z - y) / (z - x) := by positivity
  have hb : 0 ≤ (y - x) / (z - x) := by positivity
  have key := hf.2 hx hz ha hb (by field)
  simp only [smul_eq_mul] at key
  ring_nf at key
  field_simp at key ⊢
  linarith

/-- If `f : 𝕜 → 𝕜` is convex, then for any point `a` the slope of the secant line of `f` through `a`
and `b ≠ a` is monotone with respect to `b`. -/
theorem ConvexOn.secant_mono (hf : ConvexOn 𝕜 s f) {a x y : 𝕜} (ha : a ∈ s) (hx : x ∈ s)
    (hy : y ∈ s) (hxa : x ≠ a) (hya : y ≠ a) (hxy : x ≤ y) :
    (f x - f a) / (x - a) ≤ (f y - f a) / (y - a) := by
  rcases eq_or_lt_of_le hxy with (rfl | hxy)
  · simp
  rcases lt_or_gt_of_ne hxa with hxa | hxa
  · rcases lt_or_gt_of_ne hya with hya | hya
    · convert hf.secant_mono_aux3 hx ha hxy hya using 1 <;> rw [← neg_div_neg_eq] <;> simp
    · convert hf.slope_mono_adjacent hx hy hxa hya using 1
      rw [← neg_div_neg_eq]; simp
  · exact hf.secant_mono_aux2 ha hy hxa hxy

steps.text: Reduction. Delete every index i with x_i=y_i. The remaining lists are still sorted and have the same partial sum differences D_k, because each deleted term contributes 0 to every difference. Both sides of the claim lose the same amount f(x_i)=f(y_i). So we may assume x_i≠y_i for all i, and then n≥2 if some index remains.

Monotone slopes. Let f be convex. For a<b<c in I, convexity gives the three chord inequalities s(a,b)≤s(a,c)≤s(b,c). Fix v. Apply them to the three possible orders of u, u′ and v with u<u′. In each order they give s(u,v)≤s(u′,v). So u↦s(u,v) is nondecreasing on I minus the point v.

Decreasing chord slopes. Put c_i=s(x_i,y_i). We claim c_i≥c_{i+1}. If x_{i+1}≠y_i, then c_i=s(x_i,y_i)≥s(x_{i+1},y_i)≥s(x_{i+1},y_{i+1}). The first step moves the first argument down from x_i to x_{i+1}. The second step moves the second argument down from y_i to y_{i+1}. Both steps use step 2 and the symmetry of s. If x_{i+1}=y_i, then x_i≥x_{i+1}=y_i≥y_{i+1} and x_i≠y_i, so x_i≠y_{i+1}. Use the other route c_i≥s(x_i,y_{i+1})≥s(x_{i+1},y_{i+1}).

Abel summation. Put d_i=y_i−x_i and D_k=d_1+…+d_k. By the hypothesis D_k≥0 for all k and D_n=0. Because f(y_i)−f(x_i)=c_id_i, we get ∑(f(y_i)−f(x_i))=∑c_id_i=∑_{k=1}^{n−1}(c_k−c_{k+1})D_k+c_nD_n=∑_{k=1}^{n−1}(c_k−c_{k+1})D_k.
Sign. Every term (c_k−c_{k+1})D_k is the product of two nonnegative numbers. So the sum is nonnegative, and ∑f(x_i)≤∑f(y_i). This proves the inequality.

Equality for strictly convex f. Suppose some index remains after the reduction, that is x≠y. Then D_1=y_1−x_1 is nonnegative and nonzero, so D_1>0, and then n≥2 because D_n=0. For strictly convex f the slope inequalities in step 3 are strict whenever the moved argument changes. So c_k=c_{k+1} forces x_k=x_{k+1} and y_k=y_{k+1}, and hence d_{k+1}=d_k. Suppose every k with D_k>0 had c_k=c_{k+1}. Starting at k=1, induction gives d_k=d_1 for all k, so D_n=nd_1>0, a contradiction with D_n=0. So some term with D_k>0 has c_k>c_{k+1}, and the sum is positive. Therefore equality holds only if no index remains, that is x_i=y_i for all i.

Entropy case. The function f(t)=t ln t is strictly convex on [0,∞) with f(0)=0. For probability vectors p and q sorted in decreasing order with p majorized by q, the inequality gives ∑p_iln p_i≤∑q_iln q_i. This is H(p)≥H(q), because H=−∑t ln t.

steps.text: Sums. ∑x_iln x_i=6ln3+4ln2=9.3643 and ∑y_iln y_i=5ln5+3ln3=11.3430. So the first is smaller, as claimed.

Proof quantities. The pair (x_2,y_2)=(3,3) is deleted. The remaining pairs are (3,5), (2,1) and (2,1). The chord slopes are c_1=(f(5)−f(3))/2=2.3757 and c_2=c_3=f(2)−f(1)=1.3863. They decrease, as step 3 says.
Differences. d=(2,−1,−1), so D_1=2, D_2=1 and D_3=0. The Abel sum is (c_1−c_2)D_1+(c_2−c_3)D_2=0.9894×2+0=1.9788. The direct difference 11.3430−9.3643=1.9787 agrees.
Entropy. H(p)=1.2799 and H(q)=1.0297. So H(p)≥H(q). The more concentrated distribution q has lower entropy.

results.statement: Let A be an n×n positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix with diagonal entries a_11,…,a_nn. Then det A≤a_11a_22⋯a_nn. If A is positive definite, equality holds if and only if A is diagonal. For every square complex matrix M with columns m_1,…,m_n, |det M|≤‖m_1‖‖m_2‖⋯‖m_n‖, and the same holds for rows. steps.text: Zero diagonal. Suppose a_ii=0 for some i. Taking x=te_i+e_j with real t of both signs shows a_ij=0, since x*Ax=2t Re a_ij+a_jj≥0 for all t forces Re a_ij=0 and similarly Im a_ij=0. So row i is zero, det A=0, and the product of the diagonal entries is 0. The inequality holds as an equality. Assume now that all a_ii>0.
Normalization. Let D=diag(a_11^{−1/2},…,a_nn^{−1/2}) and B=DAD. Then B is positive semidefinite with b_ii=1 for all i, and det B=det A/(a_11⋯a_nn).
Spectrum of B. B is Hermitian, so B has real eigenvalues μ_1,…,μ_n≥0 with det B=∏μ_i and trace B=∑μ_i. The trace is n, since the diagonal is all ones.
Mean inequality. By the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality, det B=∏μ_i≤(∑μ_i/n)^n=1. Hence det A=det B·∏a_ii≤∏a_ii.

Equality for positive definite A. If det A=∏a_ii, then ∏μ_i=(∑μ_i/n)^n, and all μ_i>0. The equality case of the mean inequality gives μ_1=…=μ_n=1. A Hermitian matrix with all eigenvalues 1 is the identity by the spectral theorem. So B=I, A=D^{−1}D^{−1} is diagonal. Conversely a diagonal A gives equality.
Columns of a general matrix. Apply the first part to A=M*M. Then det A=|det M|² and a_jj=‖m_j‖². So |det M|²≤∏‖m_j‖². Apply this to M^T to get the row version.

Equality for M. If det M=0 and all columns are nonzero, the inequality is strict. If det M≠0, then A=M*M is positive definite, and equality holds if and only if M*M is diagonal, that is, the columns are pairwise orthogonal.
Entries ±1. If every entry of M is ±1, then every column has norm √n. So |det M|≤(√n)^n=n^{n/2}.

worked_application.title: The largest determinant of a 3×3 matrix with entries ±1
worked_application.goal: Find all values of |det M| for 3×3 matrices with entries ±1, using the Hadamard bound and a divisibility argument, then compare with n=4.
hypotheses: n=3. M has entries in {1,−1}. A second check uses n=4.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Every column of M has Euclidean norm √3, so the column form of the inequality applies.

steps.text: Bound. |det M|≤3^{3/2}=5.196. Since det M is an integer, |det M|≤5.

Divisibility. Multiply columns by −1 so that the first row is all ones. This changes only the sign of det. Subtract row 1 from rows 2 and 3. Their entries become 0 or ±2, so each of these two rows has a factor 2. Hence 4 divides det M.

Conclusion. The only multiples of 4 in [−5,5] are −4, 0 and 4. So |det M|∈{0,4}. The matrix [[1,1,1],[1,−1,1],[1,1,−1]] has determinant 4, so the value 4 occurs. An exhaustive check of all 512 matrices gives |det|=4 for 192 of them and 0 for the other 320.

Case n=4. The bound is 4^2=16. The same divisibility argument shows that 8 divides the determinant. Exhaustive check of all 65536 matrices gives |det|=16 for 768 of them, 8 for 21504 and 0 for 43264. So the bound 16 is attained by Hadamard matrices.

worked_application.result: For 3×3 matrices with entries ±1 the largest |det| is 4, while the Hadamard bound gives only 5.196. For 4×4 matrices the largest |det| is 16, equal to the Hadamard bound.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: The bound n^{n/2} for ±1 matrices is reached only when n=1, n=2 or n is a multiple of 4, and only if a Hadamard matrix exists. For n=3 the true maximum is 4, not 5.196.
The equality statement for singular matrices is not complete. The theorem names only the cases that the proof settles.
The inequality compares det with the product of the diagonal. The stronger Fischer inequality for block matrices is not proved here.

results.statement: Let a_1,…,a_n≥0 and b_1,…,b_n>0 and put a=∑a_i and b=∑b_i. Then ∑a_iln(a_i/b_i)≥a ln(a/b), with the convention 0 ln 0=0. Equality holds if and only if a_i/b_i is the same number for all i. Consequences for probability vectors p,q,p′,q′ with q_i,q′_i>0 and λ in [0,1]: (i) D(p‖q)=∑p_iln(p_i/q_i)≥0, with equality if and only if p=q. (ii) D(λp+(1−λ)p′ ‖ λq+(1−λ)q′)≤λD(p‖q)+(1−λ)D(p′‖q′). (iii) If the index set is partitioned into blocks and p̄ and q̄ are the block sums of p and q, then D(p‖q)≥D(p̄‖q̄).
hypotheses: All b_i and all q_i are strictly positive. If some b_i is zero while a_i>0, the left side is +∞ and the inequality is trivial.
The logarithm is natural. Any other base changes both sides by the same positive factor.
p, q, p′, q′ are probability vectors on the same finite set.

lemma mul_log_le_toReal_klDiv (hμν : μ ≪ ν) (h_int : Integrable (llr μ ν) μ) :
    μ.real univ * log (μ.real univ / ν.real univ) + ν.real univ - μ.real univ
      ≤ (klDiv μ ν).toReal := by
  by_cases hμ : μ = 0
  · simp [hμ, measureReal_def]
  by_cases hν : ν = 0
  · refine absurd ?_ hμ
    rw [hν] at hμν
    exact Measure.absolutelyContinuous_zero_iff.mp hμν
  refine (le_of_eq ?_).trans (mul_klFun_le_toReal_klDiv hμν h_int)
  have : ν.real univ * (μ.real univ / ν.real univ) = μ.real univ := by
    rw [mul_div_cancel₀]; simp [ENNReal.toReal_eq_zero_iff, hν, measureReal_def]
  rw [klFun, mul_sub, mul_add, mul_one, ← mul_assoc, this]

steps.text: Convex function. The function φ(t)=t ln t is strictly convex on [0,∞) with φ(0)=0. Its second derivative is 1/t on (0,∞), and it is continuous at 0.
Rewrite. Put t_i=a_i/b_i≥0 and w_i=b_i/b. Then w_i>0 and ∑w_i=1. Also ∑a_iln(a_i/b_i)=∑b_it_iln t_i=b∑w_iφ(t_i), and ∑w_it_i=a/b.
Jensen. By Jensen inequality for φ with weights w_i, ∑w_iφ(t_i)≥φ(∑w_it_i)=φ(a/b)=(a/b)ln(a/b). Multiply by b>0 to get ∑a_iln(a_i/b_i)≥a ln(a/b).
Equality. For strictly convex φ and weights all positive, equality in Jensen holds if and only if all t_i are equal. This is the equality statement.
Proof of (i). Apply the log-sum inequality to a_i=p_i and b_i=q_i. Then a=b=1 and the right side is ln 1=0. Equality holds if and only if p_i/q_i is constant, say c, and summing gives c=1, so p=q.

Proof of (ii). Let r=λp+(1−λ)p′ and s=λq+(1−λ)q′. For each index i apply the log-sum inequality to the two terms (λp_i,λq_i) and ((1−λ)p′_i,(1−λ)q′_i). It gives λp_iln(p_i/q_i)+(1−λ)p′_iln(p′_i/q′_i)≥r_iln(r_i/s_i). Sum over i. For λ=0 or λ=1 the claim is trivial.
Proof of (iii). For each block B_r apply the log-sum inequality to the terms with i in B_r. It gives ∑_{i∈B_r}p_iln(p_i/q_i)≥p̄_rln(p̄_r/q̄_r). Sum over the blocks.

results.name: Graph Laplacian: Dirichlet form, eigenvalue bounds 2Δ and n/(n−1), and connectivity
results.statement: Let G be a simple graph on n≥2 vertices with edge set E, maximum degree Δ and minimum degree δ. Let L=D−A be its Laplacian and 0=μ_1≤μ_2≤…≤μ_n its eigenvalues in increasing order. Then (a) x^TLx=∑_{uv∈E}(x_u−x_v)² for all real x. (b) μ_1=0 with eigenvector 1, and μ_n≤2Δ. (c) μ_2≤nδ/(n−1) and μ_n≥nΔ/(n−1). (d) μ_2>0 if and only if G is connected. More generally the multiplicity of the eigenvalue 0 is the number of connected components.
hypotheses: G is a finite simple graph with no loops and no multiple edges.
D is the diagonal degree matrix and A the adjacency matrix.
1 is the all-ones vector.

prerequisites.reason: Step 4 uses an orthonormal eigenbasis of the real symmetric Laplacian.

definitions.name: Laplacian
definitions.text: L=D−A. It is real symmetric. Its entries are L_vv=deg v, L_uv=−1 if u~v, and 0 otherwise.

definitions.name: Dirichlet form
definitions.text: The quadratic form x↦x^TLx. By part (a) it measures how much x varies across edges.

definitions.name: Rayleigh quotient

source.excerpt:
/-- Let $L$ be the graph Laplacian and let $x \in \mathbb{R}$, then
$$x^{\top} L x = \sum_{i \sim j} (x_{i}-x_{j})^{2}$$,
where $\sim$ denotes the adjacency relation -/
theorem lapMatrix_toLinearMap₂' [Field R] [CharZero R] (x : V → R) :
    toLinearMap₂' R (G.lapMatrix R) x x =
    (∑ i : V, ∑ j : V, if G.Adj i j then (x i - x j) ^ 2 else 0) / 2 := by
  simp_rw [toLinearMap₂'_apply', lapMatrix, sub_mulVec, dotProduct_sub, dotProduct_mulVec_degMatrix,
    dotProduct_mulVec_adjMatrix, ← sum_sub_distrib, degree_eq_sum_if_adj, sum_mul, ite_mul, one_mul,
    zero_mul, ← sum_sub_distrib, ite_sub_ite, sub_zero]
  rw [← add_self_div_two (∑ x_1 : V, ∑ x_2 : V, _)]
  conv_lhs => enter [1, 2, 2, i, 2, j]; rw [if_congr (adj_comm G i j) rfl rfl]
  conv_lhs => enter [1, 2]; rw [Finset.sum_comm]
  simp_rw [← sum_add_distrib, ite_add_ite]
  congr 2 with i
  congr 2 with j
  ring_nf

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Proof of (a). Expand x^TLx=∑_vd_vx_v²−∑_{u~v}x_ux_v, where the second sum runs over ordered adjacent pairs. Each edge uv contributes x_u²+x_v²−2x_ux_v=(x_u−x_v)² after distributing d_vx_v²=∑_{u~v}x_v². So the sum is ∑_{uv∈E}(x_u−x_v)².
Proof of (b), lower part. By (a), L is positive semidefinite, so all μ_i≥0. Each row sum of L is deg v−deg v=0, so L1=0. Hence 0 is an eigenvalue with eigenvector 1, and μ_1=0.

Proof of (b), upper part. By (a) and the inequality (s−t)²≤2s²+2t², x^TLx≤2∑_{uv∈E}(x_u²+x_v²)=2∑_vd_vx_v²≤2Δ x^Tx. The middle equality holds because the vertex v occurs in d_v edges. So every Rayleigh quotient is at most 2Δ, and μ_n=max R≤2Δ.

Choice of an eigenbasis. Since L is real symmetric, the spectral theorem gives an orthonormal eigenbasis. The eigenspace of 0 contains 1/√n, so we may take u_1=1/√n. Then for x orthogonal to 1, x=∑_{i≥2}c_iu_i and R(x)=∑_{i≥2}μ_ic_i²/∑c_i²≥μ_2. Also R(x)≤μ_n for all x≠0.

Proof of (c), lower eigenvalue. Fix a vertex v and put x=e_v−(1/n)1. Then x is orthogonal to 1. Since L1=0, x^TLx=e_v^TLe_v=d_v. Also x^Tx=1−2/n+1/n=(n−1)/n. By step 4, μ_2≤R(x)=nd_v/(n−1). Take v with d_v=δ.
Proof of (c), upper eigenvalue. The same x gives μ_n≥R(x)=nd_v/(n−1). Take v with d_v=Δ.

Proof of (d). Since L is symmetric, its eigenspace for 0 is the kernel of L. Now Lx=0 implies x^TLx=0, and the converse holds because L is positive semidefinite and symmetric. By (a), x^TLx=0 if and only if x_u=x_v on every edge. That holds if and only if x is constant on each connected component. So the kernel has dimension equal to the number of components. Hence μ_2>0 if and only if the multiplicity of 0 is 1, that is, if and only if G is connected.

results.name: Adjacency spectrum of a regular graph: |λ|≤d, multiplicity of d and of −d
results.statement: Let G be a finite simple d-regular graph with n vertices and adjacency eigenvalues λ_1≥…≥λ_n. Then (a) d is an eigenvalue with eigenvector 1, and |λ_i|≤d for all i. (b) The multiplicity of d equals the number of connected components of G. In particular λ_2<d if and only if G is connected. (c) The multiplicity of −d equals the number of bipartite connected components of G. In particular −d is an eigenvalue if and only if some component is bipartite. (d) ∑λ_i=0 and ∑λ_i²=nd.

source.alignment: The source proves that d is in the spectrum of the adjacency matrix of a d-regular graph, with eigenvector 1. This is the first half of part (a). The bound |λ|≤d, the multiplicity statements and the trace formulas are not in the source.

results.proof_status: source declaration inspected; authored proof awaits inference review; no local Lean check

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Part (a), eigenvalue d. Since every row of A sums to d, A1=d1.
Part (a), bound. Let Av=λv with v≠0 real and choose i with |v_i| maximal. Then |λ||v_i|=|∑_{j~i}v_j|≤d|v_i|. So |λ|≤d.

Part (b), upper bound on the multiplicity. Let Av=dv. Fix a component C and let M be the maximum of v over C, attained at i. Then dM=dv_i=∑_{j~i}v_j≤dM, because each of the d neighbours j lies in C and has v_j≤M. Equality forces v_j=M for every neighbour. Applying this to each neighbour and so on, connectedness gives v=M on all of C. So v is constant on each component, that is, v is a combination of the indicators χ_C.

Part (b), lower bound. Each χ_C satisfies Aχ_C=dχ_C, because every vertex has all its d neighbours inside its own component. The indicators are linearly independent. So the eigenspace of d has dimension equal to the number of components. Then λ_2<d if and only if there is exactly one component.

Part (c), structure of a −d eigenvector. Let Av=−dv, let C be a component, and let i maximize |v_j| over C with m=|v_i|. Then d·m=|∑_{j~i}v_j|≤d·m. Equality forces v_j=−v_i for every neighbour j of i. Repeating along paths, |v|=m on all of C, and adjacent vertices carry opposite values.

Part (c), bipartite or zero. If m>0, the sign of v splits C into two classes X and Y with every edge between them, so C is bipartite. Hence on a non-bipartite component v=0. On a bipartite component with parts X and Y, v=v_i·(χ_X−χ_Y) up to the sign choice, because v is fixed by the value at one vertex. So the −d eigenspace restricted to C has dimension at most 1, and χ_X−χ_Y is indeed a −d eigenvector. The multiplicity of −d is the number of bipartite components.

Part (d). The diagonal of A is zero, so tr A=0 and ∑λ_i=0. The diagonal entry (A²)_{vv} is the number of walks of length 2 from v to v, which is d. So tr A²=nd=∑λ_i², because A is diagonalizable with real eigenvalues.

Cycle C_6. The spectrum is 2, 1, 1, −1, −1, −2. The multiplicity of 2 is 1, so the graph is connected. The multiplicity of −2 is 1, so the single component is bipartite, as even cycles are.

K_4 plus K_{3,3}. The spectrum is 3, 3, 0, 0, 0, 0, −1, −1, −1, −3. The eigenvalue 3 has multiplicity 2, so there are 2 components. The eigenvalue −3 has multiplicity 1, so exactly one component is bipartite. This is K_{3,3}, since K_4 contains triangles.

results.name: Every finite stochastic matrix has a stationary distribution, and its eigenvalues lie in the unit disc
results.statement: Let P be an n×n row-stochastic matrix, that is P_ij≥0 and ∑_jP_ij=1 for each i. Let Δ be the set of probability row vectors in R^n. Then (a) P maps Δ to Δ by μ↦μP, and every complex eigenvalue λ of P satisfies |λ|≤1, with 1 an eigenvalue. (b) For every μ in Δ the Cesàro averages ν_N=(1/N)∑_{k=0}^{N−1}μP^k satisfy ‖ν_NP−ν_N‖_1≤2/N, and every limit point of (ν_N) is a stationary distribution π with πP=π. (c) The set of stationary distributions is a nonempty compact convex subset of Δ.
hypotheses: P has nonnegative entries and every row sums to 1.
‖·‖_1 is the sum of absolute values of the entries of a row vector.
No irreducibility or aperiodicity is assumed. The stationary distribution may be non-unique.

steps.text: Invariance of the simplex. Let μ∈Δ. Then (μP)_j=∑_iμ_iP_ij≥0 and ∑_j(μP)_j=∑_iμ_i∑_jP_ij=∑_iμ_i=1. So μP∈Δ. Hence μP^k∈Δ for all k, and ν_N is a convex combination of points of Δ, so ν_N∈Δ.
Eigenvalue bound. P1=1, so 1 is an eigenvalue. For a complex eigenvector v with Pv=λv choose i with |v_i| maximal. Then |λ||v_i|=|∑_jP_ijv_j|≤∑_jP_ij|v_i|=|v_i|. So |λ|≤1.
Telescoping. ν_NP−ν_N=(1/N)∑_{k=0}^{N−1}(μP^{k+1}−μP^k)=(1/N)(μP^N−μ). Both μP^N and μ lie in Δ, so ‖μP^N−μ‖_1≤2. Hence ‖ν_NP−ν_N‖_1≤2/N.
Compactness. Δ is closed and bounded in R^n, so it is compact. The sequence (ν_N) in Δ has a convergent subsequence ν_{N_m}→π, with π∈Δ.
Stationarity. The map ν↦νP is continuous. So ν_{N_m}P→πP. Also ν_{N_m}P−ν_{N_m}→0 by step 3. Hence πP−π=0. Every limit point is stationary, and the existence of π proves (a) fully.

Structure of the set. The set S of stationary distributions equals Δ∩{π : π(P−I)=0}. This is the intersection of a compact convex set and a linear subspace. So S is compact, convex and, by step 5, nonempty.

worked_application.title: A birth-death chain, a periodic chain and the identity chain
worked_application.goal: Find the stationary distribution of a three-state chain and see why Cesàro averages are needed.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Each matrix has nonnegative entries and row sums 1.

steps.text: Chain P_1. Take π=(1/4,1/2,1/4). Then πP_1=(1/8+1/8, 1/8+1/4+1/8, 1/8+1/8)=(1/4,1/2,1/4)=π. The eigenvalues of P_1 are 1, 1/2 and 0, all of modulus at most 1. They fit trace 3/2, determinant 0 and the sum of principal 2×2 minors 1/2.
Convergence for P_1. Start at μ=(1,0,0). Then μP_1³=(9/32,1/2,7/32). This is already close to π.

Periodic chain P_2. The powers μP_2^k alternate between (1,0) and (0,1) for μ=(1,0), so they do not converge. The Cesàro average over any even number N of steps is (1/2,1/2), which is stationary. For odd N the error is ‖ν_NP−ν_N‖_1=2/N, as step 3 says.
Identity chain P_3. Every probability vector is stationary. So the stationary distribution is not unique, and the set S in (c) is all of Δ.

worked_application.result: P_1 has the stationary distribution (1/4,1/2,1/4). P_2 has the stationary distribution (1/2,1/2), reached only as a Cesàro limit. P_3 has a whole simplex of stationary distributions.

results.name: Collatz-Wielandt bounds on the spectral radius of a nonnegative matrix
results.statement: Let A be an n×n real matrix with nonnegative entries and let x be a vector with all entries positive. Put r_i=(Ax)_i/x_i. Then min_ir_i≤ρ(A)≤max_ir_i, where ρ(A) is the spectral radius, the largest modulus of an eigenvalue of A. In particular, ρ(A) is at most the largest row sum (take x=1), and at most the largest column sum. If x is itself an eigenvector, Ax=λx, then ρ(A)=λ.

/-- **Gershgorin's circle theorem**: for any eigenvalue `μ` of a square matrix `A`, there exists an
index `k` such that `μ` lies in the closed ball of center the diagonal term `A k k` and of
radius the sum of the norms `∑ j ≠ k, ‖A k j‖`. -/
theorem eigenvalue_mem_ball {μ : K} (hμ : Module.End.HasEigenvalue (Matrix.toLin' A) μ) :
    ∃ k, μ ∈ Metric.closedBall (A k k) (∑ j ∈ Finset.univ.erase k, ‖A k j‖) := by
  cases isEmpty_or_nonempty n
  · exfalso
    exact hμ Submodule.eq_bot_of_subsingleton
  · obtain ⟨v, h_eg, h_nz⟩ := hμ.exists_hasEigenvector
    obtain ⟨i, -, h_i⟩ := Finset.exists_mem_eq_sup' Finset.univ_nonempty (fun i => ‖v i‖)
    have h_nz : v i ≠ 0 := by
      contrapose h_nz
      ext j
      rw [Pi.zero_apply, ← norm_le_zero_iff]
      refine (h_i ▸ Finset.le_sup' (fun i => ‖v i‖) (Finset.mem_univ j)).trans ?_
      exact norm_le_zero_iff.mpr h_nz
    have h_le : ∀ j, ‖v j * (v i)⁻¹‖ ≤ 1 := fun j => by
      rw [norm_mul, norm_inv, mul_inv_le_iff₀ (norm_pos_iff.mpr h_nz), one_mul]
      exact h_i ▸ Finset.le_sup' (fun i => ‖v i‖) (Finset.mem_univ j)
    simp_rw [mem_closedBall_iff_norm']
    refine ⟨i, ?_⟩
    calc
      _ = ‖(A i i * v i - μ * v i) * (v i)⁻¹‖ := by congr; field
      _ = ‖(A i i * v i - ∑ j, A i j * v j) * (v i)⁻¹‖ := by
                rw [show μ * v i = ∑ x : n, A i x * v x by
                  rw [← dotProduct, ← Matrix.mulVec]
                  exact congr($(Module.End.mem_eigenspace_iff.mp h_eg) i).symm]
      _ = ‖(∑ j ∈ Finset.univ.erase i, A i j * v j) * (v i)⁻¹‖ := by
                rw [Finset.sum_erase_eq_sub (Finset.mem_univ i), ← neg_sub, neg_mul, norm_neg]
      _ ≤ ∑ j ∈ Finset.univ.erase i, ‖A i j‖ * ‖v j * (v i)⁻¹‖ := by
                rw [Finset.sum_mul]
                exact (norm_sum_le _ _).trans (le_of_eq (by simp_rw [mul_assoc, norm_mul]))
      _ ≤ ∑ j ∈ Finset.univ.erase i, ‖A i j‖ :=
                (Finset.sum_le_sum fun j _ => mul_le_of_le_one_right (norm_nonneg _) (h_le j))

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Scaling. Let D=diag(x_1,…,x_n) and B=D^{−1}AD. Then B_ij=A_ijx_j/x_i≥0 and the i-th row sum of B is ∑_jA_ijx_j/x_i=(Ax)_i/x_i=r_i. The matrices A and B are similar, so they have the same eigenvalues.

Upper bound. Let Bv=λv with v≠0, possibly complex, and choose i with |v_i| maximal. Then |λ||v_i|=|∑_jB_ijv_j|≤∑_jB_ij|v_i|=r_i|v_i|. So |λ|≤r_i≤max_ir_i. This holds for every eigenvalue, so ρ(A)≤max r_i. This is a Gershgorin-type argument for the similar matrix B.
Lower bound, order step. Put r=min_ir_i. Then r≥0 and Ax≥rx entrywise. Suppose A^kx≥r^kx. Since A has nonnegative entries, A(A^kx)≥A(r^kx)=r^kAx≥r^{k+1}x. So A^kx≥r^kx for all k≥0 by induction.
Lower bound, norm step. Put m=min_ix_i and M=max_ix_i. For every k, ‖A^k‖_∞M≥‖A^kx‖_∞≥r^km. Hence ‖A^k‖_∞^{1/k}≥r(m/M)^{1/k}.
Lower bound, limit. By the Gelfand spectral radius formula, ρ(A)=lim_{k→∞}‖A^k‖_∞^{1/k}. The right side of step 4 tends to r as k→∞, since (m/M)^{1/k}→1. So ρ(A)≥r.

Consequences. For x=1 the numbers r_i are the row sums, so ρ(A)≤max row sum. Apply the same to A^T, which has the same spectral radius, to get the column sum bound. If Ax=λx with x>0, all r_i=λ, so min and max coincide and ρ(A)=λ.

results.name: Support functions: closed convex sets as intersections of half-spaces, inclusion tests and the distance formula
results.statement: Let E be a finite dimensional real inner product space. For a nonempty set K in E the support function is σ_K(u)=sup_{x∈K}⟨u,x⟩∈(−∞,+∞]. Let K and L be nonempty closed convex sets. Then (a) K={x : ⟨u,x⟩≤σ_K(u) for all u in E}. (b) K⊆L if and only if σ_K≤σ_L. So K=L if and only if σ_K=σ_L. (c) σ_{K+L}=σ_K+σ_L, σ_{tK}=tσ_K for t≥0, and σ_{conv(K∪L)}=max(σ_K,σ_L). (d) dist(x,K)=sup over unit vectors u of max(⟨u,x⟩−σ_K(u),0).

K and L are nonempty, closed and convex. The identities in (c) do not need closedness.

/-- A closed convex set is the intersection of the half-spaces containing it. -/
theorem iInter_halfSpaces_eq (hs₁ : Convex ℝ s) (hs₂ : IsClosed s) :
    ⋂ l : StrongDual ℝ E, { x | ∃ y ∈ s, l x ≤ l y } = s := by
  rw [Set.iInter_ofPred]
  refine Set.Subset.antisymm (fun x hx => ?_) fun x hx l => ⟨x, hx, le_rfl⟩
  by_contra h
  obtain ⟨l, s, hlA, hl⟩ := geometric_hahn_banach_closed_point hs₁ hs₂ h
  obtain ⟨y, hy, hxy⟩ := hx l

steps.text: Projection. Let x∉K and let p be the nearest point of K to x. Put d=‖x−p‖>0 and u=(x−p)/d. The variational inequality of the projection says ⟨x−p,y−p⟩≤0 for all y in K, that is ⟨u,y⟩≤⟨u,p⟩ for all y in K. So σ_K(u)=⟨u,p⟩ (the value is attained at y=p).
Separation gap. For this u, ⟨u,x⟩−σ_K(u)=⟨u,x−p⟩=d>0. So x violates the inequality for u in (a).
Proof of (a). If x∈K then ⟨u,x⟩≤σ_K(u) for all u by definition. If x∉K, step 2 gives a u with ⟨u,x⟩>σ_K(u). So x is outside the right side.

Proof of (d), lower bound for the distance. Let u be a unit vector and y∈K. Then ⟨u,x⟩−σ_K(u)≤⟨u,x⟩−⟨u,y⟩=⟨u,x−y⟩≤‖x−y‖ by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. Taking the infimum over y gives ⟨u,x⟩−σ_K(u)≤dist(x,K). The value 0 is also at most the distance.
Proof of (d), attainment. If x∈K both sides are 0. If x∉K, step 2 gives a unit u with ⟨u,x⟩−σ_K(u)=d=dist(x,K). So the supremum equals the distance.
Proof of (b). If K⊆L then every sup over K is at most the sup over L, so σ_K≤σ_L. Conversely, if σ_K≤σ_L, then for x in K and all u, ⟨u,x⟩≤σ_K(u)≤σ_L(u). By (a) for L, x∈L.

Proof of (c). σ_{K+L}(u)=sup_{x∈K,y∈L}(⟨u,x⟩+⟨u,y⟩)=σ_K(u)+σ_L(u), since the two choices are independent. σ_{tK}(u)=tσ_K(u) for t≥0 is clear. For the hull, a linear function on a convex combination is the same convex combination of its values, so its sup over conv(K∪L) is the sup over K∪L, which is max(σ_K(u),σ_L(u)).

steps.text: Weak duality. If x is feasible (x∈C and g(x)≤0) and λ≥0, then ∑λ_ig_i(x)≤0. So q(λ)≤f(x)+∑λ_ig_i(x)≤f(x). Taking the infimum over feasible x gives q(λ)≤p*, and then d*≤p*. This proves (a).

Convexity of A. Let (u,t),(u′,t′)∈A with witnesses x,x′∈C, and let θ∈[0,1]. The point z=θx+(1−θ)x′ is in C. By convexity of g_i and f, g_i(z)≤θg_i(x)+(1−θ)g_i(x′)≤θu_i+(1−θ)u′_i, and f(z)≤θt+(1−θ)t′. So θ(u,t)+(1−θ)(u′,t′)∈A.

Interior. A contains every (u,t) with u_i>g_i(x_0) for all i and t>f(x_0), taking the witness x_0. This is a nonempty open set, so the interior of A is nonempty. The point y=(0,p*) is not in the interior of A. Otherwise a small ball around y lies in A, so (0,p*−ε)∈A for some ε>0, which gives x∈C with g(x)≤0 and f(x)≤p*−ε, in conflict with the definition of p*.

Separation. A is convex with nonempty interior and y is not in the interior. By the supporting hyperplane form of the Hahn-Banach separation theorem in R^{m+1}, there is a nonzero linear functional, written as (u,t)↦λ·u+μt with (λ,μ)≠0, such that λ·u+μt≥μp* for all (u,t)∈A.
Signs. A is closed upward: if (u,t)∈A then (u+se_i,t)∈A and (u,t+s)∈A for s≥0. If λ_i<0, letting s→∞ drives λ·u to −∞ and breaks the bound. So λ≥0. In the same way μ≥0.

The multiplier on f is positive. Suppose μ=0. Then λ·u≥0 for all (u,t)∈A. The point (g(x_0),f(x_0)) is in A, so λ·g(x_0)≥0. But g_i(x_0)<0 and λ_i≥0, so λ·g(x_0)≤0 with equality only if λ=0. So λ=0, and then (λ,μ)=0, a contradiction. Hence μ>0.

Dual value. Put λ*=λ/μ≥0. For each x∈C the point (g(x),f(x)) is in A, so f(x)+λ*·g(x)≥p*. Taking the infimum gives q(λ*)≥p*. With part (a), p*≥d*≥q(λ*)≥p*. So d*=p*=q(λ*) and the dual value is attained. This proves (b).

Complementary slackness. Let x* be primal optimal. Then p*=q(λ*)≤f(x*)+λ*·g(x*)≤f(x*)=p*, using λ*≥0 and g(x*)≤0. So all inequalities are equalities. The sum ∑λ*_ig_i(x*) is zero and every term is at most 0, so each term is 0. Also L(x*,λ*)=p*=q(λ*)=min_xL(x,λ*). This proves (c).

hypotheses: Program P1: minimize x²+y² over C=R² subject to 1−x≤0 and 2−y≤0. Program P2: C={(x,y) : y>0}, f(x,y)=e^{−x}, g(x,y)=x²/y.

steps.text: Primal value of P1. The constraints say x≥1 and y≥2, so p*=1²+2²=5, reached at (1,2).
Dual function of P1. For λ=(λ_1,λ_2)≥0, L=x²+y²+λ_1(1−x)+λ_2(2−y) is minimized at x=λ_1/2, y=λ_2/2. So q(λ)=λ_1+2λ_2−λ_1²/4−λ_2²/4.

Dual optimum of P1. Maximizing q gives λ*=(2,4) with q(λ*)=2+8−1−4=5=p*. At the primal minimizer both constraints are active, so complementary slackness holds, and x*=λ*_1/2=1 and y*=λ*_2/2=2 as claimed.

The program P2. The constraint x²/y≤0 forces x=0, so p*=e⁰=1. For λ≥0, q(λ)=inf[e^{−x}+λx²/y]. Let y→∞ for fixed x, then x→∞, to get q(λ)=0. So d*=0<1=p*. Duality fails because no Slater point exists.

results.statement: Let L be a first-order language and let T be an L-theory. Let κ be an infinite cardinal with |L|≤κ, where |L| is the number of symbols of L. Assume three things. (i) T has a model. This means that for every L-sentence φ, either every model of T satisfies φ, or every model of T satisfies ¬φ.

steps.text: Suppose that T is not complete. Then some sentence φ has T⊭φ and T⊭¬φ. By the definition of ⊨, there is a model A of T with A⊭φ, so A⊨¬φ. There is also a model B of T with B⊭¬φ, so B⊨φ. By (ii), A and B are infinite.

Lemma. Let M be an infinite L-structure and let κ be a cardinal with κ≥ℵ₀ and κ≥|L|. Then there is a structure N with |N|=κ and N≡M. Proof. Suppose first that κ≤|M|. The downward Löwenheim–Skolem theorem gives an elementary substructure N⪯M with |N|=κ. Suppose next that |M|≤κ. The upward Löwenheim–Skolem theorem gives an elementary extension N⪰M with |N|=κ. One of the two cases holds because cardinals are comparable. An elementary substructure or extension satisfies the same sentences as M.
Apply the lemma to A and to B. We get structures A′ and B′ with |A′|=|B′|=κ, with A′≡A and with B′≡B.
Every sentence σ of T is true in A, so σ is true in A′. The same holds for B and B′. So A′ and B′ are models of T of cardinality κ. Also A′⊨¬φ because A⊨¬φ, and B′⊨φ because B⊨φ.

By (iii) there is an isomorphism h:A′→B′. An isomorphism preserves the truth of all sentences. To see this, prove by induction on formulas that A′⊨ψ[a] if and only if B′⊨ψ[h(a)] for every formula ψ and every assignment a. Terms satisfy h(t(a))=t(h(a)) because h commutes with the function symbols. Atomic formulas are preserved because h is injective and preserves the relations in both directions. Connectives are trivial. For ∃x ψ, the map h is a bijection, so a witness in A′ maps to a witness in B′ and conversely.
Hence A′ and B′ satisfy the same sentences. This contradicts the choice A′⊨¬φ and B′⊨φ. So no such sentence φ exists, and T is complete.

Remark on where each hypothesis acts. Hypothesis (i) makes T satisfiable, so that completeness is not an empty case. Hypothesis (ii) is used only to apply the lemma, because Löwenheim–Skolem needs infinite structures. The bound |L|≤κ is used only in the lemma.

worked_application.title: The theory of dense linear orders without endpoints decides its sentences
worked_application.goal: Show that the theory DLO of dense linear orders without endpoints in the language {<} is complete. Then decide two sentences by looking at the model ℚ only.
hypotheses: L={<} has one symbol, so |L|=1≤ℵ₀. Take κ=ℵ₀.
DLO is the finite list of axioms: a strict linear order, density, no least element and no greatest element.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: We must check (i) to (iii) of the test with κ=ℵ₀.

steps.text: (i) The ordered set (ℚ,<) is a model of DLO, so DLO is satisfiable.
(ii) Let M be a model. Since M has no greatest element and is nonempty, choose x₀∈M and then x_{n+1}>x_n for all n. The strict order makes x₀<x₁<x₂<… with all x_n distinct. So M is infinite.

(iii) Any two countable models of DLO are isomorphic. This is Cantor isomorphism theorem, proved by the back and forth method. A countable model has cardinality exactly ℵ₀ by (ii). So DLO is ℵ₀-categorical.
By the test, DLO is complete. So each sentence is true in all models or false in all models, and the model ℚ decides which case holds.

Sentence S: ∀x∀y (x<y → ∃u∃v∃w (x<u ∧ u<v ∧ v<w ∧ w<y)). In ℚ take d=y−x and u=x+d/4, v=x+d/2, w=x+3d/4. These satisfy x<u<v<w<y because d>0. For x=1/3 and y=1/2 the witnesses are 3/8, 5/12 and 11/24, and 1/3<3/8<5/12<11/24<1/2 holds. So ℚ⊨S, and by completeness every model of DLO satisfies S. In particular S holds in ℝ and in the lexicographic order on ℚ×ℚ.

Sentence E: ∃x∀y (x=y ∨ x<y), which says that there is a least element. In ℚ, for any x the element x−1 is smaller, so ℚ⊭E. By completeness every model of DLO satisfies ¬E. This also shows that ℚ and ℝ satisfy the same sentences in the language {<}.

worked_application.result: DLO is complete. The sentence S is a consequence of DLO and the sentence E is refuted by DLO. No proof of S inside the axioms was needed.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: The test needs a cardinal κ with |L|≤κ. For a language with uncountably many symbols, κ=ℵ₀ does not work.

Categoricity in one cardinal does not give categoricity in another. DLO is ℵ₀-categorical but it has non-isomorphic models of size 2^ℵ₀. Examples are ℝ and the lexicographic order on ℝ×ℚ. The first has no gaps and the second has.

Condition (ii) cannot be dropped. Let T say that there are at least 2 and at most 3 elements. T has no model of any infinite cardinality κ, so T is vacuously κ-categorical. But T is not complete, because it does not decide the sentence that there are at least 3 elements.

Completeness gives decidability only for theories with a recursive list of axioms. Then one can list all proofs, and for each sentence φ either a proof of φ or a proof of ¬φ appears. DLO has finitely many axioms, so it is decidable in this way.

/-- Any nonempty perfect set in a complete metric space admits a continuous injection
from the Cantor space, `ℕ → Bool`. -/
theorem Perfect.exists_nat_bool_injection
    (hC : Perfect C) (hnonempty : C.Nonempty) [CompleteSpace α] :
    ∃ f : (ℕ → Bool) → α, range f ⊆ C ∧ Continuous f ∧ Injective f := by
  obtain ⟨u, -, upos', hu⟩ := exists_seq_strictAnti_tendsto' (zero_lt_one' ℝ≥0∞)
  have upos := fun n => (upos' n).1
  let P := Subtype fun E : Set α => Perfect E ∧ E.Nonempty
  choose C0 C1 h0 h1 hdisj using
    fun {C : Set α} (hC : Perfect C) (hnonempty : C.Nonempty) {ε : ℝ≥0∞} (hε : 0 < ε) =>
    hC.small_diam_splitting hnonempty hε
  let DP : List Bool → P := fun l => by
    induction l with
    | nil => exact ⟨C, ⟨hC, hnonempty⟩⟩
    | cons a l ih =>
      cases a
      · use C0 ih.property.1 ih.property.2 (upos (l.length + 1))
        exact ⟨(h0 _ _ _).1, (h0 _ _ _).2.1⟩
      use C1 ih.property.1 ih.property.2 (upos (l.length + 1))
      exact ⟨(h1 _ _ _).1, (h1 _ _ _).2.1⟩
  let D : List Bool → Set α := fun l => (DP l).val
  have hanti : ClosureAntitone D := by
    refine Antitone.closureAntitone ?_ fun l => (DP l).property.1.closed
    intro l a
    cases a
    · exact (h0 _ _ _).2.2.1
    exact (h1 _ _ _).2.2.1
  have hdiam : VanishingDiam D := by
    intro x
    apply tendsto_of_tendsto_of_tendsto_of_le_of_le' tendsto_const_nhds hu
    · simp
    rw [eventually_atTop]
    refine ⟨1, fun m (hm : 1 ≤ m) => ?_⟩
    rw [Nat.one_le_iff_ne_zero] at hm

the diameter of the new perfect sets. -/

steps.text: Splitting lemma. Let D⊆X be nonempty and perfect, and let ε>0. Then there are disjoint nonempty perfect sets D₀,D₁⊆D with diameter at most ε. Proof. Choose p∈D. Since p is not isolated, D has a point y≠p. Let r=min(d(p,y)/3, ε/4)>0. Put D₀=closure(B(p,r)∩D) and D₁=closure(B(y,r)∩D).

Each of D₀ and D₁ is closed, nonempty (it contains p or y) and contained in D because D is closed. The closure of an open ball B(c,r) lies in the closed ball of radius r. So each has diameter at most 2r≤ε/2. The two closed balls of radius r around p and y are disjoint because 2r<d(p,y). So D₀∩D₁=∅.

D₀ is perfect. Let z∈D₀ and let W be an open neighbourhood of z. Since z is in the closure of U∩D with U=B(p,r), the open set W∩U meets D. Choose q∈W∩U∩D. The point q is not isolated in D, and W∩U is an open neighbourhood of q. In a metric space every neighbourhood of a limit point of D contains infinitely many points of D. So W∩U∩D is infinite, and it contains a point different from z. This point lies in D₀ and in W. So z is a limit point of D₀. The same argument works for D₁.

Construction of the scheme. We define sets D_s for finite binary words s by recursion on the length. Put D_∅=C. Given a nonempty perfect D_s, apply the splitting lemma with ε=2^{−(|s|+1)} to get D_{s0} and D_{s1}. They are nonempty perfect subsets of D_s, they are disjoint, and they have diameter at most 2^{−(|s|+1)}.

Definition of f. Fix x∈{0,1}^ℕ. The sets D_{x|n}, n≥1, are nonempty closed and decreasing, with diameter at most 2^{−n}. Choose p_n∈D_{x|n}. For m≥n we have p_m∈D_{x|n}, so d(p_m,p_n)≤2^{−n}. So (p_n) is Cauchy. Since X is complete, it has a limit p. Each D_{x|n} is closed and contains p_m for all m≥n, so p∈D_{x|n}. The set ⋂_n D_{x|n} has diameter 0, so it is the single point {p}. Define f(x)=p. Then f(x)∈D_{x|0}=C.
Injectivity. Let x≠y and let n be the first place where they differ. Then x|n=y|n=s and, say, x|(n+1)=s0 and y|(n+1)=s1. We have f(x)∈D_{s0}, f(y)∈D_{s1}, and D_{s0}∩D_{s1}=∅. So f(x)≠f(y).

Continuity. Let x be given and let ε>0. Choose n with 2^{−n}<ε. If y agrees with x on the first n places, then f(x) and f(y) both lie in D_{x|n}, which has diameter at most 2^{−n}<ε. So d(f(x),f(y))<ε on the cylinder [x|n], which is a neighbourhood of x.
Cardinality. f is injective, so |C|≥|{0,1}^ℕ|=2^ℵ₀=𝔠. This proves the first claim.

Polish case. Let X be Polish and let C be closed and uncountable. By the Cantor–Bendixson theorem, C=P∪N with P perfect and N countable. P is nonempty because C is uncountable. Choose a complete metric d for the topology of X. The set P is perfect and nonempty for this metric, because it depends only on the topology. The first part, applied to (X,d), gives the injection f with f({0,1}^ℕ)⊆P⊆C.

Upper bound in the Polish case. Let Q be a countable dense subset of X. For each x∈X choose, for each n≥1, a point q_n(x)∈Q with d(x,q_n(x))<1/n. The map x↦(q_n(x))_n sends X into Q^ℕ. It is injective because q_n(x)→x and limits are unique. So |X|≤|Q^ℕ|≤ℵ₀^ℵ₀=𝔠. Hence |C|≤𝔠. With the lower bound, |C|=𝔠.

worked_application.title: Embedding the Cantor space into [0,1] with explicit gaps
worked_application.goal: Run the construction in the complete metric space X=ℝ with the perfect set C=[0,1]. Compute f on two sequences and check the gap and modulus estimates.
hypotheses: Each D_s is a closed interval, so it is perfect. Its diameter 3^{−|s|} is at most 2^{−|s|}.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The scheme satisfies every requirement of the construction, so the proof gives a continuous injection into [0,1].

steps.text: D_{s0}=[a_s, a_s+3^{−|s|−1}] and D_{s1}=[a_s+2·3^{−|s|−1}, a_s+3^{−|s|}]. Both lie in D_s. The gap between them is 3^{−|s|−1}>0, so they are disjoint.
Unwinding the recursion, a_s=∑_{k<|s|} 2 s_k 3^{−k−1}. The limit point is f(x)=∑_{n≥0} 2x_n 3^{−n−1}, the Cantor ternary expansion.
The sequences agree on the first 2 places and differ at place n=2. Both images lie in D_{10}=[2/3, 7/9]. Indeed 3/4=0.75 and 19/27≈0.7037 are in [0.667,0.778].
The distance is 3/4−19/27=5/108≈0.0463. The estimates say 3^{−3}=1/27≈0.0370≤0.0463≤3^{−2}=1/9≈0.1111. So the gap bound and the modulus bound both hold.

At level n the image of the scheme is the union of 2^n intervals of length 3^{−n}. For n=5 this is 32 intervals of total length 32/243≈0.1317. The intersection over all n has length 0 but still contains a copy of {0,1}^ℕ.

results.name: A σ-algebra generated by at most 𝔠 sets has at most 𝔠 elements, so Borel sets are few
results.statement: Let X be a set and let S be a family of subsets of X. Let σ(S) be the σ-algebra generated by S. Then |σ(S)|≤max(|S|,2)^ℵ₀. In particular, if |S|≤𝔠 then |σ(S)|≤𝔠. Consequently the Borel σ-algebra of ℝ has cardinality exactly 𝔠, and there are Lebesgue measurable subsets of ℝ that are not Borel.
hypotheses: σ(S) is the smallest family of subsets of X that contains S and is closed under complements and under countable unions.
𝔠=2^ℵ₀ is the cardinality of ℝ.
The final claim uses that Lebesgue measure is complete, so every subset of a Lebesgue null set is Lebesgue measurable.

steps.text: Stage definition. Let κ=max(|S|,2)^ℵ₀. For each ordinal α<ω₁ let U_α=⋃_{β<α} G_β, with U_0=∅. Put G_α=S∪{∅}∪{X∖A : A∈U_α}∪{⋃_n A_n : (A_n) a sequence in U_α}. If α≤α′ then U_α⊆U_{α′}, so G_α⊆G_{α′}.
Let G=⋃_{α<ω₁}G_α. Claim: G=σ(S). The inclusion G⊆σ(S) follows by induction on α. The family S∪{∅} is in σ(S), and σ(S) is closed under complements and countable unions of its members.

For the inclusion σ(S)⊆G, it suffices to show that G contains S and is a σ-algebra. It contains S∪{∅} since these lie in G_0. If A∈G, then A∈G_β for some β<ω₁ and X∖A∈G_{β+1}. If A_n∈G_{β_n} for n∈ℕ, then the ordinals β_n form a countable set. Because ω₁ is regular, γ=sup_n β_n<ω₁. Then all A_n lie in U_{γ+1}, and ⋃_n A_n∈G_{γ+1}. So G is a σ-algebra and contains S.
Size of one stage. Here ℵ₀·ℵ₀=ℵ₀ and κ·κ=κ for infinite κ. Suppose |U_α|≤κ. The number of sequences in U_α is at most κ^ℵ₀=(m^ℵ₀)^ℵ₀=m^{ℵ₀·ℵ₀}=m^ℵ₀=κ, where m=max(|S|,2). So |G_α|≤|S|+1+κ+κ≤κ.

Size of the union. By induction, |U_α|≤ℵ₀·κ=κ for every α<ω₁, because U_α is a union of at most countably many sets G_β with β<α, each of size at most κ. We have ℵ₁≤2^ℵ₀≤κ. So |G|≤ℵ₁·κ=κ. Hence |σ(S)|≤max(|S|,2)^ℵ₀.
If |S|≤𝔠, then max(|S|,2)≤2^ℵ₀ and |σ(S)|≤(2^ℵ₀)^ℵ₀=2^ℵ₀=𝔠.

Borel sets of ℝ. The open intervals with rational endpoints form a countable family S that generates the Borel σ-algebra, since every open set is a countable union of members of S. So |Borel(ℝ)|≤max(ℵ₀,2)^ℵ₀=ℵ₀^ℵ₀=𝔠. Singletons are Borel, so |Borel(ℝ)|≥|ℝ|=𝔠. Hence |Borel(ℝ)|=𝔠.

Non-Borel measurable sets. Let K be the Cantor ternary set. It is closed and has Lebesgue measure 0. The map x↦∑ 2x_n3^{−n−1} is injective from {0,1}^ℕ into K, so |K|≥𝔠 and |K|=𝔠. Every subset of K is Lebesgue measurable by completeness. So there are 2^𝔠 Lebesgue measurable sets. By Cantor theorem 2^𝔠>𝔠. Since there are only 𝔠 Borel sets, some Lebesgue measurable subset of K is not Borel.

worked_application.title: Counting the algebras at the finite stages of dyadic generation
worked_application.goal: The dyadic intervals generate the Borel σ-algebra of [0,1). Count the algebra generated by the dyadic intervals of level at most n and compare with the bound.
hypotheses: Level k dyadic intervals are [j/2^k,(j+1)/2^k) for 0≤j<2^k.
S_n is the family of all dyadic intervals of level at most n. The countable family S=⋃_n S_n generates the Borel σ-algebra of [0,1).
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: Each S_n is finite, so the algebra it generates is also its σ-algebra. The finite counts show how the stages grow. The bound handles the countable limit.

steps.text: The atoms of the algebra generated by S_n are the 2^n intervals of level n, because every coarser interval is a union of them. The algebra consists of all unions of atoms.

So the algebra has 2^{2^n} elements. The values for n=0,1,2,3 are 2, 4, 16 and 256. A brute-force closure of S_n under complements and unions, computed in Python on bitmasks of the cells, gives the same four numbers.

The algebras increase with n. Their union is the algebra of finite unions of dyadic intervals. This union is countable, because it is a countable union of finite sets. It is not a σ-algebra. The singleton {0} is the countable intersection of the intervals [0,2^{−k}), but it is not a finite union of dyadic intervals.

The theorem bounds the full σ-algebra generated by S. Here |S|=ℵ₀, so |σ(S)|≤max(ℵ₀,2)^ℵ₀=ℵ₀^ℵ₀=𝔠. So the passage from the countable algebra to the σ-algebra adds at most 𝔠 sets. The lower bound 𝔠 holds because the σ-algebra contains all singletons {t}.
The Borel σ-algebra has 𝔠 members but ℝ has 2^𝔠 subsets. For the Cantor set K of cardinality 𝔠 there are 2^𝔠 subsets, all Lebesgue measurable, so most of them are not Borel.

worked_application.result: The finite stages have sizes 2, 4, 16, 256, that is 2^{2^n}. The limit σ-algebra has cardinality exactly 𝔠, and the family of Lebesgue measurable sets has cardinality 2^𝔠.

results.name: The Ackermann function dominates every primitive recursive function
results.statement: Define A:ℕ×ℕ→ℕ by A(0,n)=n+1, A(m+1,0)=A(m,1) and A(m+1,n+1)=A(m,A(m+1,n)). This recursion ends, because the pair (m,n) decreases in the lexicographic order. Let f:ℕ^k→ℕ be primitive recursive. This means that f is in the smallest class of functions that holds the zero function, the successor function and all projections, and that is closed under composition and under primitive recursion. Then there is m∈ℕ such that f(z₁,…,z_k)<A(m,max(z₁,…,z_k)) for all z∈ℕ^k, where max of the empty tuple is 0. Hence the total computable function n↦A(n,n) is not primitive recursive, and the function A of two arguments is not primitive recursive.
hypotheses: Primitive recursion defines f(0,x⃗)=g(x⃗) and f(n+1,x⃗)=h(n,f(n,x⃗),x⃗) from functions g and h that are already in the class.
Composition forms f(g₁(x⃗),…,g_l(x⃗)) from functions that are already in the class.
The theorem is about total functions on the natural numbers. A is total by the lexicographic recursion.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: No catalog entry is a prerequisite. The proof uses only induction on the construction of functions and the definition of A.

definitions.name: primitive recursive function
definitions.text: A function ℕ^k→ℕ is primitive recursive if it is built from zero, successor and projections by finitely many uses of composition and primitive recursion.

definitions.name: domination
definitions.text: A function F dominates f if f(z⃗)<F(max z⃗) holds for all z⃗ in ℕ^k. Here F=A(m,·) for a fixed m.

/-- If `f` is primitive recursive, there exists `m` such that `f n < ack m n` for all `n`. -/
theorem exists_lt_ack_of_nat_primrec {f : ℕ → ℕ} (hf : Nat.Primrec f) :
    ∃ m, ∀ n, f n < ack m n := by
  induction hf with
  | zero => exact ⟨0, ack_pos 0⟩
  | succ =>
    refine ⟨1, fun n => ?_⟩
    rw [succ_eq_one_add]
    apply add_lt_ack
  | left =>
    refine ⟨0, fun n => ?_⟩
    rw [ack_zero, Nat.lt_succ_iff]
    exact unpair_left_le n
  | right =>
    refine ⟨0, fun n => ?_⟩
    rw [ack_zero, Nat.lt_succ_iff]
    exact unpair_right_le n
  | @pair f g hf hg IHf IHg =>
    obtain ⟨a, ha⟩ := IHf; obtain ⟨b, hb⟩ := IHg
    refine ⟨max a b + 3, fun n => ?_⟩
    calc
      pair (f n) (g n) < (max (f n) (g n) + 1) ^ 2 := pair_lt_max_add_one_sq ..
      _ ≤ (ack (max a b) n + 1) ^ 2 := by rw [max_ack_left]; gcongr; exacts [(ha n).le, (hb n).le]
      _ ≤ ack (max a b + 3) n := ack_add_one_sq_lt_ack_add_three ..
  | comp hf hg IHf IHg =>
    obtain ⟨a, ha⟩ := IHf; obtain ⟨b, hb⟩ := IHg
    exact
      ⟨max a b + 2, fun n =>
        (ha _).trans <| (ack_strictMono_right a <| hb n).trans <| ack_ack_lt_ack_max_add_two a b n⟩
  | @prec f g hf hg IHf IHg =>
    obtain ⟨a, ha⟩ := IHf; obtain ⟨b, hb⟩ := IHg
    -- We prove this simpler inequality first.
    have :
      ∀ {m n},
        rec (f m) (fun y IH => g <| pair m <| pair y IH) n < ack (max a b + 9) (m + n) := by
      intro m n
      -- We induct on n.
      induction n with
      | zero => -- The base case is easy.
        grw [← le_max_left, ← le_add_right]
        exact ha m
      | succ n IH => -- We get rid of the first `pair`.
        simp only
        apply (hb _).trans ((ack_pair_lt _ _ _).trans_le _)
        -- If m is the maximum, we get a very weak inequality.
        rcases lt_or_ge _ m with h₁ | h₁
        · rw [max_eq_left h₁.le]
          gcongr <;> omega
        rw [max_eq_right h₁]
        -- We get rid of the second `pair`.
        apply (ack_pair_lt _ _ _).le.trans
        -- If n is the maximum, we get a very weak inequality.
        rcases lt_or_ge _ n with h₂ | h₂
        · rw [max_eq_left h₂.le, add_assoc]
          exact
            ack_le_ack (Nat.add_le_add (le_max_right a b) <| by simp)
              ((le_succ n).trans <| self_le_add_left _ _)
        rw [max_eq_right h₂]
        -- We now use the inductive hypothesis, and some simple algebraic manipulation.
        apply (ack_strictMono_right _ IH).le.trans
        rw [add_succ m, add_succ _ 8, succ_eq_add_one, succ_eq_add_one,
            ack_succ_succ (_ + 8), add_assoc]
        exact ack_mono_left _ (Nat.add_le_add (le_max_right a b) le_rfl)
    -- The proof is now simple.
    exact ⟨max a b + 9, fun n => this.trans_le <| ack_mono_right _ <| unpair_add_le n⟩
