steps.text: Setup for (1) to (3). Let G = Gal(L/K), cyclic with generator σ. Since L/K is Galois, |G| = n. Put σ_i = σ^i for i = 0, …, n−1. These are n distinct automorphisms of L. By the independence of characters they are linearly independent over L.

An eigenvector. For θ in L put α(θ) = Σ_{i=0}^{n−1} ζ^(−i)·σ^i(θ). Since σ^n = id and ζ^(−n) = 1, we get σ(α(θ)) = Σ ζ^(−i)·σ^(i+1)(θ) = ζ·Σ ζ^(−(i+1))·σ^(i+1)(θ) = ζ·α(θ). By linear independence the map θ ↦ α(θ) is not zero. Fix θ with α = α(θ) ≠ 0.

Generation. We have σ^i(α) = ζ^i·α for all i, and these n values are distinct because ζ has order n. So α has n distinct conjugates over K. Hence [K(α) : K] ≥ n. As K(α) ⊆ L and [L : K] = n, we get K(α) = L.
The n-th power. We have σ(α^n) = ζ^n·α^n = α^n. So α^n is fixed by the generator σ, hence by all of G. Since L/K is Galois, the fixed field of G is K. Thus α^n is in K. This proves (3).

From (3) to (2). Let α^n = a with a in K and L = K(α). The polynomial X^n − a has α as a root and degree n. The minimal polynomial of α has degree [K(α) : K] = n, so it equals X^n − a. Hence X^n − a is irreducible. Its roots are ζ^i·α for i = 0, …, n−1. They all lie in L, and L is generated by one of them. So L is a splitting field.

Separability. For (2) to (1), note first that ζ of order n forces the characteristic of K not to divide n. Indeed in characteristic p with p | n, the equation x^n = 1 equals (x^(n/p) − 1)^p, which has no element of order n. If n > 1, a = 0 is impossible, because X^n is reducible. So X^n − a has the n distinct roots ζ^i·α. A splitting field of a separable polynomial is Galois, so L/K is Galois.

The character. Let α be a root of X^n − a in L with L = K(α). For σ in G, σ(α) is again a root, so σ(α) = ζ^(i)·α for some i. Put χ(σ) = σ(α)/α. This is in μ_n. For σ, τ in G we have χ(στ) = σ(χ(τ)·α)/α = χ(τ)·σ(α)/α = χ(σ)·χ(τ), since χ(τ) lies in K and is fixed by σ. So χ is a group homomorphism G → μ_n.

Cyclic and isomorphism. If χ(σ) = 1 then σ(α) = α, and σ is the identity because L = K(α). So χ is injective. The group μ_n is cyclic, generated by ζ. A subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic. So G is cyclic. Since |G| = n = |μ_n|, the map χ is an isomorphism. The same argument applies to the α of (3) by the step from (3) to (2).

/-- If `χ` and `φ` are multiplicative characters on a finite field `F` such that
`χφ` is nontrivial, then `g(χφ) * J(χ,φ) = g(χ) * g(φ)`. -/
theorem jacobiSum_mul_nontrivial {χ φ : MulChar F R} (h : χ * φ ≠ 1) (ψ : AddChar F R) :
    gaussSum (χ * φ) ψ * jacobiSum χ φ = gaussSum χ ψ * gaussSum φ ψ := by
  classical
  rw [gaussSum_mul _ _ ψ, sum_eq_sum_sdiff_singleton_add (mem_univ (0 : F))]
  conv =>
    enter [2, 2, 2, x]
    rw [zero_sub, neg_eq_neg_one_mul x, map_mul, mul_left_comm (χ x) (φ (-1)),
      ← MulChar.mul_apply, ψ.map_zero_eq_one, mul_one]
  rw [← mul_sum _ _ (φ (-1)), MulChar.sum_eq_zero_of_ne_one h, mul_zero, add_zero]
  have sum_eq : ∀ t ∈ univ \ {0}, (∑ x : F, χ x * φ (t - x)) * ψ t =
      (∑ y : F, χ (t * y) * φ (t - (t * y))) * ψ t := by
    intro t ht
    simp only [mem_sdiff, mem_univ, mem_singleton, true_and] at ht
    exact congrArg (· * ψ t) (Equiv.sum_comp (Equiv.mulLeft₀ t ht) _).symm
  simp_rw [← sum_mul, sum_congr rfl sum_eq, ← mul_one_sub, map_mul, mul_assoc]
  conv => enter [2, 2, t, 1, 2, x, 2]; rw [← mul_assoc, mul_comm (χ x) (φ t)]
  simp_rw [← mul_assoc, ← MulChar.mul_apply, mul_assoc, ← mul_sum, mul_right_comm]
  rw [← jacobiSum, ← sum_mul, gaussSum, sum_eq_sum_sdiff_singleton_add (mem_univ (0 : F)),
    (χ * φ).map_zero, zero_mul, add_zero]

steps.text: Expand the product. We have g(χ)g(ψ) = Σ_{x,y} χ(x)ψ(y)θ(x + y). Group the terms by t = x + y. Then g(χ)g(ψ) = Σ_t θ(t)·S(t), where S(t) = Σ_x χ(x)ψ(t − x).
The term t = 0. Here S(0) = Σ_x χ(x)ψ(−x) = ψ(−1)·Σ_x (χψ)(x). Since χψ is nontrivial, orthogonality gives Σ_x (χψ)(x) = 0. So S(0) = 0.
The terms t ≠ 0. Substitute x = t·y. As x runs over F, so does y. Then S(t) = Σ_y χ(ty)ψ(t − ty) = χ(t)ψ(t)·Σ_y χ(y)ψ(1 − y) = (χψ)(t)·J(χ, ψ).
Conclusion for (i). Hence g(χ)g(ψ) = J(χ, ψ)·Σ_{t≠0} (χψ)(t)θ(t) = J(χ, ψ)·g(χψ), since (χψ)(0) = 0.

Absolute value for (ii). Let χ, ψ and χψ be nontrivial. The Gauss sum theorem gives |g(χ)|² = |g(ψ)|² = |g(χψ)|² = q. In particular g(χψ) ≠ 0. So (i) gives J = g(χ)g(ψ)/g(χψ). Then |J|² = (q·q)/q = q.
The case J(χ, χ⁻¹). Let χ be nontrivial. In the sum J(χ, χ⁻¹) the terms x = 0 and x = 1 vanish, because χ(0) = 0 and χ⁻¹(0) = 0. For x outside {0, 1} the term is χ(x)χ⁻¹(1 − x) = χ(x/(1 − x)).
A bijection. The map x ↦ x/(1 − x) is a bijection from F ∖ {0, 1} onto F ∖ {0, −1}, with inverse y ↦ y/(1 + y). Indeed x/(1 − x) = y gives x = y/(1 + y). Hence J(χ, χ⁻¹) = Σ_{y≠0,−1} χ(y).
Finish (iii). We have Σ_{y≠0} χ(y) = 0 because χ is nontrivial. Removing the term y = −1 gives Σ_{y≠0,−1} χ(y) = −χ(−1). So J(χ, χ⁻¹) = −χ(−1).

worked_application.goal: For primes p congruent to 1 mod 3 and a cubic character χ, compute J(χ, χ) and count the solutions of x³ + y³ = 1 modulo p.

steps.text: Values. A direct computation gives J(χ, χ) = 0.5 − 2.598076i for p = 7, −2.5 − 2.598076i for p = 13, 3.5 − 2.598076i for p = 19 and 2 + 5.196152i for p = 31. The numbers |J|² are 7, 13, 19, 31, as in (ii). The quotient g(χ)²/g(χ²) gives the same values as in (ii).

Evaluate the nine sums. We have J(1, 1) = p − 2, and the four sums J(1, χ), J(1, χ²), J(χ, 1), J(χ², 1) equal −1 each. By (iii), J(χ, χ²) = J(χ², χ) = −χ(−1) = −1, because χ(−1)³ = 1 and χ(−1)² = 1 give χ(−1) = 1. Also J(χ², χ²) is the complex conjugate of J(χ, χ). The total is p − 8 + 2·Re J(χ, χ).
Result and check. Therefore N = p − 2 + 2·Re J(χ, χ). The formula gives N = 6, 6, 24, 33 for p = 7, 13, 19, 31. A brute force count of all pairs (x, y) gives the same four numbers.

worked_application.result: The count of solutions of x³ + y³ = 1 modulo p equals p − 2 + 2·Re J(χ, χ), and |J(χ, χ)|² = p. Exact counts are 6, 6, 24, 33 for p = 7, 13, 19, 31.

limitations: Part (ii) needs all three characters χ, ψ and χψ to be nontrivial. Otherwise J takes values such as −1 or q − 2.
The theorem gives |J| but not its argument. The argument of a cubic Jacobi sum needs the congruence J ≡ −1 mod 3 in Z[ω].
Counting by characters needs q ≡ 1 mod 3 for cubic characters. Otherwise x ↦ x³ is a bijection of F.

results.name: Orthogonality of Dirichlet characters and the filter for a residue class
results.statement: Let N ≥ 1 and let G = (Z/N)^× with |G| = φ(N). Let Ĝ be the group of characters G → ℂ^×, and extend each Dirichlet character χ mod N by χ(n) = 0 when gcd(n, N) > 1. Then |Ĝ| = φ(N). For every g in G with g ≠ 1, Σ_χ χ(g) = 0. For a coprime to N and every integer b, Σ_χ χ̄(a)χ(b) = φ(N) if b ≡ a mod N, and 0 otherwise. Hence 1_{n ≡ a (mod N)} = (1/φ(N))·Σ_χ χ̄(a)χ(n) for all n.
hypotheses: N is a positive integer.
G = (Z/N)^× is the unit group, which is finite and abelian.
Characters take values in ℂ.

prerequisites.reason: Step 1 uses the structure theorem to count characters and to build a separating character.

definitions.name: Dirichlet character
definitions.text: A character χ of (Z/N)^×, extended to all integers by χ(n) = χ(n mod N) if gcd(n, N) = 1 and χ(n) = 0 otherwise.

definitions.name: Dual group
definitions.text: The group Ĝ of homomorphisms from a finite abelian group G to ℂ^×, with pointwise product.

source.excerpt:
/-- If `R` is an integral domain that has enough roots of unity and `n ≠ 0`, then for `a` and `b`
in `ZMod n` with `a` a unit, the sum of `χ a⁻¹ * χ b` over all Dirichlet characters
mod `n` with values in `R` vanishes if `a ≠ b` and has the value `n.totient` if `a = b`. -/
theorem sum_char_inv_mul_char_eq {a : ZMod n} (ha : IsUnit a) (b : ZMod n) :
    ∑ χ : DirichletCharacter R n, χ a⁻¹ * χ b = if a = b then (n.totient : R) else 0 := by
  simp only [← map_mul, sum_characters_eq, ZMod.inv_mul_eq_one_of_isUnit ha]

for each `a ≠ 1` in `ZMod n`, the sum of `χ a` over all Dirichlet characters mod `n`

theorem sum_characters_eq_zero ⦃a : ZMod n⦄ (ha : a ≠ 1) :
    ∑ χ : DirichletCharacter R n, χ a = 0 := by
  obtain ⟨χ, hχ⟩ := exists_apply_ne_one_of_hasEnoughRootsOfUnity R ha
  refine eq_zero_of_mul_eq_self_left hχ ?_
  simp only [Finset.mul_sum, ← MulChar.mul_apply]
  exact Fintype.sum_bijective _ (Group.mulLeft_bijective χ) _ _ fun χ' ↦ rfl

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Structure of G. By the structure theorem, G ≅ Z/n_1 × … × Z/n_r. A character of this product is determined by its values on the r generators. Each value is an n_k-th root of unity, and any choice is allowed. So |Ĝ| = n_1⋯n_r = |G| = φ(N).

Separation of points. Let g = (g_1, …, g_r) be nonzero in this product, so g_k ≠ 0 for some k. Define χ0(h) = exp(2πi·h_k/n_k). This is a character, and χ0(g) = exp(2πi·g_k/n_k) ≠ 1 because 0 < g_k < n_k. So for each g ≠ 1 there is a character χ0 with χ0(g) ≠ 1.

Sum over characters. Let S = Σ_{χ∈Ĝ} χ(g) with g ≠ 1, and pick χ0 from step 2. The map χ ↦ χ0·χ is a bijection of Ĝ, because Ĝ is a group. So S = Σ_χ (χ0χ)(g) = χ0(g)·S. Since χ0(g) ≠ 1, we get S = 0. For g = 1 every character gives 1, so the sum is |Ĝ| = φ(N).

Orthogonality for units. Let a be a unit and b a unit. Then χ̄(a) = χ(a)^(−1) = χ(a^(−1)), because |χ(a)| = 1. So χ̄(a)χ(b) = χ(a^(−1)·b). By step 3 the sum over χ is φ(N) if a^(−1)·b = 1 and 0 otherwise.

Non-units. If gcd(b, N) > 1, then χ(b) = 0 for every Dirichlet character, so the sum is 0. Also b ≢ a mod N, because a is a unit and a unit mod N has no common factor with N. So the formula holds for all integers b.

The filter. Divide the orthogonality relation by φ(N). Then 1_{n ≡ a mod N} = (1/φ(N))·Σ_χ χ̄(a)χ(n). The right side is a finite linear combination of the functions n ↦ χ(n). So a condition on residue classes becomes a combination of multiplicative functions.

worked_application.title: Primes below 100 in residue classes modulo 5
worked_application.goal: Rebuild the counts of primes below 100 in each class modulo 5 from the four Dirichlet characters.
hypotheses: 2 is a primitive root mod 5, with 2^0, 2^1, 2^2, 2^3 ≡ 1, 2, 4, 3.
The characters are χ_j(2^k) = i^(jk) for j = 0, 1, 2, 3.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The group (Z/5)^× is cyclic of order 4, so the characters are exactly these four.

steps.text: Table. Index of n: ind(1) = 0, ind(2) = 1, ind(4) = 2, ind(3) = 3. So χ_1 takes the values 1, i, −i, −1 on n ≡ 1, 2, 3, 4. Also χ_2 = (1, −1, −1, 1) and χ_3 = χ̄_1. These satisfy the relations of the theorem.

Filter. For the class a = 3, the combination (1/4)·Σ_j χ̄_j(3)χ_j(n) equals 1 for n = 3, 8 and 13. It equals 0 for n = 10, which is divisible by 5. A computer check confirms this for all n up to 100 and all four classes.

Count. There are 25 primes below 100. Apply the filter to each prime p. The sums give 5 primes with p ≡ 1 mod 5 (11, 31, 41, 61, 71), 7 with p ≡ 2, 7 with p ≡ 3 and 5 with p ≡ 4. The prime 5 gives 0 in every class.
Check. The total is 5 + 7 + 7 + 5 + 1 = 25. This matches a direct count of the primes below 100.

worked_application.result: Four characters modulo 5 reproduce the exact counts 5, 7, 7, 5 of primes below 100 in the classes 1, 2, 3, 4 modulo 5. The prime 5 lies in no unit class.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: The filter picks out residue classes only. Dirichlet theorem on primes in progressions needs also that L(1, χ) ≠ 0, which is a separate result.
The relation needs characters with values in a field that has enough roots of unity. Complex numbers have them.
For N with many prime factors, the number of characters grows like φ(N). The filter is practical only for small N.
The proof is authored. It is not checked in Lean in this repository.

results.name: Lüroth theorem: every intermediate field of K(t) is generated by one element
results.statement: Let K be a field and t transcendental over K. Let E be a field with K ⊊ E ⊆ K(t). Then there is g in K(t) ∖ K such that E = K(g). Moreover, if g = a(t)/b(t) in lowest terms and d = max(deg a, deg b), then [K(t) : E] = d.
hypotheses: K is a field and K(t) is the field of rational functions in one variable.
E is a subfield of K(t) that contains K and is not equal to K.

prerequisites.reason: Steps 4 and 5 use Gauss lemma to move between K(t)[X] and K[t][X].

definitions.name: Intermediate field
definitions.text: A field E with K ⊆ E ⊆ K(t).

definitions.name: Lowest terms
definitions.text: A fraction a/b of polynomials in K[t] with gcd(a, b) = 1 and b ≠ 0.

definitions.name: Primitive polynomial
definitions.text: A polynomial over a UFD whose coefficients have gcd 1.

results.proof_status: source declaration inspected; authored proof awaits inference review; no local Lean check

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Algebraicity of t. Let e = a_0(t)/b_0(t) be in E ∖ K. The polynomial a_0(X) − e·b_0(X) in E[X] has t as a root. It is not zero, because otherwise e would equal a quotient of corresponding coefficients and lie in K. So t is algebraic over E. Let m(X) = X^n + c_{n−1}X^(n−1) + … + c_0 be its minimal polynomial, with n ≥ 1 and c_i in E.

A non-constant coefficient. If all c_i were in K, then t would be algebraic over K. So some c_i is not in K. Put g = c_i = a(t)/b(t) with a, b in K[t] coprime and b ≠ 0. Then d = max(deg a, deg b) ≥ 1, because g is not constant. Also g is transcendental over K. Otherwise K(g) would be finite over K, and t would be algebraic over K(g) by step 1 applied to g.

The degree of K(t) over K(g). Let P(X) = a(X) − Y·b(X) in K[X, Y]. It has degree 1 in Y. A factorization P = uv has a factor with no Y, say u in K[X]. This u divides a and b, so u is a unit. Hence P is irreducible in K[X, Y]. It has degree d ≥ 1 in X. By Gauss lemma it stays irreducible in K(Y)[X]. Since K(g) ≅ K(Y), the polynomial a(X) − g·b(X) is irreducible over K(g) of degree d and has t as a root. So [K(t) : K(g)] = d.

Denominators. Write each c_j in lowest terms c_j = u_j/h_j and let h = lcm(h_j). Put f(X) = h·m(X), a polynomial in K[t][X]. It is primitive: a prime π dividing h has some h_j with the full power of π, and the coefficient h·c_j = (h/h_j)·u_j is not divisible by π. Primes not dividing h do not divide the leading coefficient h. So f is primitive in K[t][X].

Divisibility. Put G̃(X, t) = a(X)·b(t) − a(t)·b(X) in K[t][X]. Then G̃ = b(t)·(a(X) − g·b(X)). The polynomial a(X) − g·b(X) lies in E[X] and has t as a root, so m divides it in E[X]. Thus f divides G̃ in K(t)[X]. As f is primitive and K[t] is a UFD, Gauss lemma gives G̃ = f·q with q in K[t][X].

Degrees in t. The fraction g = c_i has denominator b, so b divides h. The coefficient h·g = (h/b)·a of f has t-degree deg h − deg b + deg a. If deg a ≤ deg b, then deg_t f ≥ deg h ≥ deg b = d. Otherwise deg_t f ≥ deg h − deg b + deg a ≥ deg a = d. So deg_t f ≥ d. On the other hand deg_t G̃ ≤ d. Since G̃ = f·q, we get deg_t q = 0. So q lies in K[X].

Primitivity of G̃ in K[X][t]. The coefficients of G̃ in t are b_j·a(X) − a_j·b(X), where a = Σ a_j t^j and b = Σ b_j t^j. Suppose a nonconstant w(X) divides all of them. In the field k = K[X]/(w), we have b_j·ā = a_j·b̄ for all j. If b̄ = 0, then ā ≠ 0 since gcd(a, b) = 1, so b_j = 0 for all j. That contradicts b ≠ 0. If b̄ ≠ 0, pick j with b_j ≠ 0. Then λ = ā/b̄ = a_j/b_j lies in K and a = λ·b in K[t]. Coprimality forces b constant and d = 0. This is a contradiction.

Conclusion. Now q in K[X] divides every t-coefficient of G̃ = f·q. By step 7, G̃ is primitive in K[X][t], so q is a nonzero constant. Compare degrees in X. We have deg_X f = n. Also deg_X G̃ = d by step 3. So n = d. Therefore [K(t) : E] = n = d = [K(t) : K(g)]. Since K(g) ⊆ E, this gives [E : K(g)] = 1. So E = K(g), and [K(t) : E] = d.

worked_application.title: Subfields of Q(t) generated by t^2 + t^(−2) and t^3 + t^(−3)
worked_application.goal: Find a single generator of E = Q(u, v) with u = t^2 + t^(−2) and v = t^3 + t^(−3), and test the proof steps on it.
hypotheses: K = Q and E is generated by the two elements u and v of Q(t).
Let s = t + 1/t.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: E is a subfield of Q(t) that contains Q properly. Lüroth theorem gives one generator.

steps.text: Find the generator. We have u = s² − 2 and v = s³ − 3s. So u − 1 = s² − 3 and v/(u − 1) = s·(s² − 3)/(s² − 3) = s. Hence s lies in E, and E = Q(s).
Check the proof data. The minimal polynomial of t over Q(s) is m(X) = X² − sX + 1, so n = 2. The coefficient s = (t² + 1)/t has a = t² + 1, b = t and d = 2.

Check the divisibility. We have G̃ = a(X)b(t) − a(t)b(X) = tX² + t − t²X − X = (X − t)(tX − 1). The polynomial f = t·m(X) = tX² − (t² + 1)X + t equals G̃, so q = 1. Both f and G̃ have t-degree 2 = d and X-degree 2 = n = d.
A second case. Let E = Q(t⁴, t⁶). Then t⁶/t⁴ = t² lies in E, so E = Q(t²), and g = t² gives a = t², b = 1 and d = 2. The minimal polynomial of t is X² − t², and G̃ = X² − t². Here [Q(t) : E] = 2.

worked_application.result: Q(t² + t^(−2), t³ + t^(−3)) = Q(t + 1/t), with [Q(t) : E] = 2. Also Q(t⁴, t⁶) = Q(t²).
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: The theorem is for one variable. For two variables, Lüroth theorem fails in general in positive genus in the form of a generated subfield, and the situation is more difficult.
The proof gives the degree [K(t) : E] = d but not an algorithm for g. The generator is found from a non-constant coefficient of the minimal polynomial.
The generator g is unique only up to a Möbius transformation (αg + β)/(γg + δ) with coefficients in K.
